textes.Métaphore : comparaison sans outil (« ce: Metaphor: a comparison without a connecting word (“that man is a lion”); simile: with “like” or “as”.
textes.Litote : dire moins pour suggérer plus (: Litotes: saying less to suggest more (“go, I do not hate you”). Euphemism: softening (“he has left us”).
textes.Anaphore : répétition en début de phrase: Anaphora: repetition at the start of sentences (“I have a dream”).
textes.Chiasme : structure croisée A-B / B-A («: Chiasmus: a crossed A-B / B-A structure (“eat to live, not live to eat”).
textes.Litote et euphémisme se confondent souve: Litotes and euphemism are often confused: litotes strengthens, euphemism softens.
textes.A — B / B — A : les termes se croisent: A — B / B — A: the terms cross over
textes.Schéma du chiasme : manger, vivre, puis: Chiasmus diagram: eat, live, then live, eat
textes.Pathos : les émotions qu'il suscite chez: Pathos: the emotions stirred in the audience.
textes.Logos : la force des raisons et des preu: Logos: the strength of the reasons and evidence.
textes.Un bon discours combine les trois ; la m: A good speech combines all three; manipulation plays on ethos and pathos in the absence of logos.
textes.L'ethos ne se décrète pas : c'est le pub: Ethos cannot be decreed: the audience grants its trust, or doesn't.
textes.Les trois leviers de la persuasion selon: The three levers of persuasion according to Aristotle
textes.Les raisonnements fallacieux et comment: Faulty reasoning and how to name it.
textes.Homme de paille : déformer la position a: Straw man: distorting the opposing position to refute it more easily.
textes.Ad hominem : attaquer la personne plutôt: Ad hominem: attacking the person rather than the argument.
textes.Faux dilemme : ne présenter que deux opt: False dilemma: presenting only two options when others exist.
textes.Pente glissante : affirmer sans preuve q: Slippery slope: claiming without evidence that a first step inevitably leads to the worst.
textes.Toute attaque personnelle n'est pas un a: Not every personal attack is an ad hominem: pointing out a conflict of interest can be relevant.
textes.Quatre sophismes et leur mécanisme: Four fallacies and how they work
textes.Schéma narratif : situation initiale, él: Narrative arc: initial situation, inciting incident, rising action, resolution, final situation.
textes.Le voyage du héros (Campbell) : appel, r: The hero's journey (Campbell): the call, the refusal, the mentor, the trials, the transformed return.
textes.Le suspense vient de ce que le public sa: Suspense comes from what the audience knows and the character doesn't (Hitchcock and the bomb under the table).
textes.On retient mieux une information raconté: We remember information told as a story better than a list of facts.
textes.Le fusil de Tchekhov : un détail montré: Chekhov's gun: a detail shown at the start must pay off later, otherwise it distracts.
textes.Répétition, novlangue, astroturfing et c: Repetition, newspeak, astroturfing and how to protect yourself.
textes.Répétition : plus on entend une affirmat: Repetition: the more often you hear a claim, the truer it seems (illusory truth effect).
textes.Novlangue : appauvrir ou retourner les m: Newspeak: impoverishing or twisting words to make certain thoughts hard to think (Orwell, 1984).
textes.Astroturfing : simuler un mouvement spon: Astroturfing: faking a spontaneous citizens' movement with fake accounts or paid groups.
textes.Se protéger : chercher la source, croise: Protecting yourself: find the source, cross-check, ask who benefits from the message.
textes.Savoir qu'une affirmation est fausse ne: Knowing a claim is false does not fully protect you from the repetition effect.
textes.Plus une phrase est répétée, plus elle p: The more a sentence is repeated, the truer it seems
textes.Argument = prémisses (car, puisque) + co: Argument = premises (because, since) + conclusion (therefore). Look for the unstated premise.
textes.Un argument, ce sont des prémisses, les: An argument is premises, the reasons, supporting a conclusion, what you want to establish. "We must reduce speed, because it saves lives": the conclusion is "we must reduce speed", the premise comes after "because". Spotting these words, because, since, therefore, is already taking the argument apart.
textes.Déduction valide + prémisses vraies = co: Valid deduction + true premises = certain conclusion. Valid ≠ true: the form can be fine and a premise false.
textes.Mais la validité ne concerne que la form: But validity only concerns the form. "All cats fly, Felix is a cat, so Felix flies" is perfectly valid, and false, because a premise is false. To attack a deduction there are only two routes: show the form is broken, or that a premise is false.
textes.Induction : du particulier au général, p: Induction: from the particular to the general, probable but never certain (Hume, 1739). An anecdote does not prove a rule.
textes.L'induction généralise à partir de cas :: Induction generalises from cases: the sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow. It is indispensable, we could not live without it, but it is never certain. David Hume showed this in 1739: no reasoning proves that the future will resemble the past; we believe it out of habit.
textes.Bertrand Russell l'illustre avec un poul: Bertrand Russell illustrated it with a chicken fed every morning by the farmer, ever surer of its rule, until the day the farmer wrings its neck. An anecdote, even a lived one, illustrates; it does not prove a general rule. That takes many cases, and representative ones.
textes.Comparaison = avec « comme » ; métaphore: Simile = with "like"; metaphor = no tool; metonymy = one thing for another linked to it.
textes.Ces figures ne sont pas réservées aux po: These figures are not reserved for poets. "I'm starving to death" is a hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration; "he has left us" is a euphemism; "have a glass", a metonymy. We all use them every day without knowing it. Naming them helps you spot them in people trying to convince you.
textes.Litote : dire moins pour suggérer plus (: Litotes: say less to suggest more (strengthens). Euphemism: soften (cushions). Irony: say the opposite.
textes.L'ironie dit le contraire de ce qu'on pe: Irony says the opposite of what you think, "what lovely weather!" in the rain. Paralipsis announces you will not say what you are in fact saying: "I won't mention his lies…". And the oxymoron joins two opposing words: "this dark light that falls from the stars".
textes.Le son et l'ordre des mots: The sound and order of words
Anaphora: repetition at the start of a sentence. Chiasmus: A-B / B-A. Alliteration: repetition of a sound.
textes.L'anaphore répète un mot en tête de phra: Anaphora repeats a word at the start of each sentence and hammers an idea home: "Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred!", cried de Gaulle in 1944; "I have a dream", repeated Martin Luther King in 1963. Chiasmus crosses the terms, A-B then B-A: "one must eat to live and not live to eat" (Molière, The Miser).
textes.L'allitération joue sur les sons : « Pou: Alliteration plays on sounds: "For whom are these serpents hissing on your heads?" (Racine, Andromaque) makes you hear the hissing through the repeated "s". A figure is not an ornament: it helps you remember, which is why slogans are full of them.
textes.Ethos = crédibilité ; pathos = émotion ;: Ethos = credibility; pathos = emotion; logos = reasons. Manipulating is ethos and pathos without logos.
textes.Au IVe siècle avant notre ère, Aristote: In the 4th century BCE, Aristotle distinguished three ways of persuading in his Rhetoric. Ethos, the speaker's credibility: we more readily believe someone who seems competent, honest and well-meaning. Pathos, the emotions stirred in the audience. Logos, the strength of the reasons and evidence.
textes.Un bon discours combine les trois : des: A good speech combines all three: solid evidence, carried by someone credible who knows how to move the audience. Manipulation plays on ethos and pathos when logos is missing. And ethos cannot be decreed: it is the audience that grants or withholds its trust. "Believe me, I've been a doctor for thirty years" is not evidence.
textes.Effet de cadrage (Tversky et Kahneman, 1: Framing effect (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981): "save 200" and "400 will die" are not received the same. Restate it the other way.
textes.La façon de présenter une information ch: The way information is presented changes the decision. In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman set a problem: an epidemic threatens 600 people. When a plan is presented as "saves 200 people", 72 % choose it. When the same plan is presented as "400 people will die", 78 % prefer the risky option.
textes.C'est l'effet de cadrage : « 90 % de sur: That is the framing effect: "90 % survival" reassures more than "10 % mortality". Speakers know it, and also choose their moment, what the Greeks called kairos: the same argument does not land the same way at every instant. To defend yourself, restate the figure the other way round.
textes.Cialdini (1984) : preuve sociale, autori: Cialdini (1984): social proof, authority, scarcity, reciprocity, liking, commitment. Five classical stages: inventio, dispositio, elocutio, memoria, actio.
textes.En 1984, le psychologue Robert Cialdini: In 1984 the psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence, describing the levers that make us say yes. Social proof: we judge a behaviour more correct when we see others adopt it, hence "already 10,000 satisfied customers". Authority, scarcity, reciprocity, liking, commitment: each is a useful shortcut that others can exploit.
textes.La rhétorique classique, elle, découpait: Classical rhetoric divided the preparation of a speech into five stages: finding the arguments (inventio), ordering them (dispositio), putting them into words (elocutio), memorising them (memoria), delivering them (actio). And it advised first winning the audience's goodwill, the captatio benevolentiae.
textes.Attaquer l'homme ou sa caricature: Attacking the man or his caricature
textes.Ad hominem : viser la personne. Homme de: Ad hominem: target the person. Straw man: refute a caricature. A real conflict of interest remains relevant.
textes.L'ad hominem attaque la personne au lieu: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of their argument: "you say that, but you don't even have a degree". Variant: "you smoke too, so your advice is worthless". Someone's inconsistency does not make their argument false. Careful, though: pointing out a real conflict of interest can be relevant.
textes.L'homme de paille déforme la position ad: The straw man distorts the opposing position to refute it more easily. You answer "there should be fewer cars in the city centre" with "you want to stop people getting around". You fight a caricature, not the real position. Schopenhauer, around 1831, already listed these tricks in his Art of Being Right.
textes.Faux dilemme, pente glissante, post hoc,: False dilemma, slippery slope, post hoc, circular reasoning, appeal to ignorance: the form is broken, even if the tone convinces.
textes.Post hoc : « après cela, donc à cause de: Post hoc: "after this, therefore because of this". "I took my umbrella and it rained" does not make the umbrella a rain machine. Circular reasoning puts the conclusion in the premise: "this newspaper is reliable, since it says so itself". And the appeal to ignorance: "nobody has proved ghosts don't exist, so they exist".
textes.Naturel ≠ bon ; populaire ≠ vrai. L'auto: Natural ≠ good; popular ≠ true. Authority counts within its field, never as final proof.
textes.L'appel à la nature : « c'est naturel, d: The appeal to nature: "it's natural, so it's good". Arsenic and hemlock are natural. The appeal to the crowd: "everyone does it, so it's right". The number of supporters does not prove an idea is right.
textes.Réfuter la meilleure version de l'argume: Refute the best version of the opposing argument (Rapoport's rules). Conceding strengthens. Winning ≠ being right.
textes.L'inverse de l'homme de paille : reformu: The opposite of the straw man: restate the opposing argument in its strongest version, then refute it. That is the principle of charity. The rules of the mathematician Anatol Rapoport, popularised by the philosopher Daniel Dennett in 2013, ask that before any criticism you restate the other's position so well that they would thank you, then say what you agree on and what you have learned.
textes.Concéder un point n'affaiblit pas : une: Conceding a point does not weaken you: a well-chosen concession strengthens your ethos and lets you choose the ground for the rest of the discussion. And winning a debate is not being right: you can crush a poor defender of a good idea. A bad lawyer does not make their client guilty.
textes.Un contre-exemple suffit contre « tous »: One counterexample is enough against "all". Set in advance what would change your mind. Refuting costs more than lying (Brandolini).
textes.Un seul contre-exemple suffit à abattre: A single counterexample is enough to bring down a universal claim: when Europeans described black swans in Australia in 1697, a thousand-year-old generalisation fell. You can also refute by absurdity, showing that a claim leads to an untenable consequence; Zeno of Elea made it his speciality.
textes.Méfiez-vous de celui qui déplace les pot: Beware of whoever moves the goalposts: every time the criterion is met, they demand another. A good habit, for yourself as for the other: set in advance what would change your mind. And Brandolini's law, stated in 2013, reminds us that refuting nonsense takes far more energy than producing it.
textes.Situation initiale, perturbation, péripé: Initial situation, disruption, ups and downs, resolution, final situation. Propp (1928): 31 functions; Campbell (1949): the hero's journey.
textes.Aristote l'écrit dans la Poétique : une: Aristotle wrote it in the Poetics: a well-built story has a beginning, a middle and an end. It sounds obvious. The narrative schema details it: initial situation, disruptive event, ups and downs, resolution, final situation. You can also start in medias res, in the middle of the action, like the Iliad, which Horace cites.
textes.En 1928, Vladimir Propp analyse des cont: In 1928 Vladimir Propp analysed Russian fairy tales and found 31 functions, villainy, the hero's departure, the magical object, the return, that always appear in the same order. In 1949 Joseph Campbell described the "hero's journey": the call, the refusal, the mentor, the trials, the transformed return. George Lucas said he drew on it for Star Wars.
textes.Suspense = le public sait ce que le pers: Suspense = the audience knows what the character does not (Hitchcock). Every detail shown must serve (Chekhov).
textes.Une histoire se retient bien mieux qu'un: A story is remembered far better than a list (Bower and Clark, 1969: 90 % against under 15 %). A good story is not proof.
textes.En 1969, les psychologues Gordon Bower e: In 1969 the psychologists Gordon Bower and Michael Clark gave people lists of words to learn. One group linked them by making up a little story; the other learned them as they were. After several lists, the "storytellers" recalled about 90 % of the words, the others under 15 %. Information told as a story sticks far better than a list.
textes.D'où le conseil des écrivains, « montrer: Hence writers' advice, "show, don't tell": rather than announce a character is afraid, describe their trembling hands. And hence the wariness: in 2007 Christian Salmon showed how politics and marketing use storytelling. A good story disarms the critical mind.
textes.Gettysburg (1863) : 271 mots, deux minut: Gettysburg (1863): 271 words, two minutes, against two hours for Everett. Brevity sticks.
textes.Le 19 novembre 1863, à Gettysburg, l'ora: On 19 November 1863, at Gettysburg, the star speaker was Edward Everett: he spoke for two hours, over 13,000 words. Abraham Lincoln then spoke for about two minutes, 271 words, ending on government "of the people, by the people, for the people". The next day Everett wrote to him that he wished he had come as close to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
textes.Les grands discours tiennent souvent en: Great speeches often come down to one sentence people remember. On 13 May 1940 Churchill had "nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat". In 2013, on her 16th birthday, Malala Yousafzai told the UN that "one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world".
textes.« I have a dream » (1963) était en parti: "I have a dream" (1963) was partly improvised. The 18 June appeal was not recorded; Kennedy did not say "I am a doughnut".
textes.Le 28 août 1963, à Washington, Martin Lu: On 28 August 1963, in Washington, Martin Luther King was reading a prepared text. The most famous passage, "I have a dream", was not in it: the singer Mahalia Jackson reportedly called out "Tell them about the dream, Martin!", and he left his notes. An anaphora built partly in improvisation, on phrases he had already tried out elsewhere.
textes.Méfiance aussi envers les légendes de di: Be wary of speech legends too. The appeal of 18 June 1940 was not recorded: the one often heard is the appeal of 22 June. And Kennedy did not say "I am a doughnut" in Berlin in 1963: "Ich bin ein Berliner" is correct and was understood as intended; the myth arose twenty years later in the English-language press.
textes.Veil (1974), Badinter (1981), Zola (1898: Veil (1974), Badinter (1981), Zola (1898): speeches that changed the law or public opinion.
textes.Le 26 novembre 1974, Simone Veil défend: On 26 November 1974 Simone Veil defended the law on abortion before an Assembly of 481 men and 9 women. She faced insults and threats; the law passed. On 17 September 1981 Robert Badinter argued for abolishing the death penalty: "Tomorrow, thanks to you, French justice will no longer be a justice that kills." The law was passed the next day.
textes.Le discours peut aussi s'écrire. Le 13 j: A speech can also be written. On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published "J'accuse…!" in L'Aurore to defend Captain Dreyfus; convicted of libel, he fled to London. Long before, Demosthenes thundered against Philip of Macedon: his Philippics gave their name to any violent speech against someone.
Illusory truth effect (Hasher et al., 1977): repetition makes things seem true, even when you know they are false (Fazio, 2015).
textes.En 1977, Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein et: In 1977 Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino had students rate the truth of sixty plausible statements, two weeks apart. Some came back at every session: the confidence given to them rose, whether true or false. That is the illusory truth effect: a sentence already heard is easier to process, and that ease passes for truth.
textes.Pire : en 2015, Lisa Fazio et ses collèg: Worse: in 2015 Lisa Fazio and colleagues showed that knowing the right answer does not fully protect you. Hence the "firehose of falsehood" strategy described by the RAND Corporation in 2016: lots of messages, fast, on every channel, with no concern for consistency. The aim is not to convince but to drown.
textes.Propagande vient de l'Église (1622). Ber: Propaganda comes from the Church (1622). Bernays (1928-1929), Orwell's Newspeak, talking points, the Overton window.
textes.Le mot propagande vient de la Congrégati: The word propaganda comes from the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, created by the Church in 1622; it only became pejorative in the 20th century. In 1928 Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew, published Propaganda. In 1929, for the American Tobacco Company, he had women march in New York holding cigarettes, presented as "torches of freedom".
textes.Dans 1984, George Orwell imagine la novl: In Nineteen Eighty-Four George Orwell imagined Newspeak, which impoverishes and twists words to make certain thoughts impossible. Closer to home: talking points repeated by several officials the same morning, or the dog whistle, a coded message only its intended audience hears. And the Overton window: shifting what seems sayable is often more effective than winning a debate.
textes.Inoculation (McGuire, 1961) : voir une m: Inoculation (McGuire, 1961): seeing a weakened manipulation helps resist it. Source, cross-check, who benefits.
textes.En 1961, le psychologue William McGuire: In 1961 the psychologist William McGuire proposed inoculation theory: like a vaccine, exposure to a weakened form of a manipulative argument, along with its refutation, helps resist the strong version. "Prebunking" brings it back, for example with the game Bad News by Jon Roozenbeek and Sander van der Linden, where you play a fake-news maker.
textes.Les réflexes de base restent simples : c: The basic reflexes stay simple: look for the source, cross-check with others, ask who benefits from the message. And beware of legends about other people's gullibility too: the panic caused by Orson Welles's War of the Worlds in 1938 was largely exaggerated by newspapers, happy to discredit radio, their competitor.
textes.Souvent, une prémisse reste sous-entendu: Often a premise stays unstated: that is an enthymeme. The word comes from Aristotle, in the 4th century BCE: in his Rhetoric, the enthymeme is the orator's syllogism, whose missing premise the audience supplies itself. "He has a fever, so he is ill" assumes fever signals an illness. Many arguments come from this: people fight over the conclusion when the disagreement is about the hidden premise. And the burden of proof lies with whoever puts forward a claim.
textes.La litote dit moins pour faire entendre: Litotes says less to convey more. In Le Cid, Chimène tells Rodrigue "Go, I do not hate you": she is confessing she loves him. The play is by Corneille, first staged in 1637: Rodrigue has just killed Chimène's father in a duel. Euphemism softens to spare: "he has left us" for "he has died". Both tone down the form, but litotes strengthens the meaning, euphemism cushions it.
textes.L'argument d'autorité est plus subtil :: The argument from authority is subtler: citing an expert in their field is legitimate. The fallacy is authority outside its competence, a Nobel physicist settling a medical question, or authority presented as final proof. And the Gish gallop drowns the opponent in an avalanche of weak arguments: it takes longer to refute each one than to fire them off. The name was given in 1994 by the anthropologist Eugenie Scott, after the creationist Duane Gish, a champion of the technique in debates.
textes.Hitchcock l'explique : une bombe explose: Hitchcock explained it: a bomb goes off under a table, that is fifteen seconds of surprise. Show the audience the bomb first, let the characters chat without knowing, and you have fifteen minutes of suspense. Suspense comes from what the audience knows and the character does not. He told it to François Truffaut in 1962, during a week of interviews in a room at Universal Studios; the book came out in 1966.
textes.Tchekhov, lui, donne la règle inverse :: Chekhov gave the reverse rule: if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act, it must go off in the last. He wrote it, among other places, in a letter of 1 November 1889 to the young writer Alexander Lazarev-Gruzinsky. Every detail shown must serve, otherwise it distracts. Scheherazade, in the Thousand and One Nights, takes the technique to the extreme: she stops each night at the crucial moment, and the king has to spare her to hear what happens next.
textes.Une déduction va du général au particuli: A deduction goes from the general to the particular: "all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal". If the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion is necessarily true. That is the syllogism described by Aristotle. He set it out around 350 BCE in the Prior Analytics, the first known system of logic.
textes.La comparaison rapproche deux choses ave: A simile brings two things together with a tool, like or as: "strong as a lion". A metaphor drops the tool: "this man is a lion". Metonymy names a thing by another linked to it: "have a glass", you drink the contents, not the glass. These names come from a long tradition of handbooks: Dumarsais published Des Tropes in 1730, then Pierre Fontanier catalogued them for school pupils, in 1821 and 1827.
textes.Le faux dilemme ne présente que deux opt: The false dilemma presents only two options when there are others: "either you're with us or against us". The slippery slope claims without evidence that a first step leads inevitably to the worst: "if we allow this, soon it will be chaos". Aristotle had already drawn up a list of twelve or thirteen fallacies in his Sophistical Refutations.
textes.Le mot vient d'Aristote, au IVe siècle a: The word comes from Aristotle, in the 4th century BCE: in his Rhetoric, the enthymeme is the orator's syllogism, whose missing premise the audience supplies itself.
textes.David Hume le montre en 1739 : aucun rai: David Hume showed this in 1739: no reasoning proves that the future will resemble the past; we believe it out of habit.
textes.La pièce est de Corneille, créée en 1637: The play is by Corneille, first staged in 1637: Rodrigue has just killed Chimène's father in a duel.
textes.Au IVe siècle avant notre ère, Aristote: In the 4th century BCE, Aristotle distinguished three ways of persuading in his Rhetoric.
textes.En 1981, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman set a problem: an epidemic threatens 600 people.
textes.En 1984, le psychologue Robert Cialdini: In 1984 the psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence, describing the levers that make us say yes.
textes.Schopenhauer, vers 1831, rangeait déjà c: Schopenhauer, around 1831, already listed these tricks in his Art of Being Right.
textes.Le nom est donné en 1994 par l'anthropol: The name was given in 1994 by the anthropologist Eugenie Scott, after the creationist Duane Gish, a champion of the technique in debates.
textes.Les règles du mathématicien Anatol Rapop: The rules of the mathematician Anatol Rapoport, popularised by the philosopher Daniel Dennett in 2013, ask that before any criticism you restate the other's position so well that they would thank you, then say what you agree on and what you have learned.
textes.En 1928, Vladimir Propp analyse des cont: In 1928 Vladimir Propp analysed Russian fairy tales and found 31 functions, villainy, the hero's departure, the magical object, the return, that always appear in the same order.
textes.En 1949, Joseph Campbell décrit le « voy: In 1949 Joseph Campbell described the "hero's journey": the call, the refusal, the mentor, the trials, the transformed return.
textes.En 1969, les psychologues Gordon Bower e: In 1969 the psychologists Gordon Bower and Michael Clark gave people lists of words to learn.
textes.Le 19 novembre 1863, à Gettysburg, l'ora: On 19 November 1863, at Gettysburg, the star speaker was Edward Everett: he spoke for two hours, over 13,000 words.
textes.Le 13 mai 1940, Churchill n'a « rien d'a: On 13 May 1940 Churchill had "nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat".
textes.En 2013, le jour de ses 16 ans, Malala Y: In 2013, on her 16th birthday, Malala Yousafzai told the UN that "one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world".
textes.Le 28 août 1963, à Washington, Martin Lu: On 28 August 1963, in Washington, Martin Luther King was reading a prepared text.
textes.L'appel du 18 juin 1940 n'a pas été enre: The appeal of 18 June 1940 was not recorded: the one often heard is the appeal of 22 June.
textes.Le 26 novembre 1974, Simone Veil défend: On 26 November 1974 Simone Veil defended the law on abortion before an Assembly of 481 men and 9 women.
textes.Le 17 septembre 1981, Robert Badinter pl: On 17 September 1981 Robert Badinter argued for abolishing the death penalty: "Tomorrow, thanks to you, French justice will no longer be a justice that kills."
textes.Le 13 janvier 1898, Émile Zola publie «: On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published "J'accuse…!" in L'Aurore to defend Captain Dreyfus; convicted of libel, he fled to London.
textes.En 1977, Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein et: In 1977 Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino had students rate the truth of sixty plausible statements, two weeks apart.
textes.Le mot propagande vient de la Congrégati: The word propaganda comes from the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, created by the Church in 1622; it only became pejorative in the 20th century.
textes.En 1928, Edward Bernays, neveu de Freud,: In 1928 Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew, published Propaganda.
textes.En 1961, le psychologue William McGuire: In 1961 the psychologist William McGuire proposed inoculation theory: like a vaccine, exposure to a weakened form of a manipulative argument, along with its refutation, helps resist the strong version.
textes.Ptahhotep, Enheduanna, les aèdes d'Homèr: Ptahhotep, Enheduanna, Homer's bards: the art of speaking well, centuries before it got a name.
textes.Égypte : les Maximes de Ptahhotep, vizir: Egypt: the Maxims of Ptahhotep, vizier of the 5th Dynasty, advise speaking only when you have something worth saying, and listening.
textes.Mésopotamie : Enheduanna, prêtresse à Ur: Mesopotamia: Enheduanna, priestess at Ur around 2300 BC, may be the oldest author known by name (attribution disputed).
textes.Grèce : l'Iliade et l'Odyssée viennent d: Greece: the Iliad and the Odyssey come from an oral tradition; bards improvised with ready-made formulas.
textes.Milman Parry le montre à partir de 1928: Milman Parry showed it from 1928 on: "rosy-fingered Dawn" is a formula that helps compose while singing.
textes.Le nom d'un auteur antique ne prouve pas: An ancient author's name does not prove he wrote the text: the Maxims are probably later than Ptahhotep, and Enheduanna's hymns reach us only through copies made six centuries later.
textes.Les Maximes de Ptahhotep se présentent c: The Maxims of Ptahhotep present themselves as the lessons of a vizier of King Djedkare Isesi, of Egypt's 5th Dynasty, passing his office to his son. According to William Kelly Simpson's translation, he is an elderly man of 96. The text itself was probably composed later, in the Middle Kingdom: Simpson places it in the 12th Dynasty, roughly between 2040 and 1782 BC.
textes.Une bonne partie des maximes parle de la: A good share of the maxims are about speech. "Only speak when you have something worth saying." "A perfect word is hidden more deeply than precious stones": yet it is found among the servant women working at the mill-stone. And above all, listening: the official must let the petitioner unburden himself completely before dismissing him, because "listening benefits the listener".
textes.Ptahhotep : parler peu et juste, écouter: Ptahhotep: speak little and well, listen to the end. The perfect word is rare, but it can come from anyone, even a servant at the mill-stone.
textes.Vers 2300 av. J.-C., Enheduanna, fille d: Around 2300 BC, Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, was high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. Hymns are attributed to her, including The Exaltation of Inanna, which would make her the oldest author known by name.
textes.Prudence pourtant : les copies qui nous: Caution, though: the copies we have date from about six centuries after her, and many Assyriologists doubt she wrote them. Her name might even designate her office rather than a person. Before rhetoric, then, there were already texts made to be spoken, sung before a god or a king.
textes.Enheduanna, prêtresse de Nanna à Ur vers: Enheduanna, priestess of Nanna at Ur around 2300 BC: perhaps the oldest named author, but the attribution is disputed.
textes.Aux VIIIe ou VIIe siècles av. J.-C., l'I: In the 8th or 7th century BC, the Iliad and the Odyssey took shape in Greece: two long poems in dactylic hexameter, 24 books each. They come from an oral tradition. The bards, professional singers, did not recite a text learned by heart: they composed as they sang.
textes.Leur secret : des formules toutes prêtes: Their secret: ready-made formulas that fit the metre exactly, like "rosy-fingered Dawn" or "wily Odysseus". Milman Parry showed it from 1928 on. As for Homer himself, his existence remains a mystery: this is the "Homeric question".
textes.Les aèdes improvisent avec des formules: The bards improvise with formulas that fit the metre. Parry, 1928: Homeric epic was born of oral performance.
textes.Ve siècle av. J.-C. : Corax à Syracuse,: 5th century BC: Corax in Syracuse, Protagoras and Gorgias in Athens. Speech is taught, and paid for.
textes.Syracuse, Ve siècle av. J.-C. : après la: Syracuse, 5th century BC: after the tyrant's fall, Corax and Tisias teach pleading and the argument from likelihood.
textes.Protagoras : « l'homme est la mesure de: Protagoras: "man is the measure of all things"; on every question, two arguments are opposed.
textes.Gorgias, 427 av. J.-C. : la parole est «: Gorgias, 427 BC: speech is "a powerful master", it acts on the soul as drugs act on the body.
textes.Platon, Gorgias (vers 380 av. J.-C.) : l: Plato, Gorgias (around 380 BC): rhetoric is a mere knack, a flattery, like pastry baking next to medicine.
textes.« Sophiste » n'était pas une insulte au: "Sophist" was not an insult at first: it is Plato who turns him into a seller of speeches with no care for truth. We see the sophists mostly through their opponents.
textes.Au Ve siècle av. J.-C., à Syracuse, le t: In the 5th century BC, in Syracuse, the tyrant Thrasybulus was overthrown. Citizens dispossessed under the tyrants rushed to court to recover their property, and had to plead for themselves. Corax, with his pupil Tisias, taught them how.
textes.On lui prête l'argument du vraisemblable: He is credited with the argument from likelihood, turned both ways: a weak man accused of beating a strong man will say "How could I have?"; a strong man will say "I knew I would be suspected, I would never have done it." Corax is known only through Plato, Aristotle and Cicero: he may even be legendary.
Corax and Tisias, Syracuse, 5th century BC: rhetoric is born in court, with the argument from likelihood.
textes.Protagoras, né à Abdère vers 490 av. J.-: Protagoras, born in Abdera around 490 BC, a friend of Pericles, travelled through Greece teaching for a fee. Plato credits him with inventing the professional sophist. His most famous saying: "Of all things the measure is Man, of the things that are, that they are, and of the things that are not, that they are not."
textes.Il soutient que sur toute question, deux: He held that on any question, two arguments are opposed. Aristotle reproached him for claiming "to make the weaker argument stronger". Diogenes Laërtius says his books were burned in the agora; the historian John Burnet doubts it, since no contemporary mentions it.
textes.Protagoras : l'homme est la mesure de to: Protagoras: man is the measure of all things; two opposed arguments on every question; "making the weaker argument stronger".
textes.En 427 av. J.-C., Gorgias, venu de Léont: In 427 BC, Gorgias, from Leontinoi in Sicily, came to Athens as an ambassador, aged about sixty. His prose enthralled: antitheses, clauses of equal length, matching endings. In his Encomium of Helen, he clears the most blamed woman in Greece: she may have yielded to the gods, to force, to love or to speech. And speech is "a powerful master" which, with the smallest of bodies, achieves the most divine feats.
textes.Vers 380 av. J.-C., Platon lui répond da: Around 380 BC, Plato answered him in a dialogue bearing his name, the Gorgias. Socrates there calls rhetoric a mere knack, a flattery that guesses what pleases with no thought for what is best: it is to politics what pastry baking is to medicine, and cosmetics to gymnastics.
textes.Gorgias : la parole est un puissant maît: Gorgias: speech is a powerful master. Plato: rhetoric without truth is mere flattery, pastry baking facing medicine.
textes.Périclès, Lysias, Isocrate, Démosthène :: Pericles, Lysias, Isocrates, Demosthenes: speech at the heart of Athenian democracy.
textes.Les orateurs d'Athènes dans le temps: The orators of Athens in time
textes.Périclès, oraison funèbre, fin de la pre: Pericles, funeral oration, end of the first year of the Peloponnesian War: Athens, "the school of Hellas" (reported by Thucydides).
textes.Lysias, logographe : il écrit pour ses c: Lysias, logographer: he writes made-to-measure pleas for his clients, who deliver them themselves.
Isocrates opened a school around 392 BC; too weak-voiced for the assembly, he wrote his speeches to be read.
textes.Démosthène (384-322) : les Philippiques: Demosthenes (384-322): the Philippics against Philip of Macedon, On the Crown in 330 against Aeschines.
textes.Le texte d'un discours antique n'est pas: The text of an ancient speech is not necessarily what was said: Thucydides warns that he gives the gist of speeches, not their exact words.
textes.À la fin de la première année de la guer: At the end of the first year of the Peloponnesian War, Athens buried its dead. Pericles delivered the funeral oration. Instead of singing the battles, he praised the city itself: equal justice for all, an open public life, offices given on merit. Athens, he said, is "the school of Hellas".
textes.Nous ne connaissons ce discours que par: We know this speech only through Thucydides, in Book II of his History. He presents his speeches as true to the gist of what was said, not word for word. Plato, in the Menexenus, even attributes its writing to Aspasia, Pericles' companion.
textes.Périclès fait l'éloge d'Athènes, « école: Pericles praises Athens, "the school of Hellas"; but the text is Thucydides', true to the gist, not the words.
textes.À Athènes, chacun plaide lui-même sa cau: In Athens, everyone pleaded his own case. Those who could bought a speech from a logographer. Lysias, son of a Syracusan settled in Athens at Pericles' invitation, made it his trade around 403 BC, after seeing his brother Polemarchus forced to drink hemlock under the Thirty. He fitted each speech to its client, and was the first to make this an art.
textes.Isocrate, lui, a la voix trop faible pou: Isocrates, for his part, had too weak a voice to speak before the assembly. Around 392 BC he opened a school, never more than nine pupils at a time, and wrote speeches meant to be read, like the Panegyricus of 380. He called his teaching "philosophy". The canon of the ten Attic orators, fixed later, probably in Alexandria, brings them together with Demosthenes.
textes.Lysias, logographe : des plaidoiries à l: Lysias, logographer: pleas made to measure for each client. Isocrates: a school and speeches written to be read.
textes.Démosthène, né à Athènes en 384 av. J.-C: Demosthenes, born in Athens in 384 BC, pleaded at twenty against his guardians, who had squandered his inheritance. Plutarch says he had a speech impediment: he talked with pebbles in his mouth, declaimed while running, practised in an underground study and shaved half his head so he could not go out.
textes.À partir de 351, ses Philippiques dénonc: From 351 on, his Philippics denounced Philip II of Macedon. In 330, in On the Crown, he defended his whole career against Aeschines, and won. After Athens' defeat, he poisoned himself in 322 at Kalaureia. Cicero judged him alone above all other orators.
textes.Démosthène : de ses cailloux aux Philipp: Demosthenes: from his pebbles to the Philippics (351) and On the Crown (330). Cicero places him above all.
textes.IVe siècle av. J.-C. : ethos, pathos, lo: 4th century BC: ethos, pathos, logos, the three genres of speech and the syllogism.
textes.Au IVe siècle av. J.-C., à Athènes, Aris: In the 4th century BC, in Athens, Aristotle defined rhetoric as the faculty of seeing, in each case, what may persuade. He makes it the counterpart of dialectic, the art of discussion. Plato, in the Gorgias, judged it immoral and unworthy of serious study; Aristotle studies it.
textes.Il distingue trois genres de discours, q: He distinguishes three genres of speech, matching three kinds of hearers. Deliberative, for the assembly debating political affairs; judicial, for the court, where one accuses and defends; epideictic, for praise or blame. Communication manuals still copy it.
textes.Aristote : la rhétorique voit ce qui peu: Aristotle: rhetoric sees what may persuade. Three genres: deliberative (assembly), judicial (court), epideictic (praise or blame).
textes.Royaumes combattants : le cheval blanc d: Warring States: Gongsun Long's white horse, Guiguzi's strategists, Han Fei's dragon scales.
textes.Persuader en Chine ancienne, dans le tem: Persuasion in ancient China, in time
textes.Liu Xiang compile le Zhan Guo Ce: Liu Xiang compiles the Zhan Guo Ce
textes.Gongsun Long, École des noms, IIIe siècl: Gongsun Long, School of Names, 3rd century BC: "a white horse is not a horse", a paradox on the meaning of words.
textes.Guiguzi, le « Sage de la vallée des démo: Guiguzi, the "Sage of Ghost Valley": legendary master of the travelling strategists Su Qin and Zhang Yi.
textes.Le Zhan Guo Ce rassemble des anecdotes d: The Zhan Guo Ce gathers anecdotes of political manipulation, compiled under the Han by Liu Xiang.
textes.Han Fei (mort en 233 av. J.-C.) : pour p: Han Fei (died 233 BC): to persuade a ruler, know his character and never touch his "reversed scales".
textes.En Chine ancienne, on persuade un seul h: In ancient China, one persuades a single man, the ruler, not an assembly: the art lies less in proving than in not displeasing, on pain of death.
textes.Un cheval blanc n'est pas un cheval: A white horse is not a horse
textes.Au IIIe siècle av. J.-C., Gongsun Long,: In the 3rd century BC, Gongsun Long, of the School of Names, defended a paradox that became famous: "a white horse is not a horse". The text is a dialogue between an advocate and an objector. The argument: "horse" names a shape, "white" a colour; what names a colour and a shape is not what names a shape alone.
textes.Autre exemple du texte : si l'on demande: Another example in the text: if one asks for a horse, a yellow or black horse can be brought; if one asks for a white horse, it cannot. The paradox also plays on the Chinese word 非, which can mean "is not" or "is not identical to". Only 6 of the 14 chapters of his book survive, and Mencius, Zhuangzi and the Liezi criticise him.
textes.Gongsun Long : « un cheval blanc n'est p: Gongsun Long: "a white horse is not a horse". A paradox on what words designate, in the manner of the Greek sophists.
textes.Pendant les Royaumes combattants, des co: During the Warring States period, advisers went from court to court selling their alliance plans. Tradition gives them a master, Guiguzi, the "Sage of Ghost Valley", in the 4th century BC: according to Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, he trained Su Qin and Zhang Yi, founders of the School of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances.
textes.Le livre qui porte son nom a été compilé: The book bearing his name was compiled between the late Warring States and the end of the Han. Its first chapter, "Open and Shut", teaches how to make the other speak or to keep silent, and advises staying hidden so the listener believes his decisions are his own. These strategists' anecdotes are gathered in the Zhan Guo Ce, compiled under the Han by Liu Xiang.
textes.Guiguzi, maître légendaire de Su Qin et: Guiguzi, legendary master of Su Qin and Zhang Yi: persuading without showing oneself. The Zhan Guo Ce keeps their ruses.
textes.Han Fei, né vers 280 av. J.-C. dans la f: Han Fei, born around 280 BC into the ruling family of the state of Han, stuttered, according to the historian Sima Qian, but wrote remarkably. A pupil of the Confucian Xunzi together with Li Si, he became the great thinker of Legalism. The future First Emperor, reading his writings, reportedly said he could die without regret if he could befriend this man. In 233, Li Si, jealous, drove him to drink poison.
textes.Son chapitre « Les difficultés de la per: His chapter "The Difficulties of Persuasion" is a survival manual for advisers. Talk of great men, and the ruler thinks you are hinting at his defects. The favourite Mi Zixia was first praised, then punished, for the same deeds, when the ruler's love turned to hate. Conclusion: the dragon is gentle, you can ride on its back; but under its throat it has reversed scales, and whoever touches them dies. The ruler has them too.
textes.Han Fei : persuader un prince, c'est con: Han Fei: persuading a ruler means knowing his character, and never touching his reversed scales.
textes.De l'avocat d'Arpinum au De oratore : l': From the lawyer of Arpinum to De oratore: the Roman orator, his five tasks and his memory palace.
textes.Cicéron (106-43 av. J.-C.), « homme nouv: Cicero (106-43 BC), a "new man" from Arpinum, became Rome's foremost orator by having Verres convicted in 70.
textes.Les cinq parties de la rhétorique : inve: The five parts of rhetoric: inventio, dispositio, elocutio, memoria, actio (find, arrange, phrase, memorise, deliver).
textes.De oratore (55 av. J.-C.) : l'orateur pa: De oratore (55 BC): the perfect orator can speak on every subject, richly and variously.
textes.La Rhétorique à Herennius (vers 90 av. J: The Rhetorica ad Herennium (around 90 BC) gives the first known description of the method of loci, the memory palace.
textes.La Rhétorique à Herennius a longtemps ét: The Rhetorica ad Herennium was long attributed to Cicero; its author is in fact unknown.
textes.Marcus Tullius Cicéron naît le 3 janvier: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BC at Arpinum, about a hundred kilometres from Rome, into a family of knights. With no consular ancestors, he was a "new man", who rose through speech. In 80, he defended Sextus Roscius, accused of parricide, and dared to attack Chrysogonus, a freedman of the dictator Sulla. In 70, he had Verres, the corrupt governor of Sicily, convicted against the great advocate Hortensius: he was now Rome's foremost orator.
textes.Consul en 63, il déjoue la conjuration d: Consul in 63, he foiled Catiline's conspiracy: "How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?" After Caesar's death, his Philippics, named after those of Demosthenes, attacked Mark Antony. Proscribed, he was killed on 7 December 43; his head and hands were nailed to the Rostra, the speakers' platform.
textes.Cicéron : un homme nouveau porté par la: Cicero: a new man carried by speech, from Verres (70) to the Catilinarians (63) and the Philippics against Antony. Killed in 43.
textes.En 55 av. J.-C., Cicéron écrit De orator: In 55 BC, Cicero wrote De oratore, a dialogue in the manner of Plato, in three books. The scene is set in 91, in Crassus' villa at Tusculum. Crassus defines the perfect orator there: one who can speak on every subject richly and variously. He therefore needs a broad culture, law, history, philosophy. Antonius, the dialogue's other great orator, thinks a good knowledge of people is enough.
textes.Le dialogue passe en revue les cinq tâch: The dialogue reviews the orator's five tasks: finding the arguments (inventio), arranging them (dispositio), putting them into words (elocutio), remembering them (memoria) and delivering them (actio), with voice, gesture and face. It also discusses humour: Antonius credits part of Crassus' success to his wit.
textes.De oratore, 55 av. J.-C. : l'orateur par: De oratore, 55 BC: the perfect orator speaks on everything, with culture; five tasks, from invention to delivery.
textes.Comment retenir un discours de deux heur: How do you remember a two-hour speech without notes? Cicero tells the story of Simonides of Ceos. A banquet ends with the hall collapsing; the bodies are unrecognisable. Simonides, who had stepped out just before, identifies them by remembering where each had been seated. He drew a method from it: the order of places keeps the order of things.
textes.La Rhétorique à Herennius, un manuel lat: The Rhetorica ad Herennium, a Latin manual written around 90 BC and long attributed to Cicero, contains the first known description of this method of loci. You walk in your mind through a familiar building and leave in each room a striking image of what you want to say. Today it is called the memory palace.
textes.Simonide et le banquet effondré : la mét: Simonides and the collapsed banquet: the method of loci, first described in the Rhetorica ad Herennium. The memory palace.
textes.Les Nyāya-sūtra et leurs règles du débat: The Nyāya Sūtras and their rules of debate, the five-member argument, the Buddhist controversies of the Kathāvatthu.
textes.Le débat en Inde ancienne, dans le temps: Debate in ancient India, in time
textes.Les Nyāya-sūtra, attribués à Akṣapāda Ga: The Nyāya Sūtras, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, dated between the 6th century BC and the 2nd century AD: 5 books, 528 sutras.
textes.Trois façons de débattre : la discussion: Three ways of debating: discussion (vāda), disputation to win (jalpa), cavil that only tears down (vitaṇḍā).
textes.L'argument en cinq membres : thèse, rais: The five-member argument: thesis, reason, general rule, application, conclusion. "There is fire on the hill, because there is smoke."
textes.Le Kathāvatthu, « Points de controverse: The Kathāvatthu, "Points of Controversy", lists more than 200 theses debated between Buddhist schools.
textes.L'argument indien n'est pas le syllogism: The Indian argument is not Aristotle's syllogism copied: it adds a rule confirmed by experience and repeats thesis and conclusion, to convince an audience as much as to prove.
textes.Les Nyāya-sūtra, texte fondateur de l'éc: The Nyāya Sūtras, founding text of the Nyāya school, are attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, of whom almost nothing is known; they may have several authors. Their date is uncertain: between the 6th century BC and the 2nd century AD. Five books of two chapters each, 528 aphorisms, the sutras.
textes.Le premier sūtra énumère seize catégorie: The first sutra lists sixteen categories. Among them are the means of knowing, doubt, argument and its members, but also three ways of debating: honest discussion (vāda), sophistic disputation (jalpa) and cavil (vitaṇḍā). Then the traps: fallacies (hetvābhāsa), quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti) and the ways of losing a debate (nigrahasthāna).
textes.Nyāya-sūtra : 528 sūtra, seize catégorie: Nyāya Sūtras: 528 sutras, sixteen categories. Three debates: vāda (discussion), jalpa (disputation), vitaṇḍā (cavil). And the ways of losing.
textes.Les Nyāya-sūtra décrivent l'argument cor: The Nyāya Sūtras describe the correct argument in five members. The thesis: "there is fire on the hill". The reason: "because there is smoke on the hill". The general rule, confirmed by experience: "wherever there is smoke, there is fire". The application: "the hill is smoky". The conclusion: "therefore there is fire on the hill".
textes.Le texte reconnaît quatre moyens de conn: The text recognises four means of valid knowledge: perception, inference, comparison and reliable testimony. It warns against five kinds of fallacious reasoning, and against the tricks of those who do not seek the truth.
textes.Cinq membres : thèse, raison, règle géné: Five members: thesis, reason, general rule, application, conclusion. Four means of knowing: perception, inference, comparison, testimony.
textes.Chez les bouddhistes, le Kathāvatthu, «: Among Buddhists, the Kathāvatthu, "Points of Controversy", is one of the seven books of the Abhidhamma. Tradition attributes it to Moggaliputta Tissa, at the third Buddhist council convened under the emperor Ashoka, around 240 BC; this date is debated.
textes.Il passe en revue plus de deux cents thè: It reviews over two hundred theses disputed between schools, arranged in four groups of fifty, in question-and-answer form: a thesis is stated, questioned, its contradictions shown. The text names no winner: it teaches the method as much as the doctrine.
textes.Kathāvatthu : plus de 200 points de cont: Kathāvatthu: over 200 Buddhist points of controversy, in questions and answers, attributed to Ashoka's council (around 240 BC, date debated).
textes.Ier siècle : un maître d'école de Rome é: 1st century: a Roman schoolmaster writes in twelve books how to make an orator, from cradle to grave.
textes.Quintilien, né vers 35 à Calagurris en H: Quintilian, born around 35 at Calagurris in Hispania, ran a public school of rhetoric in Rome; Pliny the Younger was his pupil.
textes.Vers 95, l'Institution oratoire, en douz: Around 95, the Institutio Oratoria, in twelve books, trains the orator from childhood.
textes.Sa définition, reprise de Caton l'Ancien: His definition, taken from Cato the Elder: the orator is "a good man skilled at speaking".
textes.Le texte complet, perdu au Moyen Âge, es: The complete text, lost in the Middle Ages, was found by Poggio at St Gall in 1416.
textes.Pour Quintilien, l'éloquence n'est pas u: For Quintilian, eloquence is not a neutral technique: a wicked man skilled at speaking is not an orator. It is a direct answer to Plato's reproach.
textes.Quintilien naît vers 35 à Calagurris, au: Quintilian was born around 35 at Calagurris, today Calahorra, in Hispania. His father sent him early to study rhetoric in Rome, at the start of Nero's reign; he took the orator Domitius Afer as his model. In 68 he returned to Rome in the retinue of the emperor Galba and, after Galba's death, opened a public school of rhetoric.
textes.Pline le Jeune est son élève, et peut-êt: Pliny the Younger was his pupil, and perhaps Tacitus. He stopped teaching and pleading in 88; in 90, the emperor Domitian entrusted him with the education of his two grand-nephews. He lost his wife young, then his two sons, and tells of it in his book.
textes.Quintilien : d'Hispanie à Rome, une écol: Quintilian: from Hispania to Rome, a public school of rhetoric, Pliny the Younger as pupil, Domitian's grand-nephews in 90.
textes.Un homme de bien habile à parler: A good man skilled at speaking
textes.Vers 95, Quintilien publie l'Institution: Around 95, Quintilian published the Institutio Oratoria, a manual in twelve books. It follows the orator "from the cradle to the grave": the small child's upbringing, the grammarian's school, then the rhetorician's, the parts of rhetoric, style, and finally the accomplished orator.
textes.Sa définition vient de Caton l'Ancien :: His definition comes from Cato the Elder: the orator is "a good man skilled at speaking". The perfect orator is first a good man, and only then a good speaker. It is an answer to Plato, for whom rhetoric was mere flattery with no care for justice.
textes.Institution oratoire, vers 95, douze liv: Institutio Oratoria, around 95, twelve books: training the orator from childhood. Vir bonus dicendi peritus: a good man skilled at speaking.
textes.Au Moyen Âge, l'Institution oratoire ne: In the Middle Ages, the Institutio Oratoria circulated only in pieces. Petrarch, who knew only an incomplete version, even addressed a letter to Quintilian. In 1416, the humanist Poggio, attending the Council of Constance, searched the abbey of St Gall and found a complete manuscript there, buried in dust.
The rediscovery nourished the humanists. Erasmus drew on it; Luther said he preferred Quintilian to almost all authors; Montaigne read him too. The idea of educating the orator from childhood became a programme for Renaissance schools.
textes.1416 : Pogge retrouve à Saint-Gall l'Ins: 1416: Poggio finds the complete Institutio Oratoria at St Gall. Erasmus, Luther, Montaigne read it.
textes.Augustin, le trivium, l'art de prêcher,: Augustine, the trivium, the art of preaching, the disputatio: rhetoric in the service of faith and teaching.
textes.La chaire et l'école dans le temps: The pulpit and the school in time
textes.Alain de Lille, l'art de prêcher: Alan of Lille, the art of preaching
textes.Augustin, ancien professeur de rhétoriqu: Augustine, a former professor of rhetoric in Milan, wrote De doctrina christiana (397-426): the preacher must teach, delight and move.
textes.Le trivium (grammaire, logique, rhétoriq: The trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) opens the seven liberal arts, before the quadrivium.
textes.Vers 1200, Alain de Lille ouvre la série: Around 1200, Alan of Lille opened the series of "arts of preaching": a biblical theme, divided and developed.
textes.La disputatio : une question, les object: The disputatio: a question, the objections, the answer. Clermont, 1095: a sermon launched the First Crusade.
textes.On n'a aucun texte exact de l'appel de C: We have no exact text of the Clermont appeal: five very different versions, all written years later. The most influential speech of the Middle Ages is unknown to us.
textes.Augustin naît en 354 à Thagaste, en Afri: Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste, in North Africa. He studied then taught rhetoric at Carthage, opened a school in Rome in 383, and in 384 won the chair of rhetoric in Milan, seat of the imperial court: the most visible academic post in the Latin world. There he admired Bishop Ambrose, "a master of rhetoric". Converted in 386, he gave up his career and became bishop of Hippo.
textes.Faut-il jeter la rhétorique païenne ? No: Should pagan rhetoric be thrown away? No, he answers in De doctrina christiana, whose first three books appeared in 397 and the fourth in 426. The preacher must, as Cicero said, teach, delight and move, and choose by subject between the subdued, the moderate and the grand style. Cicero's rhetoric thus passed into the Christian pulpit.
textes.Augustin, professeur de rhétorique à Mil: Augustine, professor of rhetoric in Milan in 384, then bishop: De doctrina christiana keeps Cicero for the pulpit. Teach, delight, move.
textes.Le trivium et l'art de prêcher: The trivium and the art of preaching
textes.Dans les écoles médiévales, les sept art: In medieval schools, the seven liberal arts began with the trivium: grammar, logic (or dialectic) and rhetoric. Then came the quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. The word trivium appeared only in the Carolingian Renaissance, but the division can already be read in Martianus Capella. And our "trivial" reportedly comes from the contrast between the simpler trivium and the harder quadrivium.
textes.Vers 1200, la Somme de l'art de prêcher: Around 1200, Alan of Lille's Summa on the art of preaching opened a new genre, the "arts of preaching". More than two hundred are known. They teach the thematic sermon: a short biblical text, the theme, divided then subdivided, each part developed with support from Scripture, the Fathers or examples. Theme, division, development: the backbone of the scholastic sermon.
textes.Trivium : grammaire, logique, rhétorique: Trivium: grammar, logic, rhetoric. Around 1200, the arts of preaching: theme, division, development.
textes.Le 27 novembre 1095, au dernier jour du: On 27 November 1095, on the last day of the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II called on Christians to set out for the East and promised remission of sins to those who went. According to Robert the Monk, the crowd cried "God wills it!". But no exact text of the speech survives: there are five very different versions, all written years later.
textes.À l'université, on enseigne par la dispu: At university, teaching proceeded by disputatio, following a set method, relying on written authorities: a question, the objections, the answer. There were also public disputations: in Barcelona in 1263, the rabbi Nahmanides defended Judaism; in Leipzig in 1519, Luther faced Johann Eck.
textes.Clermont, 1095 : un sermon lance la croi: Clermont, 1095: a sermon launched the crusade, but its text is lost. The disputatio: question, objections, answer.
textes.Al-Jāḥiẓ à Bassora, puis la balāgha d'Ib: Al-Jahiz in Basra, then the balāgha of Ibn al-Mu'tazz, al-Jurjani and al-Sakkaki: a science of eloquence.
textes.Al-Jāḥiẓ (Bassora, 776-868 ou 869), « l': Al-Jahiz (Basra, 776-868 or 869), "the bug-eyed": the Book of Eloquence and Exposition founds Arabic literary theory.
textes.Sa définition : l'éloquence, c'est faire: His definition: eloquence is delivering an effective message, brief or elaborate at will.
textes.La balāgha a trois branches : les signif: Balāgha has three branches: meanings (maʿānī), figurative expression (bayān), embellishments (badīʿ).
textes.Al-Jurjānī (mort en 1078) la fonde comme: Al-Jurjani (died 1078) founded it as a science; al-Sakkaki (died 1229) arranged it in three parts.
textes.La rhétorique arabe ne vient pas d'Arist: Arabic rhetoric does not come from Aristotle: it grew out of poetry and the Qur'an, whose style, deemed inimitable, it seeks to explain.
textes.Al-Jāḥiẓ naît à Bassora vers 776. Son su: Al-Jahiz was born in Basra around 776. His nickname means "the bug-eyed": the caliph al-Ma'mun wanted to entrust his children to him, then gave up because his eyes frightened them. Close to the Mu'tazilites, rationalist theologians, he reportedly wrote two hundred books; known works include the Book of Animals, in seven parts, and the Book of Misers, a collection of anecdotes on stinginess.
textes.Son Kitāb al-Bayān wa al-Tabyīn, le « Li: His Kitab al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin, the "Book of Eloquence and Exposition", is a wide-ranging work on human communication; it is held to have started Arabic literary theory in a formal way. His definition of eloquence was widely adopted: the ability to deliver an effective message, staying brief or elaborating, at will.
textes.Al-Jāḥiẓ, Bassora, IXe siècle : le Livre: Al-Jahiz, Basra, 9th century: the Book of Eloquence and Exposition. Eloquence: an effective message, brief or elaborate at will.
textes.La balāgha, la rhétorique arabe classiqu: Balāgha, classical Arabic rhetoric, studies how speech gets ideas across, stirs feeling and moves. It has three branches. The science of meanings (maʿānī): building the sentence that suits the situation and the audience. The science of expression (bayān): imagery, simile (tashbīh), metaphor (majāz), allusion (kināya). The science of embellishment (badīʿ): sound play (jinās), rhymed prose (saj'), antithesis (ṭibāq).
textes.Le prince-poète Ibn al-Muʿtazz, mort en: The prince-poet Ibn al-Mu'tazz, who died in 909, wrote the Kitab al-Badi'. In it he catalogues five devices, including metaphor (isti'ara) and wordplay (tajnis), and argues they are not innovations: they are already found in pre-Islamic poetry and in the Qur'an.
textes.Balāgha : maʿānī (la phrase juste), bayā: Balāgha: maʿānī (the right sentence), bayān (imagery), badīʿ (ornaments). Ibn al-Mu'tazz, died 909: figures come from ancient poetry and the Qur'an.
textes.Pour les théologiens, le Coran est inimi: For theologians, the Qur'an is inimitable: this is the doctrine of i'jaz al-Qur'an, which seeks to explain what is unique in its language and style. Al-Jurjani, who died in 1078, drew a theory from it: beauty lies not in isolated words but in their arrangement, naẓm, the link between syntax and meaning. He wrote The Proofs of Inimitability and The Secrets of Eloquence; he is held to be the founder of classical balāgha.
textes.Al-Sakkākī, mort en 1229, range la disci: Al-Sakkaki, who died in 1229, arranged the discipline in three parts in his great encyclopaedia, The Key to the Sciences. Al-Qazwini, who died in 1338, drew an abridgement from it, then a commentary: these manuals became the basis of teaching in the madrasas.
textes.Al-Jurjānī (mort en 1078) : l'éloquence: Al-Jurjani (died 1078): eloquence lies in the arrangement of words, naẓm. Al-Sakkaki (1229) codifies, al-Qazwini (1338) abridges for the madrasas.
textes.Afrique de l'Ouest : les griots, maîtres: West Africa: the griots, masters of the word, keep the history of Mali and the epic of Sundiata.
textes.Le griot (jeli en manding, gewel en wolo: The griot (jeli in Manding, gewel in Wolof): historian, genealogist, praise singer, adviser to kings and mediator.
textes.Le métier se transmet dans des familles: The craft passes down in griot families, who marry among themselves, with the kora, the ngoni or the balafon.
textes.L'épopée de Soundiata raconte le fondate: The epic of Sundiata tells of the founder of the Mali Empire (reigned 1235-1255) and his griot Balla Fasséké.
textes.En 1960, Djibril Tamsir Niane la publie: In 1960, Djibril Tamsir Niane published it in French from the account of the griot Djeli Mamoudou Kouyaté.
textes.Une tradition orale n'est pas un documen: An oral tradition is not an archival document: even the Sosso Bala, the "800-year-old" balafon listed by UNESCO, was reportedly promoted as a relic in the 1970s, according to the historians Jan Jansen and Francis Simonis.
textes.En Afrique de l'Ouest, le griot (jeli ou: In West Africa, the griot (jeli or jali in Manding, gewel in Wolof) is a historian, storyteller, praise singer, poet and musician. He keeps the oral memory of peoples and families, advises royal families and acts as mediator in disputes. The word "griot" itself may come from French, perhaps from a Portuguese word meaning servant; its origin remains obscure.
textes.Les griots forment un groupe héréditaire: Griots form a hereditary group: most marry other griots and pass their art down within the family. Their instruments: the kora, a lute-harp with 21 strings, the xalam, the ngoni, the balafon, a gourd-resonated xylophone.
textes.Le griot : historien, généalogiste, chan: The griot: historian, genealogist, praise singer, adviser and mediator. A hereditary art, carried by the kora and the balafon.
textes.L'épopée de Soundiata, poème du peuple m: The epic of Sundiata, a poem of the Malinke people, tells of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire, who reigned from 1235 until his death in 1255. As a child he cannot walk; an iron rod breaks under him, and he finally rises by leaning on a baobab branch. Grown up, he confronts Soumaoro Kanté, king of Sosso, whom the epic paints as a cruel sorcerer king.
textes.Son père lui a donné un griot, Balla Fas: His father gave him a griot, Balla Fasséké, to advise him: he is the ancestor of the Kouyaté line of griots. At his coronation, Sundiata gave the assembly an oral constitution, the Kouroukan Fouga. The epic has passed down from generation to generation, through the mouths of griots.
textes.Soundiata (règne 1235-1255) fonde le Mal: Sundiata (reigned 1235-1255) founds Mali; his griot Balla Fasséké is the ancestor of the Kouyatés. The epic lives through the griots' voice.
textes.Dans l'épopée, Balla Fasséké joue du bal: In the epic, Balla Fasséké plays Soumaoro's sacred balafon to win a place at his court. After Sundiata's victory, he becomes its guardian, and the charge passes to his descendants, the Kouyatés. This balafon, the Sosso Bala, is kept in Niagassola, Guinea; it is said to be over 800 years old. In 2001, UNESCO proclaimed it a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity.
textes.Les historiens Jan Jansen et Francis Sim: The historians Jan Jansen and Francis Simonis believe, however, that the Kouyaté family made it into a historical relic in the 1970s. The epic itself is known to us through 20th-century griots: in 1960, Djibril Tamsir Niane published in French the version of the griot Djeli Mamoudou Kouyaté.
textes.Le Sosso Bala, balafon gardé par les Kou: The Sosso Bala, a balafon kept by the Kouyatés, listed by UNESCO in 2001. Niane, 1960: the epic written down from a griot.
textes.Gutenberg, Luther, Érasme : quand la par: Gutenberg, Luther, Erasmus: when the printed word runs faster than the spoken one.
textes.L'imprimerie et les humanistes dans le t: Printing and the humanists in time
textes.Vers 1450, à Mayence, Gutenberg combine: Around 1450, in Mainz, Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press; his Bible came out around 1455.
textes.1517 : les 95 thèses de Luther sont impr: 1517: Luther's 95 Theses were printed in hundreds of copies; his Sermon on Indulgences was reprinted twenty times.
textes.Érasme, De copia (1512) : 195 façons de: Erasmus, De copia (1512): 195 ways to say "your letter delighted me greatly". At least 85 editions in his lifetime.
textes.L'Éloge de la folie (imprimé en 1511) :: The Praise of Folly (printed in 1511): Folly praises herself, and mocks everyone.
textes.L'image de Luther clouant ses thèses à l: The image of Luther nailing his theses to the church door comes from Melanchthon and remains doubtful: it is printing, more than the hammer, that spread his ideas.
textes.Vers 1450, à Mayence, Johannes Gutenberg: Around 1450, in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press, perhaps inspired by wine or olive presses. His Bible came out around 1455, in about 180 copies. Movable type already existed in China, with Bi Sheng around 1040, and in Korea.
textes.En Europe, l'imprimerie fait exploser la: In Europe, printing made the circulation of texts explode: some 27,500 different works printed before 1501 still survive. For rhetoric, everything changed: a speech, a sermon, a pamphlet could now reach thousands of readers who had never heard the speaker.
textes.Gutenberg, vers 1450 : caractères mobile: Gutenberg, around 1450: movable type, oil-based ink, screw press. 27,500 works printed before 1501 survive.
textes.Le 31 octobre 1517, Martin Luther envoie: On 31 October 1517, Martin Luther sent Albert of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz, a letter and 95 theses against the preaching of indulgences. The image of Luther nailing his theses to the door of the Wittenberg church comes from Melanchthon and remains doubtful.
textes.Ce qui est sûr, c'est l'imprimerie : des: What is certain is printing: hundreds of copies in Latin circulated from 1517, a German translation followed the same year, and his Sermon on Indulgences, written in German for everyone, was reprinted twenty times. For the first time, a theologians' quarrel was played out before a whole people of readers.
textes.Luther, 1517 : 95 thèses envoyées par le: Luther, 1517: 95 theses sent by letter, printed in hundreds of copies, translated into German. The nail on the door is doubtful.
textes.En 1512, Érasme publie chez Josse Bade,: In 1512, Erasmus published with Josse Bade, in Paris, De copia, a manual for enriching one's style. In chapter 33, he gives 195 ways of saying a single sentence: "your letter delighted me greatly". The pupil learns to vary, to rephrase, to amplify. The book went through at least 85 editions in Erasmus' lifetime; John Colet had asked him for it for his St Paul's School in London.
textes.Trois ans plus tôt, en 1509, chez son am: Three years earlier, in 1509, at his friend Thomas More's house in London, he wrote in a week, he says, the Praise of Folly, printed in 1511. The Latin title, Moriae Encomium, puns on More's name. It is Folly herself who speaks and praises herself, in the manner of Lucian, mocking princes, pedantic scholars and the abuses of the Church.
textes.Érasme : De copia (1512), 195 variations: Erasmus: De copia (1512), 195 variations of a sentence; the Praise of Folly (1511), a mock encomium in which Folly speaks.
textes.Valladolid, la Propagande de la foi, la: Valladolid, the Propaganda of the faith, the Port-Royal Logic, Pascal: debating and persuading from 1550 to 1700.
textes.Les controverses de l'âge classique dans: Controversies of the classical age in time
textes.Valladolid, 1550-1551 : Las Casas contre: Valladolid, 1550-1551: Las Casas against Sepúlveda on the fate of the Amerindian peoples; the jury never decides.
textes.1622 : le pape Grégoire XV crée la Congr: 1622: Pope Gregory XV created the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith; the word "propaganda" was born, still neutral.
textes.1662 : La Logique ou l'art de penser d'A: 1662: Logic or the Art of Thinking by Arnauld and Nicole, in French, a reasoning manual until the 20th century.
textes.Pascal, vers 1658 : l'art de persuader r: Pascal, around 1658: the art of persuading combines the art of convincing (the mind) and the art of pleasing (the heart).
textes.Un débat sans verdict n'est pas un débat: A debate without a verdict is not a useless debate: at Valladolid, each side claimed victory, neither got what it wanted, but Las Casas' arguments have crossed the centuries.
textes.Valladolid : un procès sans verdict: Valladolid: a trial without a verdict
textes.En 1550 et 1551, au collège San Gregorio: In 1550 and 1551, at the college of San Gregorio in Valladolid, two men faced each other before a junta of doctors and theologians convened by King Charles I, the emperor Charles V. The Dominican Bartolomé de las Casas defended the Amerindian peoples; the humanist Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda justified subjugating them by war.
textes.Sepúlveda s'appuie sur Aristote et sa «: Sepúlveda relied on Aristotle and his "natural slavery": some peoples were supposedly made to obey. Las Casas answered that this definition did not apply to the Indians. The judges dispersed without a decision; each side claimed victory, neither got what it wanted. A debate of ideas, on equal terms, about a conquest led by the very country that organised it.
textes.Valladolid, 1550-1551 : Las Casas contre: Valladolid, 1550-1551: Las Casas against Sepúlveda, Aristotle at the heart of the debate. No verdict.
textes.En 1662 paraît, sans nom d'auteur, La Lo: In 1662, Logic or the Art of Thinking appeared anonymously. Its authors, Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole, were Jansenists of Port-Royal, and Pascal probably contributed to it. The book was written in French, not Latin, for a wide public. It remained in use until the 20th century; the philosopher Ian Hacking called it the most influential logic book between Aristotle and the end of the 19th century.
textes.Pascal, vers 1658, rédige De l'art de pe: Pascal, around 1658, wrote On the Art of Persuasion for a work intended for the little schools of Port-Royal. He distinguishes two doors: the art of convincing, which addresses the mind and understanding and makes one hold a statement true; the art of pleasing, which addresses the heart and will and makes one love. Persuading means combining the two.
textes.Port-Royal, 1662 : la logique en françai: Port-Royal, 1662: logic in French. Pascal: persuading = convincing the mind + pleasing the heart.
textes.En 1622, en pleine Contre-Réforme, le pa: In 1622, in the midst of the Counter-Reformation, Pope Gregory XV created the Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, charged with propagating the Catholic faith in non-Catholic countries. In Latin, propaganda simply means "what must be propagated".
textes.Le mot passe aux affaires profanes à par: The word passed into secular affairs from the 1790s and took on its pejorative sense only in the 20th century, notably after the great campaigns of the First World War. A missionary congregation thus gave its name to the manipulation of crowds.
1622: Propaganda Fide, propagating the faith. The word turned secular in the 1790s, pejorative in the 20th century.
textes.De Mirabeau à Zola : la parole publique: From Mirabeau to Zola: public speech against the king, slavery and injustice.

textes.1851-1852 : Sojourner Truth à Akron, Fre: 1851-1852: Sojourner Truth in Akron, Frederick Douglass in Rochester: Black voices against slavery.
textes.1898 : « J'accuse…! », la lettre ouverte: 1898: "J'accuse…!", Zola's open letter on the Dreyfus affair, on the front page of L'Aurore.
textes.Les phrases les plus célèbres sont souve: The most famous lines are often rewritten afterwards: Mirabeau's retort belongs to legend, and the refrain "Ain't I a Woman?" appears only in a version published twelve years later.
textes.Par la volonté du peuple: By the will of the people
textes.Le 23 juin 1789, à Versailles, Louis XVI: On 23 June 1789, at Versailles, Louis XVI held a royal session in the Salle des Menus-Plaisirs. He set out a reform programme and ordered the three estates to separate. The nobility left. The Third Estate and part of the clergy stayed seated. The grand master of ceremonies, Dreux-Brézé, reminded the dean, Bailly, of the king's order; Bailly replied: "The assembled Nation cannot receive orders."
textes.Selon la légende, Mirabeau aurait lancé: According to legend, Mirabeau declared that the deputies were there by the will of the people and would be removed only by the power of bayonets. The Assembly at once voted the inviolability of its members. The king reportedly replied: "Well then, let them stay!" Speech stood up to power, and won.
textes.23 juin 1789 : Bailly, « la Nation assem: 23 June 1789: Bailly, "the assembled Nation cannot receive orders"; Mirabeau and the bayonets, partly legend.
textes.Le 29 mai 1851, à la convention pour les: On 29 May 1851, at the women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio, Sojourner Truth, a former slave born in New York State, took the floor. The convention's secretary, Marius Robinson, went over his transcription with her and published it on 21 June. In 1863, Frances Dana Gage published a very different version, with a Southern accent that Truth, who spoke only Dutch until she was nine, did not have, and a refrain: "Ain't I a Woman?".
textes.Le 5 juillet 1852, à Rochester, devant l: On 5 July 1852, in Rochester, before the Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society, Frederick Douglass asked: "What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?" Independence Day, he said, reveals to him the gross injustice and cruelty of which he is the constant victim. He turned the national holiday against those who celebrated it.
textes.Sojourner Truth (1851), dont le célèbre: Sojourner Truth (1851), whose famous refrain is an 1863 rewrite; Frederick Douglass (1852): "What, to the slave, is your 4th of July?"
textes.D'août à octobre 1858, Abraham Lincoln e: From August to October 1858, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, candidates for the Senate in Illinois, debated seven times in seven towns. The subject: should slavery be allowed in the new Western states? The rule: an hour for the first speaker, an hour and a half in reply, half an hour of rejoinder. Douglas kept his seat, but Lincoln became a national figure. On 19 November 1863, at Gettysburg, he spoke only 271 words.
textes.Le 13 janvier 1898, L'Aurore, le quotidi: On 13 January 1898, L'Aurore, Clemenceau's daily, published on its front page a letter from Émile Zola to President Félix Faure: "J'accuse…!". In it Zola named those who had had the innocent Captain Dreyfus convicted, knowing he was exposing himself to a trial. Convicted of libel on 23 February, he went into exile in England. Dreyfus was pardoned in 1899, then rehabilitated in 1906.
textes.Lincoln-Douglas, 1858 : sept débats de t: Lincoln-Douglas, 1858: seven three-hour debates; Gettysburg, 1863: 271 words. Zola, 1898: "J'accuse…!", a letter that accuses by naming.

textes.De Gaulle, 18 juin 1940, sur la BBC : pr: De Gaulle, 18 June 1940, on the BBC: almost nobody heard it, and nobody recorded it.

textes.La voix de l'appel du 18 juin qu'on ente: The voice of the 18 June appeal we hear today is that of the 22 June appeal: the founding speech was never recorded.
textes.Propp, Campbell, Queneau, Hitchcock : ce: Propp, Campbell, Queneau, Hitchcock: what the 20th century understood about stories.

textes.Un argument : des prémisses qui soutienn: An argument: premises supporting a conclusion. Induction generalises: its conclusion is only probable.
textes.L'homme d'acier : réfuter la version la: The steelman: refute the strongest version of the opposing argument (Rapoport's rules, Dennett, 2013).
