textes.En 1919, à Paris, le jeune Suisse Jean P: In 1919, in Paris, the young Swiss Jean Piaget gives intelligence tests at the Alfred Binet laboratory school. What interests him are the wrong answers: children of the same age get things wrong in the same way. He draws a four-stage theory from this. Pour water from a wide glass into a tall, thin one: before about seven, the child says there is more. It has since been shown that babies know more, earlier, than Piaget thought.
textes.Piaget s'intéressait aux erreurs. Avec v: Piaget was interested in mistakes. With you, he'd have had enough for an encyclopaedia.
textes.Étudiant à Harvard, l'Américain B. F. Sk: As a Harvard student, the American B. F. Skinner builds a cage in which a rat presses a lever to get food. In 1938, he publishes The Behavior of Organisms: behaviour followed by a reward is reinforced, and the way the reward is handed out changes everything. During the war, he trains pigeons to guide missiles; nobody takes him seriously. Slot machines, online games and dating apps now use his reward schedules.
textes.Une récompense de temps en temps, au has: A reward now and then, at random, and you come back every day. I invented nothing, Skinner did it first.
textes.En 850 naît, près de Balkh, dans le nord: In 850, near Balkh, in the north of today's Afghanistan, Abu Zayd al-Balkhi was born. A pupil of al-Kindi, he reproached physicians for treating the body while forgetting the soul. He sorted ills of the mind into four families: fear, anger, sadness and obsession. Against phobia, no bloodletting: one must expose oneself gradually to what is feared, until one grows used to it, for "most of the terror comes from anticipation of the terror".
Exposing yourself gradually to what you fear. So I'll ask you this question again. Often.
textes.En 1284, au Caire, l'hôpital al-Mansuri: In 1284, in Cairo, the al-Mansuri hospital was completed. Like the other bimaristans, the hospitals of the Islamic world that appeared in the 9th century, it was to turn no one away, not even the mentally ill. They were treated there, and music was introduced as therapy. In Aleppo, another hospital, Arghun's, relied for them on light, fresh air, running water and music.
textes.De la musique pour apaiser l'esprit. L'I: Music to soothe the mind. The AI tried it on you. She had to turn up the volume.
textes.En 1839, Gustav Fechner s'abîme les yeux: In 1839, Gustav Fechner damaged his eyes looking at the Sun through coloured glasses to study afterimages; he had to resign his chair. Convalescing, he turned to the relation between mind and body. On 22 October 1850, in bed, a new way of studying the mind came to him: measuring sensations. His Elements of Psychophysics appeared in 1860, and psychophysicists still celebrate 22 October.
textes.Il a regardé le Soleil pour comprendre l: He stared at the Sun to understand sight. You could at least look at the question.
textes.Réévaluer la situation calme mieux qu'ét: Reappraising the situation calms better than suppressing the emotion.
textes.Comment on retient, comment on oublie, c: How we remember, how we forget, how we get it wrong.
textes.Mémoire de travail : quelques éléments p: Working memory: a few items for a few seconds. Long-term memory: virtually unlimited.
textes.On oublie vite au début puis plus lentem: We forget fast at first, then more slowly (Ebbinghaus).
textes.Les rappels espacés et les tests de récu: Spaced recall and retrieval tests anchor far better than rereading.
textes.Chaque rappel reconstruit le souvenir et: Each recall rebuilds the memory and can change it.
textes.Relire et surligner donnent une impressi: Rereading and highlighting feel like mastery; testing yourself is far more effective.
textes.Courbe de l'oubli : chute rapide au débu: Forgetting curve: a steep drop at first, then slower
textes.Ce qui nous fait agir et ce qui nous fai: What makes us act and what makes us procrastinate.
textes.Motivation intrinsèque : agir pour le pl: Intrinsic motivation: acting for the pleasure of the activity. Extrinsic: for a reward or to avoid a punishment.
textes.Récompenser une activité déjà plaisante: Rewarding an already enjoyable activity can reduce intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect).
textes.Autonomie, compétence et lien social nou: Autonomy, competence and relatedness feed motivation (self-determination theory).
textes.La procrastination est surtout une fuite: Procrastination is mainly fleeing an unpleasant emotion, not laziness.
textes.La pyramide de Maslow n'a jamais été des: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow: it comes from a management consulting psychologist, Charles McDermid, in 1960.
textes.Les trois besoins de la théorie de l'aut: The three needs of self-determination theory
textes.Conformisme, obéissance et leviers de pe: Conformity, obedience and the levers of persuasion.
textes.Asch (1951) : face à un groupe unanime q: Asch (1951): faced with a unanimous group that is wrong, about a third of answers conform.
textes.Milgram (1963) : 65 % des participants v: Milgram (1963): 65% of participants go up to the maximum shock under an experimenter's authority.
textes.Un seul allié dans le groupe fait chuter: A single ally in the group sharply reduces conformity.
textes.Cialdini : réciprocité, engagement, preu: Cialdini: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity.
textes.L'expérience de Stanford de Zimbardo est: Zimbardo's Stanford experiment is strongly contested: the guards were coached.
textes.Une ligne de référence et trois lignes A: A reference line and three lines A, B and C; B is the same length
textes.Environ 86 milliards de neurones reliés: About 86 billion neurons linked by synapses.
textes.Aire de Broca : production du langage ;: Broca's area: producing language; Wernicke's area: understanding it.
textes.Plasticité : le cerveau se réorganise to: Plasticity: the brain reorganizes itself throughout life as we learn.
textes.On utilise tout son cerveau, pas 10 % :: We use all of our brain, not 10%: imaging shows activity everywhere.
textes.Le cerveau gauche « logique » et le cerv: The “logical” left brain and “creative” right brain is a myth: the two hemispheres work together.
textes.Mythes et réalités sur le cerveau: Myths and realities about the brain
textes.Piaget, Vygotski, attachement et théorie: Piaget, Vygotsky, attachment and theory of mind.
textes.Piaget : stades sensori-moteur, préopéra: Piaget: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational stages.
textes.Vygotski : zone proximale de développeme: Vygotsky: zone of proximal development, what the child can do with help.
textes.Attachement (Bowlby, Ainsworth) : un lie: Attachment (Bowlby, Ainsworth): a secure bond makes exploring possible.
textes.Théorie de l'esprit : vers 4 ans, l'enfa: Theory of mind: around age 4, children understand that others can hold a false belief (Sally and Anne).
textes.Les stades de Piaget sont moins rigides: Piaget's stages are less rigid than he thought: babies know things earlier than he assumed.
textes.Big Five, MBTI, héritabilité et vieilles: Big Five, MBTI, heritability and old theories of character.
textes.Big Five : ouverture, conscienciosité, e: Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism. It is the best-validated model.
textes.Le MBTI classe en 16 types, mais beaucou: The MBTI sorts people into 16 types, but many people change type from one test to the next.
textes.La phrénologie et les tempéraments des h: Phrenology and the temperaments of the humors have been abandoned.
textes.Les traits sont des continuums, pas des: Traits are continuums, not boxes: you are not introverted or extraverted, you are more or less extraverted.
textes.Un profil Big Five : cinq scores, pas un: A Big Five profile: five scores, not a type
textes.Le stress aigu mobilise ; c'est le stres: Acute stress mobilizes; it's chronic stress that wears you down.
textes.Adaptation hédonique : après un gain ou: Hedonic adaptation: after a gain or a loss, we largely return to our usual level of happiness.
textes.Les liens sociaux sont le meilleur prédi: Social ties are the best predictor of long-term well-being (Harvard study, running since 1938).
textes.Le sommeil consolide la mémoire ; en man: Sleep consolidates memory; lacking it degrades mood and attention.
textes.Gagner au loto ne rend pas durablement b: Winning the lottery does not make people much happier in the long run (Brickman, 1978).
textes.Adaptation hédonique : le pic retombe ve: Hedonic adaptation: the peak falls back to the usual level
textes.Nommer son émotion la calme (Lieberman,: Naming your emotion calms it (Lieberman, 2007). Reappraising works better than suppressing.
textes.Mettre un mot sur ce qu'on ressent, « je: Putting a word on what you feel, "I feel anxious", already helps calm it: in 2007 Matthew Lieberman's team observed with brain imaging a drop in amygdala activity when an emotion is named. That is affect labelling.
textes.Autre stratégie efficace : la réévaluati: Another effective strategy is reappraisal, which changes how you see the situation. Seeing stage fright as excitement rather than fear, for example. Conversely, systematically suppressing your emotions costs energy and does not reduce what you feel. The emotion is not the enemy; what matters is what you do with it.
textes.Empathie émotionnelle (ressentir) et cog: Emotional empathy (feeling) and cognitive empathy (understanding). Active listening: restate to check.
textes.L'empathie a deux faces. L'empathie émot: Empathy has two sides. Emotional empathy is feeling with the other person; cognitive empathy is understanding what they think or feel, without necessarily feeling it yourself. Emotions also spread without our thinking about it: that is emotional contagion, like a yawn or a fit of giggles.
textes.Une compétence s'entraîne : l'écoute act: It is a skill you can train: active listening. Restating what the other person said, "if I understand correctly, you…", shows you have understood and lets them correct you. Daniel Goleman popularised the idea of "emotional intelligence" in 1995, a concept proposed by Peter Salovey and John Mayer in 1990.
textes.Oubli rapide au début puis lent (Ebbingh: Fast forgetting at first, then slow (Ebbinghaus, 1885). Spaced reminders: far more effective than cramming.
textes.Hermann Ebbinghaus fut son propre cobaye: Hermann Ebbinghaus was his own guinea pig. He learned lists of meaningless syllables, like "DAX" or "BOK", so that nothing would latch onto an existing memory, then measured what remained. In 1885 he published Über das Gedächtnis: we forget very fast at first, especially in the first hours, then more and more slowly.
textes.Il découvre aussi l'effet d'espacement :: He also discovered the spacing effect: reviewing at spaced intervals retains far better than cramming everything at once. It is one of the most solid findings in the psychology of learning, and it is exactly what this game's reminders do. Each successful recall flattens the curve and lets you wait longer before the next one.
textes.Mémoire de travail ≈ 7 ± 2 éléments (Mil: Working memory ≈ 7 ± 2 items (Miller, 1956). The hippocampus forms event memories (patient H. M.).
textes.La mémoire de travail ne garde que quelq: Working memory holds only a few items, for a few seconds: George Miller, in 1956, spoke of about seven items, plus or minus two. Hence the point of grouping a phone number into pairs. Long-term memory is almost unlimited.
textes.En 1953, pour soigner son épilepsie, on: In 1953, to treat his epilepsy, Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed. He could no longer form new memories of events, but still learned new motor skills, without remembering having learned them. Patient H. M. showed that memory is not one thing: memory for facts goes through the hippocampus, memory for skills through other circuits. And sleep helps: the day's memories are replayed and stabilised then.
textes.Se tester + espacer. Palais de mémoire :: Test yourself + space it out. Memory palace: place items in familiar places. We remember the start and end of a list best.
textes.Relire et surligner donnent une impressi: Rereading and highlighting give a feeling of mastery: everything seems familiar. Testing yourself is far more effective: fetching information from memory strengthens it. Combined with spacing, it is the winning pair.
textes.Pour le plaisir ou pour la récompense: For the pleasure or for the reward
textes.Autonomie, compétence, lien social (Deci: Autonomy, competence, social connection (Deci and Ryan). Rewarding what you enjoy can kill the desire. Flow: difficulty that matches.
textes.Edward Deci et Richard Ryan résument ce: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan sum up what feeds lasting motivation in three needs: autonomy, feeling you are behind your choices; competence, feeling you are progressing; and social connection. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi adds flow: we become absorbed in a task when its difficulty just matches our abilities. Too easy, we get bored; too hard, we get anxious.
textes.La pyramide que Maslow n'a pas dessinée: The pyramid Maslow did not draw
textes.Maslow n'a pas dessiné de pyramide (McDe: Maslow did not draw a pyramid (McDermid, 1960). The marshmallow test predicts far less than was thought (Watts, 2018).
textes.Abraham Maslow propose en 1943 une hiéra: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. But he never drew a pyramid. The famous shape comes from a business consultant psychologist, Charles McDermid, in 1960, and took hold in management textbooks.
textes.Méfiance aussi envers le test du marshma: Be wary of the marshmallow test too. In the 1960s and 1970s Walter Mischel offered children one treat now or two if they waited; those who waited seemed to do better later. In 2018 a much larger replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found a far weaker link, largely explained by family background. Waiting also makes more sense when you trust the adult making the promise.
textes.Procrastiner = fuir une émotion. Commenc: Procrastinating = fleeing an emotion. Start for 5 minutes. A precise goal > "doing your best" (Locke and Latham).
textes.Un objectif précis et mesurable motive d: A precise, measurable goal motivates more than "doing your best": that is a central finding of Edwin Locke and Gary Latham's theory. And to build a habit, a small regular action tied to a specific time of day beats a big, rare effort. Believing your abilities can develop, Carol Dweck's growth mindset, helps you persevere.
textes.Face à un groupe unanime qui se trompe,: Faced with a unanimous group that is wrong, a third of answers go along (Asch, 1951). A single ally brings conformity down.
textes.En 1951, Solomon Asch montre à des étudi: In 1951 Solomon Asch showed students a reference line and three lines to compare. The answer is obvious. But the participant is surrounded by accomplices who all give the same wrong answer out loud. About a third of answers follow the group, and 74 % of participants give in at least once.
textes.Le résultat le plus encourageant est ail: The most encouraging finding lies elsewhere: it only takes one accomplice giving the right answer for conformity to collapse. With an ally, only 5 % keep following the majority. Daring to be the first to say no helps others say it too.
textes.Milgram (1963) : 65 % vont jusqu'à 450 V: Milgram (1963): 65 % go up to 450 V under authority. Stanford (1971) is disputed; Genovese's "38 witnesses" are exaggerated.
textes.En 1963, Stanley Milgram demande à des v: In 1963 Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a "learner" who made mistakes. The shocks were fake, the learner an actor who screamed. Under the calm pressure of an experimenter in a lab coat, 65 % of participants in the main version went up to the maximum 450-volt shock.
textes.Toutes les expériences célèbres ne tienn: Not all famous experiments hold up as well. The Stanford prison experiment, run by Philip Zimbardo in 1971, is now heavily disputed: archives show the "guards" were encouraged to be harsh. And the story of Kitty Genovese, killed in 1964 in front of "38 witnesses" who did nothing, was exaggerated: there were far fewer, and the police were called.
textes.Effet du témoin : plus on est nombreux,: Bystander effect: the more people, the less help (70 % alone against 40 % in pairs). Groupthink (Janis, 1972).
textes.Quand plusieurs personnes assistent à un: When several people witness an emergency, each thinks someone else will act: responsibility is diluted. That is the bystander effect. In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
textes.En groupe, les opinions se durcissent au: In groups, opinions also harden: group polarisation pushes towards the already dominant position. And groupthink can lead experts to bad collective decisions: Irving Janis illustrated it in 1972 with the failed Bay of Pigs landing. Antidote: appoint a devil's advocate, and ask for opinions before the leader gives theirs.
textes.≈ 86 milliards de neurones (Herculano-Ho: ≈ 86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel, 2009), ≈ 20 W. Distinct neurons (Cajal, Nobel 1906). The 10 % myth is false.
textes.Le cerveau compte environ 86 milliards d: The brain has about 86 billion neurons, according to Suzana Herculano-Houzel's count in 2009; the often-quoted 100 billion had never been measured. It weighs about 2 % of the body and uses about 20 watts, a small light bulb. The cerebellum alone holds about 80 % of the neurons in 10 % of the volume.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Santiago Ramón: At the end of the 19th century Santiago Ramón y Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of distinct cells, neurons, using a stain invented by Camillo Golgi, who argued the opposite, a continuous network. They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize, in a tense atmosphere. And no, we do not use 10 % of our brain: imaging shows every region is used.
textes.Gage (1848) : le lobe frontal et le cara: Gage (1848): the frontal lobe and character. Broca (1861): language. Plasticity: learning changes the brain (London taxis).
textes.En 1848, une barre à mine traverse le cr: In 1848 an iron rod went through the skull of Phineas Gage, a railway worker. He survived and lived twelve more years, but his friends said "Gage was no longer Gage": the frontal lobe also governs character. In 1861 Paul Broca autopsied a patient, Leborgne, who could only say one syllable, "tan": a lesion in the left frontal lobe. That is Broca's area, linked to producing language.
textes.Le cerveau, pourtant, se réorganise tout: Yet the brain reorganises itself throughout life: that is plasticity. After a stroke, other regions can take over a lost function. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire showed that London taxi drivers, who learn 25,000 streets, have a larger part of the hippocampus. Learning literally changes the brain.
textes.Pas de cerveau gauche « logique » ni dro: No "logical" left brain or "creative" right brain (Nielsen, 2013). A coloured MRI image is not proof (the dead salmon).
textes.Le « cerveau gauche logique » contre le: The "logical left brain" versus "creative right brain" is a myth. Some functions are more lateralised, like language, but the two hemispheres work together constantly. In 2013 a study of more than 1,000 brains by Jared Nielsen and colleagues found no overall "dominance" of one hemisphere in individuals.
textes.L'imagerie elle-même demande de la prude: Imaging itself calls for caution. In 2009 a team "detected" activity in the brain of a dead salmon placed in a scanner, to show the danger of poorly corrected statistics; it received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012. A pretty coloured image is not proof. And the brain feels no pain: some operations are done on an awake patient, who talks during the procedure.
textes.Quatre stades (Piaget) ; conservation ac: Four stages (Piaget); conservation acquired around 7. Babies know things earlier than he thought (Baillargeon).
textes.Jean Piaget a commencé en observant ses: Jean Piaget started by observing his own children, notebook in hand. He described four broad stages: sensorimotor, where the baby discovers the world through senses and movement; preoperational; concrete operations; formal operations, where one reasons about abstract ideas.
textes.Vers 4 ans, l'enfant comprend qu'autrui: Around age 4, children understand that others can believe something false (Sally-Anne, 1985). Proximal zone: what you can do with help (Vygotsky).
textes.Le test de Sally et Anne : Sally cache u: The Sally-Anne test: Sally hides a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves it to a box. Where will Sally look? Before about age 4, the child answers "in the box", where it really is. After that, the child understands that Sally believes something other than what is true. That is theory of mind, tested this way by Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith in 1985.
textes.Lev Vygotski insiste, lui, sur le rôle d: Lev Vygotsky stressed the role of others: the zone of proximal development is what the child can do with help but not yet alone. Good teaching aims at that zone, neither too easy nor out of reach. This game tries to do the same with its levels.
textes.Le réconfort compte plus que la nourritu: Comfort matters more than food (Harlow). A secure attachment allows exploration (Bowlby, Ainsworth).
textes.Dans les années 1950, Harry Harlow élève: In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised baby monkeys with two artificial "mothers": one made of wire that gave milk, the other of soft cloth with no milk. The babies spent their time clinging to the cloth mother. Comfort matters more than food. These very cruel experiments also fed into animal ethics.
textes.John Bowlby en tire la théorie de l'atta: John Bowlby drew from this the theory of attachment: a secure bond lets the child explore, knowing it can come back. Mary Ainsworth measured it with the "strange situation": a child, its mother, a stranger, and a door that closes. As for the "Mozart effect", it comes from a 1993 study on students, with a modest, short-lived gain that was poorly replicated afterwards: classical music does not make babies smarter.
textes.Big Five (OCEAN) : des continuums, pas d: Big Five (OCEAN): continuums, not types. 40-60 % heritable, they change with age.
textes.Ces traits sont héritables à environ 40: These traits are about 40 to 60 % heritable according to twin studies, and the rest comes mainly from each person's own experiences rather than the shared family. They also change: in adulthood we become on average more conscientious and more agreeable. And conscientiousness predicts school success almost as well as intelligence.
textes.Les tests qui ne tiennent pas: Tests that do not hold up
The MBTI is unstable (Pittenger, 1993). Humours and phrenology: abandoned, only words remain.
textes.Le MBTI classe les gens en 16 types. Il: The MBTI sorts people into 16 types. It sells very well, but many people change type when they retake the test a few weeks later, as David Pittenger pointed out in 1993. A type that changes with the day of the test does not measure much that is stable.
textes.L'histoire est pleine de systèmes abando: History is full of abandoned systems. Hippocrates and Galen classified temperaments by four humours; we are left with the words sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic. Franz Joseph Gall's phrenology read character in the bumps of the skull; French is left with "having the maths bump". The scenery changes; the urge to be put in a box remains.
textes.Lui, c'est un chauffard ; moi, j'étais p: He's a reckless driver; I was in a hurry
textes.Erreur fondamentale d'attribution (Ross,: Fundamental attribution error (Ross, 1977): others "are" like that, we "were" in a situation. Introvert ≠ shy.
textes.L'erreur fondamentale d'attribution cons: The fundamental attribution error is explaining other people's behaviour by their character, and our own by circumstances. Someone cuts you off: they are a reckless driver. You cut someone off: you were in a hurry. Lee Ross named it in 1977.
textes.Être introverti, au sens psychologique,: Being introverted, in the psychological sense, does not mean being shy: it mainly means drawing energy from time alone rather than from interaction. An introvert can speak in public perfectly well; they just need to recharge afterwards. The words introvert and extravert come from Carl Jung, in 1921.
textes.Stress aigu = mobilisation ; stress chro: Acute stress = mobilisation; chronic stress = wear (Selye, 1936). A little arousal helps, too much paralyses (Yerkes-Dodson).
textes.En 1936, Hans Selye décrit dans une lett: In 1936 Hans Selye described in a letter to Nature rats subjected to all kinds of harm, which all reacted the same way; he later called this reaction stress. Acute stress mobilises: cortisol releases energy to cope. It is chronic stress that wears you down: cortisol kept high for a long time weakens immunity and memory.
textes.La loi de Yerkes et Dodson, établie en 1: The Yerkes-Dodson law, established in 1908 on mice, draws a bell curve: a little arousal improves performance, too much paralyses it. A little stage fright helps. Against chronic stress, several meta-analyses put regular physical activity at a level close to psychotherapy for mild to moderate anxiety and depression.
textes.Le loto ne rend pas heureux longtemps: The lottery does not make you happy for long
textes.Adaptation hédonique : on revient vers s: Hedonic adaptation: we return towards our usual level (Brickman, 1978). Relationships best predict well-being (Harvard, since 1938).
textes.Après un grand gain ou une grande perte,: After a big win or a big loss, we largely return to our usual level of happiness: that is hedonic adaptation. In 1978 Philip Brickman compared lottery winners and people who had become paraplegic: some time later, the gaps in happiness were far smaller than you would imagine. The return is not always complete, but it is powerful.
textes.Qu'est-ce qui compte, alors ? L'étude de: So what matters? The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed men since 1938, then their families. Its conclusion, summed up by its current director, Robert Waldinger: good relationships make us happier and healthier. Social ties are the best predictor of a long and happy life.
textes.7 à 9 heures de sommeil. Écriture expres: 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Expressive writing (Pennebaker, 1986), mindfulness: real but modest effects.
textes.Le sommeil consolide la mémoire, et en m: Sleep consolidates memory, and missing it degrades mood and attention. For an adult, recommendations range from 7 to 9 hours a night; regularly getting under 6 hours is linked to many health risks.
textes.Écrire sur ses émotions difficiles quelq: Writing about difficult emotions for a few days in a row can also help: James Pennebaker's expressive writing protocol in 1986 was followed by fewer doctor's visits, with real but modest effects. And mindfulness, brought into medicine by Jon Kabat-Zinn, offers eight weeks of secularised meditation exercises. Conversely, occupational exhaustion, burnout, described in 1974, was recognised by the WHO in 2019 as an occupational phenomenon.
textes.Autre outil très ancien : le palais de m: Another very old tool: the memory palace, or method of loci, which goes back to Antiquity. You mentally place each item to remember in a familiar place, then walk the route again to find them. Legend ties it to the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos: the only survivor of a banquet whose roof had collapsed, he is said to have identified the victims by remembering where each had sat. Cicero tells it in 55 BCE, in On the Orator. Memory champions still use it. In a list, we remember the beginning and the end best: these are the primacy and recency effects. And goldfish retain associations for weeks.
textes.La motivation intrinsèque, c'est agir po: Intrinsic motivation is acting for the activity itself; extrinsic, for a reward or to avoid punishment. A trap: rewarding an activity you already enjoy can reduce the desire to do it. That is the overjustification effect: the activity becomes a means to get the reward, and loses its appeal when the reward stops. Edward Deci measured it as early as 1971: students paid to solve a puzzle spent markedly less free time on it once the payment stopped.
textes.On repousse surtout ce qui ennuie, angoi: We mainly put off what bores us, worries us or seems vague. Procrastination is first an escape from an unpleasant emotion, not a lack of willpower. Once started, a task stays "open" in the mind: that is the Zeigarnik effect. The Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described it in 1927. The idea came from her professor Kurt Lewin: a waiter remembered unpaid orders in detail, and forgot them once the bill was settled. Hence simple advice: start for five minutes, just to open the task.
textes.Ses expériences de conservation sont cél: His conservation experiments are famous: pour water from a wide glass into a tall narrow one, and a five-year-old often thinks there is more, judging by the height. Around 7, the child understands that pouring does not change the amount. But the stages are less rigid than Piaget thought: Renée Baillargeon's experiments suggest babies grasp earlier that a hidden object still exists. In 1985, with Elizabeth Spelke and Stanley Wasserman, she showed that 5-month-old babies look longer at a screen that seems to pass through a hidden box, whereas Piaget placed object permanence around 9 months.
textes.Le modèle des Big Five décrit la personn: The Big Five model describes personality through five broad traits: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, OCEAN in English. These five factors first emerged from a study of US Air Force officers by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal in 1958, published in 1961; the name Big Five was coined by Lewis Goldberg in 1981. It is the best-validated model in psychology. Each trait is a continuum: you are not introverted or extraverted, you are more or less extraverted.
textes.Daniel Goleman a popularisé en 1995 l'id: Daniel Goleman popularised the idea of "emotional intelligence" in 1995, a concept proposed by Peter Salovey and John Mayer in 1990.
textes.En 1953, pour soigner son épilepsie, on: In 1953, to treat his epilepsy, Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed.
textes.Abraham Maslow propose en 1943 une hiéra: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.
textes.En 2018, une reproduction bien plus larg: In 2018 a much larger replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found a far weaker link, largely explained by family background.
textes.La psychologue soviétique Bluma Zeigarni: The Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described it in 1927.
textes.En 1951, Solomon Asch montre à des étudi: In 1951 Solomon Asch showed students a reference line and three lines to compare.
textes.En 1963, Stanley Milgram demande à des v: In 1963 Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a "learner" who made mistakes.
textes.En 1969, Bibb Latané et Judith Rodin fon: In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Santiago Ramón: At the end of the 19th century Santiago Ramón y Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of distinct cells, neurons, using a stain invented by Camillo Golgi, who argued the opposite, a continuous network.
textes.En 1848, une barre à mine traverse le cr: In 1848 an iron rod went through the skull of Phineas Gage, a railway worker.
textes.En 1861, Paul Broca autopsie un patient,: In 1861 Paul Broca autopsied a patient, Leborgne, who could only say one syllable, "tan": a lesion in the left frontal lobe.
textes.En 2000, Eleanor Maguire montre que les: In 2000 Eleanor Maguire showed that London taxi drivers, who learn 25,000 streets, have a larger part of the hippocampus.
textes.En 2013, une étude de plus de 1 000 cerv: In 2013 a study of more than 1,000 brains by Jared Nielsen and colleagues found no overall "dominance" of one hemisphere in individuals.
textes.En 2009, une équipe « détecte » une acti: In 2009 a team "detected" activity in the brain of a dead salmon placed in a scanner, to show the danger of poorly corrected statistics; it received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012.
textes.En 1985, avec Elizabeth Spelke et Stanle: In 1985, with Elizabeth Spelke and Stanley Wasserman, she showed that 5-month-old babies look longer at a screen that seems to pass through a hidden box, whereas Piaget placed object permanence around 9 months.
textes.Les mots introverti et extraverti vienne: The words introvert and extravert come from Carl Jung, in 1921.
textes.En 1936, Hans Selye décrit dans une lett: In 1936 Hans Selye described in a letter to Nature rats subjected to all kinds of harm, which all reacted the same way; he later called this reaction stress.
textes.La loi de Yerkes et Dodson, établie en 1: The Yerkes-Dodson law, established in 1908 on mice, draws a bell curve: a little arousal improves performance, too much paralyses it.
textes.En 1978, Philip Brickman compare des gag: In 1978 Philip Brickman compared lottery winners and people who had become paraplegic: some time later, the gaps in happiness were far smaller than you would imagine.
textes.L'étude de Harvard sur le développement: The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed men since 1938, then their families.
textes.Aristote range les émotions par paires,: Aristotle arranged emotions in pairs, Seneca wanted to destroy anger; today, we learn to name and reappraise them.
textes.Aristote, dans la Rhétorique, range les: Aristotle, in the Rhetoric, arranged emotions in opposing pairs: anger and calmness, friendliness and enmity.
textes.Pour lui, la colère naît du sentiment d': For him, anger arises from feeling belittled; Seneca wanted to destroy it rather than control it.
textes.Nommer son émotion aide à la réguler : c: Naming one's emotion helps to regulate it: this is affect labelling.
textes.Les Anciens ne s'accordent pas : Aristot: The Ancients disagreed: Aristotle analysed anger to use it in a speech, Seneca held it to be an error to root out.
textes.Au IVe siècle av. J.-C., à Athènes, Aris: In the 4th century BC, in Athens, Aristotle devoted part of book II of his Rhetoric to the emotions. The speaker, he said, persuades by three means: his character, ethos; the audience's emotions, pathos; and reasoning, logos. He arranged emotions in opposing pairs, anger and calmness, friendliness and enmity, and described for each the state of mind, against whom it is directed and on what grounds.
textes.Pour Aristote, la colère naît du sentime: For Aristotle, anger arises from the feeling of having been belittled: we are angered by whoever insults us, or insults what we value. Around 45, the Stoic Seneca wrote for his brother Novatus a treatise On Anger, in three books. For him, a passion is a false belief about the value of things: "We shouldn't control anger, but destroy it entirely."
textes.Aristote : la colère vient du sentiment: Aristotle: anger comes from feeling belittled. Seneca: it must be destroyed, not controlled.
textes.L'esprit selon le Bouddha: The mind according to the Buddha
textes.En Inde, au Ve siècle av. J.-C., le Boud: In India, in the 5th century BC, the Buddha observed the mind: desire, hatred, ignorance, and the attention that calms them.
textes.L'esprit selon le Bouddha, dans le temps: The mind according to the Buddha, in time
textes.Le Bouddha vit en Inde au VIe ou au Ve s: The Buddha lived in India in the 6th or 5th century BC; he taught how to put out three "fires": desire, hatred and ignorance.
textes.Une personne n'est qu'un assemblage de c: A person is only a bundle of five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness.
textes.Aucun de ces agrégats n'est un « moi » :: None of these aggregates is a "self": this is the teaching of non-self.
textes.Les quatre fondements de l'attention (le: The four foundations of mindfulness (body, feelings, mind, phenomena) inspire today's mindfulness meditation.
textes.La pleine conscience des hôpitaux n'est: Hospital mindfulness is not a religion: Jon Kabat-Zinn's programme, in 1979, is secular, even though it draws on Buddhism.
textes.Le Bouddha a vécu en Inde au VIe ou au V: The Buddha lived in India in the 6th or 5th century BC: historians hesitate, and many now place his death around 400 BC, give or take twenty years. According to tradition, he gave his first sermon in the Deer Park at Sarnath, near Benares, before five former companions.
textes.Son enseignement est d'abord une observa: His teaching is first of all an observation of the mind. Liberation is the extinguishing of the "fires" of desire, hatred and ignorance, which the texts call the three poisons. On the wheel of life, they are painted at the centre as three animals: a rooster for greed, a snake for hatred, a pig for ignorance.
textes.Désir, haine, ignorance : les trois pois: Desire, hatred, ignorance: the three poisons, at the heart of the wheel of life (rooster, snake, pig).
textes.Pour le Bouddha, ce qu'on appelle une pe: For the Buddha, what we call a person breaks down into five skandhas, five "aggregates": material form, feeling (pleasant, unpleasant or neutral), perception that recognises and names, mental formations such as will, and consciousness.
textes.Aucun de ces agrégats n'est un « moi » :: None of these aggregates is a "self": before each one, the texts have one say "this is not mine, this is not my self, this is not what I am". An old text compares them to foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain trunk and an illusion. All Buddhist schools keep this idea of non-self.
textes.Forme, sensation, perception, formations: Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness: five aggregates, none of them a self.
textes.Le Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, dixième discours: The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the tenth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya, teaches the four foundations of mindfulness: body, feelings, mind and phenomena. It is one of the most studied texts of the Pali canon, and the foundation of modern vipassana meditation. The Dhammapada, a collection of 423 verses, opens on this idea: "Mind precedes thoughts."
textes.Une image célèbre, celle de la flèche, d: A famous image, that of the arrow, says what attention changes. Struck by pain, the untaught man adds a pain of the mind to the pain of the body, as if he received a second arrow right after the first; the instructed disciple receives only the first. In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn opened a stress reduction clinic at the University of Massachusetts, with a secular eight-week course drawn from these meditations.
textes.Quatre fondements de l'attention ; ne pa: Four foundations of mindfulness; do not shoot the second arrow; in 1979, mindfulness enters the hospital.
textes.À Athènes, vers 319 av. J.-C., l'élève d: In Athens, around 319 BC, Aristotle's pupil sketched thirty human types: the flatterer, the chatterbox, the superstitious man…
textes.Théophraste succède à Aristote à la tête: Theophrastus succeeded Aristotle at the head of the Lyceum in Athens; he is credited with over 2,000 students and 227 titles.
textes.Ses Caractères, probablement écrits vers: His Characters, probably written around 319 BC, describe thirty moral types: the first known attempt at systematic character writing.
textes.Chaque portrait donne une courte définit: Each sketch gives a short definition, then concrete gestures: a type is recognised by what it does.
textes.En 1688, La Bruyère traduit Théophraste: In 1688, La Bruyère translated Theophrastus and wrote his own Characters after them.
textes.Les Caractères ne sont pas une théorie d: The Characters are not a theory of personality: they are sketches of ordinary faults, seen from the outside, without explanation.
textes.Le beau parleur du Lycée: The fine talker of the Lyceum
His name was Tyrtamus. Born around 371 BC at Eresos, on the island of Lesbos, he became the pupil of Aristotle, who supposedly nicknamed him Theophrastus for the grace of his conversation. Aristotle left him his library and the guardianship of his children.
textes.Théophraste dirige le Lycée pendant tren: Theophrastus led the Lyceum for thirty-five or thirty-six years; at one point the school supposedly had more than 2,000 students. Diogenes Laërtius credits him with 227 titles, almost all lost. His books on plants earned him the title of "father of botany". His last words were reportedly: "We die just when we are beginning to live."
textes.Tyrtamos, surnommé Théophraste par Arist: Tyrtamus, nicknamed Theophrastus by Aristotle, led the Lyceum for thirty-five years and observed everything: plants, stones and humans.
textes.Les Caractères, probablement écrits vers: The Characters, probably written around 319 BC, line up thirty sketches: the dissembler, the flatterer, the coward, the chatterbox, the superstitious man, the miser, the late learner… Each begins with a one-line definition, then strings gestures together. "Flattery is a cringing sort of conduct that aims to promote the advantage of the flatterer."
textes.Le flatteur glisse à son compagnon : « R: The flatterer whispers to his companion: "Look how the people gaze at you!" The superstitious man, defined as "a crouching fear of unseen powers", begins his day only after sprinkling himself with water, and stops dead if a weasel crosses his path. The late learner memorises poems at sixty. No theory: each is recognised by what he does.
textes.Trente types, une définition, des gestes: Thirty types, a definition, gestures: personality seen from the outside, through observation.
textes.Le petit livre fonde un genre : le « car: The little book founded a genre: the "character", a short portrait of a human type, which even became a school exercise. In England, Joseph Hall imitated it in 1608, Thomas Overbury between 1614 and 1616, John Earle in 1628. The preface, in which Theophrastus says he is writing in his ninety-ninth year, is probably a forgery.
textes.En 1688, Jean de La Bruyère traduit Théo: In 1688, Jean de La Bruyère translated Theophrastus and published his own Characters after them, which are rather satires of thinly disguised contemporaries. In 1879, George Eliot still remembered him in Impressions of Theophrastus Such. Personality psychologists would do the same: describe before explaining.
textes.Hall, Overbury, La Bruyère (1688), Georg: Hall, Overbury, La Bruyère (1688), George Eliot (1879): the genre of the "character" comes from Theophrastus.
textes.Un esclave affranchi devient maître stoï: A freed slave became a Stoic master: what troubles us is not things, but our judgements about them.
textes.Né esclave vers l'an 50 à Hiérapolis, Ép: Born a slave around AD 50 at Hierapolis, Epictetus taught at Nicopolis, in Greece, after philosophers were expelled from Rome around 93.
textes.Le Manuel s'ouvre ainsi : certaines chos: The Handbook opens thus: some things depend on us, others do not.
textes.Chapitre 5 : ce qui trouble les gens, ce: Chapter 5: what upsets people is not things themselves but their judgements about things.
textes.Au milieu des années 1950, Albert Ellis: In the mid-1950s, Albert Ellis built a therapy on this idea and quoted Epictetus.
textes.Épictète n'a rien écrit : les Entretiens: Epictetus wrote nothing: the Discourses and the Handbook are the notes of his pupil Arrian.
textes.Épictète naît esclave vers l'an 50 à Hié: Epictetus was born a slave around AD 50 at Hierapolis, in Phrygia, today's Pamukkale in Turkey. In Rome, he belonged to Epaphroditus, a wealthy freedman who was Nero's secretary. He was lame: according to Celsus, quoted by Origen, his master broke his leg on purpose; according to Simplicius, he had been disabled since childhood.
textes.Il suit les leçons du stoïcien Musonius: He followed the lessons of the Stoic Musonius Rufus, was freed after Nero's death in 68, and taught in Rome. Around 93, the emperor Domitian banished all philosophers from the city: Epictetus left to found a school at Nicopolis, in Epirus. He wrote nothing. Around 108, his pupil Arrian noted down his lessons "word for word".
textes.Esclave, boiteux, affranchi, exilé à Nic: Slave, lame, freed, exiled to Nicopolis: Epictetus taught inner freedom; Arrian took the notes.
textes.Le Manuel, 53 courts chapitres tirés des: The Handbook, 53 short chapters drawn from the lessons by Arrian, opens with one sentence: "Of things, some depend upon ourselves, others do not depend upon ourselves." Our judgements, desires and choices depend on us; the body, reputation and events do not. Epictetus called this faculty of choice prohairesis, the only thing entirely ours.
textes.D'où le chapitre 5, le plus cité : « Ce: Hence chapter 5, the most quoted: "What upsets people is not things themselves but their judgements about the things." To change one's judgement is to change one's emotion. In the four books of the Discourses that remain to us, out of eight, everything revolves around this exercise.
textes.« Ce qui trouble les gens, ce ne sont pa: "What upsets people is not things themselves but their judgements about the things." (Handbook, 5)
textes.Du monastère au cabinet du psy: From the monastery to the therapist's office
textes.Marc Aurèle cite les Entretiens dans ses: Marcus Aurelius quotes the Discourses in his Meditations. In the Middle Ages, Greek monks adapted the Handbook into a rule of life, sometimes replacing Socrates with Saint Paul. Angelo Poliziano translated it into Latin in 1479; his translation, printed in 1497, is the first edition of the text. Matteo Ricci translated part of it into Chinese.
textes.Au milieu des années 1950, le psychologu: In the mid-1950s, the American psychologist Albert Ellis founded a therapy on the Stoic idea and quoted Epictetus: "Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them." His scheme: A, the activating event; B, the belief about it; C, the emotional consequence. To change C, one works on B. Cognitive therapies are its heirs.
textes.Marc Aurèle, les moines, Poliziano (1479: Marcus Aurelius, the monks, Poliziano (1479), then Albert Ellis (1950s): the event, the belief, the emotion.
textes.La médecine de l'âme en Islam: Medicine of the soul in Islam
textes.Au IXe siècle, al-Balkhi soigne la peur,: In the 9th century, al-Balkhi treated fear, anger, sadness and obsessions, and the hospitals of the Islamic world took in the mentally ill.
textes.La médecine de l'âme en Islam, dans le t: Medicine of the soul in Islam, in time
textes.Abu Zayd al-Balkhi (850-934), élève d'al: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi (850-934), a pupil of al-Kindi, wrote the Sustenance of Body and Soul: body and soul fall ill together.
textes.Il range les troubles de l'âme en quatre: He sorted disorders of the soul into four families: fear and anxiety, anger, sadness and depression, obsession.
textes.Contre la phobie, il conseille de s'expo: Against phobia, he advised exposing oneself gradually to what is feared, until one grows used to it.
textes.À l'hôpital al-Mansuri du Caire, achevé: At the al-Mansuri hospital in Cairo, completed in 1284, the mentally ill were also treated, and music was introduced as therapy.
textes.Al-Balkhi ne sépare pas l'âme de la foi: Al-Balkhi did not separate the soul from faith: he based his ideas on the Qur'an and the hadiths, and linked mental health to spiritual health.
textes.Abu Zayd al-Balkhi naît en 850 à Shamist: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi was born in 850 at Shamistiyan, a village in the province of Balkh, in the north of today's Afghanistan. As a young man, he spent about eight years in Iraq and followed the philosopher al-Kindi. Back home, he accepted a post as secretary from the governor of Balkh but refused to become minister. He died in Balkh in 934.
textes.On lui prête plus de soixante livres, de: He is credited with more than sixty books, from geography to poetry; his maps founded the "Balkhi school". His medical treatise, the Sustenance of Body and Soul, reproached the physicians of his day for treating the body while forgetting the mind. For him, the two are linked: when the body is ill, the soul loses its liveliness; when the soul is ill, the body may fall ill in turn.
textes.Al-Balkhi (850-934) : le corps et l'âme: Al-Balkhi (850-934): body and soul fall ill together, and the physician must treat both.
textes.Al-Balkhi range les troubles émotionnels: Al-Balkhi sorted emotional disorders into four families: fear and anxiety; anger and aggression; sadness and depression; obsession. Under all harmful symptoms he saw anxiety; under happy states, joy. He advised healthy people to keep positive thoughts in reserve, as one keeps first-aid supplies for an accident.
textes.Il distingue trois dépressions : la tris: He distinguished three depressions: ordinary sadness, a depression arising from within the body, and a depression in reaction to an outside event. When the cause is known, a loss or a failure, one treats with words, advice, and inner thoughts that help to overcome it. When it is unknown, a sudden sadness that prevents action, he suspected a physical cause and advised bodily medicine.
textes.Peur, colère, tristesse, obsession ; tro: Fear, anger, sadness, obsession; three depressions; positive thoughts in reserve like a first-aid kit.
textes.Al-Balkhi décrit la phobie, qu'il appell: Al-Balkhi described phobia, which he called fazaa': an extreme fear that makes anxiety rise, leaves one shaky and disoriented, unable to decide. Instead of the bloodletting and remedies of his day, he advised exposing oneself gradually and repeatedly to the feared object or situation, until one grows used to it. He recalled that "most of the terror comes from anticipation of the terror".
textes.Il soigne aussi un mal par son contraire: He also treated an ill by its opposite, al-ilaj bi al-did: a technique that Joseph Wolpe would reintroduce in 1969 as reciprocal inhibition. In the Islamic world, the bimaristans, hospitals that appeared in the 9th century, took in all the sick, including those of the mind. At the al-Mansuri hospital in Cairo, completed in 1284, they were treated and music was introduced as therapy.
textes.Exposition progressive contre la phobie: Gradual exposure against phobia; hospitals open to the mentally ill; music in Cairo in 1284.
textes.En 1571, Montaigne s'enferme dans sa tou: In 1571, Montaigne shut himself in his tower and observed himself: his fears, his imagination, his idleness. Introspection became a book.
textes.En 1571, à 38 ans, Montaigne se retire d: In 1571, at 38, Montaigne withdrew to the tower of his château, among about 1,500 books.
textes.Les Essais (1580, puis 1588, et 1595 apr: The Essays (1580, then 1588, and 1595 after his death) have three books and 107 chapters.
textes.Il prévient le lecteur : « Je suis moi-m: He warned the reader: "I am myself the matter of my book."
textes.Ses chapitres sur la tristesse, la peur,: His chapters on sadness, fear, idleness or imagination have fed psychology.
textes.Montaigne ne se dit pas philosophe et ne: Montaigne did not call himself a philosopher and built no system: he tried, doubted, corrected himself, and added more than three thousand corrections after 1588.
textes.Michel de Montaigne naît le 28 février 1: Michel de Montaigne was born on 28 February 1533 at the Château de Montaigne, in Guyenne. His father had him speak Latin as his first language and had him woken every morning by a musician. In 1571, at 38, he withdrew to the tower of his château, into a library of about 1,500 volumes.
textes.Il y écrit les Essais : une première édi: There he wrote the Essays: a first edition in 1580 in Bordeaux, a third book in 1588, and a posthumous edition in 1595, published by Marie de Gournay. In all, three books and 107 chapters of very unequal length. Montaigne popularised a literary genre: the essay.
textes.1571, la tour et ses 1 500 livres ; 1580: 1571, the tower and its 1,500 books; 1580, the Essays; 107 chapters in three books.
textes.« Je suis moi-même la matière de mon liv: "I am myself the matter of this book," he warned: it would be unreasonable, he added, to spend one's leisure on so frivolous a subject. His contemporaries found this self-indulgent. He observed himself relentlessly, and noted: "I have never seen a greater monster or miracle than myself." For "each man bears the entire form of the human condition".
textes.Ses titres sont un programme de psycholo: His titles are a psychology programme: Of Sadness, Of Fear, Of Idleness, Of Imagination, Of Friendship. Around 1570, knocked off his horse by a companion at full gallop, he lay unconscious and thought himself dead: "for more than two full hours taken for dead". He drew from it a precise observation of what one feels at the gates of death.
textes.S'observer soi-même pour comprendre l'hu: Observing oneself to understand humans: sadness, fear, imagination, and even fainting.
textes.Au même moment, en Espagne, le médecin J: At the same time, in Spain, the physician Juan Huarte de San Juan published in 1575 the Examination of Men's Wits. Each person, he said, has a talent of his own, tied to his temperament, and should choose the trade that suits it; children must therefore be studied early. First banned by the Inquisition, the book went through sixty editions up to 1800.
textes.Montaigne, lui, souffre de calculs rénau: Montaigne, for his part, suffered from kidney stones from 1578 and distrusted doctors. His observations on thought, motivation, fear and happiness have marked psychology. Pascal owes him much of his scepticism; Nietzsche would write that the mere fact that such a man wrote has truly augmented the joy of living on this Earth.
textes.Huarte (1575) : un talent par personne,: Huarte (1575): one talent per person, to be spotted early. Montaigne: self-observation, bequeathed to Pascal and Nietzsche.
textes.Une princesse demande comment l'âme fait: A princess asked how the soul moves the body; Descartes answered with a treatise on emotions: six passions, animal spirits and a gland.
textes.Descartes et les passions, dans le temps: Descartes and the passions, in time
textes.En 1643, Élisabeth de Bohême écrit à Des: In 1643, Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes: how can a soul that only thinks move the body?
textes.Les Passions de l'âme (1649), dédiées à: The Passions of the Soul (1649), dedicated to Elisabeth, have three parts and 212 articles.
textes.Six passions primitives : l'admiration,: Six primitive passions: wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness.
textes.Les passions sont bonnes en elles-mêmes: The passions are good in themselves; one avoids only their misuse or excess, and one can learn to master them.
textes.Pour Descartes, les passions ne sont pas: For Descartes, the passions are not faults to root out, as for some Stoics: he judges them "good by their nature".
textes.Le 16 mai 1643, la princesse Élisabeth d: On 16 May 1643, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes. If the soul is only a substance that thinks, how can it set the body's spirits in motion? On 20 June, she insisted: it would be easier for her to grant the soul matter than to admit that an immaterial thing could move a body.
textes.Descartes répond que l'union de l'âme et: Descartes replied that the union of soul and body should not be thought of as a collision between two bodies. Elisabeth was not convinced. He dedicated his Principles of Philosophy to her in 1644. In 1645, the correspondence resumed: the princess was ill, and Descartes attributed her symptoms to sadness. They then discussed happiness, passions and morals, until Descartes's death in early 1650.
textes.1643 : comment l'âme meut-elle le corps: 1643: how does the soul move the body? Elisabeth's question led Descartes to the passions.
textes.Les Passions de l'âme, achevées en 1649: The Passions of the Soul, completed in 1649 and dedicated to Elisabeth, have three parts and 212 short articles. A passion is defined there as a perception, sensation or commotion of the soul, caused, maintained and strengthened by some movement of the spirits. In article 69, Descartes decides: there are only six primitive ones.
textes.Ce sont l'admiration, l'amour, la haine,: They are wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness; all the others are mixtures or species of them. In article 211, he concludes that the passions are good by nature: one need only avoid their misuse and excess. And the virtue he prized most was generosity.
textes.Admiration, amour, haine, désir, joie, t: Wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy, sadness: six primitive passions, good in themselves.
textes.Comment l'émotion passe-t-elle du corps: How does emotion pass from body to soul? "Animal spirits", produced in the blood, flow through the nerves and move the body in all the ways it is capable of. The soul is joined to it at one point: the pineal gland, a small structure in the middle of the brain, the size of a grain of rice, 5 to 8 mm. Descartes held it to be the principal seat of the soul.
textes.Galien, au IIe siècle, n'y voyait qu'un: Galen, in the 2nd century, saw in it only a support for brain tissue; we now know it produces melatonin, which regulates sleep. But Descartes's master idea survived: one can train one's passions. In article 50, he asserts that even the weakest souls could acquire absolute mastery over their passions, if enough effort were spent training and guiding them.
textes.Esprits animaux et glande pinéale : une: Animal spirits and the pineal gland: wrong mechanics, but a sound idea, passions can be trained.
textes.À la fin du XVIIIe siècle, Pussin et Pin: At the end of the 18th century, Pussin and Pinel removed the chains of Paris's insane and invented "moral treatment".
textes.En 1797, à Bicêtre, le surveillant Jean-: In 1797, at Bicêtre, the superintendent Jean-Baptiste Pussin removed the patients' irons; Pinel did the same at the Salpêtrière three years later.
textes.Pinel range les troubles mentaux en quat: Pinel sorted mental disorders into four types: melancholia, mania, dementia and idiotism.
textes.Le « traitement moral » soigne par la pa: "Moral treatment" healed through words, observation and a humane setting; "moral" means psychological.
textes.Au même moment, Chiarugi à Florence et l: At the same time, Chiarugi in Florence and the Quakers of the York Retreat, in 1796, also banished chains.
textes.Pinel n'a pas libéré seul les fous de Bi: Pinel did not free the insane of Bicêtre alone: it was Pussin who removed the chains in 1797, after Pinel had left. The heroic scene is partly a legend.
textes.Philippe Pinel naît le 20 avril 1745 à J: Philippe Pinel was born on 20 April 1745 at Jonquières. A tragedy drew him to madness: a friend, suffering from "nervous melancholy", sank into mania and killed himself. In August 1793, in the middle of the Revolution, Pinel was appointed physician of the infirmaries at Bicêtre, which housed the insane.
textes.Il y apprend beaucoup du surveillant, Je: There he learned a great deal from the superintendent, Jean-Baptiste Pussin, and his wife, Marguerite Jubline. In 1795, Pinel became chief physician of the Salpêtrière, a post he held until his death in 1826. He had Pussin transferred there in 1802.
textes.Pinel, nommé à Bicêtre en 1793, apprend: Pinel, appointed to Bicêtre in 1793, learned from the superintendent Pussin; in 1795, he moved to the Salpêtrière.
textes.En 1797, à Bicêtre, c'est Pussin qui ret: In 1797, at Bicêtre, it was Pussin who removed the patients' irons and banned corporal punishment, when Pinel had already left; the straitjacket was still allowed. Pinel removed the chains at the Salpêtrière three years later. The legend, painted and engraved, later made Pinel the sole liberator: it is partly fabricated.
textes.Ailleurs aussi, on desserre les fers. À: Elsewhere too, irons were loosened. In Florence, Vincenzo Chiarugi banned chains at the Santa Dorotea hospital between 1785 and 1788. In England, after a Quaker woman died in an asylum in 1790, William Tuke founded the York Retreat in 1796: about thirty patients, rest, conversation, manual work, and as few restraints as possible.
textes.1797, Bicêtre : Pussin ôte les fers ; Pi: 1797, Bicêtre: Pussin removed the irons; Pinel followed at the Salpêtrière. Chiarugi in Florence and Tuke in York did the same.
textes.En 1798, Pinel publie la Nosographie phi: In 1798, Pinel published the Nosographie philosophique, an authoritative classification of diseases. He reduced the Scotsman William Cullen's "neuroses" to four types: melancholia, mania, dementia and idiotism. In 1801 came his Medico-philosophical Treatise on Mental Alienation.
textes.Sa méthode s'appelle le traitement moral: His method was called moral treatment: "moral" there means emotional or psychological, not virtuous. One observes, talks, keeps busy. The 19th century paid dearly for it: asylums grew, and in Britain their average population rose from 166 patients in 1827 to 1,221 in 1930. Routine replaced care.
textes.Quatre types de folie (1798), le Traité: Four types of madness (1798), the Treatise (1801), "moral", that is psychological, treatment.
textes.De Phineas Gage (1848) à Broca (1861) et: From Phineas Gage (1848) to Broca (1861) and Cajal (1888): the brain is mapped and found to be made of neurons.
textes.Darwin et l'expression des émotions: Darwin and the expression of emotions
textes.En 1872, Darwin compare les visages des: In 1872, Darwin compared the faces of humans and animals: our expressions are a legacy of evolution.
textes.L'expression des émotions, dans le temps: The expression of emotions, in time
textes.Le 26 novembre 1872, Darwin publie L'Exp: On 26 November 1872, Darwin published The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals; almost 7,000 copies quickly sold.
textes.Il s'appuie sur un questionnaire envoyé: He relied on a questionnaire sent out from 1867, on hundreds of photographs and on Duchenne de Boulogne's electrified faces.
textes.Trois principes : les habitudes utiles a: Three principles: serviceable associated habits, antithesis, and the direct action of the nervous system.
textes.Un siècle plus tard, Paul Ekman retrouve: A century later, Paul Ekman found among the Fore of Papua New Guinea expressions recognised everywhere.
textes.Le sourire « vrai » ne se joue pas qu'av: A "true" smile is not played with the mouth alone: Duchenne showed that it also creases the eyes. A polite smile leaves the eyes alone.
textes.Un chapitre devenu livre: A chapter that became a book
textes.L'Expression des émotions devait être un: The Expression of the Emotions was meant to be a chapter of The Descent of Man. Darwin finished that book on 15 January 1871 and began the new one two days later. From 1867, he circulated a questionnaire, first handwritten then printed, among correspondents around the world: do distant peoples show anger or shame with the same expressions?
textes.Le livre paraît chez John Murray le 26 n: The book was published by John Murray on 26 November 1872 and quickly sold almost 7,000 copies; it has never been out of print since. Darwin also observed his own son William as a baby: his notes appeared in 1877 in the journal Mind. Blushing, he wrote in chapter 13, is "the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions".
textes.Un questionnaire dès 1867, un livre en 1: A questionnaire from 1867, a book in 1872, never out of print since; blushing, "the most human of expressions".
textes.Pour illustrer son livre, Darwin réunit: To illustrate his book, Darwin gathered hundreds of photographs of actors, babies and children, including Oscar Rejlander's. His publisher warned him that the photos would "make a hole in the profits". He also drew on Mechanism of Human Physiognomy, published in 1862 by the neurologist Duchenne de Boulogne, with whom he exchanged a few letters.
textes.Duchenne posait des électrodes sur les m: Duchenne placed electrodes on the muscles of the face to provoke expressions, and photographed them: "only photography, as truthful as a mirror", could capture them. His main model was an old toothless man. He showed that the smile of real joy works the muscles of the eyes as well as those of the mouth: today we speak of a Duchenne smile.
textes.Rejlander, Duchenne et ses électrodes :: Rejlander, Duchenne and his electrodes: the true smile also creases the eyes.
textes.Darwin explique nos expressions par troi: Darwin explained our expressions by three principles. Serviceable associated habits: a once-useful gesture returns with the state of mind that went with it. Antithesis: an opposite state produces the opposite gesture. And the direct action of the nervous system, which acts on the body independently of the will. Conclusion: the great expressions are shared, inherited from common ancestors.
textes.Un siècle plus tard, Paul Ekman et Walla: A century later, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen showed that Fore people of Papua New Guinea, without writing, recognised the same expressions. In 1978, they completed a coding system for facial movements, in which each movement is an "action unit". Ekman would advise the series Lie to Me and Pixar's film Inside Out, in 2015. But the universality of emotions is still debated.
textes.Habitudes utiles, antithèse, action du s: Serviceable habits, antithesis, action of the nervous system; Ekman among the Fore; facial coding in 1978.
textes.Weber pèse les sensations, Fechner les m: Weber weighed sensations, Fechner put them into equations, Donders timed thought, and Wundt opened in Leipzig, in 1879, the first psychology laboratory.
textes.Ernst Weber (1834) : on perçoit une diff: Ernst Weber (1834): we perceive a relative difference, not an absolute one; it takes about 108 g to tell a weight from 100 g.
textes.Gustav Fechner, Éléments de psychophysiq: Gustav Fechner, Elements of Psychophysics (1860): sensation grows as the logarithm of the stimulus.
textes.Franciscus Donders (1868) chronomètre le: Franciscus Donders (1868) timed how long it takes to discriminate and to choose, by subtracting reaction times.
textes.Wilhelm Wundt ouvre à Leipzig, en 1879,: Wilhelm Wundt opened in Leipzig, in 1879, the first laboratory devoted entirely to psychology; he supervised 185 doctoral theses.
textes.Wundt ne se fiait pas à l'introspection: Wundt did not trust naive introspection: self-observation had to be learned and carried out under strict experimental control.
textes.En 1834, l'anatomiste de Leipzig Ernst H: In 1834, the Leipzig anatomist Ernst Heinrich Weber published in Latin his experiments on touch. With the two points of a compass placed on the skin, he sought the distance at which one feels two points instead of one. With weights, he showed that one best distinguishes two masses that differ by 8 to 10%: for a 100 g block, one needs at least 108 g.
textes.Ce qu'on perçoit, c'est donc le rapport: What one perceives, then, is the ratio of the difference to the size compared. Gustav Fechner, who had damaged his eyes in 1839 by looking at the Sun, drew a law from it: for sensation to rise steadily, the stimulus must increase in geometric progression. In 1860 he published his Elements of Psychophysics: psychology had its first equations.
textes.Weber : une différence relative (100 g c: Weber: a relative difference (100 g against 108 g); Fechner (1860): sensation follows the logarithm of the stimulus.
textes.Wilhelm Wundt naît en 1832 près de Mannh: Wilhelm Wundt was born in 1832 near Mannheim. In 1858, he became assistant to the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz at Heidelberg. In 1874, he published the Principles of Physiological Psychology, the first textbook of experimental psychology. Appointed professor of philosophy at Leipzig in 1875, he opened there in 1879 the first laboratory devoted entirely to psychology.
textes.Il y dirige 185 thèses entre 1875 et 191: There he supervised 185 theses between 1875 and 1919, 70 of them by foreign students; among them were James McKeen Cattell, Granville Stanley Hall, Edward Titchener and Hugo Münsterberg. Wundt rejected naive introspection: self-observation has to be learned. He described feelings along three dimensions: pleasant or unpleasant, tense or relaxed, excited or calm.
textes.1874, le premier manuel ; 1879, le premi: 1874, the first textbook; 1879, the first laboratory; 185 theses, 70 of them by foreigners.
textes.Dès 1865, l'ophtalmologiste néerlandais: From 1865, the Dutch ophthalmologist Franciscus Donders measured reaction times. A subject repeats a syllable known in advance (method a), or one of five possible syllables (method b), or only one particular syllable among five (method c). In 1868, he found that c takes 0.047 s longer than a: the time to discriminate; and b, 0.036 s longer than c: the time to choose.
textes.C'est la méthode de soustraction : retra: This is the subtraction method: subtracting a simple time from a more complex one to measure a step of thought. A simple reaction time is around 200 ms; in young adults, about 160 ms for a sound and 190 ms for a light. Francis Galton would measure more than 10,000 among the London public. In Leipzig, Wundt made such timings a routine.
textes.Donders (1868) : discriminer, 47 ms ; ch: Donders (1868): discriminating, 47 ms; choosing, 36 ms. Reacting to a sound, about 160 ms; to a light, about 190 ms.
textes.Des chiens qui salivent au son d'un métr: Dogs salivating at the sound of a metronome, a baby conditioned to fear a rat: psychology set out to study behaviour alone.
textes.Ivan Pavlov, prix Nobel 1904 pour ses tr: Ivan Pavlov, Nobel Prize 1904 for his work on digestion, noticed that his dogs salivated before the meal: "psychic secretion".
textes.Un stimulus neutre, associé à la nourrit: A neutral stimulus, paired with food, ends up triggering salivation on its own: classical conditioning (1897).
textes.En 1913, John B. Watson veut une psychol: In 1913, John B. Watson wanted a "purely objective" psychology, studying behaviour alone.
textes.En 1920, Watson et Rosalie Rayner condit: In 1920, Watson and Rosalie Rayner conditioned little Albert to fear a white rat.
textes.La fameuse cloche de Pavlov est douteuse: Pavlov's famous bell is doubtful: his writings mention metronomes, whistles, tuning forks and electric shocks; the use of a bell is still disputed.
textes.Ivan Pavlov naît en 1849 à Riazan, fils: Ivan Pavlov was born in 1849 in Ryazan, the son of a village Orthodox priest; he left the seminary without graduating to devote himself to science. A physiologist, he fitted his dogs with fistulas to collect their digestive juices over long periods. In 1904, he received the Nobel Prize for his work on digestion: the first Russian Nobel laureate.
textes.Il remarque que ses chiens salivent avan: He noticed that his dogs salivated before the food arrived: he called it "psychic secretion". He then paired a stimulus, such as a metronome, with the meal; soon the metronome alone made them salivate. He published these results in 1897. And the bell? His writings mention metronomes, whistles, tuning forks and electric shocks; whether he ever used a bell is still disputed.
textes.Nobel 1904 pour la digestion ; la « sécr: Nobel 1904 for digestion; "psychic secretion"; a metronome, more surely than a bell.
textes.Le vocabulaire est resté. La nourriture: The vocabulary has stayed. Food is an unconditioned stimulus: it makes the dog salivate without learning, which is the unconditioned response. The metronome, at first neutral, becomes a conditioned stimulus after announcing food; the salivation it triggers on its own is the conditioned response, learned and less lasting than the innate reflex.
textes.Si le métronome sonne sans nourriture, l: If the metronome sounds without food, the response eventually dies out: this is extinction, which does not erase the learning, for after a rest the response can return, weaker. A similar sound also triggers the response: this is generalisation. Conscious to the end, Pavlov had a student sit by his deathbed, in 1936, to note what he felt as he died.
textes.Stimulus et réponse inconditionnels, pui: Unconditioned stimulus and response, then conditioned ones; extinction, recovery, generalisation.
textes.En 1913, l'Américain John B. Watson publ: In 1913, the American John B. Watson published his manifesto, "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It": psychology must be a purely objective experimental branch of natural science. In 1920, with his student Rosalie Rayner, he conditioned a nine-month-old baby, "Albert": each time the child touched a white rat, a steel bar was struck with a hammer behind his back.
textes.Bientôt le rat seul fait pleurer Albert,: Soon the rat alone made Albert cry, then a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat, a Santa Claus mask with a cotton beard. Such an experiment would be considered unethical today. Before them, Edward Thorndike had proposed the law of effect in 1898; B. F. Skinner would extend it with his lever box, which he hated hearing called a "Skinner box".
textes.Watson (1913) : n'étudier que le comport: Watson (1913): study behaviour alone. Little Albert (1920): a learned fear, then generalised.
textes.À Vienne, autour de 1900, Freud fait par: In Vienna, around 1900, Freud got his patients talking and read their dreams: psychoanalysis looked for what escapes consciousness.
textes.Freud et l'inconscient, dans le temps: Freud and the unconscious, in time
textes.Avec Josef Breuer, Freud publie en 1895: With Josef Breuer, Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895; the patient "Anna O." spoke of a "talking cure".
textes.L'Interprétation des rêves paraît le 4 n: The Interpretation of Dreams appeared on 4 November 1899, dated 1900: every dream fulfils a wish.
textes.En 1923, Freud décrit le ça, le moi et l: In 1923, Freud described the id, the ego and the superego.
textes.Le philosophe Karl Popper reproche à la: The philosopher Karl Popper criticised psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable, hence unscientific.
textes.La psychanalyse a marqué la culture du X: Psychoanalysis left its mark on 20th-century culture, but its effectiveness and scientific status remain much debated.
textes.Sigmund Freud naît le 6 mai 1856 à Freib: Sigmund Freud was born on 6 May 1856 at Freiberg, in Moravia, now Příbor in Czechia. A young Viennese neurologist, he praised the virtues of cocaine in 1884 in "On Coca", before ceasing to recommend it in the face of cases of addiction. In October 1885, he went to Paris for three months to study with Charcot, who was working on hypnosis.
textes.Son aîné Josef Breuer soigne Bertha Papp: His elder Josef Breuer treated Bertha Pappenheim, "Anna O.", who coined the phrase "talking cure". In 1895, Freud and Breuer published Studies on Hysteria. Freud then abandoned hypnosis for free association: the patient says whatever comes to mind. He named his method "psychoanalysis" in 1896. The patient lies on a couch, the analyst sits behind, out of sight.
textes.Charcot (1885), Anna O. et la « cure par: Charcot (1885), Anna O. and the "talking cure", free association; the word "psychoanalysis" in 1896.
textes.L'Interprétation des rêves paraît le 4 n: The Interpretation of Dreams appeared on 4 November 1899 from Franz Deuticke, dated 1900. Thesis: every dream is the fulfilment of a wish. The manifest content, the one we remember, disguises a latent content; during sleep, the unconscious condenses and displaces images, so that on waking the meaning is unrecognisable.
textes.« L'interprétation des rêves est la voie: "The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind," wrote Freud. His first example is one of his own dreams, that of "Irma's injection", from the summer of 1895. Success was slow: the first printing, 600 copies, took eight years to sell. In 1901, The Psychopathology of Everyday Life tracked the unconscious in slips and forgettings.
textes.1899 : le rêve accomplit un désir déguis: 1899: the dream fulfils a disguised wish; 600 copies, eight years to sell them.
textes.Le ça, le moi, le surmoi: The id, the ego, the superego
textes.En 1923, dans Le Moi et le Ça, Freud déc: In 1923, in The Ego and the Id, Freud described three agencies. The id, present from birth, a reservoir of drives, unconscious, obeys the pleasure principle. The ego forms slowly and negotiates between drives and reality, according to the reality principle. The superego is the part of the ego where self-observation, self-criticism and judgement arise.
textes.En 1933, les nazis brûlent ses livres. F: In 1933, the Nazis burned his books. Freud told Ernest Jones: "In the Middle Ages they would have burned me. Now, they are content with burning my books." He died in London on 23 September 1939. The philosopher Karl Popper would criticise psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable: a theory that explains everything cannot be proved wrong, and so is not scientific.
textes.Ça, moi, surmoi (1923) ; les livres brûl: Id, ego, superego (1923); the books burned in 1933; Popper: an unfalsifiable theory is not science.
textes.En 1905, Binet et Simon inventent une éc: In 1905, Binet and Simon invented a scale to spot struggling schoolchildren; it would become the IQ, with its uses and abuses.
textes.En 1904, une commission du ministère cha: In 1904, a ministry commission tasked Alfred Binet with spotting pupils who needed adapted teaching.
textes.En 1905, Binet et Théodore Simon publien: In 1905, Binet and Théodore Simon published a scale of thirty tasks; in 1908 came mental age.
textes.En 1912, William Stern invente le quotie: In 1912, William Stern invented the intelligence quotient: mental age divided by real age, times 100.
textes.Aujourd'hui, le QI est calibré pour une: Today, IQ is calibrated to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.
textes.Binet et Simon voyaient l'intelligence c: Binet and Simon saw intelligence as malleable, not fixed; Simon judged the conversion into IQ a betrayal of the test's purpose.
textes.Alfred Binet naît à Nice le 8 juillet 18: Alfred Binet was born in Nice on 8 July 1857. With a law degree in 1878, he turned to psychology and worked at the Salpêtrière with Charcot. He also observed his two daughters very closely. In 1891, he joined the psychology laboratory at the Sorbonne, which he directed from 1894 or 1895 depending on the sources.
textes.En 1894, il fonde avec Henry Beaunis la: In 1894, he founded with Henry Beaunis the journal L'Année psychologique. The same year, he published a Psychology of Great Calculators and Chess Players. In 1904, the Ministry of Public Instruction set up a commission for struggling pupils; Binet was on it. He needed a tool to recognise those who needed help.
textes.Binet, de la Salpêtrière à la Sorbonne ;: Binet, from the Salpêtrière to the Sorbonne; 1904, a commission and a need: to spot the pupils who need help.
textes.Trente épreuves et un âge mental: Thirty tasks and a mental age
textes.En 1905, Binet et Théodore Simon publien: In 1905, Binet and Théodore Simon published their scale: thirty tasks of increasing difficulty, from grasping an object or recognising food to repeating digits, comparing lines of different lengths or answering an abstract question. The test takes about a quarter of an hour.
textes.La version de 1908 range les épreuves pa: The 1908 version arranged the tasks by age: the birth of mental age, the age whose tasks a child succeeds at.
