Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series, voltage with a voltmeter connected across the terminals.
textes.Série : R = R₁ + R₂. Dérivation : 1/R =: Series: R = R₁ + R₂. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (two 100 Ω = 50 Ω). Kirchhoff's laws, 1845.
textes.En série, le courant traverse les résist: In series, the current goes through the resistors one after the other: they add up, R = R₁ + R₂. The current is the same everywhere, the voltage is shared. In parallel, the current has several paths: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. For two 100 Ω resistors: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so R = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 Ω. Two paths let twice as much current through.
textes.Ces règles se déduisent de la loi d'Ohm: These rules follow from Ohm's law and the two laws Gustav Kirchhoff published in 1845, while still a student. Junction rule: all the current arriving at a junction leaves it again, nothing is lost. Loop rule: around a loop, the voltages balance out. With these two laws you can work out any circuit, however complicated.
textes.C'est le courant qui tue: It is the current that kills
textes.Le danger, c'est le courant à travers le: The danger is current through the body: 30 mA for the RCD. One wire, no current: the bird survives.
textes.Ce qui blesse, c'est le courant qui trav: What harms is the current passing through the body, more than voltage alone. A few tens of milliamperes are enough to cause serious heart trouble. That is why homes have a 30 mA residual-current device: it compares the current going out and the current coming back, and cuts off within a fraction of a second if some escapes, for example through someone.
textes.Un oiseau posé sur un seul câble haute t: A bird sitting on a single high-voltage line is safe: both its feet are at the same potential, no current passes through it. The danger would come from touching two lines at once, or a line and the pylon. In France the household supply is 230 V AC, 50 Hz; North America uses about 120 V at 60 Hz.
textes.P = U × I : 230 V × 10 A = 2 300 W. Watt: P = U × I: 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. Watt = joule per second.
textes.Le watt et le joule ne mesurent pas la m: The watt and the joule do not measure the same thing. The joule is an energy, the watt a power, that is, energy per second: 1 W = 1 J/s. A 5 W bulb spends 5 joules every second. An LED gives as much light as an incandescent bulb using about 5 to 8 times less, because the old one turned most of the electricity into heat.
textes.P = R × I² (Joule, 1841). Haute tension: P = R × I² (Joule, 1841). High voltage = low current = losses divided by the square.
textes.En 1841, James Prescott Joule mesure la: In 1841 James Prescott Joule measured the heat given off by a wire carrying a current: it is proportional to the resistance and to the square of the current. Combining P = U × I with Ohm's law U = R × I gives P = R × I². That is Joule heating: the toaster, the kettle, the heater and the fuse that melts all use it.
textes.Ce carré explique le transport à très ha: That square explains transmission at very high voltage. For the same power P = U × I, raising the voltage lowers the current. Yet losses in the cables equal R × I²: dividing the current by 10 divides the losses by 10 × 10 = 100. That is why lines leave power stations at hundreds of thousands of volts.
textes.Un courant crée un champ magnétique (Ørs: A current creates a magnetic field (Ørsted, 1820). Electromagnet: Sturgeon, 1824. Motor: electricity → motion.
textes.En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying a current deflects the needle of a nearby compass. Tradition says it happened during a lecture. It is the proof that electricity and magnetism are linked: a current creates a magnetic field around it. André-Marie Ampère worked out the laws within a few weeks; the unit of current bears his name.
textes.Enroulez le fil autour d'un noyau de fer: Wind the wire around an iron core and the field concentrates: that is the electromagnet, invented by William Sturgeon in 1824. Unlike a magnet, it can be switched on and off: scrapyard cranes, doorbells, loudspeakers. In an electric motor, these forces turn a shaft: electrical energy becomes motion.
textes.Un champ qui varie crée un courant (Fara: A changing field creates a current (Faraday, 1831). Alternator = magnet turning past coils.
textes.En 1831, Michael Faraday fait l'inverse: In 1831 Michael Faraday did the reverse: he moved a magnet near a coil of wire, and a current appeared in it. Not when the magnet is still, only when the field changes. That is electromagnetic induction. Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice who became Humphry Davy's assistant, used little beyond the simplest algebra: he thought in lines of force, an image that would guide Maxwell.
textes.Presque toute notre électricité vient de: Almost all our electricity comes from this. In an alternator, a magnet turns past coils: coal, gas, nuclear, dam or wind turbine only serve to turn it. The motor does the reverse, and some electric cars do both, recovering energy when braking. The induction hob too: its changing field creates currents in the bottom of the pan, which heats by Joule heating.
textes.Maxwell (1865) : la lumière est une onde: Maxwell (1865): light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz (1886): radio waves exist. Marconi (1901): the Atlantic.
textes.En 1865, James Clerk Maxwell met en équa: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell put electricity and magnetism into equations. His equations predict waves travelling at a speed he calculates: that of light. He concluded that light is itself an electromagnetic wave. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which in turn creates an electric field: the wave sustains itself, even in a vacuum.
textes.Restait à le prouver. À partir de 1886,: It still had to be proved. From 1886 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves in his laboratory. Asked about their applications, he is said to have answered: "Nothing, I guess." Fifteen years later, in 1901, Guglielmo Marconi sent an "S" in Morse across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
textes.Même onde, fréquences différentes. c = λ: Same wave, different frequencies. c = λ × f: Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz = 12.5 cm. Ionising: part of UV, X, gamma.
textes.Plus la fréquence est haute, plus chaque: The higher the frequency, the more energy each grain of light, each photon, carries. Only part of the ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have enough to tear off electrons and damage DNA: they are ionising radiation, hence sunburn. Radio waves and Wi-Fi do not have enough: they can heat, not break DNA.
textes.Röntgen (1895) : rayons X, premier Nobel: Röntgen (1895): X-rays, first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Spencer (1945): the microwave, born of a melted chocolate bar.
textes.En 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen découvre des ra: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered unknown rays, which he called X, able to pass through flesh and reveal bones. In 1901 he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, and refused to patent his discovery. About six weeks after the discovery he was already X-raying his wife's hand.
textes.Le radar, développé intensément pendant: Radar, developed intensively during the Second World War, sends out waves and listens for their echo. In 1945 at Raytheon, engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket: from this came the microwave oven, which agitates the water molecules in food.
textes.ENIAC : plus de 17 000 tubes. Diode = se: ENIAC: more than 17,000 tubes. Diode = one way. Capacitor = store of charges released at once.
textes.Les premiers ordinateurs calculaient ave: The first computers calculated with vacuum tubes, glass bulbs that let a current of electrons through or block it. ENIAC, completed in 1945 in the United States, had more than 17,000 of them. They got hot, used a lot of power and burned out regularly: finding the dead tube was part of the job.
textes.Tout l'enjeu de l'électronique est là :: That is what electronics is all about: controlling one current with another. The diode, the simplest component, lets current through in one direction only; it is used to turn alternating current into direct current. The capacitor stores charges and releases them in one go, as in a camera flash.
textes.Un interrupteur sans pièce mobile: A switch with no moving parts
textes.Transistor : Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobe: Transistor: Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobel 1956. A small signal controls a large current.
textes.En décembre 1947, aux laboratoires Bell,: In December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain got the first transistor working, a small germanium device; William Shockley, their boss, soon designed a more practical version. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Bardeen received a second in 1972, for superconductivity.
textes.Le transistor est fait d'un semi-conduct: The transistor is made of a semiconductor: a material that conducts less well than a metal, but whose conduction can be controlled. A small current or voltage on one terminal controls a large current between the other two. It serves as an amplifier in a radio, and as an ultra-fast switch in a computer. Silicon replaced germanium, hence Silicon Valley.
textes.Circuit intégré : Kilby 1958 (germanium): Integrated circuit: Kilby 1958 (germanium), Noyce 1959 (silicon). Moore's law: doubling every two years.
textes.Le 12 septembre 1958, chez Texas Instrum: On 12 September 1958 at Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit: several components on a single piece of germanium. About six months later Robert Noyce, at Fairchild, made a silicon version, much easier to manufacture. Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000; Noyce, who died in 1990, could no longer share it.
textes.En 1965, Gordon Moore remarque que le no: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling at a steady rate: every year, then, in 1975, he revised it to every two years. This "Moore's law" held for decades. A large 2023 processor has from a few tens to more than a hundred billion transistors. LEDs are diodes too: the blue LED, which made white light possible, won the 2014 Nobel Prize.
textes.Thermique = eau chauffée, vapeur, turbin: Thermal = heated water, steam, turbine, alternator. Plumes = water vapour. Solar: Becquerel, 1839.
textes.Une centrale thermique, au charbon, au g: A thermal power station, coal, gas or nuclear, always does the same thing: heat water. The steam turns a turbine, the turbine drives an alternator, and Faraday's induction does the rest. In a nuclear plant the heat comes from the fission of uranium nuclei. The big white plumes from the cooling towers are not smoke but water vapour.
textes.Les éoliennes et les barrages font tourn: Wind turbines and dams turn the alternator directly, without steam. The solar panel has nothing that turns: it converts light into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839, at 19. In 2023, according to RTE, nuclear power produced about 65 % of France's electricity.
textes.Edison : continu. Westinghouse et Tesla: Edison: direct current. Westinghouse and Tesla: alternating current. AC won thanks to the transformer.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Thomas Edison d: At the end of the 19th century Thomas Edison championed direct current; George Westinghouse, who licensed Nikola Tesla's motor patents, championed alternating current. Edison's 110 V DC did not reach beyond about a mile: a small power station was needed for each neighbourhood. In 1882 his lighting company set up in New York on that model.
textes.L'alternatif gagne grâce au transformate: Alternating current won thanks to the transformer, which only works with a varying current, since it relies on induction. It lets you raise the voltage to transmit far with few losses, then lower it again at the user's end. In France the current changes direction a hundred times a second: 50 Hz. The 1892 merger that created General Electric ended the battle.
textes.Production = consommation à chaque insta: Production = consumption at every moment, otherwise the frequency drifts. Storage: pumped storage, batteries (Nobel 2019).
textes.Le réseau a une contrainte que peu de ge: The grid has a constraint few people know: at every moment, production must equal consumption. If more is consumed than produced, the frequency drops below 50 Hz; too large a gap, and outages are triggered to protect the grid. On a winter evening, when everyone gets home and cooks, you need sources that start fast.
textes.Le vent et le soleil ne se commandent pa: Wind and sun cannot be ordered: you have to store or supplement. Pumped-storage stations pump water up into a lake when electricity is plentiful and run it through turbines when it is short. Lithium-ion batteries play the same role on a smaller scale; they earned Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
textes.1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8 bits = 256 values. A transistor: on or off.
textes.En binaire, on n'a que deux chiffres, 0: In binary there are only two digits, 0 and 1, and each place is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8… So 1011 = 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 11. Leibniz set out this arithmetic in a memoir published in 1705. With 3 bits you can code 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 values; with an 8-bit byte, 2⁸ = 256.
textes.Pourquoi deux chiffres ? Parce qu'un tra: Why two digits? Because a transistor is very good at two things: letting through or blocking. Text, images, sounds: everything is coded in 0s and 1s. A detail about units: under the International System, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes; 1,024 bytes is called a kibibyte.
textes.Boole : la logique devient algèbre. Shan: Boole: logic becomes algebra. Shannon (1937): circuits compute it. AND, OR, NOT are enough for everything.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, George Boole fait de la: In the 19th century George Boole turned logic into algebra: true and false become 1 and 0, and "and", "or", "not" become operations. In 1937, aged 21, Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis at MIT, published in 1938, that relay circuits can carry out all of this algebra. It has been called possibly the most important master's thesis of the century.
textes.La porte ET donne 1 seulement si ses deu: The AND gate gives 1 only if both its inputs are 1; the OR gate gives 1 if at least one is 1; the NOT gate inverts. Built from a few transistors, these gates are assembled into adders, memories, then processors. A computer is, at bottom, just a huge assembly of these three decisions.
textes.Des plans de Babbage au bug de 1947: From Babbage's plans to the 1947 bug
textes.Babbage : la machine jamais construite ;: Babbage: the machine never built; Lovelace (1843): the first program. Von Neumann (1945): program and data together.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, Charles Babbage conçoit: In the 19th century Charles Babbage designed the analytical engine, a programmable mechanical calculator. It was never built in his lifetime. Yet in 1843 Ada Lovelace published its first program: a calculation of the Bernoulli numbers. She also sensed that the machine could handle things other than numbers, music for example.
textes.La guerre accélère tout. En 1943-1944, C: The war sped everything up. In 1943-1944 Colossus helped Bletchley Park break encrypted German messages; it remained secret until the 1970s. In 1945 John von Neumann described the architecture in which program and data share the same memory, that of almost all our computers. And in 1947 Grace Hopper's team taped into their logbook a moth found in a relay: "first actual case of bug being found".
textes.Un courant ne circule que dans une boucl: A current flows only in a closed loop: from the battery, through the wires, through the lamp, and back to the battery. An open switch breaks the loop and the lamp goes out. Metals conduct because some of their electrons are free to move; plastic, glass or rubber hold them back: they are insulators, hence cable sheathing. This difference between conductors and insulators was discovered by the Englishman Stephen Gray in 1729: a thread held up by metal lost its charge, one held up by silk kept it, and he made electricity travel 800 feet, about 240 m.
textes.La puissance électrique P, en watts, est: Electrical power P, in watts, is the product of voltage U and current I: P = U × I. An appliance on 230 V drawing 10 A uses P = 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. The other way round, a 2,000 W kettle draws I = P ÷ U = 2,000 ÷ 230 ≈ 8.7 A. The watt is named after James Watt, the steam-engine engineer. His great improvement to Newcomen's engine, the separate condenser, dates from 1769.
textes.Radio, micro-ondes, infrarouge, visible,: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays: it is the same wave at different frequencies. All travel at the speed of light c, about 300,000 km/s, and satisfy c = λ × f: wavelength times frequency. For Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz: λ = c ÷ f = 300,000,000 m/s ÷ 2,400,000,000 Hz = 0.125 m, that is 12.5 cm. Our eye sees only a thin slice, from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). The two invisible neighbours of that slice were discovered one after the other: infrared in 1800 by William Herschel, with a thermometer placed beyond the red of a prism's spectrum, and ultraviolet in 1801 by Johann Ritter, with silver chloride paper that darkened beyond the violet.
textes.En 1600, dans De Magnete, le médecin ang: In 1600, in De Magnete, the English physician William Gilbert drew from the Greek elektron, amber, a Latin word for bodies that attract: that is where our "electricity" comes from.
textes.Au XVIIIe siècle, Benjamin Franklin appe: In the 18th century Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of charge positive and negative, and coined the word "charge".
textes.Georg Ohm les relie en 1827 dans Die gal: Georg Ohm related them in 1827 in Die galvanische Kette: U = R × I.
textes.En 1841, James Prescott Joule mesure la: In 1841 James Prescott Joule measured the heat given off by a wire carrying a current: it is proportional to the resistance and to the square of the current.
textes.En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying a current deflects the needle of a nearby compass.
textes.Enroulez le fil autour d'un noyau de fer: Wind the wire around an iron core and the field concentrates: that is the electromagnet, invented by William Sturgeon in 1824.
textes.En 1831, Michael Faraday fait l'inverse: In 1831 Michael Faraday did the reverse: he moved a magnet near a coil of wire, and a current appeared in it.
textes.En 1865, James Clerk Maxwell met en équa: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell put electricity and magnetism into equations.
textes.À partir de 1886, Heinrich Hertz produit: From 1886 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves in his laboratory.
textes.Quinze ans plus tard, en 1901, Guglielmo: Fifteen years later, in 1901, Guglielmo Marconi sent an "S" in Morse across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
textes.En 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen découvre des ra: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered unknown rays, which he called X, able to pass through flesh and reveal bones.
textes.En 1945, chez Raytheon, l'ingénieur Perc: In 1945 at Raytheon, engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket: from this came the microwave oven, which agitates the water molecules in food.
textes.En décembre 1947, aux laboratoires Bell,: In December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain got the first transistor working, a small germanium device; William Shockley, their boss, soon designed a more practical version.
textes.Le 12 septembre 1958, chez Texas Instrum: On 12 September 1958 at Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit: several components on a single piece of germanium.
textes.En 1965, Gordon Moore remarque que le no: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling at a steady rate: every year, then, in 1975, he revised it to every two years.
textes.En 2023, selon RTE, le nucléaire a produ: In 2023, according to RTE, nuclear power produced about 65 % of France's electricity.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Thomas Edison d: At the end of the 19th century Thomas Edison championed direct current; George Westinghouse, who licensed Nikola Tesla's motor patents, championed alternating current.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, George Boole fait de la: In the 19th century George Boole turned logic into algebra: true and false become 1 and 0, and "and", "or", "not" become operations.
textes.En 1937, à 21 ans, Claude Shannon montre: In 1937, aged 21, Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis at MIT, published in 1938, that relay circuits can carry out all of this algebra.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, Charles Babbage conçoit: In the 19th century Charles Babbage designed the analytical engine, a programmable mechanical calculator.
textes.Ada Lovelace en publie pourtant, en 1843: Yet in 1843 Ada Lovelace published its first program: a calculation of the Bernoulli numbers.
textes.En 1943-1944, Colossus aide à Bletchley: In 1943-1944 Colossus helped Bletchley Park break encrypted German messages; it remained secret until the 1970s.
textes.En 1945, John von Neumann décrit l'archi: In 1945 John von Neumann described the architecture in which program and data share the same memory, that of almost all our computers.
textes.Bien avant les piles, des poissons donna: Long before batteries, fish gave shocks: the Egyptians, Greeks and Romans knew them, and doctors used them.
textes.Des textes égyptiens de 2750 av. J.-C. p: Egyptian texts from 2750 BC already speak of the Nile's electric fish, "protectors" of the other fish.
textes.La torpille, une raie électrique, tire s: The torpedo, an electric ray, takes its name from the Latin torpere, "to be numb": that is what it does to whoever touches it.
textes.Vers 47, Scribonius Largus, médecin de l: Around AD 47, Scribonius Largus, physician to the emperor Claudius, treated headaches and gout with the torpedo's shock.
textes.On compte quelque 350 espèces de poisson: There are some 350 species of electric fish; the electric eel reaches up to 860 volts.
textes.L'anguille électrique n'est pas une angu: The electric eel is not an eel: it is a South American knifefish, not closely related to true eels.
textes.Le poisson-chat électrique vit en Afriqu: The electric catfish lives in tropical Africa and in the Nile. The Egyptians knew it well and painted it on walls: it already appears on King Narmer's palette, around 3100 BC. Egyptian texts from 2750 BC describe these fish as the "protectors" of the other fish.
textes.Au XIIe siècle, le médecin de Bagdad Abd: In the 12th century, the Baghdad physician Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi described its properties in turn. In Arabic its name, ra'ad, means "thunder". Long before anyone knew what electricity was, people had noticed that this fish strikes like lightning.
textes.Poisson-chat électrique du Nil : peint s: Electric catfish of the Nile: painted under Narmer (c. 3100 BC), a "protector" in texts from 2750 BC, "thunder" in Arabic.
textes.La torpille est une raie électrique. Son: The torpedo is an electric ray. Its name comes from the Latin torpere, "to be numb", the effect it has on whoever touches it. Depending on the species, it delivers 8 to 220 volts, thanks to two kidney-shaped organs at the base of its fins. The Greeks already used it to numb the pain of childbirth and operations.
textes.Chez Platon, Ménon accuse Socrate d'« en: In Plato, Meno accuses Socrates of "numbing" people with his questions, like a torpedo. Around AD 47, Scribonius Largus, a physician at the court of the emperor Claudius, gathered 271 prescriptions; in them he treated headaches and gout with the torpedo's shock. It is the first known electrotherapy, seventeen centuries before the battery.
textes.Torpille : de torpere, « engourdir » ; 8: Torpedo: from torpere, "to numb"; 8 to 220 V. Scribonius Largus (c. AD 47) treated migraine and gout with it.
textes.L'anguille qui foudroie les chevaux: The eel that strikes down horses
textes.En Amérique du Sud vit l'anguille électr: In South America lives the electric eel, which is not an eel but a knifefish. It can exceed 2 metres and deliver up to 860 volts. In 1800, the explorer Alexander von Humboldt followed indigenous fishermen who drove about thirty horses into a pond: the eels came out of the mud and attacked. Two horses, stunned, drowned.
textes.Ces poissons ont nourri la science de l': These fish fed the science of electricity. In 1773, John Walsh received the Copley Medal for a paper on the electrical properties of the torpedo. In 1839, Michael Faraday studied an eel from Surinam and confirmed, with sparks, that its discharges really were electrical. Some 350 species of electric fish are known today; the electric organ appeared eight times in the course of evolution.
textes.Anguille électrique : poisson-couteau, j: Electric eel: a knifefish, up to 860 V. Humboldt (1800), Walsh (1773), Faraday (1839). Electric organ evolved eight times.
textes.Une résine fossile qui attire la paille,: A fossil resin that attracts straw, a stone that attracts iron: the two mysteries that gave us the words electricity and magnetism.
textes.Vers 600 av. J.-C., Thalès de Milet aura: Around 600 BC, Thales of Miletus is said to have noticed that rubbed amber attracts light objects.
textes.L'ambre se dit êlektron en grec : de ce: Amber is called ēlektron in Greek: from this word come "electric" and "electricity".
textes.La pierre d'aimant est de la magnétite a: Lodestone is magnetite magnetised naturally, probably by lightning; "magnet" may come from Magnesia, in Anatolia.
In China, the Guiguzi, in the 4th century BC, is the oldest mention of magnetism.
textes.Thalès croyait que l'ambre frotté devena: Thales believed rubbed amber became magnetic: electricity and magnetism would be confused until the 16th century.
textes.Thalès et la pierre qui a une âme: Thales and the stone with a soul
textes.Thalès de Milet, né vers 625 av. J.-C.,: Thales of Miletus, born around 625 BC, is regarded as the first Greek philosopher. According to much later authors, around 600 BC he noticed that amber rubbed with fur attracts dust and light straws. He thought the rubbing made the amber magnetic: he was wrong, it was static electricity.
textes.Aristote rapporte une autre idée de Thal: Aristotle reports another idea of Thales: "all things are full of gods". The lodestone would have a soul, since it makes iron move. The reasoning is simple: what causes movement is alive, and what is alive has a soul. Wrong, but it is the first known attempt to explain the magnet.
textes.Thalès (v. 600 av. J.-C.) : l'ambre frot: Thales (c. 600 BC): rubbed amber attracts, the magnet has a soul. He confuses electricity and magnetism.
textes.L'ambre est une résine d'arbre fossilisé: Amber is fossilised tree resin. The oldest pieces are about 320 million years old, and most of the world's extractable amber comes from the Kaliningrad region, on the Baltic. The Greeks called it ēlektron, a word linked to the sun's brilliance. From this word come "electric" and "electricity".
textes.Au Ier siècle, Pline l'Ancien raconte qu: In the 1st century, Pliny the Elder relates that in Syria women made their spindle whorls of amber and called it harpax, "the snatcher", because it attracts leaves and straw. In 1550, the Italian Gerolamo Cardano distinguished, perhaps for the first time, the attraction of amber from that of the magnet. The English word electricity appeared in 1646, in Thomas Browne.
textes.Ambre = résine fossile = êlektron en gre: Amber = fossil resin = ēlektron in Greek: hence "electricity". Pliny: harpax. Cardano (1550) separates amber and magnet.
textes.La pierre d'aimant est un morceau de mag: Lodestone is a piece of magnetite, an iron ore, magnetised naturally. The most common explanation: lightning, striking the ground, aligns its magnetic domains. That is why it is found mostly near the surface. The English word lodestone means "leading stone"; "magnet" may come from the stones of Magnesia, in Anatolia.
textes.La Grèce n'est pas seule. En Chine, le G: Greece was not alone. In China, the Guiguzi, in the 4th century BC, is the oldest literary mention of magnetism; in the 2nd century BC, the Lüshi Chunqiu notes that "the lodestone makes iron come, or it attracts it". The same stone would become, in China, the first compass.
textes.Pierre d'aimant = magnétite aimantée, sa: Lodestone = magnetite magnetised, probably by lightning. China: Guiguzi (4th c. BC), Lüshi Chunqiu.
textes.Une cuillère qui montre le sud, un poiss: A spoon that points south, an iron fish, then Shen Kuo's needle: China invented the compass and gave it to sailors.
textes.Vers 70-80, Wang Chong décrit une « cuil: Around AD 70-80, Wang Chong described a "south-pointing spoon"; it is often seen as the first compass, without certainty.
textes.En 1088, Shen Kuo décrit une aiguille ai: In 1088, Shen Kuo described a needle magnetised with lodestone and hung from a silk thread.
textes.Entre 1111 et 1117, Zhu Yu note que les: Between 1111 and 1117, Zhu Yu noted that sailors look at the needle in dark weather: the first attested use at sea.
textes.La boussole est mentionnée en Europe ver: The compass is mentioned in Europe around 1190 and in the Muslim world in 1232.
textes.La boussole chinoise « montre le sud » :: The Chinese compass "points south": it is the same needle, they just chose the other end.
textes.Vers 70-80, le philosophe chinois Wang C: Around AD 70-80, the Chinese philosopher Wang Chong wrote in his Lunheng: "when the south-pointing spoon is thrown upon the ground, it comes to rest pointing at the south". It is often seen as the earliest form of the compass. But the text does not mention a magnet, and historians still debate it.
textes.Le Wujing Zongyao, un traité militaire a: The Wujing Zongyao, a military treatise completed around 1044, is clearer. It describes a "south-pointing fish", a thin leaf of iron floated on a bowl of water, to be used in the darkness of night. The iron was magnetised by heating it and cooling it in the right direction: today this is called thermoremanence.
textes.Cuillère du sud (Wang Chong, v. 70-80),: South spoon (Wang Chong, c. 70-80), debated. Floating iron fish (Wujing Zongyao, 1044), magnetised by heat.
textes.Shen Kuo, né en 1031 à Hangzhou, est un: Shen Kuo, born in 1031 in Hangzhou, was a scholar and senior official of the Song dynasty: he headed the bureau of astronomy and the Hanlin Academy, and commanded armies. In 1088, retired to his garden, he completed his Dream Pool Essays.
textes.On y trouve la première mention indiscut: It contains the first incontestable mention of a magnetised needle: geomancers rub it on a lodestone and hang it from a single silk thread. It points south, he remarks, with a slight deviation to the east: he saw that magnetic north is not true north. The same book discusses fossils, changing climate and movable-type printing.
textes.Shen Kuo (1088) : aiguille frottée sur l: Shen Kuo (1088): needle rubbed on lodestone, hung from a silk thread, and the first observation of declination.
textes.La boussole a d'abord servi aux géomanci: The compass first served geomancers, to orient tombs and houses. The first attested use at sea comes from Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks, written between 1111 and 1117: "in dark weather they look at the south-pointing needle".
textes.L'Europe la mentionne vers 1190, chez l': Europe mentioned it around 1190, in the Englishman Alexander Neckam: sailors "touch the magnet with a needle". In the Muslim world, the first mention dates from 1232, in a Persian book of tales; in 1282, in Cairo, Baylak al-Qibjaqi described a floating iron fish seen on a crossing to Alexandria, around 1242.
textes.En mer : Zhu Yu (1111-1117). Europe : Ne: At sea: Zhu Yu (1111-1117). Europe: Neckam (c. 1190). Muslim world: 1232, then al-Qibjaqi (1282).
textes.Pierre de Maricourt et les pôles: Peter of Maricourt and the poles
textes.En 1269, un savant picard écrit une lett: In 1269, a Picard scholar wrote a letter on the magnet: two poles, which attract or repel, and two compasses.
textes.La Lettre sur l'aimant de Pierre de Mari: Peter of Maricourt's Letter on the Magnet is dated 8 August 1269.
textes.C'est le premier texte conservé qui expl: It is the first surviving text that explains how to find a magnet's north and south poles.
textes.Pôles semblables se repoussent, pôles co: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; the magnetisation of a piece of iron can also be reversed.
textes.Il décrit une boussole flottante et une: He described a floating compass and a dry pivoted compass; Gilbert would acknowledge his debt in 1600.
textes.Pierre de Maricourt pense que l'aimant s: Peter of Maricourt thought the magnet turns towards the poles of the sky, not those of the Earth.
textes.Une lettre écrite sous les murs: A letter written under the walls
textes.Pierre de Maricourt, dit Pierre le Pèler: Peter of Maricourt, called Peter the Pilgrim, came from Picardy, around Maricourt. On 8 August 1269, he dated a letter addressed to Sygerus of Foucaucourt, a Picard soldier, perhaps a friend or neighbour: the Epistola de magnete, the Letter on the Magnet.
textes.Une note finale la situe au siège de Luc: A final note places it at the siege of Lucera, in southern Italy. But only one of the 39 manuscript copies bears that note: the evidence is weak. The letter circulated in manuscript for three centuries before being printed in Augsburg in 1558. In 1562, Jean Taisnier copied it without credit: a plagiarism.
textes.Lettre sur l'aimant, 8 août 1269, à Syge: Letter on the Magnet, 8 August 1269, to Sygerus of Foucaucourt. Lucera: one copy out of 39. Printed in 1558.
textes.La lettre est le premier texte conservé: The letter is the first surviving text to explain the magnet's polarity: how to locate its north pole and its south pole. Peter showed that two like poles repel and that two unlike poles attract. He explained how to magnetise iron, and even how to reverse the magnetisation of iron already magnetised.
textes.Pour expliquer pourquoi l'aimant s'orien: To explain why the magnet orients itself, he invoked the poles of the sky and not those of the Earth. It took William Gilbert, in 1600, to understand that the Earth itself is a magnet. Gilbert acknowledged his debt to Peter of Maricourt in De Magnete.
textes.Premier exposé de la polarité : pôles se: First account of polarity: like poles repel, unlike attract. For him, the poles of the sky guide the magnet.
textes.La seconde partie de la lettre décrit de: The second part of the letter describes two instruments. A "wet" compass, where the magnet floats in a vessel of water, and a "dry" compass, where the needle turns freely on a pivot. It is the oldest detailed description of a needle mounted on a pivot, the ancestor of our compasses.
textes.Pierre propose aussi une machine à mouve: Peter also proposed a perpetual motion machine: a toothed wheel that the magnet would turn endlessly, by attracting then repelling its teeth. It never worked, and for good reason: no machine produces energy from nothing.
textes.Boussole humide (flottante) et sèche (à: Wet (floating) and dry (pivoted) compass; a perpetual-motion wheel, impossible.
textes.En 1600, un médecin anglais fait des exp: In 1600, an English physician did experiments instead of copying the Ancients: the Earth is a magnet, and amber is not alone in attracting.
textes.William Gilbert, médecin d'Élisabeth Ire: William Gilbert, physician to Elizabeth I, published De Magnete in London in 1600, in Latin, in six books.
textes.Avec une petite Terre en aimant, la terr: With a small Earth made of lodestone, the terrella, he showed that the Earth itself is a magnet: hence the orientation of compasses.
textes.Il forge le mot latin electricus, « comm: He coined the Latin word electricus, "like amber", and showed that rubbed sulphur, wax or glass also attract.
textes.Son versorium, une aiguille sur pivot se: His versorium, a pivoted needle sensitive to rubbed amber, is the first electrical measuring instrument.
textes.Gilbert croyait électricité et magnétism: Gilbert believed electricity and magnetism were different: Ørsted and Maxwell would show they are two faces of one force.
textes.William Gilbert naît à Colchester en 154: William Gilbert was born in Colchester in 1544. A renowned physician in London, he became physician to Queen Elizabeth I in 1601. A year earlier, in 1600, he published with Peter Short a large book in Latin, in six books: De Magnete, "On the Magnet, Magnetic Bodies, and the Great Magnet the Earth".
textes.Son idée maîtresse vient d'une maquette: His key idea came from a model: a ball carved from lodestone, the terrella, the "little Earth". Moving a needle over its surface, he found everything compasses do on the real Earth, including dip: at the equator the needle stays flat, towards the poles it plunges. Conclusion: the Earth itself is a magnet.
textes.De Magnete (1600) : la terrella, petite: De Magnete (1600): the terrella, a little Earth of lodestone, shows that the Earth is a magnet. Dip increases towards the poles.
textes.Gilbert s'intéresse aussi à l'ambre. Il: Gilbert also took an interest in amber. He coined for it the Latin adjective electricus, "like amber", from the Greek ēlektron. He discovered that many other rubbed bodies attract light straws: sulphur, wax, glass. To see it, he invented the versorium, a metal needle set on a pivot, which turns towards the rubbed object. It is the first electrical measuring instrument.
textes.Il sépare nettement les deux forces : l': He clearly separated the two forces: the magnet attracts only iron, rubbed amber attracts anything light. It was progress, but also a lasting error: two centuries later, Ørsted then Maxwell would show that electricity and magnetism are two aspects of one force, electromagnetism.
textes.Electricus = « comme l'ambre » (Gilbert): Electricus = "like amber" (Gilbert). Versorium: the first electrical instrument. Sulphur, wax, glass also attract.
textes.De Magnete passe en revue tout ce qu'on: De Magnete reviews everything known about the magnet since Antiquity, then submits it to experiment. Gilbert dealt with declination, the gap between magnetic north and true north, and with dip, with an instrument to measure it. The last book even defends the Earth's rotation and the Copernican system.
textes.Gilbert meurt à Londres le 30 novembre 1: Gilbert died in London on 30 November 1603. A unit is named after him, the gilbert, now replaced by the ampere-turn. His book was translated into English only in 1893, by Paul Fleury Mottelay: for three centuries, one had to read Latin to follow the birth of the science of electricity.
textes.De Magnete : histoire de l'aimant, décli: De Magnete: history of the magnet, declination, dip, the Earth's rotation. Translated into English only in 1893.
textes.Au XVIIIe siècle, l'électricité devient: In the 18th century, electricity became a show: rubbing machines, conducting threads, and a bottle that keeps the spark.
textes.En 1663, Otto von Guericke construit ce: In 1663, Otto von Guericke built what is regarded as one of the first electrostatic generators.
textes.En 1729, Stephen Gray montre que l'élect: In 1729, Stephen Gray showed that electricity travels along a thread: there are conductors and insulators.
textes.En 1745, Ewald von Kleist puis, à Leyde,: In 1745, Ewald von Kleist then, at Leiden, Musschenbroek and Cunaeus invented the bottle that stores charge.
textes.La bouteille de Leyde est le premier con: The Leyden jar is the first capacitor: two metal foils separated by glass.
textes.La charge n'est pas dans l'eau de la bou: The charge is not in the water of the bottle but in the glass, between the two coatings: Franklin showed it.
textes.En 1663, Otto von Guericke frotte de la: In 1663, Otto von Guericke rubbed by hand a sulphur globe fixed on an iron rod: today it is seen as one of the first electrostatic generators, even though he did not take it for an electrical machine. In 1729, the Englishman Stephen Gray showed that electricity can travel along a thread: with Granville Wheler, he sent it along a pack-thread for 800 feet, about 240 metres, across a paddock.
textes.Il distingue ainsi les conducteurs, qui: He thus distinguished conductors, which let electricity through, from insulators, which hold it back. His most famous experiment: a boy suspended by silk cords, electrified by bringing a rubbed glass tube near his feet; his face and hands then attracted light straws. Gray received the very first Copley Medal in 1731. In 1733, the Frenchman du Fay distinguished two electricities, "vitreous" and "resinous".
textes.Guericke (1663) : globe frotté. Gray (17: Guericke (1663): rubbed globe. Gray (1729): conductors and insulators, 800 feet of thread, the suspended boy. Du Fay (1733): two electricities.
textes.En octobre 1745, le clerc allemand Ewald: In October 1745, the German cleric Ewald Georg von Kleist tried to keep electricity in a bottle of alcohol pierced by a nail. At Leiden, in 1745-1746, Pieter van Musschenbroek and Andreas Cunaeus obtained the same effect independently, and understood why the bottle had to be held in the hand.
textes.La version classique est un bocal de ver: The classic version is a glass jar covered with metal foil inside and out, with a rod touching the inner foil. It is the first capacitor: two conductors separated by an insulator. Abbé Nollet popularised the device and gave it the name Leyden jar.
textes.Kleist (oct. 1745), Musschenbroek et Cun: Kleist (Oct. 1745), Musschenbroek and Cunaeus (Leiden, 1745-1746): the bottle that stores charge, the first capacitor.
textes.Moines et gardes en chaîne: Monks and guards in a chain
textes.L'abbé Jean-Antoine Nollet fait de la bo: Abbé Jean-Antoine Nollet turned the jar into a show. Before King Louis XV, he sent the discharge through 180 royal guards holding hands. In 1746, he linked about 200 monks with iron wire, in a circle about a mile round, some 1.6 km: they all jumped almost at the same moment. Electricity spreads very fast.
textes.Benjamin Franklin étudie la bouteille et: Benjamin Franklin studied the jar and showed that the charge is stored in the glass, not in the water. In a 1749 letter, he used for the first time the term "electrical battery" for several linked jars. In 1767, Joseph Priestley told this whole story in a book of about 700 pages, The History and Present State of Electricity.
Nollet: 180 guards, 200 monks (1746). Franklin: the charge is in the glass; "battery" (1749).
textes.Un imprimeur de Philadelphie montre que: A Philadelphia printer showed that lightning is a giant spark, invented the lightning rod and named plus and minus.
textes.Franklin est le premier à appeler les de: Franklin was the first to call the two kinds of charge positive and negative.
textes.Il découvre le principe de conservation: He discovered the principle of conservation of charge: electricity is not created, it is moved.
textes.En mai 1752, Dalibard réalise en France: In May 1752, Dalibard performed in France the rod experiment Franklin had proposed; in June, Franklin flew his kite.
textes.En 1752, des paratonnerres sont posés su: In 1752, lightning rods were installed on the Academy and the Pennsylvania State House, in Philadelphia.
textes.La foudre n'a pas frappé le cerf-volant: Lightning did not strike the kite: the charge was induced by a nearby charged cloud.
textes.Benjamin Franklin, imprimeur de Philadel: Benjamin Franklin, a Philadelphia printer, became passionate about electricity in the late 1740s. He wrote up his discoveries in letters to Peter Collinson, who passed them on to the Royal Society in London; they appeared as a book in 1751 under the title Experiments and Observations on Electricity, and went through five editions.
textes.Pour Franklin, il n'y a pas deux électri: For Franklin, there were not two electricities, vitreous and resinous, but a single fluid, in excess or in deficit. He was the first to speak of positive and negative charge, and he discovered the conservation of charge: what one body gains, another loses. In 1748, he linked several Leyden jars into an "electrical battery".
textes.Franklin : positif et négatif, conservat: Franklin: positive and negative, conservation of charge, "battery". His letters became a book in 1751.
textes.Franklin propose d'attirer la foudre dan: Franklin proposed attracting lightning into a Leyden jar with a long metal rod. It was in France that the experiment first succeeded: in May 1752, at Marly-la-Ville, Thomas-François Dalibard succeeded with the rod experiment. For lack of a tall enough spire in Philadelphia, Franklin used a kite, in June 1752.
textes.Avec son fils William, il attache une cl: With his son William, he tied a metal key to the hemp string, held it all by an insulating silk cord, and charged a Leyden jar. The kite was not struck by lightning: the charge came from a nearby cloud. The experiment remains dangerous: in August 1753, in Saint Petersburg, Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed repeating it.
textes.Dalibard (mai 1752) puis Franklin (juin: Dalibard (May 1752) then Franklin (June 1752): lightning is electrical. Richmann died of it in 1753.
textes.De ses expériences, Franklin tire une in: From his experiments Franklin drew an invention: the lightning rod, a pointed metal rod connected to the ground, which conducts lightning harmlessly. In 1752, after trials on his own house, rods were installed on the Academy of Philadelphia and on the Pennsylvania State House.
textes.La Royal Society lui décerne la médaille: The Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal in 1753, and elected him in 1756, a rare honour for an American. Franklin did not write the detailed account of the kite himself: it comes from Joseph Priestley, in 1767. Franklin had only published a short letter in the Pennsylvania Gazette, on 19 October 1752, without specifying the circumstances of his own experiment.
textes.Paratonnerres en 1752 à Philadelphie. Co: Lightning rods in 1752 in Philadelphia. Copley in 1753. Account of the kite: Priestley, 1767.
textes.En 1785, un ingénieur militaire mesure l: In 1785, a military engineer measured the force between two charges with a twisted wire: it follows the inverse square of the distance.
textes.Loi de Coulomb : F = k × q₁ × q₂ ÷ r², a: Coulomb's law: F = k × q₁ × q₂ ÷ r², with k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
textes.Doubler la distance divise la force par: Doubling the distance divides the force by four; doubling one charge doubles the force.
textes.Coulomb la mesure en 1785 avec une balan: Coulomb measured it in 1785 with a torsion balance of his own invention.
textes.Même forme que la gravitation de Newton,: Same form as Newton's gravitation, but the electric force can attract or repel.
textes.Coulomb n'est pas le premier à soupçonne: Coulomb was not the first to suspect the inverse square: Aepinus, Priestley and Cavendish had anticipated it, but Cavendish published nothing.
textes.Charles-Augustin Coulomb naît à Angoulêm: Charles-Augustin Coulomb was born in Angoulême on 14 June 1736. An officer of military engineering, he was sent to Martinique to build the new Fort Bourbon, a project that kept him there from 1764 to 1772. Back in France, he presented his first work to the Academy of Sciences in 1773.
textes.Ingénieur avant tout, il étudie ce qui g: An engineer above all, he studied what hinders machines: in 1779, he published a major study of friction, whose laws still bear his name. In 1784, he published experiments on the torsion of metal wires. This twisted wire would serve him to weigh the electric force.
textes.Coulomb (1736-1806) : officier du génie,: Coulomb (1736-1806): military engineer, Fort Bourbon (1764-1772), friction (1779), torsion of wires (1784).
textes.Sa balance de torsion est faite pour dét: His torsion balance was made to detect tiny forces: a light bar hung from a thin wire, with a small charged ball at the end. Another ball with the same charge is brought near; the bar turns and twists the wire, and the angle of twist measures the force. For attractive forces, Coulomb studied the bar's oscillations instead.
textes.En 1785, dans son premier mémoire sur l': In 1785, in his first memoir on electricity and magnetism, he concluded that the repulsion between two charged balls "follows the inverse ratio of the square of the distances". He was not the first to suspect it: Aepinus in 1758, Priestley in 1767, Robison in 1769, and Cavendish, who published nothing. But he measured and published it: the law bears his name.
textes.Balance de torsion : l'angle du fil tord: Torsion balance: the angle of the twisted wire measures the force. 1785: the force varies as 1 ÷ r².
textes.La loi de Coulomb s'écrit F = k × q₁ × q: Coulomb's law is written F = k × q₁ × q₂ ÷ r². The force F, in newtons, is proportional to the product of the two charges q₁ and q₂, in coulombs, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance r, in metres. The constant is k = 1 ÷ (4π ε₀) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Doubling the distance divides the force by 2 × 2 = 4.
textes.C'est la même forme que la gravitation d: It has the same form as Newton's gravitation, with one difference: gravity always attracts, the electric force attracts or repels depending on the signs. And it is far stronger. In 1880, the unit of charge was named the coulomb; since 2019, the charge of an electron has been fixed at exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Coulomb's name is one of the 72 engraved on the Eiffel Tower.
textes.F = k q₁ q₂ / r², k ≈ 8,99 × 10⁹. Distan: F = k q₁ q₂ / r², k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹. Distance × 2 → force ÷ 4. Like Newton, but attracts or repels.
textes.Des cuisses de grenouille qui sautent, u: Frog legs that twitch, a quarrel between two Italians, and the first source of continuous current.
textes.À Bologne, à partir de 1780, Luigi Galva: In Bologna, from 1780, Luigi Galvani saw the legs of dead frogs twitch under a spark.
textes.En 1791, il publie dix ans de recherches: In 1791, he published ten years of research and defended an "animal electricity", belonging to living tissue.
textes.Pour Alessandro Volta, l'effet vient des: For Alessandro Volta, the effect came from the metals; on 20 March 1800, he described to the Royal Society his pile of zinc and copper discs.
textes.La pile donne enfin un courant continu :: The pile finally gave a continuous current: water was electrolysed in 1800, Davy isolated sodium and potassium.
textes.Galvani n'avait pas tout faux : l'influx: Galvani was not entirely wrong: nerve signals are indeed electrical. But his frogs were reacting mostly to the metals.
textes.Luigi Galvani naît à Bologne en 1737. Mé: Luigi Galvani was born in Bologna in 1737. A physician and anatomist, he married in 1762 Lucia Galeazzi, daughter of his teacher, herself a scientist. From 1780, he observed that the leg muscles of dead frogs twitched when struck by an electric spark.
textes.En 1791, il publie dix ans de recherches: In 1791, he published ten years of research in his Commentary on the Effects of Electricity on Muscular Motion. For him, electricity arises in the animal's tissue: this is "animal electricity". The book caused a stir throughout Europe. Mary Shelley would read these accounts before writing Frankenstein, and we still say "galvanise".
textes.Galvani (1780) : grenouilles et étincell: Galvani (1780): frogs and sparks; 1791: "animal electricity". Hence "galvanise".
textes.Alessandro Volta, né à Côme en 1745, est: Alessandro Volta, born in Como in 1745, had been professor of physics at Pavia since 1779. He had already improved the electrophorus, in 1775, and discovered marsh methane in 1776. He repeated Galvani's experiments and reached another conclusion: the twitching depends on the metals linking nerve and muscle. The frog is only a detector.
textes.Les deux hommes s'opposent avec respect: The two men disagreed respectfully; it was Volta who coined the word "galvanism". Galvani left the defence of his ideas mostly to his nephew, Giovanni Aldini. In 1798, he refused to swear allegiance to the Cisalpine Republic, lost his posts and died poor the same year. Volta was right about the frogs; Galvani, about the nerves, which do run on electricity.
Volta: the twitching comes from the metals. Galvani: animal electricity. Each had his share of truth.
textes.Pour prouver qu'il a raison, Volta empil: To prove he was right, Volta stacked pairs of copper, or silver, and zinc discs, separated by cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water. On 20 March 1800, he described the device in a letter to the Royal Society in London. It was the first battery able to supply a continuous current to a circuit. Each cell gives about 0.76 volt: six cells, 4.56 volts.
textes.La science s'en empare aussitôt. En 1800: Science seized on it at once. In 1800, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle decomposed water with it; Humphry Davy then used it to isolate sodium, potassium and magnesium. Volta had received the Copley Medal in 1794, Napoleon made him a count in 1810, and the volt bears his name.
textes.Pile de Volta (20 mars 1800) : zinc, cui: Volta's pile (20 March 1800): zinc, copper, salt water; ~0.76 V per cell. Electrolysis of water the same year.
textes.1820-1831 : le courant fait tourner l'ai: 1820-1831: current turns the needle, two currents attract, the magnet gives birth to current.
textes.En septembre 1820, François Arago racont: In September 1820, François Arago told the Academy of Sciences about Ørsted's discovery: a current deflects a magnetised needle. André-Marie Ampère, born in Lyon in 1775, seized on it at once. He showed that two parallel wires carrying currents attract when the currents flow in the same direction, and repel when they flow in opposite directions.
textes.Il bâtit une théorie mathématique de ces: He built a mathematical theory of these forces, which he called electrodynamics, and coined the word "solenoid" for a coil of wire. His great memoir appeared in 1826. James Clerk Maxwell would call him "the Newton of electricity", and the unit of current, the ampere, bears his name. His life was hard: his father had been guillotined on 24 November 1793.
textes.Ampère (1820) : deux courants parallèles: Ampère (1820): two parallel currents attract or repel. Electrodynamics, the solenoid, the ampere.
textes.En 1827, Georg Ohm lie tension, intensit: In 1827, Georg Ohm linked voltage, current and resistance: U = R × I. Volts, amperes, ohms.
textes.Charges, conducteurs, boucles, série et: Charges, conductors, loops, series and parallel, and Kirchhoff's two laws (1845) for calculating any network.
textes.En 1845, Gustav Kirchhoff, étudiant né e: In 1845, Gustav Kirchhoff, a student born in 1824, at the University of Königsberg, formulated two rules for a seminar exercise set by Franz Neumann. They generalise Georg Ohm's work and make it possible to calculate any network of wires, however complicated. Kirchhoff would become a great physicist: with Robert Bunsen, he discovered caesium and rubidium in 1861.
textes.Loi des nœuds : en un point où plusieurs: Junction rule: at a point where several wires meet, the sum of the currents arriving equals the sum of the currents leaving; charge does not pile up. Loop rule: along a closed loop, the voltages add up to zero. With these two rules and Ohm's law, an engineer can calculate any circuit, from a torch to the power grid.
textes.Kirchhoff (1845) : ce qui entre dans un: Kirchhoff (1845): what enters a node leaves it; around a loop, the voltages cancel out.
textes.Des aiguilles qui tremblent, des points: Trembling needles, dots and dashes, a cable under the Atlantic: information travels at the speed of electricity.
textes.En 1833, à Göttingen, Gauss et Weber rel: In 1833, in Göttingen, Gauss and Weber linked the university to the observatory with a wire about 1,200 m long, using a binary code.
textes.En 1837, Cooke et Wheatstone brevettent: In 1837, Cooke and Wheatstone patented a needle telegraph; it equipped the Great Western Railway in 1838.
textes.Le 24 mai 1844, Samuel Morse envoie de W: On 24 May 1844, Samuel Morse sent from Washington to Baltimore: "What hath God wrought".
textes.Le premier câble transatlantique, en 185: The first transatlantic cable, in 1858, lasted only three weeks; the 1866 one worked.
textes.Morse n'a pas inventé le télégraphe élec: Morse did not invent the electric telegraph: Schilling, Gauss and Weber, Cooke and Wheatstone came before him.
textes.Les premiers télégraphes électriques son: The first electric telegraphs were electrochemical: Francisco Salvá's in 1804, Samuel Thomas von Sömmering's in 1809. After Ørsted's discovery, in 1820, a magnetised needle deflected by the current was used instead. In 1832, Pavel Schilling, in Russia, reduced the number of wires from eight to two.
textes.En 1833, à Göttingen, le mathématicien C: In 1833, in Göttingen, the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss and the physicist Wilhelm Weber linked the university to the observatory, about 1,200 metres away, with a binary code. In 1837, the Englishmen William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented their needle telegraph; in 1838, a five-needle version equipped the Great Western Railway. The needles pointed directly to the letters: no code to learn.
textes.Sömmering (1809), Schilling (1832), Gaus: Sömmering (1809), Schilling (1832), Gauss and Weber (1833), Cooke and Wheatstone (1837): the current moves a needle.
textes.Samuel Morse est d'abord un peintre : il: Samuel Morse was first a painter: he painted the portrait of Lafayette and co-founded in 1826 the National Academy of Design in New York. He teamed up with Alfred Vail, a machinist at the Speedwell ironworks, who invented the first sending key. On 6 January 1838, at Speedwell, a message crossed two miles of wire: "A patient waiter is no loser".
textes.En 1843, le Congrès vote 30 000 dollars: In 1843, Congress voted 30,000 dollars for a 38-mile line between Washington and Baltimore. On 24 May 1844, Morse sent from the Capitol a Bible phrase chosen by Annie Ellsworth: "What hath God wrought". The code is made of dots and dashes; the most frequent letter in English, E, has the shortest sign, a single dot. In 1865, a conference in Paris set an international code.
textes.Morse et Vail : Speedwell (1838), Washin: Morse and Vail: Speedwell (1838), Washington-Baltimore (24 May 1844). E = one dot. International code: Paris, 1865.
textes.Les câbles sous-marins commencent en 185: Submarine cables began in 1850. In August 1858, a cable linked Ireland to Newfoundland. Queen Victoria's message to President Buchanan, 98 words, took 16 hours to get through. Three weeks later, the cable died: the engineer Wildman Whitehouse had tried to drive up to 2,000 volts through it and damaged the insulation.

textes.Professeur de lycée à Cologne, Georg Ohm: A secondary-school teacher in Cologne, Georg Ohm passes current through wires of different lengths and measures what happens. He derives a simple law: the current is proportional to the voltage, and inversely proportional to the circuit's resistance. He takes inspiration from how heat spreads along a bar, studied by Fourier. The German scientific community gives this work a poor reception, calling it a “web of naked fancies”, and Ohm leaves his post. Not until 1841 does the Royal Society honor him.

textes.Fils de brasseur, James Joule mesure ave: A brewer's son, James Joule measures with obsessive precision the heat given off by a wire carrying a current. He shows it is proportional to the wire's resistance and to the square of the current: doubling the current quadruples the heat. This is Joule heating, which makes filament bulbs glow and toasters heat up, but also wastes energy in power lines, which is why electricity is transmitted at very high voltage. These measurements later lead him to the equivalence between work and heat, which he defended alone against the scientific establishment.

Arriving in the United States, he works briefly for Edison, a champion of direct current, then teams up with Westinghouse. This is the “war of the currents”. The mathematician John von Neumann writes a memo describing its organization: an arithmetic unit, a control unit, a memory, inputs and outputs. Above all, the program is stored in the same memory as the data, instead of being wired by hand. So programs can be changed in seconds. This organization, known as the “von Neumann architecture”, is still that of almost every computer.

In a silicon or germanium crystal, current is carried by electrons, but also by “holes”, empty places that move like positive charges. By dosing impurities, the current can be controlled. textes.Le transistor a été inventé en 1947 aux: The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs by:

textes.Le circuit intégré, réunissant plusieurs: The integrated circuit, bringing several components together on a single chip, was invented in 1958-1959 by:

It changes direction a hundred times a second. The United States uses 60 Hz.

textes.Edison, partisan du continu, et Westingh: Edison, for direct current, against Westinghouse and Tesla, for alternating current
textes.L'alternatif l'emporte car il se transpo: Alternating current wins because transformers make it easier to transmit.
textes.Un transformateur ne fonctionne qu'avec: A transformer only works with alternating current.

textes.On transporte l'électricité sous très ha: Electricity is transmitted at very high voltage because:

textes.Pour une même puissance, plus de tension: For the same power, more voltage means less current, so fewer losses.

textes.un alternateur entraîné par les pales: a generator driven by the blades
textes.Comme dans presque toutes les centrales: As in almost every power plant: a magnet spinning near coils.
textes.Les panneaux photovoltaïques transformen: Photovoltaic panels convert light directly into electricity.
textes.Par l'effet photovoltaïque, observé par: Through the photovoltaic effect, observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839, at 19.
textes.Environ quelle part de l'électricité fra: Roughly what share of French electricity was produced by nuclear power in 2023, in percent?
textes.Environ 65 % selon RTE, la plus forte pr: About 65% according to RTE, the highest proportion in the world.
textes.La plus ancienne grande forme d'électric: The oldest major form of renewable electricity is:

textes.Une batterie lithium-ion stocke l'énergi: A lithium-ion battery stores energy in chemical form.

textes.Elle la turbine plus tard, quand la dema: It runs it through turbines later, when demand is high.

textes.1011 = 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 1: 1011 = 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 11. Leibniz set out this binary arithmetic, using only the digits 0 and 1, in a paper published in 1705.

textes.L'équipe de Grace Hopper l'a collé dans: Grace Hopper's team taped it into the logbook with the note “First actual case of bug being found”.
