textes.Le mot « groupthink » apparaît en 1952 s: The word "groupthink" appeared in 1952, written by the journalist William H. Whyte in Fortune magazine; he borrowed it from Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. In 1972, the psychologist Irving Janis, of Yale, turned it into a theory in Victims of Groupthink: a close-knit group, eager to agree, stops examining its choices.
textes.Janis relève huit symptômes, dont l'illu: Janis listed eight symptoms, including the illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship and the illusion of unanimity. Textbook case: in 1961, Kennedy's team accepted without scrutiny the CIA's plan to land in Cuba, at the Bay of Pigs; it was a disaster. In 1962, during the missile crisis, Kennedy brought in outside experts, split the group into subgroups and left the room. Same men, another method.
textes.Whyte, 1952 ; Janis, 1972 : un groupe qu: Whyte, 1952; Janis, 1972: a group that wants to agree stops thinking. Remedies: outside views, subgroups, an absent boss.
textes.Le mot « groupthink » apparaît en 1952 s: The word "groupthink" appeared in 1952, written by the journalist William H. Whyte in Fortune magazine; he borrowed it from Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four.
textes.En 1968, Robert Rosenthal et Lenore Jaco: In 1968, Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson led the teachers of a Californian school to believe that 20% of their pupils, picked at random, were about to bloom. By the end of the study, the youngest of them had progressed more: the "Pygmalion effect". But later studies judged it small and often temporary; it nearly vanishes when the teacher already knows the pupils.
textes.Les autres pèsent aussi sur l'action. En: Others also weigh on action. In 1964, it was said that 38 neighbours let Kitty Genovese be killed without reacting; the figure was false, the New York Times admitted in 2016. But experiments confirm a dilution: alone, 70% of participants help a woman in distress, 40% next to a stranger. In the street, though, cameras show that at least one passer-by intervenes in over 90% of disputes.
textes.Pygmalion (1968) : les attentes pèsent,: Pygmalion (1968): expectations matter, but little and not for long. Bystanders: responsibility is diluted, but in real streets someone almost always helps.
textes.En 1968, Robert Rosenthal et Lenore Jaco: In 1968, Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson led the teachers of a Californian school to believe that 20% of their pupils, picked at random, were about to bloom.
textes.Bartlett, 1932 : la mémoire reconstruit: Bartlett, 1932: memory reconstructs; what does not fit our schemas drops out or changes.
textes.Loftus et Palmer, 1974 : le verbe de la: Loftus and Palmer, 1974: the verb in the question changes the estimated speed and makes people "see" broken glass.
textes.Effet de désinformation : une informatio: Misinformation effect: information received afterwards slips into the memory.
textes.Biais rétrospectif (Fischhoff, 1975) : u: Hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975): once the outcome is known, we believe we foresaw it.
textes.Être sûr de son souvenir ne prouve rien: Being sure of a memory proves nothing: flashbulb memories are special only in their perceived accuracy.
textes.À Cambridge, Frederic Bartlett fait lire: At Cambridge, Frederic Bartlett had English people read a Native American tale, The War of the Ghosts, then retell it several times, weeks apart. With each version, what seemed strange to them disappeared or became familiar: "canoes" became "boats". The longer the interval, the further the story drifted from the original.
textes.Il en tire, dans Remembering, en 1932, u: In Remembering, in 1932, he drew an idea that would last: memory is not a recording but a reconstruction. We do not replay a memory, we rebuild it from a few traces, guided by schemas, our usual frames, our knowledge and our expectations. Bartlett then held the chair of experimental psychology at Cambridge.
textes.Bartlett, 1932 : se souvenir, c'est reco: Bartlett, 1932: to remember is to reconstruct. What does not fit our schemas drops out or changes (canoes become boats).
textes.À chaque version, ce qui leur semble étr: With each version, what seemed strange to them disappeared or became familiar: "canoes" became "boats".
textes.En 1974, Elizabeth Loftus et John Palmer: In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed 45 students films of car crashes, then asked: how fast were the cars going when they "smashed", "hit", "contacted" each other? With smashed, the mean estimate was about 41 miles per hour; with contacted, about 32. The verb changed what they believed they had seen.
textes.Une semaine plus tard, une autre série d: A week later, another set of participants had to say whether they had seen broken glass. There was none. With "smashed", 32% said yes, against 14% with "hit". In 1978, a false mention of a "Yield" sign replaced in memory the "Stop" sign actually seen: the misinformation effect. Loftus has since testified in more than 300 trials.
textes.Loftus et Palmer, 1974 : « smashed » fai: Loftus and Palmer, 1974: "smashed" raises the speed and makes people see broken glass. Information received afterwards slips into memory.
textes.Une semaine plus tard, une autre série d: A week later, another set of participants had to say whether they had seen broken glass.
textes.En 1977, Roger Brown et James Kulik nomm: In 1977, Roger Brown and James Kulik named "flashbulb memories" the memories of the moment one learns shocking news: we think we see it all again, the place, the people, the time. After the Challenger shuttle exploded in 1986, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch questioned students; three years later, their memories were not very accurate, yet they remained very sure of them.
textes.La mémoire réécrit aussi nos propres pré: Memory also rewrites our own forecasts. In 1975, Baruch Fischhoff described hindsight bias, the "I knew it all along". Before Nixon's trip to Beijing and Moscow, his participants estimated the odds of various events; afterwards, they remembered giving higher odds to what happened. Remedy: explicitly imagine the other possible outcomes.
textes.Souvenirs flash : très vifs, très sûrs,: Flashbulb memories: very vivid, very sure, often wrong. Hindsight bias (Fischhoff, 1975): knowing the outcome rewrites what we believed before.
textes.En 1977, Roger Brown et James Kulik nomm: In 1977, Roger Brown and James Kulik named "flashbulb memories" the memories of the moment one learns shocking news: we think we see it all again, the place, the people, the time.
textes.Effet Dunning-Kruger : les moins compéte: Dunning-Kruger effect: the least competent overestimate their level the most, since they don't know what they don't know.
textes.Les plus compétents ont tendance à se so: The most competent tend to slightly underestimate themselves.
textes.La courbe en « montagne de la stupidité: The “Mount Stupid” curve circulating on the Internet is not in the original paper.
textes.Métacognition : s'entraîner à dire « je: Metacognition: practice saying “I'm 70% sure” and check whether you're right 7 times out of 10.
textes.Dunning-Kruger ne dit pas que les ignora: Dunning-Kruger doesn't say ignorant people think they're experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top.
textes.En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves. Those in the bottom quarter placed themselves on average around the 62nd percentile, when they were near the 12th. The skills they lack are precisely the ones that would let them see their mistakes. The best slightly underestimated themselves.
textes.Attention aux caricatures. Les moins com: Beware of caricatures. The least competent do not think they are experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top, and always below the best. The famous "Mount Stupid" curve does not come from the paper. And some researchers think a good part of the effect is a statistical artefact, linked to regression to the mean; Dunning defends his findings.
textes.Les moins compétents se surestiment (12e: The least competent overestimate themselves (12th percentile actual, 62nd estimated), without thinking they are experts. "Mount Stupid" is not in the paper.
textes.En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves.
textes.La métacognition, c'est savoir ce qu'on: Metacognition is knowing what you know, and spotting what you do not. A simple exercise: instead of answering yes or no, say "I'm 70 % sure", then check. If you are right about 7 times out of 10 when you say you are 70 % sure, you are well calibrated. Most people discover they are wrong far more often than they thought at "90 %".
textes.La surconfiance est partout. En 1981, Ol: Overconfidence is everywhere. In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers. And the planning fallacy makes us underestimate how long our projects will take, even when we know previous ones ran late. Conversely, impostor syndrome credits one's successes to luck.
textes.Se calibrer : « sûr à 70 % » doit tomber: Calibrate yourself: "70 % sure" should be right 7 times out of 10. 93 % of drivers think they are in the better half (Svenson, 1981).
textes.En 1981, Ola Svenson trouve que 93 % des: In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers.
textes.Relire un cours donne une impression tro: Rereading a lesson gives a misleading sense of mastery: everything feels familiar, so it seems known. Testing yourself, fetching the answer from memory without looking, strengthens the memory far better. That is the testing effect, or retrieval practice, and it is the very principle of this game.
textes.Il y a aussi un angle mort : nous repéro: There is also a blind spot: we spot other people's biases very well, our own far less. Emily Pronin and colleagues described it in 2002. The more you learn in a field, the more you measure how much you do not know: that is the flip side of Dunning-Kruger, and rather a good sign.
textes.Se tester bat la relecture (effet de tes: Testing beats rereading (testing effect). We see others' biases, not our own (blind spot, Pronin, 2002).
textes.À Athènes, au Ve siècle av. J.-C., Thucy: In Athens, in the 5th century BC, Thucydides refused to believe the first story he heard; in 1377, Ibn Khaldun listed the errors of historians.
textes.En 430 av. J.-C., la peste frappe Athène: In 430 BC, plague struck Athens; in Piraeus, the Peloponnesians were accused of poisoning the reservoirs.
textes.Thucydide : la plupart des gens se donne: Thucydides: most people take little trouble to seek the truth and accept the first story that comes along.
textes.Il note aussi l'habitude des hommes de c: He also noted mankind's habit of entrusting to careless hope what they long for: wishful thinking.
textes.En 1377, Ibn Khaldun compte sept causes: In 1377, Ibn Khaldun counted seven causes of error among historians, including partisanship and overconfidence in sources.
textes.Une histoire que tout le monde répète n': A story everyone repeats is no truer for it: the Athenians were wrong about their own heroes, the tyrannicides.
textes.En 430 av. J.-C., deuxième année de la g: In 430 BC, the second year of the Peloponnesian War, an epidemic fell upon Athens. It first struck the port of Piraeus, where people said the Peloponnesians had poisoned the reservoirs, there being as yet no wells there. The historian Thucydides caught it himself and survived. It is thought to have killed about a quarter of the population.
textes.Les Athéniens se rappellent alors un vie: The Athenians then recalled an old verse: "A Dorian war shall come and with it death." Some argued the word had been "dearth", but with the plague upon them, "death" won. Thucydides drily notes that people made their recollection fit their sufferings, and that if another war ever brought a famine, the verse would be read differently.
textes.Face au malheur, on cherche un coupable: In misfortune, people look for a culprit and reread the past in the light of the present: Thucydides saw it in 430 BC.
textes.Les héros qui ont raté le tyran: The heroes who missed the tyrant
textes.Les Athéniens honorent Harmodios et Aris: The Athenians honoured Harmodius and Aristogeiton, who killed Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, in 514 BC, during the Panathenaic festival. Everyone believed they had struck down the tyrant. Wrong, Thucydides reminds us: the tyrant in power was his elder brother Hippias, who was only driven out in 510 BC, by a Spartan army.
textes.Il relève d'autres idées reçues : chaque: He points out other received ideas: each king of Sparta does not have two votes in council, but one, and the "company of Pitane" never existed. His conclusion: most people take very little trouble to seek the truth and accept the first story that comes along. He says he relied neither on the first witness to hand nor on his own impression, and checked every fact.
textes.« Tout le monde le dit » n'est pas une p: "Everyone says so" is not proof: Thucydides checks stories, even those his city is proud of.
textes.Né à Tunis en 1332, Ibn Khaldun perd ses: Born in Tunis in 1332, Ibn Khaldun lost both his parents at about 17, in the plague that struck the city in 1348-1349. After a turbulent political life, he withdrew for several years to Qal'at Ibn Salama, under the protection of a Berber tribe, and there completed in 1377 a first version of the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his universal history.
textes.Il l'ouvre par les erreurs des historien: He opens it with the errors of historians. He counts seven, including partisanship towards an opinion, overconfidence in sources and flattery of the powerful: a partisan soul, he writes, accepts without hesitation the information that is agreeable to it. When al-Masudi reports that Moses counted over 600,000 soldiers, he objects that the land could not have held such an army, nor could so large an army manoeuvre as one body.
textes.Ibn Khaldun, 1377 : un récit se juge d'a: Ibn Khaldun, 1377: a story is judged first on its plausibility, not only on the reputation of those who pass it on.
textes.L'éléphant et les aveugles: The elephant and the blind men
textes.Dans l'Inde ancienne, des aveugles se ba: In ancient India, blind men fight over an elephant; around 80 AD, in China, Wang Chong weighs beliefs in the balance.
textes.L'éléphant et les aveugles, dans le temp: The elephant and the blind men, in time
textes.Le Kalama Sutta conseille de ne pas croi: The Kalama Sutta advises not to believe something on the sole strength of tradition, rumour, scripture or a teacher.
textes.Dans l'Udana, texte bouddhique, des aveu: In the Udana, a Buddhist text, blind men each touch one part of an elephant and end up fighting.
textes.Les jaïns en tirent l'anekantavada : la: The Jains drew from it anekantavada: reality has many sides, and no single viewpoint grasps it alone.
textes.Vers 80, en Chine, Wang Chong publie le: Around 80 AD, in China, Wang Chong published the Lunheng: thunder comes from fire or heat, not from Heaven's anger.
textes.Le Kalama Sutta n'autorise pas à croire: The Kalama Sutta does not license believing whatever one likes: the monk Bhikkhu Bodhi points out that it also gives criteria, such as what the wise approve.
textes.Dans le canon bouddhique en pali, l'Angu: In the Buddhist Pali canon, the Anguttara Nikaya contains a short sermon, the Kalama Sutta. The Kalamas, a clan of the town of Kesaputta, see many teachers pass through, each with his doctrine. Which should they follow? they ask the Buddha.
textes.La réponse est restée célèbre : ne pas s: The answer became famous: do not rely, on its own, on what you have heard repeated, on tradition, on rumour, on scripture, on surmise, on specious reasoning, on a long-pondered notion, nor on a teacher's prestige. But when you know for yourself that a thing is good, praised by the wise and beneficial, you may adopt it. The monk Bhikkhu Bodhi warns that this is no licence to believe whatever one likes.
textes.Le Kalama Sutta : ni la rumeur, ni la tr: The Kalama Sutta: neither rumour, nor tradition, nor authority is enough; one must examine for oneself.
textes.Les aveugles et l'éléphant: The blind men and the elephant
textes.Dans l'Udana, un recueil bouddhique, un: In the Udana, a Buddhist collection, a king has blind men and an elephant brought to the palace. Each touches one part and compares it to an object: a pot, a plough, a pillar… They quarrel, then come to blows, to the king's great delight. The Buddha compares these blind men to preachers and scholars who quarrel, each clinging to his one point of view.
textes.Le conte voyage. Les jaïns s'en servent: The tale travelled. The Jains used it to explain anekantavada, the idea that reality has many sides. The Persian poet Rumi set it in a dark room and concluded that if each had had a candle, their differences would have disappeared. In the 19th century, the American John Godfrey Saxe drew a famous poem from it: "It was six men of Indostan".
textes.Chacun ne touche qu'une partie de l'élép: Each touches only one part of the elephant: being right about a piece is not being right about the whole.
textes.Wang Chong naît en 27, sous les Han de l: Wang Chong was born in 27 AD, under the Eastern Han. Too poor to buy books, he is said to have read standing at the booksellers' stalls of Luoyang. Around 80 AD his great work appeared, the Lunheng, which Joseph Needham rendered as "Discourses Weighed in the Balance": 85 chapters, one of which keeps only its title, often rebutting popular beliefs.
textes.Le tonnerre n'est pas la colère du Ciel: Thunder is not Heaven's anger at the wicked, he writes, but the effect of fire or heat. If ghosts were the souls of the dead, there would be far more of them than living people, and they should appear naked, since clothes have no souls. He does not deny all spirits for all that; he demands evidence: a belief must rest on experience, just as an action is judged by its results.
textes.Wang Chong, vers 80 : avant d'accuser le: Wang Chong, around 80 AD: before blaming Heaven, look for a natural cause and for evidence.
textes.Au IVe siècle av. J.-C., Aristote dresse: In the 4th century BC, Aristotle listed false reasonings; Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus taught how to suspend judgement.
textes.Au Caire, au début du XIe siècle, Ibn al: In Cairo, in the early 11th century, Ibn al-Haytham showed that light enters the eye, and that seeing is already judging: the Moon on the horizon proves it.
textes.Entre 1011 et 1021, Ibn al-Haytham écrit: Between 1011 and 1021, Ibn al-Haytham wrote his Book of Optics, in seven volumes.
textes.La lumière va des objets à l'œil, et non: Light goes from objects to the eye, not the other way round as Euclid and Ptolemy believed.
textes.La Lune paraît plus grosse à l'horizon,: The Moon looks bigger on the horizon, although its apparent size does not change: it is an illusion.
textes.Pour lui, la vision se fait dans le cerv: For him, vision happens in the brain and depends on experience: without notions of distance and size, sight tells us next to nothing.
textes.Ce n'est pas l'air qui grossit la Lune à: It is not the air that enlarges the Moon on the horizon: a pebble held at arm's length covers it just as well high and low, and photos show the same size.
textes.Ibn al-Haytham, que l'Occident appellera: Ibn al-Haytham, whom the West would call Alhazen, was born in Basra around 965 and died in Cairo around 1040. A legend says he feigned madness to escape the caliph al-Hakim and stayed in hiding until the caliph's death in 1021. It was between 1011 and 1021 that he wrote his Book of Optics, the Kitab al-Manazir, in seven volumes.
textes.Euclide et Ptolémée pensaient que l'œil: Euclid and Ptolemy thought the eye sends out rays towards objects. Ibn al-Haytham argued the opposite: light, coming from objects, enters the eye, and it travels in straight lines. He described the camera obscura, where a small hole projects an image. His book is famous above all for its method: experiment rather than the mere authority of the ancients.
textes.Ibn al-Haytham, 1011-1021 : la lumière e: Ibn al-Haytham, 1011-1021: light enters the eye, and experiment decides between theories.
textes.Au ras de l'horizon, la pleine Lune para: Just above the horizon, the full Moon looks huge; high in the sky, it seems smaller. Yet, measured with a theodolite or photographed, it keeps the same apparent size, and a pebble held at arm's length covers it just as well in both positions. The perceived enlargement is usually about 50 percent.
textes.Aristote et Ptolémée connaissaient déjà: Aristotle and Ptolemy already knew the illusion. Ptolemy first blamed the atmosphere, then apparent distance. Ibn al-Haytham proposed an explanation based on intervening objects: we judge a distance by the series of things between us and the target. Between the Earth and the high Moon there is nothing: it seems closer, and so smaller, than on the horizon. Even today, no single theory has won outright.
textes.La Lune ne grossit pas à l'horizon : c'e: The Moon does not grow on the horizon: it is our judgement of distance that changes its perceived size.
textes.Pour Ibn al-Haytham, la vision se fait d: For Ibn al-Haytham, vision happens in the brain, and it is subjective, shaped by each person's experience. He wrote: without tangible notions of distance and size for correlation, sight can tell us next to nothing. His explanation of colour constancy is an early form of unconscious inference: our vision corrects what it receives without our willing it.
textes.Traduit en latin à la fin du XIIe ou au: Translated into Latin in the late 12th or early 13th century as De aspectibus, or Perspectiva, his book fed European optics from the 13th to the 17th century. In 1267, Roger Bacon drew on it in the optics part of his Opus Majus. In 1572, Friedrich Risner printed it in his Opticae thesaurus.
textes.Ce que nous voyons est déjà une interpré: What we see is already an interpretation: hence illusions, which deceive even scholars.
textes.Du bouc chassé au désert aux massacres d: From the goat driven into the wilderness to the massacres of 1349 and the witches' pyres: when misfortune strikes with no known cause, people find a culprit.
textes.La peste et les boucs émissaires, dans l: The plague and the scapegoats, in time
textes.Le mot vient du Lévitique : le jour du G: The word comes from Leviticus: on the Day of Atonement, a goat laden with the people's sins is driven into the wilderness.
textes.De 1348 à 1351, pendant la peste noire,: From 1348 to 1351, during the Black Death, Jews were accused of poisoning wells; confessions were extracted under torture.
textes.Le pape Clément VI répond en 1348 : les: Pope Clement VI replied in 1348: Jews are dying of the plague too, and it strikes regions where there are no Jews.
textes.Les procès de sorcellerie font de 40 000: Witch trials killed 40,000 to 60,000 people in Europe, mostly from 1560 to 1630; about 80 percent of those convicted were women.
textes.Un coupable désigné n'explique rien : à: A designated culprit explains nothing: in Strasbourg, Jews were burned on 14 February 1349, although the plague had not yet reached the city.
textes.Le bouc chassé au désert: The goat driven into the wilderness
textes.Dans le Lévitique, au chapitre 16, le jo: In Leviticus, chapter 16, on the Day of Atonement, two goats are chosen by lot: one is sacrificed, the other is driven into the wilderness, after the High Priest has confessed the people's sins over its head. It carries all their iniquities away with it. In 1530, translating the Bible into English, William Tyndale coined the word scapegoat; in French, one says bouc émissaire.
textes.Les Grecs aussi avaient leurs boucs émis: The Greeks had their scapegoats too, human ones. In times of famine, drought or plague, one or two poor people, slaves or criminals were driven out to save the city. In Abdera, a poor man was well fed, led around the walls, then driven out with stones. In Massalia, one was fed for a year before being cast out to stop an epidemic.
textes.Le bouc émissaire porte les fautes de to: The scapegoat bears everyone's sins: an ancient rite turned reflex, naming a culprit when misfortune strikes.
textes.La peste noire atteint l'Europe en 1347: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 and within a few years killed 30 to 60 percent of Europeans, depending on the estimate. No one knew its cause. From 1348 to 1351, a rumour spread: Jews were said to be poisoning the wells. Some, under torture, ended up "confessing". Massacres followed one another, from Toulon in April 1348 to Basel, Erfurt, Mainz, Frankfurt or Zurich; some 510 Jewish communities were destroyed.
textes.Le 14 février 1349, à Strasbourg, enviro: On 14 February 1349, in Strasbourg, about 2,000 Jews were burned alive, although the plague had not yet reached the city. Pope Clement VI had nevertheless issued two bulls, on 6 July and 26 September 1348: Jews are dying of the plague too, and it strikes regions where there are none. The argument was unanswerable; the rumour was stronger. In Poland, King Casimir III welcomed the refugees.
textes.1348-1351 : face à une cause inconnue, l: 1348-1351: faced with an unknown cause, rumour names a culprit, and even an unanswerable argument does not stop it.
textes.Des années 1400 aux années 1770, l'Europ: From the 1400s to the 1770s, Europe tried witches. The Hammer of Witches, by the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer, appeared in Speyer in 1486; it claims that women yield more easily to the devil and served as a manual for secular courts. The trials peaked from 1560 to 1630 and killed 40,000 to 60,000 people; about 80 percent of those convicted were women.
textes.Des historiens comme Wolfgang Behringer: Historians such as Wolfgang Behringer or Emily Oster note that trials increased as the climate cooled: lost harvests, wars, diseases, and witches as culprits. The explanation is judged too simple, but it recalls the plague. As early as 1563, the physician Johann Weyer argued that accused women who confessed were sick, melancholic, not allies of the devil.
textes.Les sorcières ont servi de boucs émissai: Witches served as scapegoats for Europe's misfortunes: 40,000 to 60,000 dead.
textes.Les idoles des deux Bacon: The idols of the two Bacons
textes.En 1267, Roger Bacon dénonce quatre caus: In 1267, Roger Bacon denounced four causes of error; in 1620, Francis Bacon listed the idols that distort the mind.
textes.Les idoles des deux Bacon, dans le temps: The idols of the two Bacons, in time
textes.Roger Bacon, Opus majus, 1267 : se fier: Roger Bacon, Opus Majus, 1267: relying on weak authority, custom, the ignorance of the crowd, and ignorance hidden behind a show of knowledge.
textes.Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, 1620 : les: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, 1620: the idols of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre.
textes.Une fois une opinion adoptée, l'esprit h: Once an opinion is adopted, the human understanding draws everything else to support it: confirmation bias, three centuries before it had a name.
textes.« Où sont les portraits de ceux qui se s: "Where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?": counting only the survivors misleads.
textes.Les idoles de Bacon ne sont pas des stat: Bacon's idols are not statues: they are false images in the mind, from the Latin idola.
textes.En 1267, à la demande du pape Clément IV: In 1267, at the request of Pope Clement IV, the scholar Roger Bacon sent him his Opus Majus, the "Greater Work". The first of its seven parts deals with the obstacles to wisdom and truth. He sorts four causes of error: relying on weak or unreliable authority, following custom, sharing the ignorance of the crowd, and hiding one's own ignorance behind a show of knowledge.
textes.Le reste de l'ouvrage fait la part belle: The rest of the work gives pride of place to observation. The fifth part, on optics, draws on the Arab scholars al-Kindi and Alhazen; the sixth is devoted to "experimental science". There is also alchemy and a taste for magic: Bacon was a man of his time, but he had seen that authority and habit lead the mind astray.
textes.Roger Bacon, 1267 : l'autorité, la coutu: Roger Bacon, 1267: authority, custom, the opinion of the crowd and false knowledge are the four sources of error.
textes.En 1620, le philosophe anglais Francis B: In 1620, the English philosopher Francis Bacon published, in Latin, the Novum Organum, the second part of a grand project to renew the sciences, the Instauratio Magna. On the frontispiece, a galleon sails past the Pillars of Hercules. But before proposing his method, Bacon lists the "idols", the false images that clutter the mind.
textes.Les idoles de la tribu tiennent à la nat: The idols of the tribe are rooted in human nature: we see more order in nature than there is. Those of the cave come from each individual, from temperament and upbringing: each has his own cave, which scatters and discolours the light. Those of the marketplace arise from misunderstood words. Those of the theatre, finally, come from philosophical systems accepted without examination, like those of Aristotle or Plato.
textes.Tribu, caverne, place publique, théâtre: Tribe, cave, marketplace, theatre: the species, the individual, words and doctrines distort our judgement.
textes.Dans l'aphorisme 46, Bacon décrit avec t: In aphorism 46, Bacon described three centuries ahead what would be called confirmation bias: once it has adopted an opinion, the human understanding draws everything else to support and agree with it. It keeps the favourable cases, and neglects or sets aside those that contradict it.
textes.Il raconte qu'on montra à un homme, dans: He tells how a man was shown, in a temple, the pictures offered by those who had made a vow and escaped shipwreck, to make him acknowledge the power of the gods. He asked: "But where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?" According to ancient sources, the retort belongs to Diagoras, in Cicero, or to Diogenes the Cynic.
textes.Ne compter que les rescapés, c'est se tr: Counting only the survivors is a sure way to be wrong: one must also look for the drowned.
textes.À Paris et à Londres, en 1720, les actio: In Paris and London, in 1720, Mississippi and South Sea shares soared then collapsed: everyone was counting on selling for more.
textes.1720, l'année des bulles, dans le temps: 1720, the year of bubbles, in time
textes.À Paris, l'action de la Compagnie du Mis: In Paris, John Law's Mississippi Company share went from 500 to 10,000 livres, then collapsed in 1720.
textes.À Londres, l'action de la Compagnie des: In London, the South Sea Company share rose from £128 in January 1720 to £1,000 in August, and fell back to £150 by the end of September.
textes.Le mot « bulle » vient de cet épisode :: The word "bubble" comes from this episode: prices inflated with nothing but air.
textes.Théorie du plus grand imbécile : on achè: Greater fool theory: people buy too dear, counting on selling dearer still. The bubble bursts when there are no more buyers.
textes.La phrase de Newton sur « la folie des g: Newton's line about "the madness of people" is known only at second hand, and no one knows how much he really lost.
textes.À Paris, l'économiste écossais John Law: In Paris, the Scottish economist John Law founded in 1717 a company that received all of Louisiana and a monopoly on its trade: the future Mississippi Company. Its shares, issued at 500 livres, stayed at that price until mid-1719. Then the fever rose: the price reached 10,000 livres. People fought over them in the open air, on the rue Quincampoix. In February 1720, the company even bought the Banque Royale.
textes.Pour suivre la demande d'actions, il fau: To keep up with the demand for shares, ever more bank notes were needed, and inflation reached 23 percent a month in January 1720. Then the bubble burst: 2,000 livres in September 1720, 1,000 in December. By the end of the year, the Regent, Philippe d'Orléans, had dismissed Law, who fled to Brussels, then to Venice.
textes.Paris, 1719-1720 : de 500 à 10 000 livre: Paris, 1719-1720: from 500 to 10,000 livres, then 1,000. The rise drew buyers, and the buyers made the rise.
textes.À Londres, la même année, l'action de la: In London, the same year, the South Sea Company share went from about £128 in January 1720 to £550 at the end of May, then £1,000 in early August. In the fever, many dubious companies sprang up, already called "bubbles". The most famous supposedly raised funds "for carrying out an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is"; it is probably a legend.
textes.Fin septembre, l'action ne vaut plus que: By the end of September, the share was worth only £150, and about £100 by the end of the year. The 33 directors were removed and lost on average 82 percent of their wealth. Isaac Newton held nearly £22,000 of stock in 1722; he is said to have lost up to £20,000 and to have said he "could not calculate the madness of people", but these words are known only at second hand.
textes.Londres, 1720 : 128 £, 1 000 £, puis 150: London, 1720: £128, £1,000, then £150. A bubble rises because people buy, and bursts when they stop buying.
textes.Pourquoi acheter une action manifestemen: Why buy a share that is plainly too dear? Because you count on selling it dearer still to someone else: that is the greater fool theory. As long as new buyers arrive, drawn by the first ones' gains and the fear of missing out, the price rises. But, as the economist Burton Malkiel puts it, eventually one runs out of greater fools.
textes.L'économiste Charles Kindleberger, auteu: The economist Charles Kindleberger, author in 1978 of a history of financial crises, described bubbles in five phases: a shock that opens new opportunities for profit, the boom, euphoria, distress when prices level off, then revulsion when everyone sells. Every time, people tell themselves that "this time is different". The word bubble itself comes from the South Sea affair: prices inflated with nothing but air.
textes.Une bulle vit de l'espoir de revendre pl: A bubble lives on the hope of selling for more: it bursts when there is no greater fool left.
textes.De Charles Mackay, en 1841, à Allport et: From Charles Mackay, in 1841, to Allport and Postman, in 1947: how a false idea runs faster than the true one.
textes.En 1785, Condorcet calcule quand une maj: In 1785, Condorcet calculated when a majority is right; in 1907, Galton saw a crowd guess the weight of an ox. Provided everyone thinks alone.
textes.La sagesse des foules, dans le temps: The wisdom of crowds, in time
textes.Théorème du jury de Condorcet, 1785 : si: Condorcet's jury theorem, 1785: if each voter has more than an even chance of being right and votes independently, the more voters there are, the likelier the majority is to be right.
textes.Galton, 1907 : à Plymouth, l'estimation: Galton, 1907: at Plymouth, the median estimate of 787 tickets, 1,207 pounds, came within 9 pounds of the ox's real weight, 1,198.
textes.Surowiecki, 2004 : une foule est sage si: Surowiecki, 2004: a crowd is wise if opinions are diverse, independent, decentralised and well aggregated.
textes.Zurich, 2011 : montrer aux gens les esti: Zurich, 2011: showing people the others' estimates reduces diversity without making the crowd more accurate.
textes.Si chacun a moins d'une chance sur deux: If each has less than an even chance of being right, adding voters makes things worse: the best jury is then a single voter.
textes.Bien avant les sondages, Aristote notait: Long before opinion polls, Aristotle noted in his Politics that the many may be better, not individually but collectively, like a dinner to which each contributes. In 1785, Condorcet gave a mathematical version of it in his Essay on the Application of Analysis to the Probability of Majority Decisions.
textes.C'est le théorème du jury : si chaque vo: This is the jury theorem: if each voter has a probability p, greater than 1/2, of voting correctly, independently of the others, then the more voters there are, the likelier the majority is to be right, approaching certainty. With three voters at p = 0.8, the majority is right with a probability of 0.896. But if p is below 1/2, each extra voter makes things worse.
textes.Condorcet, 1785 : une majorité de votant: Condorcet, 1785: a majority of independent voters, each a little better than chance, is very often right.
textes.À une foire aux bestiaux de Plymouth, en: At a livestock fair in Plymouth, in 1906, about 800 visitors placed bets on the weight of an ox once slaughtered and dressed. The statistician Francis Galton collected the 787 legible tickets.
textes.En 1907, il publie le résultat dans la r: In 1907, he published the result in the journal Nature, under the title Vox Populi. The median estimate, 1,207 pounds, was only 9 pounds off the real weight, 1,198: under 1 percent. The mean of the tickets, published later, came to 1,197. Taken together, the crowd had got it right.
textes.Galton, 1907 : la médiane de 787 estimat: Galton, 1907: the median of 787 estimates came within 1 percent of the ox's true weight.
textes.Quand la foule perd sa sagesse: When the crowd loses its wisdom
textes.En 2004, James Surowiecki popularise l'i: In 2004, James Surowiecki popularised the idea in The Wisdom of Crowds. A crowd is wise under four conditions: diversity of opinion, independence, decentralisation, and a good way to aggregate views. It fails through homogeneity, centralisation, division, imitation or emotionality.
textes.En 2011, à l'École polytechnique fédéral: In 2011, at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich, researchers had 144 students estimate six quantities, such as the population density of Switzerland. When shown the others' answers, their estimates converged without becoming more accurate, and their confidence rose. Social influence destroys the diversity that made the crowd wise.
textes.Une foule n'est sage que si chacun pense: A crowd is wise only if each person thinks alone: imitation makes it confident, not more accurate.
textes.En 1932, Frederic Bartlett montre que se: In 1932, Frederic Bartlett showed that remembering is rebuilding; in 1974, Elizabeth Loftus changed a memory with a single verb.
textes.En 1943, Abraham Wald blinde les avions: In 1943, Abraham Wald armoured planes where no hits could be seen; in 1973, Tversky and Kahneman showed that we judge frequency by what comes to mind.
textes.En 1951, Solomon Asch montre qu'on cède: In 1951, Solomon Asch showed that people yield to a unanimous group that is wrong; in 1972, Irving Janis named groupthink.
textes.En 1948, Skinner rend des pigeons supers: In 1948, Skinner made pigeons superstitious; in 1956, Festinger observed believers whose prophecy failed.
textes.En 1960, Peter Wason invente le jeu 2-4-: In 1960, Peter Wason invented the 2-4-6 game, then in 1966 his four cards: we look for what proves us right and ignore the rest.
textes.Berkeley, 1973 : des chiffres qui s'inve: Berkeley, 1973: figures that reverse when grouped; then regression to the mean and false positives.
textes.En 1974, Tversky et Kahneman font tourne: In 1974, Tversky and Kahneman spun a rigged wheel: a first number, however absurd, pulls our estimates.
textes.En 1979, Kahneman et Tversky publient la: In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky published prospect theory: losing hurts more than winning pleases. Then sunk costs and nudges.
textes.En 1986, Harry Frankfurt distingue le me: In 1986, Harry Frankfurt distinguished the liar from the bullshitter; in 2013, Alberto Brandolini measured what it costs to refute nonsense.
textes.Frankfurt, 1986 : le menteur connaît la: Frankfurt, 1986: the liar knows the truth and hides it; the bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true.
textes.D'où sa formule : le baratin est un plus: Hence his formula: bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are.
textes.Pennycook, 2015 : des phrases fabriquées: Pennycook, 2015: sentences randomly built from buzzwords are rated fairly profound, 2.6 out of 5 on average.
textes.Loi de Brandolini, 2013 : réfuter une ân: Brandolini's law, 2013: refuting nonsense takes ten times more energy than producing it.
textes.Une phrase creuse peut être grammaticale: A hollow sentence can be grammatically perfect: "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty" means nothing.
textes.En 1986, le philosophe Harry Frankfurt p: In 1986, the philosopher Harry Frankfurt published in the journal Raritan an essay with an unacademic title, On Bullshit. He starts from a notion of the philosopher Max Black, humbug, more polite but close.
textes.Sa distinction est restée célèbre : le m: His distinction became famous: the liar cares about the truth, since he tries to hide it. The bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true or false; only the effect counts. Hence his conclusion: bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are. Republished as a small book in 2005, the essay spent 27 weeks on the New York Times best-seller list.
textes.Le menteur cache la vérité ; le baratine: The liar hides the truth; the bullshitter ignores it. Frankfurt, 1986: the second is the more dangerous.
textes.En 2015, Gordon Pennycook et quatre coll: In 2015, Gordon Pennycook and four colleagues built meaningless sentences out of buzzwords, using two online generators, one of which drew on the tweets of the author Deepak Chopra. Example: "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty." The grammar is perfect; the meaning, absent.
textes.Les participants notent la profondeur de: Participants rated the profundity of each sentence from 1 to 5. Average: 2.6, between "somewhat" and "fairly" profound. Those who saw the most profundity did worse on reflective-thinking tests and made more ontological confusions. In a second study, real vague tweets by Chopra received ratings similar to those of the random sentences.
textes.Une phrase qui sonne profond n'est pas p: A sentence that sounds profound is not profound: ask what exactly it claims.
textes.En janvier 2013, le programmeur italien: In January 2013, the Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini formulated his law: the amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it. He had just read Daniel Kahneman's book on the two systems of thought, then watched a TV debate with Silvio Berlusconi and Marco Travaglio.
textes.L'idée est ancienne. En 1710, Jonathan S: The idea is old. In 1710, Jonathan Swift wrote that falsehood flies, and truth comes limping after it. In 1845, Frédéric Bastiat noted in his Economic Sophisms that a half-truth can be stated in a few words, but refuting it requires long and dry dissertations. An order of magnitude is a factor of ten.
textes.Produire du baratin coûte peu, le démont: Producing bullshit costs little, taking it apart costs ten times more: hence the point of not passing it on.
textes.En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger measured the gap between what we know and what we think we know.

textes.Trente-sept livres pour tout dire du mon: Thirty-seven books to say everything about the world: astronomy, geography, humans, animals, plants, remedies, metals, stones. He describes the anatomy of the eye, reflection in mirrors and refraction, the change of direction when light passes from air to water. He studies the camera obscura, a dark room where an inverted image forms through a small hole. Above all, he tests every claim by experiment, and criticizes the ancient authorities when they are wrong.

Three centuries ahead of time, he describes confirmation bias: once an opinion is adopted, the mind draws everything back to it, keeps the cases that support it and neglects or dismisses those that contradict it.

textes.Ce recueil rassemble les études qui ont: This collection gathers the studies that showed our judgments follow predictable shortcuts. The founding 1974 paper describes three. Representativeness: we judge a case by its resemblance to a stereotype, forgetting proportions. Availability: we estimate how frequent an event is by how easily examples come to mind. Anchoring: a number we've just seen, even one drawn at random, pulls our estimates toward it. These biases are not random errors, but slopes, the same for everyone.

He offers a “baloney detection kit”: seek independent confirmation of the facts, consider several hypotheses, beware of arguments from authority, quantify, check that every link in a chain of argument holds, apply Occam's razor, and ask whether a claim can be falsified. He reminds us that science is not a body of truths, but a method for correcting its errors.

Journalist Dan Gardner shows that our brain judges risks by the images in our heads, not by the numbers. A spectacular event, repeated by the media, seems frequent. He cites a striking case: after September 11, 2001, many Americans drove rather than flew, and road deaths rose in the following year.

textes.Puisque nos décisions sont biaisées, peu: Since our decisions are biased, can choices be arranged to help people without constraining them? That is the idea of the “nudge”. Economist Thaler and legal scholar Sunstein show that the way options are presented matters enormously. The default option is often the one people keep: automatically enrolling employees in a retirement savings plan, while leaving them free to opt out, multiplies enrollment. Putting healthy food at eye level in the cafeteria gets more of it eaten. The authors call this libertarian paternalism.

textes.Kahneman décrit notre pensée comme le tr: Kahneman describes our thinking as the work of two systems. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, completes “bread and…”, answers 10 cents to the bat-and-ball question. System 2 is slow, attentive and costly: it calculates, checks, reflects. The problem is that System 2 is lazy and often lets the first decide. Hence our biases: anchoring, availability, loss aversion, overconfidence. The book sums up forty years of research carried out largely with Amos Tversky, who died in 1996.

textes.Sextus Empiricus, médecin de l'école emp: Sextus Empiricus, a physician of the Empiric school, lived around the late 2nd century. His Outlines of Pyrrhonism set out the scepticism inherited from Pyrrho: every argument meets an argument of equal force, so the sceptic suspends judgement, epoché, and gains tranquillity of mind, ataraxia. The book preserves Aenesidemus' ten modes of doubt and Agrippa's five: dissent, infinite regress, relativity, hypothesis and circularity. Henri Estienne translated it into Latin and printed it in Geneva in 1562; the Greek text appeared only in 1621. Widely read in Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, it deeply marked Montaigne, then Hume.

textes.Irving Janis, psychologue à Yale, repren: Irving Janis, a Yale psychologist, took up a word coined in 1952 by the journalist William H. Whyte, inspired by Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four: groupthink. His book, subtitled "a psychological study of foreign-policy decisions and fiascoes", asks how teams of competent leaders could decide so badly. Central case: in 1961, Kennedy's team accepted without scrutiny the CIA's plan to land in Cuba, at the Bay of Pigs; objections were brushed aside, doubts went unspoken. Janis lists eight symptoms, from the illusion of invulnerability to self-censorship and the "mindguards" who filter out dissenting views. He contrasts this fiasco with the 1962 missile crisis, in which the same men, with other methods, decided better. A new edition appeared in 1982 under the title Groupthink.

textes.En 1932, Frederic Bartlett, titulaire de: In 1932, Frederic Bartlett, who had held the chair of experimental psychology at Cambridge since the year before, published Remembering. In it he reports his repeated-reproduction experiments: English people read a Native American tale, The War of the Ghosts, then retold it several times, at longer and longer intervals. Much of the story was forgotten, and what did not fit their culture disappeared or became familiar: canoes became boats. Bartlett drew from it a theory of schemas: remembering is not replaying a trace, it is reconstructing, from one's experience, knowledge and expectations. He also treats memory as a social fact and describes transmission-chain studies, in which a story passes from person to person.
textes.C'est le livre qui présente la mémoire c: It is the book that presents memory as a reconstruction rather than a recording.

textes.En 1841, le journaliste écossais Charles: In 1841, the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay published Memoirs of Extraordinary Popular Delusions, in three volumes: national delusions, peculiar follies and philosophical delusions. In it he gathers history's collective follies: three financial bubbles, Law's Mississippi scheme, the South Sea Bubble and tulip mania; but also the Crusades, the witch hunts of the 16th and 17th centuries, the alchemists, fortune-tellers, haunted houses, relics and prophecies. The 1852 edition reorganised it into two volumes; later editions took the title that stuck, Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds. The book has its own exaggerations: the historian Anne Goldgar does not find in the archives the general ruin it ascribes to tulip mania.

textes.Thucydide, général athénien exilé après: Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled after the loss of Amphipolis in 424 BC, tells of the war between Athens and Sparta from 431 BC. He brings in no god: he looks for human causes of events. He relies on witnesses, documents and what he saw himself, such as the plague of 430 BC, which he caught. The speeches he gives the actors, like Pericles' funeral oration, are reconstructions: he writes what each had to say, as close as possible to the sense of what was said. He wanted a work made to last for ever, rather than a piece to please for a moment. The account breaks off mid-sentence in 411 BC; scholars later divided it into eight books, and Xenophon continued it in his Hellenica.
textes.C'est le premier grand livre d'histoire: It is the first great history book to distrust rumours and seek causes without appealing to the gods.

textes.Le Lunheng, publié vers 80 sous les Han: The Lunheng, published around 80 AD under the Eastern Han, gathers 85 chapters, one of which keeps only its title. Its author, Wang Chong, was a poor scholar said to have learned by reading standing at the booksellers' stalls of Luoyang. He writes about natural science, mythology, philosophy and literature, often to rebut popular beliefs. Thunder is not a punishment from Heaven but an effect of fire or heat; Heaven has no purpose towards us, either benevolent or hostile; and if the dead became ghosts, they would outnumber the living. Wang Chong asks that what is too quickly attributed to divine will be put to the test of repeated experience.
textes.C'est l'un des grands livres sceptiques: It is one of the great sceptical books of ancient China: it demands evidence before blaming Heaven.
textes.Peu lu du vivant de son auteur, le livre: Little read in its author's lifetime, the book later won admirers: Cai Yong appreciated it, and Wang Lang took a copy to court in 198.

textes.Le Malleus maleficarum, ou Marteau des s: The Malleus Maleficarum, or Hammer of Witches, appeared in Speyer in 1486. Its main author is the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer; Jacob Sprenger was only associated with it from 1519, and his role is disputed. The preface reproduces Pope Innocent VIII's bull Summis desiderantes affectibus, of 1484, to suggest papal approval. textes.Thucydide l'observait déjà au Ve siècle: Thucydides already observed it in the 5th century BC: people entrust to careless hope what they long for and use reason to thrust aside what they do not fancy. Francis Bacon, in the Novum Organum, noted that the mind "draws all things else to support and agree with it".
textes.Peter Cathcart Wason invente ce test des: Peter Cathcart Wason devised this four-card test in 1966: in his study, not even 10% of participants found the right answer. The same rule becomes easy when it is about social exchange, such as the age for drinking alcohol.
textes.Le militant d'Internet Eli Pariser forge: Internet activist Eli Pariser coined the phrase "filter bubble" around 2010 and popularised it in 2011. He showed that two people searching "BP" on Google got investment news for one, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill for the other.
textes.Dans des expériences, on donne de fausse: In experiments, participants are given fake evidence, then told it was fake: part of the belief remains. Lee Ross and Craig Anderson concluded that beliefs can survive potent logical or empirical challenges.
textes.Francis Bacon le notait déjà au XVIIe si: Francis Bacon already noted it in the 17th century: a mind that has adopted an opinion draws in everything that supports it and neglects the rest.
textes.Tolstoï écrivait en 1894 que la chose la: Tolstoy wrote in 1894 that the simplest thing cannot be made clear to the most intelligent man if he is firmly persuaded that he knows it already. Recent studies show this bias depends more on the ability to reason than on the level of intelligence.
textes.Bertram Forer donne à ses 39 étudiants u: Bertram Forer gave his 39 students the same profile, presented as personal: they rated it 4.3 out of 5 on average. The text came from a newsstand astrology book. Paul Meehl named the effect after the showman P. T. Barnum in 1956.
textes.Dans l'étude de Stanford de 1979, chaque: In the 1979 Stanford study, each side judged the study that contradicted it to be flawed. The authors concluded that people set higher standards of evidence for hypotheses that go against their expectations.
textes.L'expression vient de l'acoustique, où l: The phrase comes from acoustics, where an echo chamber makes sounds bounce and repeat. Its real effect online is debated: according to several studies, it is weaker than often assumed.
textes.Wason n'emploie pas encore l'expression: Wason did not yet use the phrase in 1960. It was in rereading these results, which show a preference for confirmation over falsification, that he later coined the term "confirmation bias".
textes.Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman décriven: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described anchoring in 1974 with a rigged wheel stopping at 10 or 65: those who saw 10 estimated the share of African countries in the UN at 25% on average, those who saw 65, at 45%.
textes.Dans leur expérience de 1974, la roue ét: In their 1974 experiment, the wheel was rigged to stop at 10 or 65. That irrelevant number was enough to move the average estimate from 25% to 45%.
textes.Une étude de Kristensen et Gärling, en 1: A 1997 study by Kristensen and Gärling showed that the first offer weighs more on the outcome of a negotiation than the counter-offers that follow.
textes.En 1996, Wilson et ses collègues montren: In 1996, Wilson and colleagues showed that neither incentives nor warnings eliminate the anchoring effect.
textes.C'est l'expérience de Tversky et Kahnema: This is Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 experiment: with 10, the average estimate was 25%; with 65, 45%.
textes.En 2006, Englich et Mussweiler montrent: In 2006, Englich and Mussweiler showed that even experienced legal professionals are anchored. Early studies had thought experts more resistant.
textes.Huber, Payne et Puto décrivent ce leurre: Huber, Payne and Puto described this "asymmetrically dominated" decoy in 1982. Dan Ariely cites the real case of The Economist: nobody took the decoy offer, but removing it reversed the choices.
textes.Tversky et Kahneman décrivent cette heur: Tversky and Kahneman described this heuristic in 1973: we judge an event more frequent when examples come easily to mind.
Tversky and Kahneman described this heuristic in 1973. Massive coverage of rare events makes them more present in the mind, and so more likely in our eyes.
textes.C'est l'expérience de Tversky et Kahnema: This is Tversky and Kahneman's 1973 experiment: people think words starting with "k" are more common because they come to mind faster, whereas a typical text has twice as many with "k" as the third letter.
textes.Une attaque de requin fait la une, la mo: A shark attack makes headlines, death by falling aircraft parts almost never. As a result, people overestimate the first risk and underestimate the second, as Tversky and Kahneman described in 1973.
textes.Wald travaillait au Statistical Research: Wald worked at Columbia University's Statistical Research Group, which issued eight memoranda on analysing damaged combat aircraft. The planes hit in vital spots never came back to be counted.
textes.En 1973, Kahneman et Tversky montrent qu: In 1973, Kahneman and Tversky showed that students ignore grade statistics as soon as a particular student is described to them: we judge by resemblance, not by frequency.
textes.Kahneman introduit WYSIATI, « ce que tu: Kahneman introduced WYSIATI, "what you see is all there is", in Thinking, Fast and Slow, published in 2011, to explain overconfidence: the mind reasons with what it has and rarely accounts for what it lacks.
textes.Darwin l'avait remarqué : « L'ignorance: Darwin had noticed it: "Ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge." Kruger and Dunning received an Ig Nobel Prize for their paper in 2000. Some researchers see it mainly as a statistical artefact.
textes.L'article de 1999, dans le Journal of Pe: The 1999 paper, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, is titled "Unskilled and Unaware of It". In 2000 it earned its authors an Ig Nobel Prize.
textes.En 1995 à Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler b: In 1995 in Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler robbed banks bare-faced, his face smeared with lemon juice. His photo was shown on the 11 pm news on 19 April; he was arrested less than an hour later and protested: "But I wore the lemon juice."
textes.Le psychologue américain John Flavell do: The American psychologist John Flavell named metacognition in 1979. But Aristotle already discussed it in the 4th century BC, in his treatise On the Soul and the Parva Naturalia.
textes.En 1981, Ola Svenson interroge des étudi: In 1981, Ola Svenson surveyed students: 93% of the Americans and 69% of the Swedes put themselves in the top half of drivers. It is also called the "Lake Wobegon" effect, after the fictional town where all the children are above average.
textes.Kahneman et Tversky proposent l'erreur d: Kahneman and Tversky proposed the planning fallacy in 1979. The Sydney Opera House was meant to be finished in 1963 for 7 million dollars; a scaled-down version opened in 1973, for 102 million.
textes.Pauline Clance et Suzanne Imes décrivent: Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described this "impostor phenomenon" in 1978, in high-achieving women: an inner feeling of intellectual phoniness.
textes.Francis Bacon conseillait déjà cette mét: Francis Bacon already recommended this method in 1620, and William James noted in 1890 that memory retains better through active than passive repetition. The first experimental study was published by Edwina Abbott in 1909.
textes.Emily Pronin, à Princeton, crée l'expres: Emily Pronin, at Princeton, coined the phrase in 2002 with Daniel Lin and Lee Ross. In a survey of more than 600 Americans, over 85% judged themselves less biased than average; only one person judged themselves more biased.
textes.Kahneman et Tversky décrivent l'aversion: Kahneman and Tversky described loss aversion in prospect theory, published in 1979 in Econometrica. This work underpinned Kahneman's 2002 Nobel Prize in economics.
textes.Dans la théorie des perspectives (1979),: In prospect theory (1979), the pain of losing 1,000 dollars is only offset by the pleasure of gaining about 2,000.
textes.On l'appelle aussi « sophisme du Concord: It is also called the "Concorde fallacy": the British and French governments kept funding the supersonic plane long after it was clear it would not pay off.
textes.Richard Thaler nomme l'effet en 1980. Da: Richard Thaler named the effect in 1980. In the 1990 Cornell experiment, students who had been given a mug wanted about 7 dollars for it, while buyers offered only about 3.
textes.Samuelson et Zeckhauser le mettent en év: Samuelson and Zeckhauser demonstrated it with a questionnaire in 1988. In the early 1990s, New Jersey and Pennsylvania inadvertently ran the experiment: drivers mostly kept the default insurance option.
textes.En 2003, Eric Johnson et Daniel Goldstei: In 2003, Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein argued that this default rule, presumed consent or consent to be given, is the main cause of the gap in donor rates between countries.
textes.Barry Schwartz publie Le Paradoxe du cho: Barry Schwartz published The Paradox of Choice in 2004. A 2010 meta-analysis of 50 studies, however, found no meaningful link between abundant choice and anxiety.
textes.Les premières inversions de préférence o: The first preference reversals were observed in rats and pigeons, as in George Ainslie's 1974 study on impulse control in pigeons.
textes.Sur le conseil de Circé, Ulysse met de l: On Circe's advice, Ulysses put wax in his sailors' ears and had himself tied to the mast. Some psychiatric advance directives are today called "Ulysses pacts".
textes.Nudge, de Richard Thaler et Cass Sunstei: Nudge, by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, came out in 2008. It defends "libertarian paternalism": arranging how choices are presented without banning any. Thaler received the Nobel Prize in economics in 2017.
textes.Ce Nobel 2002 récompense la théorie des: This 2002 Nobel rewarded prospect theory, written with Amos Tversky and published in Econometrica in 1979.
textes.Herbert Simon forge l'expression ; il dé: Herbert Simon coined the phrase; he developed the idea in Models of Man, in 1957. He received the Nobel Prize in economics alone in 1978, and in 1975 the Turing Award with Allen Newell for his work on artificial intelligence.
textes.Edward Simpson le décrit en 1951, mais K: Edward Simpson described it in 1951, but Karl Pearson in 1899 and Udny Yule in 1903 had already noted similar effects. Colin Blyth gave it the name "Simpson's paradox" in 1972.
textes.L'étude de Bickel, Hammel et O'Connell,: The study by Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell, "Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data From Berkeley", was published in 1975 and became the classic example of Simpson's paradox.
textes.Les expressions « sophisme du procureur: The terms "prosecutor's fallacy" and "defense attorney's fallacy" were introduced in 1987 by William Thompson and Edward Schumann.
textes.L'expert, le pédiatre Roy Meadow, sous-e: The expert, the paediatrician Roy Meadow, also underestimated how often such deaths occur. The Royal Statistical Society issued a statement pointing out the errors, and Sally Clark's conviction was quashed on 29 January 2003.
textes.Francis Galton popularise l'idée à la fi: Francis Galton popularised the idea at the end of the 19th century, in 1886, with "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature". Kahneman showed it explains why rebukes seem to work and praise to backfire.
textes.Un sportif arrive en couverture après un: An athlete makes the cover after an exceptional run; their results then drift back toward average, which looks like a curse. Galton had described this regression as early as 1886.
textes.Le mot « p-hacking » est forgé en 2014 p: The word "p-hacking" was coined in 2014 by the three researchers behind the Data Colada blog. In 2015, journalist John Bohannon revealed he had rigged a study on chocolate for weight loss: it took 18 variables to get below p < 0.05.
textes.Darrell Huff le décrit en 1954 dans Comm: Darrell Huff described it in 1954 in How to Lie with Statistics, illustrated by Irving Geis: cutting off the bottom of a chart magnifies differences. It is one of the best-selling statistics books in history.
textes.Le raisonnement vient de Thomas Bayes :: The reasoning comes from Thomas Bayes: his essay, reworked by Richard Price after his death, appeared in 1763. Laplace found the same rule independently in 1774.
textes.Le Literary Digest avait envoyé 10 milli: The Literary Digest had sent out 10 million ballots and got 2.38 million replies, drawn from lists of telephone users and car owners. George Gallup, with only 50,000 people, got it right. The magazine folded in 1938.
textes.Joseph Berkson montre en 1946 qu'étudier: Joseph Berkson showed in 1946 that studying only hospital patients creates false associations between diseases, because people end up in hospital precisely because they are ill.
textes.Des chercheurs parlent d'un « détecteur: Researchers speak of a "hyperactive agent detection device": wrongly imagining a predator behind a snapping twig costs little, while missing a real one can be fatal.
textes.Le cliché de Viking 1 date du 25 juillet: The Viking 1 image dates from 25 July 1976. The sharper images from Mars Global Surveyor led NASA to describe a natural hill whose face-like look depends on the viewing angle.
textes.La maxime paraît en 1980 dans un livre d: The maxim appeared in 1980 in a book by Arthur Bloch on Murphy's law, attributed to a certain Robert J. Hanlon. Robert Heinlein had written in 1941: "You have attributed conditions to villainy that simply result from stupidity."
textes.Gérald Bronner publie La Démocratie des: Gérald Bronner published La Démocratie des crédules in 2013, then Apocalypse cognitive in January 2021. He shows how hoaxes and fake news pile up in layers of arguments.
textes.Une étude a montré que croire que Ben La: One study showed that believing Bin Laden was already dead before his compound in Pakistan was raided makes people more likely to believe… that he is still alive.
textes.Skinner nourrissait des pigeons à interv: Skinner fed pigeons at regular intervals, whatever they did. The birds started repeating "rituals": they behaved, he wrote, as if there were a causal relation between their behaviour and the food.
textes.L'Américaine Dorothy Martin annonçait un: The American Dorothy Martin predicted a flood before dawn on 21 December 1954. Festinger, Riecken and Schachter infiltrated her group, the Seekers, and published When Prophecy Fails in 1956. Archival work has since cast doubt on part of the account.
textes.En 2007, Leman et Cinnirella font lire à: In 2007, Leman and Cinnirella had 64 participants read about the assassination, attempted or successful, of a fictional president: the graver the consequences, the more they believed in a conspiracy.
textes.L'étude de Tuskegee dure de 1932 à 1972: The Tuskegee study ran from 1932 to 1972: 399 Black men with syphilis were left untreated, even after 1947 when penicillin became standard therapy. Whistleblower Peter Buxtun had it exposed by Jean Heller of the Associated Press in July 1972.
textes.James Randi lance son défi en 1964 avec: James Randi launched his challenge in 1964 with 1,000 dollars; a friend, Rick Adams, raised it to a million in 1996. About a thousand people applied, none succeeded, and the challenge ended in 2015.
textes.Le nom vient de Fiona Broome, chercheuse: The name comes from Fiona Broome, a paranormal researcher, who remembered news coverage of Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s. He died in 2013.
textes.L'idée est ancienne : Hume écrivait en 1: The idea is old: Hume wrote in 1748 that testimony loses force the more unusual the fact, and Laplace that the weight of evidence must be proportioned to the strangeness of the claim. Marcello Truzzi had put it this way in 1978.
textes.Gary Klein décrit la méthode en 2007 dan: Gary Klein described the method in 2007 in the Harvard Business Review: you start from the assumption that "the patient has died". It formalises the "prospective hindsight" studied by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington in 1989.
textes.L'idée vient de Kahneman et Tversky. Ben: The idea comes from Kahneman and Tversky. In 2004 Bent Flyvbjerg turned it into a practical method, reference class forecasting, published in June 2004 by the UK Department for Transport.
textes.Dans le Good Judgment Project de Tetlock: In Tetlock's Good Judgment Project, the best forecasters did about 30% better than the average intelligence analyst with access to secret data. Tetlock told the story in Superforecasting, in 2015, with Dan Gardner.
textes.Philip Tetlock publie ces résultats en 2: Philip Tetlock published these results in 2005 in Expert Political Judgment: experts often predict no better than other people, and are rarely held to account when wrong.
textes.Le théorème de Thomas Bayes paraît en 17: Thomas Bayes's theorem appeared in 1763 after his death, edited by Richard Price. Harold Jeffreys said it is to probability theory what Pythagoras's theorem is to geometry.
textes.Karl Pearson regroupe dès 1904 plusieurs: Karl Pearson pooled several studies on the typhoid vaccine as early as 1904. The word "meta-analysis" was coined in 1976 by the statistician Gene Glass: "the analysis of analyses".
textes.Le mot vient du grec zētētikós, « qui ai: The word comes from the Greek zētētikós, "one who likes to search", a name given to the sceptics who followed Pyrrho. Henri Broch revived it in the 1980s and founded the zetetics laboratory at the University of Nice in 1998.
textes.Cicéron raconte qu'on montra à Diagoras: Cicero tells how Diagoras of Melos was shown the votive paintings of sailors saved from shipwreck. He replied that the pictures of those who drowned were missing, and they were far more numerous.
textes.L'Allemand Karl Kahlbaum introduit le mo: The German Karl Kahlbaum introduced the word in 1866, from the Greek pará, "beside", and eídōlon, "image". Leonardo da Vinci already advised painters to look for scenes in the stains on walls.
textes.Dans les Réfutations sophistiques, Arist: In the Sophistical Refutations, Aristotle draws up:
textes.un catalogue des faux raisonnements qui: a catalogue of false reasonings that look valid
textes.un traité de rhétorique pour gagner les: a rhetoric manual for winning lawsuits
textes.Un sophisme est un raisonnement qui a l': A sophism is a reasoning that looks like a proof without being one. Naming them is learning to spot them.
textes.Les Réfutations sophistiques font partie: The Sophistical Refutations belong to the Organon, Aristotle's set of treatises on logic. Six of its fallacies depend on language: equivocation, amphiboly, composition, division, accent and form of expression.
textes.« Chaque joueur de l'équipe est excellen: "Every player on the team is excellent, so the team is excellent." This fallacy of Aristotle's is called:
textes.la composition : prêter au tout ce qui v: composition: giving the whole what holds for its parts
textes.Ce qui est vrai de chaque partie ne l'es: What is true of each part is not necessarily true of the whole. The reverse error, giving each part what holds for the whole, is called division.
textes.Aristote range la composition et la divi: Aristotle counts composition and division among the fallacies that arise from language, alongside equivocation: one word taken in two senses.
textes.Pour les sceptiques pyrrhoniens, suspend: For the Pyrrhonian sceptics, suspending judgement (epoché) leads to:
textes.Le pyrrhonien ne dit ni oui ni non : il: The Pyrrhonist says neither yes nor no: he notes that every argument meets an argument of equal force. Ceasing to decide frees him from worry.
textes.Pyrrhon d'Élis, qui a donné son nom à l': Pyrrho of Elis, who gave the school its name, went with Alexander the Great as far as India, where he met the gymnosophists, naked sages.
textes.Lequel de ces arguments fait partie des: Which of these arguments is one of Agrippa's five modes?
textes.Les cinq modes : le désaccord, la régres: The five modes: dissent, infinite regress, relativity, hypothesis and circularity. Together, they show that no justification comes to rest on firm ground.
textes.On ne connaît Agrippa que par Sextus Emp: Agrippa is known only through Sextus Empiricus, who reports his five modes. Before him, Aenesidemus, in the 1st century BC, had proposed ten.
textes.Combien de modes du doute Agrippa propos: How many modes of doubt does Agrippa propose?
textes.Cinq : désaccord, régression à l'infini,: Five: dissent, infinite regress, relativity, hypothesis, circularity. Aenesidemus counted ten; Agrippa tightens them.
textes.Tous les modes mènent au même point : l': All the modes lead to the same point: epoché, suspension of judgement.
textes.« Ce journal est fiable : il l'écrit lui: "This paper is reliable: it says so itself in its editorial." Which of Agrippa's modes targets this argument?
textes.la circularité : la preuve suppose ce qu: circularity: the proof assumes what it proves
textes.Le journal se sert de sa propre parole p: The paper uses its own word to vouch for its word: the conclusion is already in the premise.
textes.Sextus Empiricus était aussi médecin, de: Sextus Empiricus was also a physician, of the so-called Empiric school, which relied on observation rather than hidden causes. He lived around the late 2nd century.
textes.En 1562, les Esquisses pyrrhoniennes de: In 1562, Sextus Empiricus' Outlines of Pyrrhonism returned to Europe thanks to:
textes.une traduction latine d'Henri Estienne,: a Latin translation by Henri Estienne, printed in Geneva
textes.un manuscrit offert au pape: a manuscript given to the pope
textes.L'imprimerie fait circuler le doute anti: Printing spread ancient doubt: within a few decades, European scholars were reading the Greek sceptics' arguments.
textes.Cette traduction a profondément marqué M: This translation deeply marked Montaigne. The Greek text itself was printed only in 1621.
textes.Qui écrit que celui qui étudie les livre: Who wrote that whoever studies the books of scientists must "make himself an enemy of all that he reads"?
textes.Le savant arabe recommande d'attaquer un: The Arab scholar advises attacking a text from every side, and suspecting oneself during the examination, so as to fall into neither prejudice nor leniency.
textes.Il applique ce programme dans ses Doutes: He applied this programme in his Doubts concerning Ptolemy, published between 1025 and 1028: he lists the contradictions of the Greek astronomer Ptolemy.
textes.Selon ses biographes, Ibn al-Haytham aur: According to his biographers, Ibn al-Haytham feigned madness to escape the anger of the caliph al-Hakim.
textes.Il avait promis de régler les crues du N: He had promised to regulate the Nile floods, then realised it was impossible. He reportedly played mad, then lived in hiding until the caliph's death, in 1021.
textes.C'est dans ces années qu'il écrit son Li: It was during these years that he wrote his Book of Optics (1011-1021), in which he describes the camera obscura and holds that light enters the eye.
textes.Le premier précepte de la méthode de Des: The first precept of Descartes' method asks you to:
textes.ne rien tenir pour vrai qu'on ne connais: hold nothing true that one does not know clearly and distinctly
textes.Les trois autres préceptes : diviser cha: The three other precepts: divide each difficulty, go from the simplest to the most complex, review everything so as to omit nothing.
textes.Le Discours de la méthode paraît sans no: The Discourse on Method appeared anonymously in Leiden in 1637, in French rather than Latin, as a preface to three essays: the Dioptrics, the Meteorology and the Geometry.
textes.diviser chaque difficulté pour mieux l'e: dividing each difficulty to examine it better
textes.Un problème trop gros se découpe en morc: A problem that is too big is cut into pieces that can be examined one by one. It is still used to debug a program or check a rumour.
textes.Descartes écrit en français, la « langue: Descartes wrote in French, the "vulgar tongue", to be read beyond the scholars who read Latin; men of letters soon identified him as the author.
textes.Le doute de Descartes est un doute métho: Descartes' doubt is methodical: he doubts in order to find a certainty, not to give up on all truth.
textes.Le pyrrhonien suspend son jugement pour: The Pyrrhonist suspends judgement to be at peace; Descartes doubts everything once, then builds on what resists doubt.
textes.Les Esquisses pyrrhoniennes, très lues e: The Outlines of Pyrrhonism, widely read in Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries, nourished a line of French thinkers: Montaigne, Descartes, Pascal.
textes.Dans l'expérience de Solomon Asch (1951): In Solomon Asch's experiment (1951), the participants had to:
textes.dire laquelle de trois lignes avait la m: say which of three lines matched a model line in length
textes.deviner le nombre de billes dans un boca: guess the number of marbles in a jar
textes.La tâche était facile : seuls, presque t: The task was easy: alone, almost everyone answered correctly. But the other "participants" were confederates who unanimously gave a wrong answer.
textes.L'expérience se déroule au Swarthmore Co: The experiment took place at Swarthmore College, in Pennsylvania, with 50 students. In the control group, with no confederates, errors stayed under 1%.
textes.Chez Asch, quelle part des participants: In Asch's study, what share of the participants followed the majority's error at least once?
textes.Environ 74 % ont cédé au moins une fois: About 74% gave in at least once; about a quarter never did. Across all critical trials, a little over a third of answers followed the group.
textes.Chaque participant passait 18 essais, do: Each participant went through 18 trials, 12 of them "critical", in which the confederates gave the same wrong answer.
textes.Dans une variante d'Asch, un seul compli: In a variant of Asch's study, a single confederate gives the right answer. What happens to conformity?
textes.elle s'effondre : un seul allié suffit à: it collapses: one ally is enough to resist
textes.le participant suit l'allié dans l'erreu: the participant follows the ally into error
textes.L'unanimité fait la force du groupe. Ave: Unanimity is what gives the group its power. With one partner telling the truth, only 5% of participants keep following the majority.
textes.Asch résume son inquiétude : que des jeu: Asch summed up his concern: that intelligent, well-meaning young people are willing to call white black is a matter of concern.
textes.Chez Asch, quand les participants écrive: In Asch's study, when participants write their answer instead of saying it aloud, they conform less.
textes.La pression du groupe tient en partie au: Group pressure partly rests on others' eyes. A private answer frees judgement: the secret ballot rests on the same idea.
textes.Les variantes d'Asch montrent aussi le p: Asch's variants also show the weight of unanimity: a single dissenter in the group is enough to make conformity drop.
textes.le journaliste William H. Whyte, dans Fo: the journalist William H. Whyte, in Fortune
Whyte borrowed it from Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. The psychologist Irving Janis, without citing him, coined it again twenty years later and turned it into a theory.
textes.Irving Janis, professeur à Yale, publie: Irving Janis, a professor at Yale, published Victims of Groupthink in 1972 and described eight symptoms, including the illusion of unanimity and self-censorship.
textes.Quel fiasco Irving Janis prend-il comme: Which fiasco does Irving Janis take as the textbook case of groupthink?
