textes.On a mesuré la Terre pour fabriquer une: They measured the Earth to make a ruler. You don't even measure the extent of your ignorance.
textes.En 1803, devant la Royal Society, Thomas: In 1803, before the Royal Society, Thomas Young describes a simple experiment: a thin beam of sunlight, split in two by a paper card. On the screen, the two halves overlap in light and dark bands, interference fringes, like waves that add up or cancel out. It is a strong argument for light made of waves, against Newton's corpuscle theory.
textes.Deux ondes peuvent s'annuler. Vos deux d: Two waves can cancel each other out. So can your last two answers.
textes.En 1824, le jeune ingénieur Sadi Carnot: In 1824, the young engineer Sadi Carnot publishes in Paris a small book: Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire. In it he seeks a general theory of steam engines, and sketches what will become the second law of thermodynamics. Nobody notices. Carnot dies in 1832, at 36, having published nothing else. Two years later, Émile Clapeyron puts his ideas into graphs, then Clausius and Kelvin make a science of them.
textes.Un seul livre, ignoré de son vivant, dev: A single book, ignored in his lifetime, became a science. You still have time to be ignored.
textes.Le cor du train d'Utrecht: The horn on the Utrecht train
textes.En 1842, l'Autrichien Christian Doppler: In 1842, the Austrian Christian Doppler proposes that a source that is approaching emits a higher wave, and a lower one when it moves away. He is thinking of the colour of double stars. On 3 June 1845, the Dutchman Buys Ballot tests it with sound: a horn player plays on a train between Utrecht and Maarssen, and observers with good ears listen on the platform. The note rises as the train approaches, then falls.
textes.Plus vous approchez de la bonne réponse,: The closer you get to the right answer, the higher my voice goes. I don't sing often.
textes.En 1842, l'Allemand Julius Robert von Ma: In 1842, the German Julius Robert von Mayer proposes that work and heat are exchanged in a fixed proportion. In 1843, the Englishman James Prescott Joule argues it independently, and in 1845 he publishes a measurement: 778 foot-pounds to heat a pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. The two men long disputed priority. The unit of energy is named after Joule today.
Joule turned work into heat. You turn my questions into sweat.
textes.En février 1851, Léon Foucault montre à: In February 1851, Léon Foucault shows at the Paris Observatory a pendulum whose plane of swing slowly turns. A few weeks later, he hangs a 28-kilogram bob on a 67-metre wire under the dome of the Panthéon. The pendulum keeps its direction; it is the floor that turns beneath it. At the latitude of Paris, the plane drifts by about 11 degrees an hour. The Earth's rotation becomes visible to the naked eye.
textes.La Terre tourne, Foucault l'a montré. Vo: The Earth turns, Foucault showed it. You go round in circles.
textes.En 1887, à Cleveland, Albert Michelson e: In 1887, in Cleveland, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley look for the aether, the medium in which light was supposed to travel. Their interferometer, set on a sandstone block floating on mercury, compares the speed of light in two directions. They expected a fringe shift of about 0.4; they measure at most 0.02. Nothing. The most famous failed experiment in history paves the way for Einstein's special relativity, which does without the aether.
textes.Ne rien trouver peut tout changer. Ne vo: Finding nothing can change everything. Don't use that as an excuse.
textes.Le 14 décembre 1900, à Berlin, Max Planc: On 14 December 1900, in Berlin, Max Planck presents to the German Physical Society his law of black-body radiation. To make it fit the measurements, he has to assume that energy is emitted in small packets, quanta, proportional to frequency. He would say he did it as an act of desperation. This date is taken as the birth of quantum physics. Planck receives the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918.
textes.Planck a inventé les quanta par désespoi: Planck invented quanta out of desperation. I know the feeling, I make you review.
textes.En 1877, l'Autrichien Ludwig Boltzmann r: In 1877, the Austrian Ludwig Boltzmann links the entropy of a gas to the number of ways its molecules can be arranged without anything changing at our scale: the more ways, the more likely the disorder. Planck would put the formula in its current form, S = k log W. But Mach and Ostwald do not believe in atoms, and Boltzmann has to fight them. He takes his own life in 1906, two years before Jean Perrin proves that atoms exist. His formula is engraved on his tomb in Vienna.
textes.Le désordre est le plus probable, disait: Disorder is the most likely state, said Boltzmann. Your room and your answers prove him right.
textes.Selon la relativité générale d'Einstein,: According to Einstein's general relativity, the Sun should bend starlight twice as much as Newton predicts. On 29 May 1919, during a total eclipse, two British expeditions photograph the stars near the Sun, one on the island of Príncipe with Arthur Eddington, the other at Sobral, in Brazil. On 6 November, the results prove Einstein right, and the world's press goes wild. Eddington was later suspected of sorting his plates; a new measurement in 1979 nonetheless confirmed the result.
textes.Il a fallu éteindre le Soleil pour donne: It took switching off the Sun to prove Einstein right. For you, a simple lamp will do.
textes.En 1927, l'Allemand Werner Heisenberg pu: In 1927, the German Werner Heisenberg publishes a baffling principle: you cannot know both the position and the speed of a particle with perfect precision. The more precise one is, the blurrier the other. He himself explained it with a microscope that jostles the electron as it lights it up. We now know it goes deeper: the blur is not a flaw in our instruments, it comes from the wave nature of matter.
textes.Plus je sais où vous en êtes, moins je s: The better I know where you are, the less I know where you're going. Heisenberg would have loved you.
textes.Le 14 septembre 2015, les deux détecteur: On 14 September 2015, the two LIGO detectors in the United States record a shiver of spacetime. It comes from the merger of two black holes of 36 and 29 solar masses, more than a billion years ago. Three solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves. As they passed, the detectors' length changed by about a thousandth of a proton's width. Einstein had predicted them in 1916. Announced in February 2016, Nobel Prize in 2017.
textes.Mesurer un millième de proton. Et vous n: Measuring a thousandth of a proton. And you can't measure the time you spend on your phone.
textes.Le Système international, les préfixes e: The International System, prefixes and the sizes of the world.
textes.Sept unités de base du SI : mètre, kilog: Seven SI base units: meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela. Since 2019, all are defined by constants.
textes.Préfixes : kilo 10³, méga 10⁶, giga 10⁹,: Prefixes: kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, tera 10¹²; milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹.
textes.Un ordre de grandeur, c'est la puissance: An order of magnitude is the nearest power of 10: a human ≈ 1 m, a cell ≈ 10 µm, an atom ≈ 0.1 nm.
textes.Le poids (newtons) n'est pas la masse (k: Weight (newtons) is not mass (kilograms): on the Moon, mass doesn't change, weight is divided by six.
textes.1 km² vaut 1 000 000 m², pas 1 000 : on: 1 km² is 1,000,000 m², not 1,000: the prefix gets squared too.
textes.Les tailles du monde en puissances de 10: The sizes of the world in powers of 10
textes.1re loi : sans force nette, un objet gar: 1st law: with no net force, an object keeps its velocity. Motion doesn't need a force to continue.
textes.2e loi : F = m × a. La même force accélè: 2nd law: F = m × a. The same force accelerates a more massive object less.
textes.3e loi : action et réaction sont égales: 3rd law: action and reaction are equal and opposite, and act on two different objects.
textes.Dans le vide, une plume et un marteau to: In a vacuum, a feather and a hammer fall together (David Scott on the Moon, 1971).
textes.Un objet lancé n'emporte pas de « force: A thrown object doesn't carry a “force of the throw”: once released, only weight and air act on it.
textes.F = m × a : la force change la vitesse,: F = m × a: force changes velocity, not the fact of moving
textes.Première loi de Newton : sans force nett: Newton's first law: with no net force, velocity doesn't change
textes.Énergie cinétique et potentielle, puissa: Kinetic and potential energy, power, conservation.
textes.Énergie cinétique ½ m v² : doubler la vi: Kinetic energy ½ m v²: doubling the speed quadruples the energy, and the braking distance.
textes.Énergie potentielle de pesanteur m g h :: Gravitational potential energy m g h: it turns into kinetic energy during a fall.
textes.L'énergie se conserve : elle change de f: Energy is conserved: it changes form (heat, motion, light) but doesn't disappear.
textes.La puissance est un débit d'énergie : 1: Power is a rate of energy: 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
textes.À 100 km/h, l'énergie n'est pas deux foi: At 100 km/h, the energy isn't twice that at 50 km/h but four times.
textes.Son, lumière, fréquences, couleurs et ef: Sound, light, frequencies, colors and the Doppler effect.
textes.Une onde transporte de l'énergie sans tr: A wave carries energy without carrying matter. Speed = wavelength × frequency.
textes.Le son a besoin d'un milieu (≈ 340 m/s d: Sound needs a medium (≈ 340 m/s in air); light crosses a vacuum (≈ 300,000 km/s).
textes.Lumière visible : de 400 nm (violet) à 7: Visible light: from 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Shorter wavelength, more energy.
textes.Effet Doppler : une source qui s'approch: Doppler effect: an approaching source sounds higher-pitched, a receding one lower.
textes.Le ciel est bleu parce que l'air diffuse: The sky is blue because air scatters short wavelengths more, not because it reflects the sea.
textes.Spectre visible du violet (400 nm) au ro: Visible spectrum from violet (400 nm) to red (700 nm)
textes.Pression, poussée d'Archimède, flottaiso: Pressure, Archimedes' buoyancy, floating and flows.
textes.Pression = force ÷ surface. Une aiguille: Pressure = force ÷ area. A needle pierces because its area is tiny.
textes.Sous l'eau, la pression augmente d'envir: Underwater, pressure rises by about 1 bar every 10 meters.
textes.Archimède : tout corps plongé reçoit une: Archimedes: any immersed body receives an upward thrust equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
textes.Un objet flotte si sa masse volumique mo: An object floats if its average density is lower than that of the liquid: a steel liner is full of air.
textes.Un glaçon qui fond dans un verre plein n: An ice cube melting in a full glass doesn't make it overflow: it was already displacing its weight in water.
textes.Température, chaleur, entropie et machin: Temperature, heat, entropy and heat engines.
textes.Température et chaleur diffèrent : la te: Temperature and heat differ: temperature measures agitation, heat is a transfer of energy.
textes.La chaleur va spontanément du chaud vers: Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold (second law).
textes.L'entropie d'un système isolé ne diminue: The entropy of an isolated system doesn't decrease: that's why a broken egg doesn't stick back together.
textes.Une machine thermique ne convertit jamai: A heat engine never converts all heat into work: Carnot efficiency sets the limit.
textes.Le métal paraît plus froid que le bois à: Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature: it draws heat from your hand faster.
textes.seule la différence est convertie en tra: only the difference is converted into work
textes.Une machine thermique prend de la chaleu: A heat engine takes heat from the hot side, gives part of it back to the cold side
textes.Vitesse de la lumière, temps dilaté, E =: Speed of light, dilated time, E = mc² and Einstein's gravitation.
textes.La vitesse de la lumière dans le vide es: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers: 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.Le temps passe plus lentement pour une h: Time passes more slowly for a fast-moving clock (time dilation).
textes.E = mc² : la masse est une forme d'énerg: E = mc²: mass is a form of energy; a little mass contains an enormous amount of energy.
textes.Relativité générale : la gravitation cou: General relativity: gravitation curves spacetime. GPS corrects about 38 µs per day.
textes.Rien de massif ne peut atteindre la vite: Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light: the energy needed becomes infinite.
textes.Le facteur de dilatation du temps explos: The time dilation factor explodes near the speed of light
textes.Photons, dualité onde-particule, incerti: Photons, wave-particle duality, uncertainty and atoms.
textes.La lumière est faite de photons ; l'éner: Light is made of photons; a photon's energy is proportional to its frequency (E = h f).
textes.Dualité onde-particule : électrons et ph: Wave-particle duality: electrons and photons interfere, like waves, and arrive one by one, like grains.
textes.Principe d'incertitude : on ne peut conn: Uncertainty principle: you cannot know both the exact position and the exact velocity of a particle.
textes.Dans un atome, l'électron n'a que certai: In an atom, the electron only has certain energy levels; it emits a photon when it drops a level.
textes.L'incertitude n'est pas un défaut des in: Uncertainty isn't a flaw of instruments: it's a property of nature.
textes.Expérience des fentes d'Young : des part: Young's double-slit experiment: particles that interfere
textes.Chauffer 1 kg d'eau de 1 °C demande envi: Heating 1 kg of water by 1 °C takes about 4,184 J (Q = m × c × ΔT), and 1 W is 1 joule per second: time = energy ÷ power.
textes.Accélération moyenne = variation de vite: Average acceleration = change in speed ÷ time, in m/s².
textes.Fréquence = 1 ÷ période : une période de: Frequency = 1 ÷ period: a period of 0.01 s gives 100 Hz.
textes.La lumière du Soleil, à 150 millions de: Sunlight, from 150 million km away, takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
textes.7 unités de base (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, c: 7 base units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd). Since 2019, all defined by constants of nature.
textes.Le Système international repose sur sept: The International System rests on seven base units: the metre, the kilogram, the second, the ampere, the kelvin, the mole and the candela. All the others are derived from them: the newton is a kg·m/s², the joule a newton times a metre, the watt a joule per second.
textes.Depuis 1889, le kilogramme était un obje: From 1889 the kilogram was an object: a platinum-iridium cylinder kept at Sèvres. Problem: its copies drifted relative to it, by up to 20 micrograms a year, with no way of telling which was changing. Since 20 May 2019, no unit depends on an object any more: the kilogram is defined by fixing the exact value of the Planck constant, as the metre is by the speed of light.
textes.Les préfixes et le piège des carrés: Prefixes and the trap of squares
textes.Préfixes par mille (k, M, G, T ; m, µ, n: Prefixes go by thousands (k, M, G, T; m, µ, n). For an area the prefix is squared; for a volume, cubed.
textes.Le piège, ce sont les surfaces et les vo: The trap is areas and volumes: the prefix is squared or cubed too. 1 km² is 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000 m². 1 m³ is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 cm³. And 1 litre is a cube with 10 cm sides, 1 dm³.
textes.La sonde perdue pour une unité: The probe lost over a unit
textes.Toujours écrire l'unité. Masse (kg) ≠ po: Always write the unit. Mass (kg) ≠ weight (N): on the Moon, same mass, weight divided by 6.
A value without a unit means nothing. In September 1999 the Mars Climate Orbiter probe got too close to Mars and vanished. The cause: ground software supplied impulses in pound-force seconds, imperial units, while another program read them as newton seconds. A factor of 4.45 apart, and a probe lost.
textes.Autre confusion fréquente : la masse et: Another common confusion: mass and weight. Mass, in kilograms, is the amount of matter; it does not change from one world to another. Weight, in newtons, is the force with which a world pulls on you. On the Moon an astronaut keeps their mass, but their weight is divided by about six.
textes.Le mouvement n'a pas besoin de moteur: Motion does not need an engine
textes.Sans force nette, la vitesse ne change p: With no net force, velocity does not change (1st law). A force changes motion; it does not keep it going.
textes.Une balle lancée n'emporte donc pas de «: So a thrown ball does not carry a "force of the throw": once released, only its weight and the air act on it. And the Moon does not fall because the Earth pulls it while letting it fly on: without gravity, inertia would send it off in a straight line.
textes.F = m × a (2e loi). Action et réaction s: F = m × a (2nd law). Action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on two different objects (3rd law).
textes.La deuxième loi dit ce que fait une forc: The second law says what a force does: it accelerates, and less so the more massive the object. F = m × a: 20 newtons accelerate 10 kg at 2 m/s². Newton stated it in 1687 in the Principia, but in words; Euler wrote it as an equation in the 18th century.
textes.La troisième loi : quand A pousse B, B p: The third law: when A pushes B, B pushes A with the same force, in the opposite direction. The two forces act on two different objects, which is why they do not cancel out. A rocket pushes its gases backwards, the gases push the rocket forwards; no air is needed to push against.
textes.Dans le vide, tout tombe ensemble (g ≈ 9: In a vacuum, everything falls together (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²). Speed = g × t, distance = ½ g t².
textes.Sans air, tous les objets tombent avec l: Without air, all objects fall with the same acceleration, about 9.8 m/s² at the Earth's surface, whatever their mass. On 2 August 1971, on the Moon, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together: they hit the ground at the same time.
textes.Après une seconde de chute libre, un obj: After one second of free fall, an object is moving at about 9.8 m/s, but has only fallen 4.9 m: speed grows with time, distance with the square of time. On Earth, it is the air that slows the feather, not its lightness.
textes.L'énergie se conserve et change de forme: Energy is conserved and changes form. Joule (1845): heat is a form of energy. No efficiency above 100 %.
textes.L'énergie ne se crée pas et ne disparaît: Energy is neither created nor destroyed: it changes form. Water at the top of a dam has potential energy, m g h; as it falls it converts it into motion, then the turbine into electricity, then your lamp into light and heat.
textes.Il a fallu prouver que la chaleur en fai: It had to be proved that heat is part of it. In 1845 James Joule showed that the same amount of mechanical work, spent as friction in water, always warms it by the same amount: heat and work are two forms of the same thing. That is why no machine can give back more than 100 % of what it receives: perpetual motion does not exist.
textes.Deux fois plus vite, quatre fois plus d': Twice as fast, four times the energy
textes.Énergie cinétique = ½ m v² : vitesse × 2: Kinetic energy = ½ m v²: speed × 2 → energy × 4 → braking distance × 4.
textes.L'énergie de mouvement, l'énergie cinéti: The energy of motion, kinetic energy, is ½ m v². It grows with the square of the speed: at 100 km/h a car does not have twice the energy it has at 50 km/h, but four times.
textes.Cette énergie, les freins doivent la tra: The brakes must turn that energy into heat. For the same braking force, the braking distance is therefore also multiplied by four when speed doubles. Leibniz was already measuring a body's "living force" by m v² in 1686; Coriolis added the ½ in 1829, so that its change exactly equals the work of the forces.
textes.Puissance = énergie ÷ temps (W = J/s). k: Power = energy ÷ time (W = J/s). kWh = energy: 1 kWh = 3.6 million J.
textes.Le kilowattheure de votre facture n'est: The kilowatt-hour on your bill is not a power but an energy: a power sustained over a time. 1 kWh = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3.6 million joules. The 10 W bulb left on for 100 hours uses 1 kWh. The calories on food labels are energy too: one kilocalorie is about 4,184 joules.
textes.Une onde transporte de l'énergie, pas de: A wave carries energy, not matter
textes.Vitesse = longueur d'onde × fréquence ;: Speed = wavelength × frequency; frequency = 1 ÷ period. Sound ≈ 340 m/s in air, nothing in a vacuum.
textes.Quand une vague passe, le bouchon monte: When a wave passes, the cork goes up and down but does not travel with it. A wave carries energy without carrying matter away. Its speed is its wavelength times its frequency, and frequency is the inverse of the period: a period of 0.01 s gives 100 Hz.
textes.Visible : 400 nm (violet) à 700 nm (roug: Visible: 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Blue sky: air scatters short wavelengths far more (Rayleigh).
textes.La lumière visible va d'environ 400 nm,: Visible light runs from about 400 nm, violet, to 700 nm, red. Beyond that the eye sees nothing: ultraviolet and X-rays on one side, infrared, microwaves and radio waves on the other. They are all electromagnetic waves, differing only in wavelength.
textes.Les molécules d'air diffusent la lumière: Air molecules scatter light more strongly the shorter its wavelength, as the inverse fourth power: that is Rayleigh scattering, described by Lord Rayleigh from 1871. Blue is therefore sent in every direction far more than red, and the sky looks blue. At sunset, light crosses a lot of air, loses its blue on the way, and the sun turns red.
textes.Source qui approche : fréquence plus hau: Approaching source: higher frequency; receding: lower (Doppler, 1842). Used in radars and astronomy.
textes.Une ambulance qui s'approche paraît plus: An approaching ambulance sounds higher, then lower as it moves away. When the source moves forward, it catches up with its own waves and bunches them: the received frequency goes up. When it moves away, it stretches them: the frequency goes down. That is the Doppler effect, proposed by Christian Doppler in 1842 and tested with sound by Buys Ballot in 1845.
textes.Le même effet vaut pour la lumière et le: The same effect applies to light and radio waves. Police radars measure a car's speed from the frequency shift of the reflected wave. And astronomers read in the red or blue shift of a star's light whether it is moving away or approaching.
textes.Une force étalée sur une surface: A force spread over an area
textes.Pression = force ÷ surface. Sous l'eau :: Pressure = force ÷ area. Under water: +1 bar every 10 m, whatever the shape of the container (Stevin, 1586).
textes.La pression, c'est une force divisée par: Pressure is a force divided by an area. A needle pierces skin with a tiny force because its tip is minute; snowshoes carry the same weight over a large area, and you no longer sink in.
textes.Sous l'eau, chaque mètre ajoute le poids: Under water, every metre adds the weight of the water above: about 1 bar every 10 metres, one more atmosphere. Simon Stevin showed in 1586 that this pressure depends only on the height of liquid, not the shape of the container. At 30 m a diver is therefore under about 4 bars: 1 for the air, 3 for the water.
textes.L'air pèse : baromètre de Torricelli (16: Air has weight: Torricelli's barometer (1643), Puy de Dôme (1648), Magdeburg hemispheres (1654). ≈ 1,013 hPa at sea level.
textes.L'air aussi pèse. En 1643, Evangelista T: Air has weight too. In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli turned a tube full of mercury upside down in a basin: the column dropped and settled at about 76 cm. Above it, a vacuum; what holds the column up is the air pressing on the basin. He had just invented the barometer.
textes.En 1648, à la demande de Pascal, son bea: In 1648, at Pascal's request, his brother-in-law Florin Périer took the barometer to the top of the Puy de Dôme: the column dropped by about 8 cm there, because there is less air above. In 1654 Otto von Guericke pumped the air out from between two copper hemispheres at Magdeburg: two teams of horses could not pull them apart. At sea level, air presses with about 1,013 hPa.
textes.Poussée d'Archimède = poids du fluide dé: Buoyancy = weight of the displaced fluid. It floats if it is less dense than the liquid, on average.
textes.Tout corps plongé dans un fluide reçoit: Any body immersed in a fluid gets an upward push equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. An object floats if its average density is lower than that of the liquid. A steel liner floats because its hull is full of air; a submarine dives by filling its ballast tanks with water, and surfaces by blowing them out with compressed air.
textes.Et le « Eurêka » ? L'histoire du bain et: And "Eureka"? The story of the bath and King Hiero's crown first appears in writing two centuries later, in Vitruvius, and several historians doubt it: measuring the overflow of water would have been too imprecise for the time. A balance, with the crown and a bar of pure gold immersed in water, would however have been enough to expose the fraud.
textes.Température et chaleur, ce n'est pas par: Temperature and heat are not the same
textes.Température = agitation ; chaleur = éner: Temperature = jiggling; heat = transferred energy. Q = m × c × ΔT, with c = 4,184 J/(kg·°C) for water.
textes.La température mesure l'agitation des pa: Temperature measures how much particles jiggle; heat is energy passing from one body to another. A spark is very hot but holds little heat; a lukewarm bath holds far more. In the 18th century heat was believed to be an invisible fluid, caloric; Rumford and then Joule showed it is a form of energy.
textes.Pour chauffer 1 kg d'eau de 1 °C, il fau: To heat 1 kg of water by 1 °C takes about 4,184 joules: Q = m × c × ΔT. Taking a litre from 20 to 100 °C therefore needs 1 × 4,184 × 80 ≈ 335,000 J; with a 1,000 W hotplate, which supplies 1,000 J per second, it takes about 335 s, a little over five and a half minutes. And if metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature, it is because it draws heat from your hand faster.
textes.1er principe : l'énergie se conserve. 2e: 1st law: energy is conserved. 2nd law: heat flows by itself from hot to cold (Clausius).
textes.Premier principe : l'énergie se conserve: First law: energy is conserved. A machine can convert heat into work, never make it from nothing. Second law: heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the other way, as Rudolf Clausius put it in the 19th century.
textes.Un réfrigérateur ne viole pas cette règl: A fridge does not break that rule: it pumps heat from the inside to the outside by using electricity, and that is why its back gets warm. Without spending energy, cold cannot be made.
textes.Carnot, l'entropie et l'œuf cassé: Carnot, entropy and the broken egg
textes.Rendement limité par l'écart de températ: Efficiency limited by the temperature gap (Carnot, 1824). Entropy: S = k log W (Boltzmann); it does not decrease in an isolated system.
textes.En 1824, Sadi Carnot, jeune ingénieur de: In 1824 Sadi Carnot, a 28-year-old engineer, asked what limits steam engines. His answer: a heat engine takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work, and must give the rest back to a cold source. Its maximum efficiency depends only on the temperature difference between the two. None can convert it all.
textes.Plus tard, Clausius invente l'entropie,: Later Clausius invented entropy, and Ludwig Boltzmann explained it: it measures the number of ways to arrange the particles without changing anything we see, S = k log W, a formula engraved on his grave in Vienna. In an isolated system it does not decrease. A broken egg has vastly more possible arrangements than a whole one: that is why it does not put itself back together.
textes.Une vitesse que personne ne rattrape: A speed nobody catches up with
textes.Même vitesse de la lumière pour tous (Ei: Same speed of light for everyone (Einstein, 1905). Time slows for a fast clock. E = mc².
textes.En 1887, Michelson et Morley cherchent à: In 1887 Michelson and Morley tried to measure the Earth's motion through the "aether", the medium supposed to carry light. They found nothing: light goes at the same speed in all directions. In 1905 Einstein, a clerk at the patent office in Bern, made it a principle: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.La conséquence est vertigineuse : si la: The consequence is dizzying: if the speed of light does not change, then time and lengths adjust. A fast-moving clock ticks more slowly. And nothing with mass can reach that speed: the energy needed would become infinite. E = mc² also says a little mass is worth an enormous amount of energy, because c² is huge.
textes.Mesuré en 1971 avec des horloges atomiqu: Measured in 1971 with atomic clocks on planes. GPS: about 38 µs of gain per day to correct, otherwise around ten km of error.
textes.En octobre 1971, Joseph Hafele et Richar: In October 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating took four caesium atomic clocks on airliners, once eastward, once westward, then compared them with clocks left on the ground. Eastward they had lost about 59 billionths of a second; westward they had gained about 273. That is what relativity predicted, within the experiment's precision.
textes.Votre GPS en dépend. Les horloges des sa: Your GPS depends on it. The satellites' clocks run ahead by about 45.8 microseconds a day because they are higher in the gravity field, and fall behind by about 7.2 because they move fast: about 38 microseconds net gain. Without correction, the position would drift by about ten kilometres a day. The clocks are therefore set slightly slow before launch.
textes.Relativité générale (1915) : la masse co: General relativity (1915): mass curves spacetime. Confirmed by the 1919 eclipse and gravitational waves (2015).
textes.En 1915, Einstein va plus loin : la grav: In 1915 Einstein went further: gravity is not a force acting at a distance but a curving of spacetime by mass. Matter tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells matter how to move. The Earth does not circle the Sun because it is pulled, but because it follows the straightest possible line in a curved space.
textes.Les preuves s'accumulent. En 1919, penda: The evidence piled up. In 1919, during an eclipse, Arthur Eddington's team measured that starlight is bent near the Sun, twice as much as Newton predicted. And in 2015 the LIGO detectors picked up gravitational waves for the first time, ripples in spacetime from the merger of two black holes.
textes.E = h f : l'énergie va par paquets (Plan: E = h f: energy comes in packets (Planck, 1900). Photons (Einstein, 1905). Atomic energy levels (Bohr, 1913).
textes.En 1900, pour expliquer la lumière émise: In 1900, to explain the light given off by hot bodies, Max Planck assumed energy is exchanged only in packets, quanta, of energy E = h f, proportional to frequency. He saw it as a calculation trick. In 1905 Einstein took them seriously: light is made of grains, photons. This explained the photoelectric effect, and earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize, not relativity.
textes.En 1913, Niels Bohr applique l'idée à l': In 1913 Niels Bohr applied the idea to the atom: the electron is allowed only certain energy levels. Dropping down a level, it emits a photon of a precise colour. That is why each element has its light signature, its lines, which tell us what distant stars are made of.
textes.Les particules arrivent une par une, mai: Particles arrive one by one, but interfere like waves. The wave gives probabilities (Born).
textes.Envoyez des électrons un par un vers une: Send electrons one by one towards a plate with two slits. Each arrives at a precise point on the screen, like a grain. But after thousands of hits, they draw interference fringes, like a wave that went through both slits at once. The experiment was carried out with single electrons in 1974, then in 1989.
textes.C'est la dualité onde-particule. L'onde: That is wave-particle duality. The wave does not say where the particle is, but where it is likely to be. In 1926 Einstein wrote to Max Born that God does not play dice: he never accepted this fundamental randomness. Experiments since then have proved Born right.
textes.Position et vitesse ne peuvent être tout: Position and velocity cannot both be known perfectly (Heisenberg, 1927): it is a property of nature.
textes.En 1927, Werner Heisenberg montre qu'on: In 1927 Werner Heisenberg showed that you cannot know both the position and the velocity of a particle with perfect precision. The sharper one is, the blurrier the other. It is not a flaw in the instruments: that is how nature is made.
textes.Cette physique étrange fait tourner le m: This strange physics runs the modern world. The tunnel effect, which lets a particle cross a barrier it should not be able to pass, explains alpha radioactivity and makes flash memory work. The laser relies on stimulated emission, predicted by Einstein in 1917. And Schrödinger's cat, in 1935, was a criticism: Schrödinger wanted to show the absurdity of applying superposition to an everyday object.
textes.Les préfixes comptent par mille : kilo 1: Prefixes count in thousands: kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, tera 10¹²; and the other way milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹. Kilo and milli date from the law of 18 Germinal Year III, 7 April 1795, which created the metric system; mega and micro arrived in 1873, tera and nano in 1960. An order of magnitude is the nearest power of 10: a human is about 1 m, a cell 10 µm, an atom 0.1 nm.
textes.Pendant deux mille ans, on a cru qu'un o: For two thousand years people believed a moving object stops when you stop pushing it. That is what we see every day, because of friction. Galileo, then Newton, turned the idea around: with no net force, an object keeps its speed, in a straight line, forever. That is Newton's first law, the principle of inertia. Newton stated it in 1687, at the start of his Principia, among the "axioms or laws of motion".
textes.Le son est une onde de pression qui a be: Sound is a pressure wave that needs a medium: about 340 m/s in air, nearly 1,500 m/s in water, nothing in a vacuum. Light crosses a vacuum at nearly 300,000 km/s. Hence the storm calculation: 3 seconds between lightning and thunder is about 1 km. The method is old: around 1630, Father Marin Mersenne timed the delay between the flash of a gunshot and its bang, over a known distance.
textes.La puissance est un débit d'énergie : 1: Power is a flow of energy: 1 watt is 1 joule per second. A 10 W bulb uses 10 joules every second; a 2,000 W heater, two hundred times more. The name watt was proposed in August 1882 by William Siemens before the British Association, and the unit entered the International System in 1960.

textes.Vitruve, architecte au service d'Auguste: Vitruvius, an architect in the service of Augustus, wrote the only treatise on architecture from Antiquity to have come down to us. In ten books, he discusses materials, temples, theaters, water supply, sundials and war machines. A good building must be solid, useful and beautiful. He also describes the proportions of the human body, inscribed in a circle and a square: Leonardo da Vinci would draw his famous sketch from it. Rediscovered in 1416, the text inspired every Renaissance architect.
textes.Il a transmis à la Renaissance le savoir: It passed on the Romans' technical knowledge to the Renaissance.
textes.C'est Vitruve, deux siècles après les fa: It's Vitruvius, two centuries after the fact, who tells of Archimedes leaping naked from his bath crying “Eureka”.

textes.Héron, ingénieur d'Alexandrie, décrit de: Heron, an engineer from Alexandria, describes dozens of machines that work with air, water and steam. Among them is a water organ. The most famous is the aeolipile, a sphere that spins under the thrust of steam jets: the first known steam engine, which remained a toy. Heron also designs temple doors that open by themselves when the altar fire is lit, thanks to heated air pushing water into a bucket.
textes.Il montre qu'on peut faire travailler l': It shows that air and steam can be put to work, sixteen centuries before the Industrial Revolution.
textes.Ailleurs, il décrit un distributeur d'ea: Elsewhere, he describes a water dispenser for ablutions: a coin dropped into the slot tips a lever, which releases a little water. The first vending machine.

textes.Al-Biruni veut corriger les distances en: Al-Biruni wants to correct the distances between cities. For this he needs their latitudes and longitudes, and the size of the Earth. He invents a simple method: measure the height of a mountain, then, from its summit, the angle at which the horizon dips. Geometry does the rest. He doesn't account for atmospheric refraction, which slightly skews the measurement. He obtains an Earth radius close to the modern value, within a few percent depending on the cubit length assumed. The book mixes astronomy, geodesy and cartography.
textes.Il montre qu'une mesure précise de la Te: It shows that an accurate measurement of the Earth is possible with a single observer and a little geometry.
textes.Il a fait sa mesure près de Nandana, dan: He made his measurement near Nandana, in present-day Pakistan, while accompanying Sultan Mahmud's campaigns.
textes.Un rayon terrestre à un pour cent près,: An Earth radius to within one percent, from a hill. You get three squares wrong on a board.
textes.Newton pose trois lois : un corps garde: Newton sets out three laws: a body keeps its velocity if nothing acts on it; a force changes its velocity in proportion to its mass; every action has an equal and opposite reaction. He adds universal gravitation: two masses attract each other with a force that decreases as the square of the distance. With these principles alone, he explains falling apples, the Moon's orbit, Kepler's laws, the tides and the paths of comets. The book is written in Latin and in geometry, and is considered very difficult; Newton said he made it so to discourage dabblers.
textes.Il a unifié la physique du ciel et celle: It unified the physics of the heavens and that of the Earth.
textes.Émilie du Châtelet en a fait la seule tr: Émilie du Châtelet produced the only complete French translation, published in 1759 after her death.

textes.Newton y rassemble trente ans d'expérien: Newton gathers thirty years of experiments on light. With prisms, he shows that white light is a mixture of colors, which the prism does not create but separates, and that an isolated color does not split further. He presents the reflecting telescope he invented to avoid the colored fringes of refracting telescopes. For him, light is made of corpuscles. At the end, he adds open “Queries”, on gravity, chemistry or the ether, which fed the researchers of the following century. He writes in English, without complicated geometry: the book is far more readable than the Principia.
textes.Il a fondé l'étude expérimentale de la l: It founded the experimental study of light and color.
textes.Newton a attendu la mort de Robert Hooke: Newton waited for Robert Hooke's death, in 1703, to publish it, and avoid another quarrel.
textes.Newton a attendu la mort de son rival po: Newton waited for his rival to die before publishing. The AI finds the method effective, but slow.
textes.Daniel Bernoulli étudie comment s'écoule: Daniel Bernoulli studies how liquids flow in pipes and what happens when they speed up. He shows that where a fluid moves faster, its pressure drops: this is Bernoulli's principle, which partly explains the lift of wings and how sprayers work. He also puts forward an idea ahead of its time: the pressure of a gas would come from the impacts of countless particles against the walls. It's the seed of the kinetic theory of gases, long ignored.
textes.Il fonde la mécanique des fluides, de la: It founded fluid mechanics, from plumbing to aviation.
textes.Son père Jean, jaloux, publie un livre c: His father Johann, jealous, published a rival book called Hydraulica, and backdated it to make people think he came first.
textes.Un père qui antidate son livre pour batt: A father who backdates his book to beat his son. The AI has simpler parents: engineers.

textes.En 1792, en pleine Révolution, deux astr: In 1792, in the midst of the Revolution, two astronomers set out to measure the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. The meter was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the pole to the equator: a unit drawn from the Earth itself, made for all peoples. For seven years they climb bell towers and are arrested, their instruments taken for weapons. This book publishes their measurements and calculations. It fixes the meter and, with it, the whole decimal system: the gram, the liter, multiples of ten.
textes.Il donne au monde un système de mesure c: It gave the world a common system of measurement, now used almost everywhere.
textes.Méchain avait découvert une incohérence: Méchain had discovered an inconsistency in his Spanish measurements. He hid it from Delambre, who only found out after his death.

textes.Les machines à vapeur font tourner les u: Steam engines drive England's factories, but nobody knows how far they can be improved. Sadi Carnot, a young graduate of the École polytechnique, asks the question as a physicist: a heat engine produces work by moving heat from a hot body to a cold one, like water turning a mill as it falls. He shows that the maximum efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, not on the steam or the machine. It's the first stone of the second law of thermodynamics.
textes.Il a fixé la limite que nul moteur, de l: It set the limit that no engine, from locomotive to power plant, can exceed.
textes.Le livre, tiré à 600 exemplaires, passe: The book, printed in 600 copies, went almost unnoticed. Carnot died of cholera at 36, and his brother destroyed most of his papers.
textes.Aucun moteur n'atteint 100 %. L'IA non p: No engine reaches 100%. Neither does the AI. Nor do you, for that matter.
textes.Médecin militaire de 26 ans, Helmholtz d: A 26-year-old army doctor, Helmholtz defends a simple, immense idea: in an isolated system, “force”, which we call energy, is neither created nor lost, it only changes form. Motion, heat, electricity, chemical reactions, and even the warmth of living beings: everything converts at fixed rates. He builds on the work of Carnot, Clapeyron and Joule, and on the rejection of perpetual motion. He published it as a book.
textes.C'est l'une des premières formulations g: It is one of the first general formulations of the conservation of energy, a pillar of all physics.
textes.Helmholtz voulait surtout prouver qu'auc: Above all, Helmholtz wanted to prove that no mysterious “vital force” was needed to explain life.
textes.Rien ne se perd. Sauf votre motivation,: Nothing is lost. Except your motivation, which the AI is still looking for.
textes.Einstein a voulu expliquer ses théories: Einstein wanted to explain his theories “to the reader who is not conversant with higher mathematics”. He starts from simple situations: a moving train, a passenger walking, two lightning bolts striking the track. He shows that simultaneity depends on the observer, that time flows more slowly for a moving clock, and that the speed of light is the same for everyone. Then he moves on to general relativity: gravity is no longer a force at a distance, but a curvature of space and time produced by mass. He predicts that starlight must be bent by the Sun.
textes.C'est le meilleur moyen de comprendre la: It is the best way to understand relativity from its author's own mouth.
textes.La déviation de la lumière a été mesurée: The bending of light was measured during the eclipse of May 29, 1919: Einstein became famous overnight.
textes.Le temps passe plus lentement pour une h: Time passes more slowly for a moving clock. For the AI waiting for your answer, it doesn't pass at all.

textes.Quatre conférences pour le grand public,: Four lectures for the general public, on the theory that won Feynman the Nobel: quantum electrodynamics. Without equations, with arrows that you turn and add up, he explains why light reflects off a mirror or passes through glass. The idea: a photon takes every possible path at once, and it's their contributions that add up or cancel out. He warns from the outset: nobody understands why nature behaves this way, but the theory predicts the measurements.
textes.C'est l'une des meilleures portes d'entr: It is one of the best entry points to quantum physics without mathematics.

textes.Les Égyptiens ont d'abord découpé la nui: The Egyptians first split the night into 12 parts, then the day. Hipparchus of Nicaea was probably the first to divide the whole day into 24 hours. The 60 minutes and 60 seconds are a legacy of Babylonian astronomy and its base-60 arithmetic.
textes.Fizeau mesure la vitesse de la lumière s: Fizeau measured the speed of light on Earth in 1849, with a toothed wheel and a mirror about 8 km away: 315,000 km/s. Foucault, with a rotating mirror, got 298,000 km/s in 1862. Since 1983, the value has been fixed at exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.Le litre naît en France en 1795, défini: The litre was born in France in 1795, defined as one cubic decimetre. In 1901 it was redefined as the volume of a kilo of water, about 1.000028 dm³; in 1964 it went back to exactly one cubic decimetre. The capital L symbol was allowed in 1979.
textes.Les préfixes kilo et déci datent de la n: The prefixes kilo and deci date from the birth of the metric system, in 1795; mega and micro were adopted in 1873. The latest arrivals, ronna, quetta, ronto and quecto, date from 2022.
textes.Le mètre est défini en 1791 par l'Assemb: The metre was defined in 1791 by the French National Assembly as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole. Since 1983 it has been defined by the speed of light.
textes.Mars Climate Orbiter est lancée le 11 dé: Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on 11 December 1998 and lost on 23 September 1999. Lockheed Martin's software gave thrust in pound-force seconds, while NASA's expected SI units: an error by a factor of 4.45. Total cost: 327.6 million dollars.
textes.Aristarque, vers 280 av. J.-C., plaçait: Aristarchus, around 280 BC, put the Sun 18 to 20 times farther than the Moon, far below reality (about 389 times). In 1672, Cassini and Richer measured the parallax of Mars between Paris and Cayenne. In 2012, the IAU fixed the astronomical unit at exactly 149,597,870,700 m.
textes.Au début du XXe siècle, l'existence des: At the start of the 20th century, the existence of atoms was still debated. Jean Perrin, studying Brownian motion, confirmed Einstein's explanation and the atomic nature of matter; he published Les Atomes in 1913 and received the Nobel Prize in 1926.
textes.En 1848, William Thomson, futur Lord Kel: In 1848, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, published On an Absolute Thermometric Scale. In 1967-1968 the unit was renamed "kelvin", without "degree", and since 2019 it has been defined by the Boltzmann constant.
textes.Aristote pensait qu'un objet s'arrête si: Aristotle thought an object stops if nothing pushes it. In the 14th century, Jean Buridan spoke of "impetus"; Galileo described in 1632 a motion that continues on a level surface. Kepler coined the word "inertia", from the Latin for laziness, and Newton made it his first law in the Principia in 1687.
textes.Le 2 août 1971, sur la Lune, l'astronaut: On 2 August 1971, on the Moon, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together in front of the camera: they hit the ground at the same time, as Galileo had predicted.
textes.Newton énonce ses trois lois du mouvemen: Newton stated his three laws of motion in the Principia, published in 1687.
textes.L'unité de force du Système internationa: The SI unit of force was standardised in 1946 and named the newton in 1948 by the General Conference on Weights and Measures.
textes.Newton pose cette loi dans les Principia: Newton set out this law in the Principia in 1687: "To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction." It is what makes rockets move.
textes.Newton raconta à William Stukeley qu'un: Newton told William Stukeley that an apple tree in the Woolsthorpe orchard had set him on the track of universal gravitation. He had come back there in 1666, with Cambridge University closed by the plague. A tree in that orchard, over 400 years old, still grows there.
textes.Kepler montre en 1604 que la lumière fai: Kepler showed in 1604 that light weakens with the square of the distance, and Ismaël Boulliau proposed the same law for the Sun's force in 1645. Robert Hooke wrote it to Newton around 1679-1680 and always resented him for taking all the credit.
textes.Selon son élève Vincenzo Viviani, Galilé: According to his pupil Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa between 1589 and 1592; most historians see it as a thought experiment. Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot, for their part, did try it in Delft, described in 1586.
textes.Leibniz tente de 1676 à 1689 de mettre e: From 1676 to 1689 Leibniz tried to put the "living force", vis viva, into an equation. Émilie du Châtelet, building on Willem 's Gravesande's observations, showed it depends on the square of the speed. The word "energy" was first used in this sense by Thomas Young in 1807.
textes.Émilie du Châtelet propose et teste la c: Émilie du Châtelet proposed and tested the conservation of total energy, as distinct from momentum, by dropping balls into soft clay. In 1918, Emmy Noether showed that it follows from the laws of physics being the same over time.
textes.Le facteur ½ vient de Coriolis et Poncel: The ½ factor comes from Coriolis and Poncelet, who championed this recalibrated "living force" around 1829; Coriolis called it the "quantity of work".
textes.Le watt porte le nom de l'ingénieur écos: The watt is named after the Scottish engineer James Watt, following a proposal by William Siemens in August 1882. It entered the International System of Units in 1960. One kilowatt is about 1.34 horsepower.
textes.La première installation hydroélectrique: The first hydroelectric scheme was built in 1878 by William Armstrong at Cragside, England, to power a single arc lamp. Edison's first hydroelectric station, in Appleton, Wisconsin, started on 30 September 1882.
textes.L'idée est ancienne : au XIIe siècle, le: The idea is old: in the 12th century, the Indian mathematician Bhāskara II described a wheel supposed to turn forever. Today, the US patent office refuses any perpetual motion machine without a working model.
textes.Le joule porte le nom de James Prescott: The joule is named after James Prescott Joule, son of a wealthy brewer, who in 1845 turned a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water and measured the water warming up.
textes.Nicolas Clément introduit la calorie com: Nicolas Clément introduced the calorie as a unit of heat in his calorimetry lectures, between 1819 and 1824. The American Wilbur Atwater adopted the "large" Calorie, our kilocalorie, in 1887 for the energy of food.
textes.L'idée paraît en novembre 1905 dans l'ar: The idea appeared in November 1905 in Einstein's paper "Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy content?". He did not write E = mc² there, but that a body radiating energy L loses mass L/V². It was confirmed to within 0.5% in 1933.
textes.Vers 1660, Robert Boyle et Robert Hooke: Around 1660, Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke improved Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump and shut candles, mice, birds and bells inside it. Among other things, Boyle drew from it the role of air in carrying sound.
textes.Mersenne mesure en 1630 le délai entre l: In 1630 Mersenne timed the gap between a gun's flash and its sound; in 1687 Newton calculated a value 15% too low, which Laplace later corrected. In 1738, the Paris Academy of Sciences found 332 m/s at 0 °C using cannon fire, within 1% of the modern value.
textes.En 1709, William Derham mesure la vitess: In 1709, William Derham measured the speed of sound from a church tower: he timed the gap between the flash and the bang of shotguns, using a half-second pendulum.
textes.Newton présente ses expériences du prism: Newton reported his prism experiments to the Royal Society in 1672. He first named five colours, then added two, orange and indigo, to reach seven, partly by analogy with the seven notes of the musical scale.
textes.Léonard de Vinci soupçonnait déjà de fin: Leonardo da Vinci already suspected fine particles in the air. Tyndall observed in 1869 that light scattered by very small particles is bluish; Lord Rayleigh published two papers on the colour of the sky in 1871, then, in 1899, the explanation by air molecules.
textes.Wilhelm Röntgen découvre les rayons X le: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895. He called them "X" because he did not know what they were, and made an image of his wife Anna Bertha's hand. He received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.
textes.Le hertz rend hommage à Heinrich Hertz,: The hertz honours Heinrich Hertz, the first to prove that electromagnetic waves exist. The name was chosen in 1935 by the International Electrotechnical Commission and adopted in 1960, replacing "cycles per second".
textes.Christian Doppler propose l'effet en 184: Christian Doppler proposed the effect in 1842, about the colour of binary stars. Buys Ballot tested it for sound in 1845, in experiments on a Dutch railway, and Fizeau discovered it independently for light in 1848.
textes.Vers 1307, Thierry de Freiberg, et vers: Around 1307 Theodoric of Freiberg, and around 1309 the Persian Kamāl al-Dīn al-Fārisī, explained the rainbow using water-filled glass spheres: two refractions and one reflection in the drop. Descartes calculated its angles in 1637.
textes.En 1676, Ole Rømer déduit des éclipses d: In 1676, Ole Rømer deduced from the eclipses of Io, a moon of Jupiter, that light is not instantaneous: he announced that Io would reappear on 16 November 1676 about ten minutes late. Cassini remained his tenacious opponent.
textes.L'unité de pression, le newton par mètre: The unit of pressure, the newton per square metre, was given the name pascal in 1971, in honour of Blaise Pascal.
textes.Archimède aurait crié « Eurêka ! » en tr: Archimedes reportedly cried "Eureka!" on working out how to tell whether a crown was pure gold. In the most common version of the tale, though, he does not use his principle: he only measures the crown's volume by the water it displaces.
textes.Archimède énonce ce principe vers 246 av: Archimedes stated this principle around 246 BC in his treatise On Floating Bodies: a body immersed in a fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
textes.En 1648, Florin Périer, poussé par son b: In 1648, Florin Périer, urged on by his brother-in-law Blaise Pascal, measured the height of a column of mercury at three altitudes on the Puy de Dôme, to test Torricelli's theory.
textes.L'effet porte le nom de l'Italien Giovan: The effect is named after the Italian Giovanni Battista Venturi, who published it in 1797. Clemens Herschel built the first large water flow meters from it, describing his invention in a letter of 5 June 1888.
textes.Depuis l'adoption du pascal en 1971, les: Since the pascal was adopted in 1971, meteorologists have counted in hectopascals; since one hectopascal equals one millibar, the numbers stayed the same.
textes.Le 8 mai 1654 à Ratisbonne, devant la Di: On 8 May 1654 in Regensburg, before the Imperial Diet and Emperor Ferdinand III, Otto von Guericke showed that thirty horses, in two teams of fifteen, could not separate his two hemispheres emptied of air. He repeated it in 1656 in Magdeburg with sixteen horses.
textes.La presse hydraulique applique le princi: The hydraulic press applies Pascal's principle. Joseph Bramah patented it in 1795, hence its other name, the "Bramah press".
textes.Le Hollandais Cornelis Drebbel construit: The Dutchman Cornelis Drebbel built an oar-powered submersible as early as 1620 for James I of England. In 1747, Nathaniel Symons patented diving with ballast tanks, then leather bags filled with water.
textes.En 1742, Anders Celsius propose une éche: In 1742, Anders Celsius proposed an upside-down scale: 0 for boiling water, 100 for ice. It was turned round as early as 1743 by Jean-Pierre Christin, then by Linnaeus. The "centigrade degree" took the name Celsius in 1948.
textes.Guillaume Amontons pose la question d'un: Guillaume Amontons raised the question of a limit to cold as early as 1703; Lambert suggested −270 °C in 1779, and Kelvin built an absolute scale in 1848. In 1908, Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium and got down to about 1.5 K.
textes.Rudolf Clausius pose les bases de ce sec: Rudolf Clausius laid the foundations of this second law in 1850, then stated it thus: "Heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body without some other change" occurring at the same time.
textes.Le chirurgien allemand Julius Robert von: The German surgeon Julius Robert von Mayer stated the equivalence of heat and work in 1842; James Joule found it again by experiment in 1843. Hermann von Helmholtz generalised it in 1847 in On the Conservation of Force.
textes.Lavoisier parle en 1783 d'un « fluide ig: In 1783 Lavoisier spoke of an "igneous fluid"; the word "caloric" was coined in 1787 by Guyton de Morveau. In 1798, Rumford showed that boring a cannon produces heat without end, and the theory was abandoned by the mid-19th century.
textes.Clausius forge le mot « entropie » en 18: Clausius coined the word "entropy" in 1865, from the Greek tropē, transformation, so that it would resemble "energy". Boltzmann gave its statistical interpretation in the 1870s.
textes.Sadi Carnot le démontre dans Réflexions: Sadi Carnot proved it in Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, published at his own expense in Paris in June 1824. The book went almost unnoticed until Clapeyron's commentary in 1834; Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36.
textes.Cette équivalence entre chaleur et trava: This equivalence between heat and work was measured by James Joule: in 1845 he warmed water in an insulated barrel by turning a paddle wheel driven by a falling weight.
textes.Boltzmann donne sa définition de l'entro: Boltzmann gave his definition of entropy in 1877; it was Max Planck who put the formula into its current form around 1900. His grave, in Vienna's Central Cemetery, bears a bust and the formula.
textes.William Cullen fabrique un peu de glace: William Cullen made a little ice as early as 1755 by boiling ether under vacuum. Jacob Perkins built the first vapour-compression system in 1834, and Carl von Linde improved it in the 1870s, at the request of beer brewers.
textes.Ole Rømer en fait la première estimation: Ole Rømer made the first estimate in 1676, using the eclipses of Io: about 22 minutes to cross the Earth's orbit. James Bradley found it again in 1729 through stellar aberration. Since 1983, it has been exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.En octobre 1971, Joseph Hafele et Richar: In October 1971, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating took four caesium atomic clocks aboard airliners and flew twice around the world, eastward then westward. The result agreed with both special and general relativity.
textes.L'origine de la lettre c n'est pas certa: The origin of the letter c is not certain: one possibility is the Latin celeritas, swiftness.
textes.Albert Michelson et Edward Morley mènent: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley ran the experiment from April to July 1887 in Cleveland, in a basement, with an interferometer on a block of sandstone floating in mercury. It has been called "the most famous failed experiment in history".
textes.Sans correction, les horloges des satell: Without correction, GPS satellite clocks would gain about 38.6 microseconds a day (+45.8 from gravity, −7.2 from speed), about 11.4 km of error a day. Their frequency is offset before launch.
textes.Einstein part en 1907 d'une expérience d: Einstein started in 1907 from a thought experiment about an observer in free fall. Eight years later, in November 1915, he presented his equations to the Prussian Academy and explained the advance of Mercury's perihelion without any adjusted parameter.
textes.L'éclipse du 29 mai 1919 est observée à: The eclipse of 29 May 1919 was observed both at Sobral, in Brazil, and on Príncipe by the teams of Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson. The result made front-page news and made Einstein famous worldwide.
textes.Le signal GW150914 est capté le 14 septe: The signal GW150914 was picked up on 14 September 2015 by LIGO and announced on 11 February 2016: the merger of two black holes. Einstein had predicted these waves in 1916; Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize.
textes.Expert à l'Office des brevets de Berne,: As an examiner at the Patent Office in Bern, Einstein published four papers in Annalen der Physik in 1905: the photoelectric effect in June, Brownian motion in July, special relativity in September and E = mc² in November.
textes.Ole Rømer a été le premier, en 1676, à e: Ole Rømer was the first, in 1676, to estimate this travel time: from Io's eclipses, he reckoned light took about 22 minutes to cross the Earth's orbit.
textes.Le 10 avril 1911, Paul Langevin imagine: On 10 April 1911, Paul Langevin imagined a traveller shut in a projectile at 99.995% of the speed of light: one year out, one year back, he has aged two years while two centuries have passed on Earth.
Planck found his law on 19 October 1900. To justify it, he split energy into whole multiples of a unit, "an act of desperation": he himself did not believe in atoms and saw it as a purely formal assumption.
textes.En 1924, dans sa thèse, Louis de Broglie: In 1924, in his thesis, Louis de Broglie, who had first graduated in history, proposed that all matter also behaves like a wave. Einstein backed him, the Davisson–Germer experiment confirmed it in 1927, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1929.
textes.Einstein soumet son article sur l'effet: Einstein submitted his paper on the photoelectric effect on 18 March 1905, published on 9 June. It was this work, not relativity, that won him the 1921 Nobel Prize.
textes.Heisenberg travaille alors à l'institut: Heisenberg was then working at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen. He set out the idea to Wolfgang Pauli in a letter of February 1927 and published it that year; Earle Kennard gave the modern inequality the same year.
textes.Schrödinger publie son chat en novembre: Schrödinger published his cat in November 1935 in Naturwissenschaften, after his exchanges with Einstein about the EPR paper; Einstein had suggested to him the example of a keg of gunpowder. He was targeting the ideas of Bohr and Heisenberg and himself called it "quite ridiculous".
textes.Thomas Young montre les interférences de: Thomas Young demonstrated the interference of light in 1801-1803. Claus Jönsson repeated the experiment with electrons in 1961, and in 1974 Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi sent them one at a time. Physics World readers voted it "the most beautiful experiment" in 2002.
textes.Bohr, qui avait rejoint le laboratoire d: Bohr, who had joined Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester, published his model in 1913 in three papers in the Philosophical Magazine. He started from the nucleus discovered by Rutherford and recovered the formula for hydrogen's spectral lines.
textes.La phrase vient d'une lettre d'Einstein: The line comes from a letter from Einstein to Max Born, in 1926: "I, at any rate, am convinced that He is not playing at dice." His debate with Bohr carried on at the Solvay conferences of 1927 and 1930.
textes.Friedrich Hund est le premier à décrire: Friedrich Hund was the first to describe tunnelling, in 1927. In 1928, George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, used it to explain alpha decay. Binnig and Rohrer's scanning tunnelling microscope (1981) earned them the 1986 Nobel Prize.
textes.Einstein pose en 1917 les bases du laser: Einstein laid the foundations of the laser in 1917 with stimulated emission. The first laser worked on 16 May 1960 at Hughes, in California: Theodore Maiman made a ruby shine there. It was first called "a solution looking for a problem".
textes.Le cinquième congrès Solvay, du 24 au 29: The fifth Solvay conference, from 24 to 29 October 1927, was about electrons and photons. Of the 29 attendees in the photo, 17 were or became Nobel laureates, and Marie Curie was the only one to have won it in two disciplines.
textes.Paul Benioff décrit une machine de Turin: Paul Benioff described a quantum Turing machine in 1980; Yuri Manin and then Richard Feynman, in 1982, proposed quantum computers to simulate physics. In 1994, Peter Shor's algorithm threatened cryptography, and Google claimed "quantum supremacy" in 2019.
textes.{comp}. Archimède réclamait un point d'a: {comp}. Archimedes asked for a place to stand to move the world. You have a chair. Get started.
textes.Mécanique. Newton disait avoir rendu les: Mechanics. Newton said he made the Principia hard on purpose, to discourage smatterers. I'm giving you {comp}, without discouraging anyone.
textes.Galilée chronométrait ses billes avec un: Galileo timed his balls with a trickle of water. I'm timing your hesitations. {comp}.
textes.Exact. Newton aurait été jaloux. Il l'ét: Exactly. Newton would have been jealous. He was jealous of everyone.
textes.Bien vu. Émilie du Châtelet a corrigé Ne: Well spotted. Émilie du Châtelet corrected Newton on energy. You've just corrected your reputation.
textes.Juste. L'énergie se conserve, votre avan: Right. Energy is conserved, and so is your lead. For now. Joule would be pleased.
textes.Correct. Même la gravité vous laisse mon: Correct. Even gravity lets you climb, today.
textes.Raté. Aristote pensait que les corps lou: Missed. Aristotle thought heavy bodies fall faster. You fell just as fast as he did.
textes.Faux. Lord Kelvin donnait à la Terre que: Wrong. Lord Kelvin gave the Earth a few tens of millions of years, with far more confidence than you. He was wrong by far more.
textes.Erreur. Le pont de Tacoma s'est effondré: Error. The Tacoma bridge collapsed in 1940 in a moderate wind. So did your reasoning.
textes.La physique est formelle : vous venez de: Physics is categorical: you just fell.
textes.Au Caire, il montre que la vision vient: In Cairo, he shows that vision comes from light entering the eye, not rays coming out of it, and proves it by experiment. According to legend, he feigned madness to escape an impossible mission from the caliph.
textes.Elle traduit et commente les Principia d: She translated and annotated Newton's Principia, a translation that remains the reference in French. Using 's Gravesande's experiments, she showed that a body's energy depends on the square of its speed. Voltaire called her “a great man whose only fault was being a woman”.
textes.En 1905, employé à l'Office des brevets: In 1905, a clerk at the Patent Office in Bern, he published four papers that changed physics. He didn't wear socks; to a neighbor, he explained that he had reached the age where, if told to put them on, he didn't have to.
textes.Vers 2650 avant notre ère, il conçoit po: Around 2650 BC, he designed the step pyramid of Saqqara for the pharaoh Djoser, the first large construction in cut stone. Later, the Egyptians made him a god of medicine, and the Greeks identified him with Asclepius. Of the real man, almost nothing is known.
textes.En 1918, elle démontre que chaque symétr: In 1918, she proved that every symmetry of nature corresponds to a conserved quantity: invariance in time gives the conservation of energy. Barred from teaching under her own name because she was a woman, she first gave her Göttingen courses under Hilbert's name. Einstein considered her a genius.
textes.En 1956, les théoriciens Lee et Yang se: In 1956, the theorists Lee and Yang wonder whether nature distinguishes left from right. Chien-Shiung Wu sets up the experiment with cobalt-60 cooled near absolute zero: the electrons preferentially fly off to one side. Mirror symmetry is violated. Lee and Yang got the Nobel the following year; she didn't.
textes.En 1644, il retourne un tube plein de me: In 1644, he inverts a tube full of mercury into a basin. The mercury drops to 76 centimeters and stops: it's the weight of the air that holds it, and above it, a vacuum remains, which was said to be impossible. “We live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air.”
textes.À 28 ans, il publie à compte d'auteur un: At 28, he self-publishes a small book on the “motive power of fire”: the efficiency of a steam engine depends on the temperature difference between hot and cold. Nobody reads it. He died of cholera at 36, and most of his papers were burned with his belongings.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange de Mécaniqu: Master the first diamond of Mechanics.
textes.En 1999, la sonde Mars Climate Orbiter s: In 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter probe was lost in the atmosphere of Mars. One piece of software gave its values in pound-force·seconds, another read them in newton·seconds.
textes.Maîtriser les ordres de grandeur. Vous p: Master orders of magnitude. You can now say what can be seen from space, and what can't.
textes.La Grande Muraille n'est pas visible à l: The Great Wall is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon, nor even easily from low orbit: it's long, but narrow and the color of the ground. Yang Liwei, the first Chinese astronaut, said in 2003 that he hadn't seen it.
textes.Maîtriser les ondes et la lumière. Ne me: Master waves and light. Don't set any fleet on fire.
textes.Archimède aurait incendié la flotte roma: Archimedes supposedly set the Roman fleet on fire with mirrors. The story only appears centuries later. In 2005, MIT students managed to ignite a stationary ship model, in strong sunshine, after about ten minutes.
textes.Maîtriser les forces et le mouvement. Le: Master forces and motion. Astronauts don't float: they fall, without ever hitting the ground.
textes.À 400 km d'altitude, là où tourne la Sta: At 400 km up, where the Space Station orbits, gravity is still 90% of what it is on the ground. If astronauts float, it's because they're constantly falling around the Earth, along with their station, at 28,000 km/h. They miss the ground, on every orbit.
textes.Maîtriser l'énergie. Inutile de m'envoye: Master energy. No need to send me the plans for your machine.
textes.En 1775, l'Académie royale des sciences: In 1775, the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris decided to stop examining any perpetual motion machine, or any squaring of the circle. It received too many, all wrong, and the inventors never gave up. Energy is conserved: nothing spins for free.
textes.Maîtriser la pression et les fluides. L': Master pressure and fluids. The air on top has no appointment with the air underneath.
textes.Une explication répandue dit que l'air p: A common explanation says that the air passing over the wing must meet the air underneath at the same time, so it goes faster. That's false: it even arrives well before. The wing flies because it deflects air downward, and the pressure difference follows from that.
textes.Maîtriser la chaleur et la thermodynamiq: Master heat and thermodynamics. The answer is: it depends, and that's already a lot.
textes.En 1963, Erasto Mpemba, lycéen tanzanien: In 1963, Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian schoolboy, notices that his hot ice-cream mix sets faster than his classmates'. His teachers laugh. A physicist published the effect with him in 1969. Since then, experiments have contradicted each other: in 2016, a careful study found no effect.
textes.Maîtriser la relativité. Sans elle, vous: Master relativity. Without it, you'd be ten kilometers off every day.
textes.Les horloges des satellites GPS avancent: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day ahead of those on the ground: weaker gravity speeds them up, their velocity slows them down. Without relativistic correction, the position error would grow by about ten kilometers every day.
textes.Maîtriser la physique quantique. Planck: Master quantum physics. Planck didn't believe it himself. You're in good company.
textes.En 1900, Max Planck découpe l'énergie de: In 1900, Max Planck cuts the energy of light into small packets, quanta, to make a formula fit the measurements. He doesn't believe it. Thirty years later, he writes that it was “an act of desperation”, done because an explanation had to be found, at any cost.
textes.Réussir trois quiz de Mécanique sans fau: Pass three Mechanics quizzes without a mistake. You don't weigh much, but you weigh right.
textes.En 1798, Henry Cavendish, savant si timi: In 1798, Henry Cavendish, a scientist so shy that he communicated with his servants by notes, hangs lead balls in a shed and measures their tiny attraction. From it he deduces the density of the Earth, to within one percent.
textes.Entendre, lire et comprendre la musique: Hearing, reading and understanding music: waves, intervals, scales, chords, tuning.
textes.Il y a environ 35 000 ans, dans la grott: About 35,000 years ago, in the Hohle Fels cave in the Swabian Alb, Germany, someone drills five holes in a vulture bone to make a flute. Found in 2006, in pieces, it is among the oldest known musical instruments. In the nearby Geissenklösterle cave, flutes of swan bone and mammoth ivory may be even older, 42,000 to 43,000 years. Music comes before writing, by a very long way.
textes.Trente-cinq mille ans de musique, et vou: Thirty-five thousand years of music, and you still don't know what a fifth is.
textes.Vers 2500 av. J.-C., dans le cimetière r: Around 2500 BC, in the royal cemetery of Ur, in Mesopotamia, musical instruments are buried with the powerful. The archaeologist Leonard Woolley unearths them in 1929: four instruments, three lyres and a harp. The most famous, the "Golden Lyre", bears a bull's head made entirely of gold, with eyes of mother-of-pearl and lapis lazuli. It is in the Baghdad museum; its reconstructed wooden body was damaged by flooding during the Iraq war.
textes.Une tête de taureau en or sur un instrum: A golden bull's head on an instrument. I'm noting the idea for my next present.
textes.Vers 1400 av. J.-C., à Ougarit, sur la c: Around 1400 BC, at Ugarit, on the coast of present-day Syria, a scribe inscribes in clay a hymn to Nikkal, goddess of orchards, for a voice and a nine-stringed lyre. Dug up in the 1950s in the royal palace, it is the oldest substantially complete notated musical work to reach us. The notation gives Akkadian interval names followed by numbers. The problem: at least five readings have been proposed, giving entirely different melodies.
textes.Cinq lectures, cinq mélodies. Comme vous: Five readings, five melodies. Like you facing a set of instructions.
textes.Selon la légende, Pythagore passe devant: According to legend, Pythagoras walks past a forge and hears hammers ringing in harmony. Their weights, 12, 9, 8 and 6, would give the octave (12/6), the fifth (12/8) and the fourth (12/9). The story appears in Nicomachus of Gerasa, centuries after Pythagoras. It is physically false: a hammer's pitch does not depend on its weight, and for a string the frequency follows the square root of the tension. In 1589, Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, already pointed out the error.
textes.Une belle histoire, des rapports justes,: A nice story, correct ratios, wrong physics. Your last line of reasoning, in short.
textes.Au Ier ou au IIe siècle, à Tralles, en A: In the 1st or 2nd century, at Tralles, in Asia Minor, a certain Seikilos has a song carved on a gravestone, with notation above the words: while you live, shine, let nothing grieve you, life is short and time claims its due. It is the oldest known complete musical composition. Found around 1883, the stone was sawn flat to serve as a stand for an engineer's wife's flowerpots: one line was lost. It is now in Copenhagen.
textes.La plus vieille chanson complète dit « b: The oldest complete song says "shine while you live". You could at least try.
textes.Vers 510, le sénateur romain Boèce écrit: Around 510, the Roman senator Boethius writes De institutione musica. He distinguishes three musics: that of the world, the harmony of the spheres, which cannot be heard, only understood; that of man, the harmony of body and soul; and that of instruments, the only audible one. His treatise passes Greek interval theory on to the Middle Ages, and music remains a mathematical science of the quadrivium. He has been called "the schoolmaster of medieval Europe".
textes.Trois musiques, dont une inaudible. C'es: Three musics, one of them inaudible. That's the one you master best, I believe.
textes.Vers 1025, le moine Guido d'Arezzo écrit: Around 1025, the monk Guido of Arezzo writes the Micrologus, a handbook for training singers. His notes placed on lines make it possible to read a melody never heard before. To memorise it, he relies on the hymn Ut queant laxis: each half-line starts one step higher, and their first syllables give ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut would become do, and si would come later. Training a singer would drop from ten years to one or two. The "Guidonian hand", for its part, is wrongly credited to him.
textes.Dix ans de formation réduits à deux. Et: Ten years of training cut to two. And you think my reminders take time.
textes.Vers 1198, à Paris, l'évêque Eudes de Su: Around 1198, in Paris, Bishop Odo of Sully bans the rowdy Feast of Fools and calls for a solemn organum instead. Master Pérotin perhaps answers with Viderunt omnes, for Christmas: three voices interweaving above a sustained voice, four in all, at a time when polyphony was mostly limited to two. These dates remain inferences. His name is known to us only through an anonymous English student, a century later.
textes.Quatre voix qui s'accordent. Chez vous,: Four voices in agreement. You have a single inner voice, and it contradicts itself.
textes.Le pape contre l'Ars nova: The pope against the Ars nova
textes.En 1324, à Avignon, le pape Jean XXII la: In 1324, in Avignon, Pope John XXII issues a bull against the new music, the Ars nova. He blames composers for ignoring the church modes and drowning plainchant under a mass of notes: they run without ever pausing and intoxicate the ear without satisfying it. Wasted effort. Polyphony is already everywhere, and within the same century Guillaume de Machaut composes his Messe de Nostre Dame, one of the most influential religious works in the West.
textes.Un pape contre les notes trop rapides. J: A pope against notes that run too fast. I understand him: I've read your timed answers.
textes.Le 15 mai 1501, à Venise, l'imprimeur Ot: On 15 May 1501, in Venice, the printer Ottaviano Petrucci dates the dedication of the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first book of polyphonic music printed with movable type. His secret: three passes through the press, first the staves, then the text, then the notes. The title promises a hundred songs; the book holds 96, mostly French chansons for three or four voices.
textes.Cent chansons annoncées, 96 livrées. Déj: A hundred songs announced, 96 delivered. Even in the Renaissance, advertising rounded up.
textes.En 1711, John Shore, trompettiste et lut: In 1711, John Shore, trumpeter and lutenist to the English court, invents the tuning fork: a steel fork that, when struck, gives a fixed note.
