Its first overtone is about six times higher than the base note and dies away quickly, hence an almost pure sound. The fork he gives Handel sounds a C at 512 Hz. From now on, a reference pitch can be kept that does not shift with temperature, unlike strings.
textes.Une fourche qui donne toujours la même n: A fork that always gives the same note. More reliable than you, and less chatty.
textes.En 1722, à Köthen, Jean-Sébastien Bach r: In 1722, in Köthen, Johann Sebastian Bach assembles The Well-Tempered Clavier: 24 preludes and fugues, one in each major and minor key, for the instruction of young musicians. For much of the 20th century, it was believed he was championing equal temperament, the tuning of our pianos. Specialists now lean towards an unequal temperament, in which all keys sound good without being identical. A second book of 24 follows twenty years later.
textes.Bien tempéré ne veut pas dire égal. Vous: Well-tempered does not mean equal. Neither are you: your good days are rare.
textes.En 1787, Ernst Chladni publie ses Découv: In 1787, Ernst Chladni publishes his Discoveries in the Theory of Sound. He sprinkles sand on a metal plate and makes it vibrate with a violin bow: the sand leaves the moving areas and gathers on the still lines, drawing figures. In 1808, he shows them in Paris before Napoleon, who offers a prize for their mathematical explanation. Sophie Germain is the only one with the right approach, but her first entry is rejected for its errors.
textes.On voit le son avec du sable. Moi, je vo: Sound can be seen with sand. I can see your gaps with nothing at all.
textes.En 1814, à Amsterdam, Dietrich Nikolaus: In 1814, in Amsterdam, Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel invents a compact spring-driven pendulum to beat time. Johann Maelzel adds a scale, calls it a metronome and mass-produces it from 1816 under his own name, a borrowing considered dubious. In December 1815, Beethoven writes his first metronome marking. A score can now say how fast to play, in beats per minute.
textes.Maelzel a pris l'invention de Winkel, et: Maelzel took Winkel's invention, and his name is the one that stuck. Don't take inspiration from that.
textes.En 1859, une loi française fixe le la à: In 1859, a French law sets A at 435 vibrations per second: the "diapason normal". A had kept rising, and singers complained of straining their voices; old tuning forks range from 409 to over 455 Hz. In 1939, an international conference recommends 440 Hz, which ISO adopts in 1955. Orchestras often tune a little higher today. As for the "natural" A at 432 Hz, it is a legend.
textes.Même le la n'arrivait pas à rester juste: Even A couldn't stay in tune. You see, you're not alone.
textes.En 1857, le Français Édouard-Léon Scott: In 1857, the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville patents the phonautograph, which traces sound vibrations on soot-blackened paper. He wants to see sound, not hear it: the device cannot play anything back. In 1860, he records Au clair de la lune with it. In 2008, a team of researchers scans the trace and plays it for the first time. Played too fast, it is first taken for a woman's or child's voice; it is in fact Scott himself, singing slowly.
textes.Le premier enregistrement de l'histoire: The first recording in history is a nursery rhyme sung slowly. You have your pace, Scott had his.
textes.En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie Di: In 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publishes On the Sensations of Tone. To break down a complex sound, he invents resonators, hollow spheres that respond to a single frequency. Held to the ear, they let you pick out, one by one, the pure components hidden in a note. Combined, they can even imitate vowels. His book founds musical acoustics and inspires musicologists into the 20th century.
textes.Helmholtz entendait les harmoniques cach: Helmholtz heard the overtones hidden in a note. I hear the panic hidden in your silence.
textes.En 1895, à Harvard, on confie au jeune p: In 1895, at Harvard, the young physicist Wallace Sabine is handed a failed lecture hall: in the Fogg room, a spoken word echoes for about five and a half seconds. With his assistants, he borrows hundreds of seat cushions from Sanders Theatre, moves them around and times how sounds die away. One listener absorbs as much as six cushions. He derives a law of reverberation, then advises on Boston's Symphony Hall, the first concert hall designed by calculation. The unit of absorption bears his name, the sabin.
textes.Un humain absorbe le son comme six couss: A human absorbs sound like six cushions. And information like... I'll let you finish.
textes.Le 29 mai 1913, au théâtre des Champs-Él: On 29 May 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the Ballets Russes premiere Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, choreographed by Nijinsky. The bassoon opens in a register so high it is barely recognisable; laughter, then uproar. Legend speaks of a riot. But the word only appears in reviews in 1924, accounts contradict each other, and the performance went on to the end. For some historians, it was the dance more than the music that shocked.
textes.Une émeute apparue onze ans après les fa: A riot that appeared eleven years after the event. Your revision memories work the same way.
textes.Vers 1921, Arnold Schoenberg met au poin: Around 1921, Arnold Schoenberg develops his method of composing with twelve tones: a row contains each of the twelve notes of the chromatic scale once, and the whole work is built on it. No more tonic, no note ruling the others: the row replaces the functions of tonal harmony. He describes it to his pupils around 1923. The Austrian Josef Matthias Hauer had published his own "law of the twelve tones" as early as 1919.
textes.Douze notes, aucune ne domine. Chez vous: Twelve notes, none dominates. In your case, the lowest mark dominates.
textes.En 1920, en Russie soviétique, Léon Ther: In 1920, in Soviet Russia, Leon Theremin invents an instrument played without touching it. Two antennas: the distance of one hand from the first sets the pitch, that of the other hand from the second sets the volume. Patented in 1928, the theremin triumphs in concert with Clara Rockmore, then gives films their shiver, such as Hitchcock's Spellbound or The Day the Earth Stood Still.
textes.Un instrument qu'on joue sans le toucher: An instrument played without touching it. Like your revision, in short.
textes.En 1964, l'Américain Robert Moog présent: In 1964, the American Robert Moog unveils a modular synthesizer: oscillators, filters and amplifiers linked by cables. His key idea: control everything with an electrical voltage, one volt per octave. You start from a wave rich in harmonics and take some away with a filter: that is subtractive synthesis. In 1968, Wendy Carlos plays Bach on the Moog in Switched-On Bach: three Grammys and the first classical album certified platinum.
textes.Retirer des harmoniques pour faire un so: Remove harmonics to make a sound. Remove a few certainties to make a right answer.
textes.En 1993, la revue Nature publie une étud: In 1993, the journal Nature publishes a study: 36 students who have just listened to a Mozart sonata do slightly better on spatial reasoning tests, for about fifteen minutes. IQ was never measured. Yet the press turns it into "Mozart makes you smarter". In 1998, the governor of Georgia proposes giving a classical music recording to every newborn. Later meta-analyses find a tiny effect, better explained by the pleasure of listening than by Mozart.
textes.Écouter Mozart ne vous rendra pas plus i: Listening to Mozart won't make you smarter. Revising will. Step back two spaces, with music.
textes.Au début des années 1990, à l'institut F: In the early 1990s, at the Fraunhofer institute in Germany, Karlheinz Brandenburg's team develops MP3, published as a standard in 1993. Its principle comes from psychoacoustics: a loud sound masks a quieter one close by, so there is no point keeping what the ear will not hear. At 128 kbit/s, the file is eleven times smaller than on a CD. To tune the voice, Brandenburg listens over and over to Tom's Diner, sung a cappella by Suzanne Vega, the "mother of MP3".
textes.Le MP3 jette ce que l'oreille n'entend p: MP3 throws away what the ear can't hear. Your memory throws away what you just learned.
textes.En 1584, en Chine, Zhu Zaiyu, héritier d: In 1584, in China, Zhu Zaiyu, heir to a Ming dynasty principality, describes equal temperament through precise calculation: the octave is cut into twelve perfectly equal semitones, each multiplying the frequency by the twelfth root of two. Every key then sounds alike, so you can move from one to another without retuning. In 1593, he inherits the title of prince and immediately hands it to his cousin to devote himself to his studies.
textes.Il a renoncé à une principauté pour des: He gave up a principality for calculations. You give up calculations for a TV series.
textes.En 1700, à Florence, un inventaire des i: In 1700, in Florence, an inventory of Prince Ferdinando de' Medici's instruments describes an "arpicembalo" that plays "piano and forte": soft and loud. Its maker, Bartolomeo Cristofori, has replaced the harpsichord's plectra with hammers. An ingenious mechanism, the escapement, lets them bounce off the string instead of sticking to it. The oldest surviving piano, from 1720, is at the Metropolitan Museum in New York.
textes.Doux et fort à la fois. Vous, vous êtes: Soft and loud at once. You are mostly loud with excuses.
textes.Le 24 février 1607, à la cour des Gonzag: On 24 February 1607, at the Gonzaga court in Mantua, Claudio Monteverdi stages L'Orfeo, to a libretto by Alessandro Striggio: the myth of Orpheus, who goes down to the Underworld to fetch Eurydice by the sole power of his song. Opera was born in Florence a few years earlier, with Peri's Dafne in 1598, but L'Orfeo is the oldest still regularly performed. Its score, printed in 1609, names some forty instruments.
textes.Orphée a perdu Eurydice pour s'être reto: Orpheus lost Eurydice by looking back. Don't look back at your mistakes: fix them.
textes.Vers 433 av. J.-C., en Chine, on enterre: Around 433 BC, in China, Marquis Yi of Zeng was buried with twenty-one women and a whole orchestra: sounding stones, zithers, flutes, mouth organs, and 65 bronze bells hung from great beams. Struck in the centre, each bell gives one note; on the side, another, a third higher. The tomb slept for twenty-four centuries, until 1977, when soldiers levelled the hill to build a factory.
textes.Soixante-cinq cloches, deux notes chacun: Sixty-five bells, two notes each. And you, always the same wrong note.
textes.Safi al-Din et la chute de Bagdad: Safi al-Din and the fall of Baghdad
textes.En février 1258, les Mongols de Houlagou: In February 1258, Hulagu's Mongols took Baghdad and executed the last Abbasid caliph, al-Mustasim. His copyist, the calligrapher and musician Safi al-Din al-Urmawi, survived thanks to his musical talent: he hosted one of Hulagu's officers, and the conqueror, impressed, doubled his income. In his Kitab al-Adwar, he divided the octave into 17 steps, described twelve modes and notated melodies with letters and numbers, a first.
textes.Sauvé par la musique pendant un siège. V: Saved by music during a siege. Your revision playlist will not save you from the quiz.
textes.Le 30 avril 1877, Charles Cros dépose à: On 30 April 1877, Charles Cros deposited a sealed envelope with the Academy of Sciences describing a "paleophone". That same year, Thomas Edison built the phonograph: a stylus linked to a membrane engraves sound into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder, and a horn gives it back. To test it, Edison recited Mary Had a Little Lamb. That recording was not preserved; a 1927 film of him reciting it is sometimes wrongly presented as the original.
textes.Le premier enregistrement rejouable est: The first playable recording is a nursery rhyme, and it is lost. Your lecture notes are heading the same way.
textes.En 1944, au Caire, un étudiant en génie: In 1944, in Cairo, an agricultural engineering student, Halim El-Dabh, borrowed a wire recorder from Middle East Radio and recorded a zaar ceremony in the street. He transformed the sound with reverberation, echo chambers and a re-recording room with movable walls, and removed the fundamentals to keep only the high overtones. The Expression of Zaar was presented in a Cairo gallery, four years before Pierre Schaeffer's musique concrète.
textes.Un étudiant en agronomie invente la musi: An agriculture student invented electronic music. And you study what, again?
textes.Le son est une onde de pression : l'air: Sound is a pressure wave: the air compresses and expands. Without matter, no sound: it does not cross a vacuum.
textes.La fréquence, en hertz (Hz), compte les: Frequency, in hertz (Hz), counts vibrations per second. It gives the pitch: the higher it is, the higher the sound.
textes.L'amplitude donne l'intensité, que l'on: Amplitude gives the intensity, which is measured in decibels (dB).
textes.Dans l'air à 20 °C, le son parcourt envi: In air at 20 °C, sound travels about 343 m/s; in water, nearly 1,500 m/s.
textes.Un son plus fort n'est pas plus aigu : l: A louder sound is not higher: intensity (amplitude) and pitch (frequency) are independent.
textes.fréquence f = 1 / T, en hertz (vibration: frequency f = 1 / T, in hertz (vibrations per second)
textes.Une onde sonore : la période donne la ha: A sound wave: the period gives the pitch, the amplitude gives the intensity
textes.La portée a cinq lignes : plus une note: The staff has five lines: the higher a note is placed, the higher it sounds.
textes.La clé donne le nom d'une ligne : la clé: The clef names one line: the treble (G) clef puts G on the 2nd line, the bass (F) clef puts F on the 4th.
textes.Une ronde vaut 2 blanches, 4 noires ou 8: A whole note is worth 2 half notes, 4 quarter notes or 8 eighth notes. A dot after a note adds half its value.
textes.La mesure 4/4 compte quatre temps d'une: 4/4 time counts four quarter-note beats; 3/4 time, three beats, the waltz time.
textes.Le chiffre du bas d'une mesure ne compte: The bottom number of a time signature does not count beats: it says which note gets one beat (4 for the quarter note, 8 for the eighth).
textes.Durées : une ronde vaut deux blanches, q: Note values: a whole note equals two half notes, four quarter notes or eight eighth notes
textes.Monter d'une octave double la fréquence: Going up an octave doubles the frequency: the A at 440 Hz has the A at 880 Hz as its octave.
textes.La quinte juste répond au rapport 3/2 de: The perfect fifth matches a 3/2 frequency ratio, the fourth a 4/3 ratio. On a string, two thirds of the length sound the fifth.
textes.L'octave occidentale compte 12 demi-tons: The Western octave has 12 semitones; a whole tone equals two semitones.
textes.Un dièse (♯) monte une note d'un demi-to: A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone; a flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone.
textes.Les marteaux de forgeron de Pythagore so: Pythagoras's blacksmith hammers are a legend: a hammer's note does not follow its weight the way a string's note follows its length.
textes.Une corde : sa moitié sonne l'octave, se: A string: half of it sounds the octave, two thirds the fifth, three quarters the fourth
textes.La gamme majeure suit le motif ton, ton,: The major scale follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half: C D E F G A B C, on the white keys alone.
textes.La gamme mineure naturelle suit ton, dem: The natural minor scale follows whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. A minor has the same notes as C major: it is its relative.
textes.L'armure, au début de la portée, liste l: The key signature, at the start of the staff, lists the key's sharps or flats: one F♯ for G major, one B♭ for F major.
textes.De quinte en quinte (do, sol, ré, la…),: From fifth to fifth (C, G, D, A…), each major key gains one more sharp: this is the circle of fifths.
textes.Do majeur et la mineur partagent exactem: C major and A minor share exactly the same notes: only the starting note, the tonic, changes.
textes.Gamme de do majeur : ton, ton, demi-ton,: C major scale: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
textes.Une note d'instrument contient sa fréque: An instrument's note contains its fundamental frequency f and harmonics at 2f, 3f, 4f…
textes.Le timbre, qui distingue un violon d'une: Timbre, which tells a violin from a flute on the same note, depends mostly on the mix of these harmonics and on the attack of the sound.
textes.Joseph Fourier a montré en 1822 qu'un si: Joseph Fourier showed in 1822 that a periodic signal breaks down into a sum of sine waves.
textes.Un tuyau ouvert aux deux bouts produit t: A pipe open at both ends produces all the harmonics; closed at one end, mostly the odd ones, like the clarinet in its low register.
textes.Deux instruments qui jouent la même note: Two instruments playing the same note have the same fundamental: it is not the pitch that differs, it is the timbre.
textes.le timbre dépend du dosage de chaque har: timbre depends on the strength of each harmonic
textes.Une corde vibre à la fois sur sa fondame: A string vibrates at once on its fundamental f and on its harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f
textes.L'accord parfait majeur empile une tierc: The major triad stacks a major third (4 semitones) then a minor third (3): C, E, G.
textes.L'accord parfait mineur inverse l'ordre,: The minor triad reverses the order, minor third then major third: A, C, E.
textes.Les intervalles aux rapports simples son: Intervals with simple ratios sound consonant: octave 2/1, fifth 3/2, major third 5/4.
textes.Rameau, en 1722 : do-mi-sol, mi-sol-do e: Rameau, in 1722: C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted.
textes.Un accord ne prend pas le nom de sa note: A chord is not named after its lowest note but after its root: E-G-C is still a C chord.
textes.Accord parfait de do majeur : do, mi, so: C major triad: C, E, G; major third then minor third
textes.Douze quintes pures (3/2) dépassent sept: Twelve pure fifths (3/2) overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%: this is the Pythagorean comma.
textes.Le tempérament égal divise l'octave en 1: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 identical semitones, with a ratio of ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595.
textes.Ses quintes sont un peu trop petites (≈: Its fifths are slightly too small (≈ 1.4983 instead of 1.5), but every key becomes playable.
textes.L'octave vaut 1 200 cents, le demi-ton t: The octave is 1,200 cents, the tempered semitone 100 cents.
textes.« Bien tempéré » ne veut pas forcément d: “Well-tempered” does not necessarily mean “equally tempered”: the exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
textes.l'écart, le comma pythagoricien, vaut en: the gap, the Pythagorean comma, is about 1.4%
textes.le tempérament égal le répartit sur les: equal temperament spreads it over the 12 fifths
textes.Douze quintes pures dépassent sept octav: Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%: this is the Pythagorean comma
textes.Décibels, limites de l'oreille et émotio: Decibels, the limits of the ear and musical emotion.
textes.Une oreille jeune entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: A young ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; with age, the high frequencies go first.
textes.Le décibel est logarithmique : +10 dB mu: The decibel is logarithmic: +10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10, +3 dB roughly doubles it.
textes.À intensité égale, l'oreille est plus se: At equal intensity, the ear is more sensitive around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz than in the bass (Fletcher and Munson curves, 1933).
textes.Les frissons musicaux s'accompagnent d'u: Musical chills come with a release of dopamine in the brain (Salimpoor et al., 2011).
textes.L'« effet Mozart », qui rendrait plus in: The “Mozart effect,” supposed to make you smarter, was not confirmed: the effect described in 1993 was small, brief and poorly replicated.
textes.L'oreille humaine entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: The human ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, with peak sensitivity around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz
textes.Fréquence = 1 ÷ période, et longueur d'o: Frequency = 1 ÷ period, and wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.
textes.Le son est une onde de pression, pas de: Sound is a pressure wave, no sound in a vacuum. 343 m/s in air: 3 seconds per kilometre.
textes.Une corde pincée, une membrane de haut-p: A plucked string, a loudspeaker cone or your vocal cords push the air, which compresses, then relaxes. This compression is passed along step by step, like a push in a queue of people: it is a pressure wave. The air does not travel, only the push moves forward. Without matter there is nothing to push: sound does not cross a vacuum.
textes.Fréquence = hauteur, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitud: Frequency = pitch, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitude = loudness. λ = v ÷ f: A 440 Hz is 0.78 m long.
textes.La fréquence f, en hertz, compte les vib: Frequency f, in hertz, counts the vibrations per second; it gives the pitch. The higher it is, the higher the sound. It is the inverse of the period T, the duration of one vibration: f = 1 ÷ T. For a period of 0.002 s, f = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 Hz. The tuning fork, invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter at the English court, vibrates 440 times a second: that is the A.
textes.L'amplitude, elle, donne l'intensité, me: Amplitude gives the intensity, measured in decibels. The two are independent: a low A can be very loud, a high A very soft. And the wave has a length: the distance covered during one vibration, λ = v ÷ f. For A at 440 Hz in air: λ = 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m. Bass notes have wavelengths of several metres, hence big loudspeakers.
textes.Cinq lignes, l'aigu en haut. Clé de sol: Five lines, high at the top. Treble clef: 2nd line. Bass clef: 4th. Ut, re, mi: Guido of Arezzo, around 1030.
textes.La portée a cinq lignes et se lit comme: The staff has five lines and reads like a graph: time runs from left to right, high notes at the top, low at the bottom. The clef, at the start, names one line, and all the others follow from it. The treble clef curls around the 2nd line: that line carries G. The bass clef puts F on the 4th line, for low instruments.
textes.Les noms des notes ont une histoire. Ver: The note names have a history. Around 1030 Guido of Arezzo had the idea of taking the first syllable of each line of the Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, each line of which starts one step higher: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut would later become do, easier to sing.
textes.Couper une ronde en morceaux: Cutting a whole note into pieces
textes.Ronde = 2 blanches = 4 noires = 8 croche: Whole = 2 halves = 4 quarters = 8 eighths. The dot adds half: dotted half = 3 quarters.
textes.Un point juste après une note ajoute la: A dot just after a note adds half its value. A dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = 3 quarter notes; a dotted quarter note, one and a half quarters, that is 3 eighth notes. Careful: a dot above or below the note is something else, it asks for it to be played detached.
textes.Haut : nombre de temps. Bas : quelle fig: Top: number of beats. Bottom: which note is one beat. 3/4 = the waltz. Petrucci (1501): printed music.
textes.La mesure regroupe les temps. Le chiffre: The time signature groups the beats. The top number counts the beats; the bottom one says which note value is one beat: 4 for the quarter note, 8 for the eighth. In 4/4, four quarter notes per bar, the most common time. In 3/4, three quarter notes: that is the waltz, first beat stressed, oom, pah, pah.
textes.Pendant des siècles, la musique se copia: For centuries music was copied by hand. In 1501 in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed with movable type: notes, staves and words went under the press in several passes. The score became an object that travels.
textes.Octave = fréquence × 2, corde ÷ 2 (Philo: Octave = frequency × 2, string ÷ 2 (Philolaus). A 440 Hz: London 1939, ISO 16 standard.
textes.Monter d'une octave, c'est doubler la fr: Going up an octave means doubling the frequency: f = 2 × 440 = 880 Hz for the A above. The two notes blend so well that they get the same name. On a string it is half: a string half as long vibrates twice as fast. In the 5th century BC the Pythagorean Philolaus already linked the octave to the ratio 2/1.
textes.Le la de référence à 440 Hz a été recomm: The reference A at 440 Hz was recommended in London in 1939, then adopted by the ISO 16 standard. Before that it varied from city to city: France had set its own at 435 Hz in the mid-19th century. A touring orchestra could find itself out of tune with the local organ.
textes.Quinte 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), quarte 4/3, t: Fifth 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), fourth 4/3, third 5/4. Pythagoras' hammers: a legend.
textes.La légende veut que Pythagore ait découv: Legend has it that Pythagoras discovered these ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers of different weights. Nicomachus of Gerasa and then Boethius tell it. It is physically false: a hammer's note does not follow its weight the way a string's follows its length. The ratios themselves are true, and can be checked on a string.
textes.12 demi-tons par octave, un ton = 2 demi: 12 semitones per octave, a tone = 2 semitones, fifth = 7. Sharp raises, flat lowers, natural cancels.
textes.L'octave occidentale compte 12 demi-tons: The Western octave has 12 semitones: on a piano, seven white keys and five black before you reach the same note again. A tone is two semitones: from C to D you pass through C♯. The perfect fifth has seven: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G.
textes.Le dièse (♯) monte une note d'un demi-to: The sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, the flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone, and the natural (♮) cancels both. On a piano C♯ and D♭ fall on the same black key; on a violin a player may play them very slightly differently.
textes.Majeure : T T ½ T T T ½. Do majeur = tou: Major: T T ½ T T T ½. C major = white keys. The key signature keeps the pattern: G has F♯, F has B♭.
textes.Partez d'une autre note et, pour garder: Start from another note and, to keep the pattern, you need accidentals. From G, the F must go up: G major has an F♯. From F, the B must come down: F major has a B♭. They are written once and for all at the start of the staff: that is the key signature.
textes.La mineur = notes de do majeur, départ e: A minor = notes of C major, starting on A (relative). Pentatonic: 5 notes, the black keys.
textes.La gamme mineure naturelle suit ton, dem: The natural minor scale follows tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone. Start from A on the white keys and you get it: A minor has exactly the same notes as C major. It is called its relative. Only the tonic, the note of departure and arrival, changes, and with it the whole colour: darker, more melancholy.
textes.De quinte en quinte, un dièse de plus :: Fifth by fifth, one more sharp: C 0, G 1, D 2. Bach: 24 preludes and fugues per book.
textes.Bach a célébré ce cercle complet. Chaque: Bach celebrated this complete circle. Each book of The Well-Tempered Clavier offers a prelude and fugue in each of the 12 major and 12 minor keys: 24 pairs per book. It still required a keyboard tuning that made all these keys playable.
textes.fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701) : 3e harmoniq: fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701): 3rd harmonic of 110 Hz = 330 Hz. Between 2f and 3f, a hidden fifth.
textes.Une corde ne vibre pas seulement en enti: A string does not vibrate only as a whole. It also vibrates in two halves, three thirds, four quarters, all at once. Each mode gives a frequency: the fundamental f, then the harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f… The n-th harmonic is fₙ = n × f. For a fundamental at 110 Hz, the 3rd harmonic is 3 × 110 = 330 Hz. Joseph Sauveur gave them the name harmonics in 1701.
textes.Sauveur appela aussi « nœuds » les point: Sauveur also called the still points "nodes". A string vibrating in 4 loops at 400 Hz has a fundamental of f = 400 ÷ 4 = 100 Hz. And between the 2nd and 3rd harmonics the ratio is 3f ÷ 2f = 3/2: every note contains a hidden fifth.
textes.Pourquoi une flûte n'est pas un violon: Why a flute is not a violin
textes.Même note, même fondamentale : le timbre: Same note, same fundamental: timbre is the mix of harmonics and the attack. Helmholtz (1863): the resonators.
textes.Une flûte et un violon qui jouent le mêm: A flute and a violin playing the same A have the same fundamental. What sets them apart is timbre: the mix of harmonics, and the way the sound begins, the attack. The violin is rich in harmonics, the flute has few. A pipe open at both ends produces all the harmonics; closed at one end, it favours the odd ones, like the clarinet in its low register, hence its rather hollow tone.
textes.En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie sa: In 1863 Hermann von Helmholtz published his great study of the sensations of tone. To isolate harmonics he used hollow resonators, each tuned to a single frequency, which he held against the ear: you could then hear one harmonic at a time in a sound that seemed single.
textes.Fourier (1822) : tout signal périodique: Fourier (1822): any periodic signal = sum of sine waves. The spectrum analyser shows it.
textes.En 1822, dans sa Théorie analytique de l: In 1822, in his Analytical Theory of Heat, Joseph Fourier showed that a periodic signal, however complicated, can be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves. He was working on heat, not music, but his tool applies to everything that vibrates.
textes.C'est exactement ce que fait un analyseu: That is exactly what a spectrum analyser does: it breaks a sound down into its frequencies and displays the fundamental and its harmonics, each with its own height. Electronic tuners, MP3 compression and song recognition rest on this idea.
textes.Majeur : tierce majeure (4) + mineure (3: Major: major third (4) + minor (3). Minor: the reverse. Rameau (1722): inversions.
textes.L'accord parfait majeur empile deux tier: The major triad stacks two thirds: a major third of 4 semitones, then a minor third of 3. On C: C, E, G, the root, its third and its fifth. The minor triad reverses the order, minor third then major: A, C, E. C minor is formed by lowering the third: C, E♭, G.
textes.En 1722, Jean-Philippe Rameau publie son: In 1722 Jean-Philippe Rameau published his Treatise on Harmony Reduced to its Natural Principles. In it he showed that C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted: it takes the name of its root, not of its lowest note. He also set out the fundamental bass, which explains chord progressions.
textes.Rapports simples = consonance (Helmholtz: Simple ratios = consonance (Helmholtz, beats). Zarlino (1558): third 5/4, 264 → 330 Hz.
textes.Les intervalles aux rapports simples son: Intervals with simple ratios sound consonant: the octave 2/1, the fifth 3/2, the major third 5/4, the minor third 6/5. Helmholtz explained it by beats: with a simple ratio few neighbouring harmonics rub against each other; with a complicated ratio they grate.
textes.En 1558, Gioseffo Zarlino défend les tie: In 1558 Gioseffo Zarlino championed pure thirds at ratio 5/4 against the Pythagorean third of 81/64, too wide. The calculation: the natural major third of a C at 264 Hz is f = 264 × 5/4 = 330 Hz. After a perfect cadence, the dominant G resolving onto the tonic C, you hear that the piece is over.
textes.Tonique = repos, dominante = tension. Ca: Tonic = rest, dominant = tension. Perfect cadence: G → C. A chord takes the name of its root.
textes.En harmonie, chaque accord a un rôle dan: In harmony each chord has a role in the key. The tonic, built on the first note, is rest. The dominant, on the fifth, creates a tension that calls for a return. The perfect cadence, dominant then tonic, G then C in C major, has the effect of a full stop.
textes.Les quintes ne retombent pas juste: The fifths do not land true
textes.(3/2)¹² ≈ 129,75 contre 2⁷ = 128 : 1,4 %: (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75 versus 2⁷ = 128: a 1.4 % gap, the Pythagorean comma.
textes.Empilez douze quintes pures depuis un do: Stack twelve pure fifths from a C: you should land on a C seven octaves up. The calculation says no. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is 129.75 ÷ 128 − 1 ≈ 0.0137, that is 1.4 %. That is the Pythagorean comma, named after Pythagoras because it comes from his tuning by pure fifths.
textes.Conséquence : impossible d'accorder un c: Consequence: you cannot tune a keyboard with all its fifths pure. The error has to be spread somewhere. Meantone temperament, for example, keeps eleven nearly pure fifths and concentrates the error in the twelfth, so grating that it is called the wolf fifth: music that modulated too far became unplayable on a single keyboard.
textes.Demi-ton tempéré = ¹²√2 ≈ 1,0595 (Zhu Za: Tempered semitone = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595 (Zhu Zaiyu, 1584). Fifths barely too small, every key playable.
textes.Le tempérament égal répartit l'erreur pa: Equal temperament spreads the error everywhere: it divides the octave into 12 identical semitones. Twelve semitones must make an octave, so r¹² = 2 and r = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595. Each fifth becomes slightly too small, about 1.4983 instead of 1.5, 2 cents less: the ear barely notices. But every key becomes playable.
textes.En 1584, en Chine, le prince Zhu Zaiyu c: In 1584, in China, Prince Zhu Zaiyu calculated the twelfth root of 2 on an abacus to 24 correct decimal places: it was the first exact calculation of this division. In Europe Simon Stevin was working on the same idea at the same time. Almost all pianos are tuned this way today: every interval is slightly off, but all equally so.
textes.Dans les années 1880, Alexander Ellis in: In the 1880s Alexander Ellis invented the cent: one hundredth of a tempered semitone. The octave therefore has 12 × 100 = 1,200. Tuners and music software use it to say how far out a note is: within a few cents, most ears cannot tell the difference.
textes.Et Bach ? Le titre du Clavier bien tempé: And Bach? The title of The Well-Tempered Clavier does not prove he tuned in equal temperament. "Well-tempered" means tuned well enough to play in every key, which other unequal temperaments also allowed. The exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
textes.20 Hz à 20 000 Hz, les aigus partent d'a: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, high frequencies go first. Peak sensitivity around 2,000-5,000 Hz (Fletcher and Munson, 1933).
textes.Une oreille jeune entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: A young ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below are infrasounds; above, ultrasounds, which bats hear. With age you lose the high frequencies first: that is presbycusis. Nor is the ear equally sensitive everywhere: it is most sensitive around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz, where much of speech intelligibility lies.
textes.En 1933, Harvey Fletcher et Wilden Munso: In 1933 Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson measured it: their curves show that a low sound must be far more intense than a 3,000 Hz sound to seem as loud. That is why the bass seems to disappear when you turn the volume down.
textes.L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20 dB = × 100, +3 dB ≈ × 2. The bel: Graham Bell.
textes.Cette échelle colle à notre oreille, qui: This scale fits our ear, which perceives ratios rather than differences. But it misleads: two speakers instead of one add only 3 dB, not twice the perceived noise. And with too many decibels, the hair cells of the inner ear are damaged for good.
textes.Frissons musicaux = dopamine (Salimpoor,: Musical chills = dopamine (Salimpoor, 2011). The Mozart effect does not hold. Beethoven deaf, Vienna 1824.
textes.En 2011, Valorie Salimpoor et ses collèg: In 2011 Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues measured with brain imaging what happens during musical chills: the brain releases dopamine, the same molecule as for food. Music activates the reward circuit, even before the awaited passage: the pleasure of anticipation.
textes.L'« effet Mozart », lui, ne s'est pas co: The "Mozart effect" was not confirmed. The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task; in 1999 a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ. And Beethoven composed his Ninth almost totally deaf: at the premiere, in 1824 in Vienna, the singer Caroline Unger had to turn him towards the audience so he could see the applause.
textes.Dans l'air à 20 °C, le son parcourt envi: In air at 20 °C sound travels about 343 m/s; nearly 1,500 m/s in water, and 5,000 to 6,000 m/s in steel. Hence the thunderstorm rule: time equals distance divided by speed, t = d ÷ v. For 1 km: t = 1,000 m ÷ 343 m/s ≈ 2.9 s. Count about 3 seconds between lightning and thunder per kilometre. Newton was the first to calculate the speed of sound. That was in 1687, in the Principia: he found 298 m/s, about 15% too low, because he assumed the air keeps its temperature as it is compressed. Laplace would correct the error.
textes.Les durées se divisent par deux : une ro: Durations are divided by two: a whole note is worth 2 half notes, a half note 2 quarter notes, a quarter note 2 eighth notes. So a whole note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 quarter notes, or 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 eighth notes, and a half note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 eighth notes. The shorter the note, the more beams or flags it gets. The idea that a note's shape sets its duration goes back to Franco of Cologne, in his Ars cantus mensurabilis, around 1250.
textes.Un accord ne prend pas le nom de sa note: A chord takes its name not from its lowest note but from its root: E-G-C is still a C chord. That is Rameau's contribution, which lets you recognise the same function in very different layouts, from a Bach chorale to a pop song. Rameau published this idea in 1722, in his Treatise on Harmony.
textes.Le décibel est logarithmique : L = 10 lo: The decibel is logarithmic: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀), where I is the intensity and I₀ the threshold of hearing. In practice, +10 dB multiply the intensity by 10. Going from 60 dB to 80 dB is +20 dB, so an intensity multiplied by 10 × 10 = 100. And +3 dB roughly double it, since 10^(3/10) ≈ 2. The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell; the decibel is a tenth of it. The unit was born in telephony: the Bell System measured its line losses in "transmission units", renamed decibels in 1928.
textes.Après l'octave, l'intervalle le plus sim: After the octave, the simplest interval is the perfect fifth, at ratio 3/2: on a string, two thirds of the length. Above an A at 440 Hz, the fifth vibrates at f = 440 × 3/2 = 660 Hz. Next come the fourth, 4/3, and the natural major third, 5/4. Philolaus already gave the fifth the ratio 3/2. This Pythagorean lived in the 5th century BCE.
textes.La gamme majeure suit toujours le même m: The major scale always follows the same pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Start from C and you get C D E F G A B C, on the white keys alone: the semitones fall between E and F, and between B and C, between the 3rd and 4th notes then the 7th and 8th. The note names come from a monk, Guido of Arezzo, around 1025: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la are the openings of the lines of the hymn Ut queant laxis, which he used as a memory aid. Ut later became do, and si was added.
textes.Il existe d'autres gammes. La pentatoniq: There are other scales. The pentatonic has only five notes, as its name says: the five black keys of the piano form one. It is found in many of the world's musics, from the blues to traditional songs. The oldest notated music to have reached us almost complete, a Hurrian hymn to the goddess Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet from Ugarit around 1400 BCE, even gives instructions for tuning a nine-stringed lyre.
textes.Montez de quinte en quinte depuis do : d: Go up fifth by fifth from C: C, G, D, A… Each major key gains one more sharp. C has none, G has F♯, D has F♯ and C♯, A has three. The other way, going down fifth by fifth, you gain a flat at each step. The twelve keys close up into a circle. The first known diagram of this circle appears in Mykola Dyletsky's Grammatika, in 1677; Johann David Heinichen published another in 1711.
textes.Le diapason, inventé en 1711 par John Sh: The tuning fork, invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter at the English court, vibrates 440 times a second: that is the A.
textes.Vers 1030, Guido d'Arezzo a l'idée de pr: Around 1030 Guido of Arezzo had the idea of taking the first syllable of each line of the Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, each line of which starts one step higher: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.
textes.En 1501, à Venise, Ottaviano Petrucci pu: In 1501 in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed with movable type: notes, staves and words went under the press in several passes.
textes.Au Ve siècle avant notre ère, le pythago: In the 5th century BC the Pythagorean Philolaus already linked the octave to the ratio 2/1.
textes.Les noms des notes viennent d'un moine,: The note names come from a monk, Guido of Arezzo, around 1025: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la are the openings of the lines of the hymn Ut queant laxis, which he used as a memory aid.
textes.La plus ancienne musique notée qui nous: The oldest notated music to have reached us almost complete, a Hurrian hymn to the goddess Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet from Ugarit around 1400 BCE, even gives instructions for tuning a nine-stringed lyre.
textes.Le premier schéma connu de ce cercle fig: The first known diagram of this circle appears in Mykola Dyletsky's Grammatika, in 1677; Johann David Heinichen published another in 1711.
textes.En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie sa: In 1863 Hermann von Helmholtz published his great study of the sensations of tone.
textes.En 1822, dans sa Théorie analytique de l: In 1822, in his Analytical Theory of Heat, Joseph Fourier showed that a periodic signal, however complicated, can be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves.
textes.En 1722, Jean-Philippe Rameau publie son: In 1722 Jean-Philippe Rameau published his Treatise on Harmony Reduced to its Natural Principles.
textes.En 1558, Gioseffo Zarlino défend les tie: In 1558 Gioseffo Zarlino championed pure thirds at ratio 5/4 against the Pythagorean third of 81/64, too wide.
textes.En 1584, en Chine, le prince Zhu Zaiyu c: In 1584, in China, Prince Zhu Zaiyu calculated the twelfth root of 2 on an abacus to 24 correct decimal places: it was the first exact calculation of this division.
textes.L'unité naît dans les téléphones : le Be: The unit was born in telephony: the Bell System measured its line losses in "transmission units", renamed decibels in 1928.
textes.En 2011, Valorie Salimpoor et ses collèg: In 2011 Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues measured with brain imaging what happens during musical chills: the brain releases dopamine, the same molecule as for food.
textes.L'étude de 1993 décrivait un gain bref s: The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task; in 1999 a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ.
textes.Des flûtes taillées dans des os il y a 4: From flutes carved from bones 40,000 years ago to the golden lyres of Ur: music is far older than writing.
textes.En Allemagne, des flûtes en os de cygne: In Germany, flutes of swan bone and mammoth ivory are 42,000 to 43,000 years old; the one from Hohle Fels, of vulture bone, about 35,000.
textes.En Chine, à Jiahu, on a trouvé 33 flûtes: In China, at Jiahu, 33 flutes made from crane wing bones were found, from 7000 to 5700 BC: they can still be played.
textes.Les lyres d'Ur, vers 2550 à 2450 av. J.-: The lyres of Ur, from about 2550 to 2450 BC, are the oldest surviving stringed instruments.
textes.En 1914, Hornbostel et Sachs rangent tou: In 1914, Hornbostel and Sachs sorted all instruments into four families according to what vibrates: the body, a membrane, a string or the air.
textes.Un os percé n'est pas forcément une flût: A pierced bone is not necessarily a flute: the Divje Babe "flute", in Slovenia, may have been holed by a carnivore's teeth.
textes.Il y a environ 35 000 ans, dans la grott: About 35,000 years ago, in the Hohle Fels cave, in the Swabian Jura, someone drilled five holes in a vulture's radius. Found in 2006, this flute is among the oldest known instruments. In the nearby Geissenklösterle cave, two flutes of swan bone and one of mammoth ivory were dated in 2012 to 42,000 to 43,000 years.
textes.Un candidat plus ancien divise les cherc: An older candidate divides researchers: at Divje Babe, in Slovenia, a cave bear femur pierced with holes, found in 1995, may be 50,000 to 60,000 years old. For its discoverer, the holes are man-made; for others, an animal simply chewed the bone.
textes.Geissenklösterle 42 000 à 43 000 ans, Ho: Geissenklösterle 42,000 to 43,000 years, Hohle Fels 35,000 years: flutes are among the oldest objects made for art.
textes.En Chine, dans la province du Henan, prè: In China, in Henan province, near the Yellow River, the Neolithic village of Jiahu was inhabited from about 7000 to 5700 BC. Thirty-three flutes were found there, carved from the wing bones of red-crowned cranes, a large bird about 1.5 m tall. They are 18 to 25 cm long, about twenty are intact, and they can still be played.
textes.Ces flûtes étaient précieuses : l'une, c: These flutes were precious: one, broken, was repaired by drilling fourteen small holes along the crack. They are among the oldest playable instruments in the world. The same site yielded eleven signs carved on tortoise shells and bones, which some see as proto-writing.
textes.Jiahu, 7000 à 5700 av. J.-C. : 33 flûtes: Jiahu, 7000 to 5700 BC: 33 crane-bone flutes, still playable.
textes.Les lyres d'Ur, et quatre familles: The lyres of Ur, and four families
textes.Vers 2550 à 2450 av. J.-C., dans le cime: Around 2550 to 2450 BC, in the royal cemetery of Ur, in Mesopotamia, four instruments were buried with the powerful: three lyres and a harp, the oldest surviving stringed instruments. Leonard Woolley uncovered them among the skeletons of ten women. The "golden lyre", with its bull's head all in gold, is in the Baghdad museum; its reconstructed sound box was damaged by flooding during the Iraq war.
textes.Comment ranger tant d'instruments ? En 1: How to sort so many instruments? In 1914, Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs proposed classifying them by what vibrates: the body of the instrument (idiophones), a stretched membrane (membranophones), a string (chordophones) or the air itself (aerophones). In 1940 Sachs added a fifth family, the electrophones.
textes.Ur : les plus vieux instruments à cordes: Ur: the oldest surviving stringed instruments. Hornbostel-Sachs: an instrument is classified by what vibrates.
textes.D'une tablette d'argile à Ougarit à une: From a clay tablet at Ugarit to a Greek gravestone: the first attempts to write down a melody, and how hard they are to read back.
textes.Vers 1400 av. J.-C., à Ougarit, en Syrie: Around 1400 BC, at Ugarit, in Syria, a hymn to the goddess Nikkal was written on clay: it is the oldest substantially complete notated work.
textes.Sa notation donne des noms d'intervalles: Its notation gives Akkadian interval names followed by numbers; at least five different readings have been proposed.
textes.L'épitaphe de Seikilos, au Ier ou IIe si: The Seikilos epitaph, from the 1st or 2nd century, is the oldest complete musical composition: letters above the words give the melody.
textes.Au IVe siècle, Alypius dresse les tables: In the 4th century, Alypius drew up the tables of Greek signs, for voice and for instruments: thanks to them Seikilos can be read today.
textes.Une notation ancienne ne se lit pas comm: An ancient notation is not read like a score: without the reading rules, the same tablet gives entirely different melodies.
textes.Dans les années 1950, au palais royal d': In the 1950s, in the royal palace of Ugarit, on the coast of present-day Syria, fragments of clay tablets were dug up bearing about 36 hymns in the Hurrian language. They date from about 1400 BC. Only one, tablet h.6, is substantially complete: a hymn to Nikkal, goddess of orchards, for a voice and a nine-stringed lyre.
textes.Sous les paroles, la notation aligne des: Below the words, the notation lines up Akkadian interval names, each followed by a number. What do these numbers mean? Should two notes be played at once? At least five rival decipherments have been proposed, giving entirely different melodies. And the Hurrian language itself is still poorly understood.
textes.Ougarit, vers 1400 av. J.-C. : la plus v: Ugarit, around 1400 BC: the oldest substantially complete notated music, and at least five ways to read it.
textes.Au Ier ou au IIe siècle, à Tralles, près: In the 1st or 2nd century, at Tralles, near present-day Aydın, in Turkey, a man named Seikilos had a song carved on a stone: while you live, shine, life is short. Above each line of words, letters and signs give the notes. It is the oldest known complete musical composition.
textes.Retrouvée vers 1883 lors de la construct: Found around 1883 during the building of a railway, the stone fell into the hands of the engineer Edward Purser, who had its base sawn flat to hold his wife's flowerpots: one line was lost, known only from a rubbing. Taken from Smyrna in 1922, kept in The Hague, it then entered the National Museum of Denmark, in Copenhagen.
textes.Seikilos : la plus vieille chanson compl: Seikilos: the oldest complete song, notated by letters above the words, and narrowly saved from a flowerpot.
textes.Comment sait-on quelle note désigne chaq: How do we know which note each Greek letter stands for? Thanks to Alypius of Alexandria, a 4th-century author. Only a fragment of his Introduction to Music remains, but it holds the essentials: the vocal and instrumental signs for every sound, in 45 scales, that is fifteen modes in three genera, diatonic, chromatic and enharmonic.
textes.Les Grecs avaient donc deux alphabets mu: So the Greeks had two musical alphabets, one for singing, one for playing. Alypius's text, judged hopelessly corrupt by an earlier editor, was restored by the Dane Marcus Meibom, who printed it with its tables in Amsterdam in 1652. It is now the best source for reading Greek notation.
textes.Alypius : les tables des signes grecs, p: Alypius: the tables of Greek signs, for voice and for instruments. Without him, Seikilos would be silent.
textes.Octave, quinte, quarte : des rapports si: Octave, fifth, fourth: simple ratios, which legend attributes to Pythagoras's hammers.
textes.Dans la Chine des Zhou, des carillons de: In Zhou China, bronze chimes played melodies. Each bell sounds two notes, and a marquis took 65 of them to his tomb.
textes.Les bianzhong sont des jeux de cloches d: Bianzhong are sets of tuned bronze bells, struck with mallets to play melodies, symbols of power under the Zhou.
textes.Frappée au centre, une cloche donne sa n: Struck in the centre, a bell gives its main note; struck on the side, a second note, a major or minor third higher.
textes.Le tombeau du marquis Yi de Zeng, vers 4: The tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, around 433 BC, held 65 bells covering five octaves, chromatic over the three central octaves.
textes.Leurs inscriptions mettent en correspond: Their inscriptions relate the pitch systems of several states: Zeng, Chu and Zhou.
textes.Une cloche n'est pas forcément un instru: A bell is not necessarily a one-note instrument: a Chinese zhong bell gives two clear notes depending on where it is struck.
textes.Des flûtes du phénix aux cloches de bron: From the phoenix's flutes to bronze bells
textes.Selon la légende, Ling Lun, le fondateur: According to legend, Ling Lun, the founder of Chinese music, cut bamboo flutes that imitated birdsong, even that of the fenghuang, the mythical bird likened to the phoenix. He is also credited with the five notes of the pentatonic scale. The Yellow Emperor is then said to have had bells cast in tune with these flutes.
textes.La réalité est plus belle encore. Sous l: Reality is even finer. Under the Shang and Zhou dynasties, the Chinese made the world's first bronze chime-bells, for ritual music. This set of bells, the bianzhong, was reserved for the elite: a sign of power and wealth. They are also the only Bronze Age instruments that can still be played.
textes.Légende : Ling Lun et ses flûtes. Histoi: Legend: Ling Lun and his flutes. History: the bronze chimes of the Shang and Zhou, signs of power.
textes.En 1977, à Suizhou, dans le Hubei, des s: In 1977, at Suizhou, in Hubei, soldiers levelling a hill to build a factory stumbled on a tomb: that of Marquis Yi of Zeng, who died around 433 BC. Twenty-one women were buried there with him, and a whole orchestra: sounding stones, qin and se zithers, panpipes, flutes, sheng mouth organs.
textes.Et surtout, sorti de terre en 1978 presq: And above all, brought out in 1978 almost intact, a complete set of 65 bronze bells hung from great wooden beams. They cover five octaves and are chromatic over the three central octaves. Inscriptions on them relate the pitch systems of the states of Zeng, Chu and Zhou. The chime is on display at the Hubei Provincial Museum, in Wuhan.
textes.Marquis Yi de Zeng, vers 433 av. J.-C. :: Marquis Yi of Zeng, around 433 BC: 65 bells, five octaves, and inscriptions comparing systems of notes.
Zhong bells hide a surprise. Struck in the centre, a bell gives its main note; struck near a corner, it gives a second note, a major or minor third higher.
textes.Un jeu de 65 cloches offre donc bien plu: A set of 65 bells therefore offers far more than 65 notes. The archaeologist Lothar von Falkenhausen devoted a whole book to them in 1993, Suspended Music, with chapters on their acoustics, their manufacture, how they were played and the measurement of their notes.
textes.Cloche zhong : au centre, la note princi: Zhong bell: in the centre, the main note; on the side, a third higher.
textes.Pour Boèce à Rome comme pour al-Farabi à: For Boethius in Rome as for al-Farabi in Baghdad, music is a science: numbers, ratios, and effects on the soul.
textes.Boèce et la musique savante, dans le tem: Boethius and learned music, in time
textes.Vers 510, Boèce écrit De institutione mu: Around 510, Boethius wrote De institutione musica, based on Nicomachus of Gerasa and Ptolemy's Harmonics.
textes.Il distingue trois musiques : celle du m: He distinguished three musics: that of the world, understood but not heard, that of man, and that of instruments, the only audible one.
textes.Son traité fait de la musique une scienc: His treatise made music a science of the quadrivium, with arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, throughout the Middle Ages.
textes.À Bagdad, au Xe siècle, al-Farabi, le «: In Baghdad, in the 10th century, al-Farabi, the "second teacher" after Aristotle, wrote the Great Book of Music: theory, instruments and effects on the soul.
textes.La musica mundana de Boèce n'est pas une: Boethius's musica mundana is not music one hears: it is the wholly mathematical harmony of the movement of the heavens.
textes.Boèce naît à Rome vers 480. Sénateur, co: Boethius was born in Rome around 480. A senator, consul in 510, he became master of offices to the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. He wanted to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, and wrote manuals for arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. Around 510, his De institutione musica, in five books left unfinished, drew on a lost work by Nicomachus of Gerasa and on Ptolemy's Harmonics.
textes.Il y distingue trois musiques. La musica: In it he distinguished three musics. Musica mundana, that of the world, the harmony of the spheres, which cannot be heard but only understood. Musica humana, the harmony of body and soul. And the music of instruments, the only audible one. For him, "music is so naturally united with us that we cannot be free from it even if we so desired".
textes.Trois musiques : du monde (inaudible), d: Three musics: of the world (inaudible), of man, of instruments. Only the last can be heard.
textes.Vers 523, Boèce prend la défense d'un an: Around 523, Boethius defended a former consul, Albinus. Theodoric had him imprisoned; while awaiting execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy. He was executed in 524, at Pavia. His treatise on music, however, would survive a thousand years.
textes.À partir du IXe siècle, les théoriciens: From the 9th century on, medieval theorists used it to understand Greek music; about 140 medieval manuscripts of it survive, and it was printed in Venice in 1491-1492. The anonymous 9th-century treatise Musica enchiriadis often circulated with it. The historian Richard Southern called Boethius "the schoolmaster of medieval Europe".
textes.Exécuté en 524, Boèce reste le manuel de: Executed in 524, Boethius remained Europe's music textbook for a thousand years: 140 manuscripts, then print.
textes.Né vers 870 à Farab, al-Farabi passe l'e: Born around 870 in Farab, al-Farabi spent most of his scholarly life in Baghdad and died in Damascus around 950. He is called the "second teacher", just after Aristotle. He was both a practising musician and a theorist. For a vizier of the caliph al-Radi who wanted to learn the music of the Greek theorists, he wrote the Kitab al-musiqi al-kabir, the Great Book of Music.
textes.Le livre part de la philosophie et de la: The book starts from philosophy and the production of sound, then moves on to the instruments of his day, the oud lute and the tanbur, to intervals and kinds of melody. Al-Farabi shows that music borrows its principles from mathematics, and that each kind of music acts differently on the soul. Legend credits him with the power to make his audience laugh, cry or sleep against their will.
textes.Al-Farabi, Bagdad, Xe siècle : la musiqu: Al-Farabi, Baghdad, 10th century: music is mathematical, and it acts on the soul.
textes.Depuis Guido d'Arezzo, vers 1025, des no: Since Guido of Arezzo, around 1025, notes placed on lines: staff, clefs, durations and time signatures.
textes.Du plain-chant à quatre voix : à Notre-D: From plainchant to four voices: at Notre-Dame in Paris and then with the Ars nova, Europe learned to sing several melodies at once.
textes.L'organum ajoute au plain-chant au moins: Organum adds at least one voice to plainchant; the 9th-century treatise Musica enchiriadis gives the first surviving rules for it.
textes.À Notre-Dame de Paris, Léonin écrit des: At Notre-Dame in Paris, Léonin wrote two-voice organa; Pérotin moved to three, then four with Viderunt omnes and Sederunt principes, in 1198 and 1199.
textes.Au XIVe siècle, l'Ars nova, attachée à P: In the 14th century, the Ars nova, linked to Philippe de Vitry, freed rhythm; in 1324, Pope John XXII condemned it, in vain.
textes.Avant 1365, Guillaume de Machaut compose: Before 1365, Guillaume de Machaut composed the Messe de Nostre Dame, the oldest complete Mass by a single composer.
textes.Ars antiqua et Ars nova ne désignent pas: Ars antiqua and Ars nova do not mean Antiquity and the Renaissance: they are two periods of the Middle Ages, before and after the 1320s.
textes.Le plain-chant de l'Église est une seule: The Church's plainchant is a single melody, sung in unison. Organum adds at least one other voice to it to enrich the harmony. The first text to describe it and give rules for it is the Musica enchiriadis, an anonymous 9th-century treatise, long wrongly attributed to Hucbald.
textes.C'est la première tentative conservée d': It is the first surviving attempt to set up rules for polyphony in Western art music. The added voice follows the chant at a perfect interval, most often a fourth below. The treatise also uses a very rare notation, called daseian, in which signs rotated by a quarter turn indicate different pitches.
textes.Organum : le chant plus une voix parallè: Organum: the chant plus a parallel voice, often at the fourth. Musica enchiriadis, 9th century: the first rules.
textes.À la fin du XIIe siècle, la cathédrale N: At the end of the 12th century, the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris became the great workshop of polyphony. Léonin, master of chant, compiled the Magnus liber organi, a great book of two-voice organa. The Notre-Dame composers also developed the rhythmic modes, fixed patterns of long and short notes.
textes.Pérotin passe à trois voix, puis à quatr: Pérotin moved to three voices, then four: Viderunt omnes and Sederunt principes were sung at Notre-Dame in 1198 and 1199, three intertwined voices above a held voice. His name is known to us only through an anonymous English student, Anonymous IV, writing around 1275, who judged him the best composer of discant.
textes.Léonin : deux voix. Pérotin : trois, pui: Léonin: two voices. Pérotin: three, then four, in 1198 and 1199. And an anonymous student to remember it.
textes.L'Ars nova et le pape: The Ars nova and the pope
textes.Vers 1322, un ensemble d'écrits attribué: Around 1322, a collection of writings attributed to Philippe de Vitry, later bishop of Meaux, gave its name to an era: the Ars nova, the new art. Its notation allowed far freer rhythms to be written than the earlier rhythmic modes, now called Ars antiqua. Vitry is also credited with isorhythm, in which the same pattern of durations returns under different melodies. But the attribution, and even the existence of the treatise, are debated.
textes.En 1324, à Avignon, le pape Jean XXII co: In 1324, at Avignon, Pope John XXII condemned the new music, which drowned plainchant under a multitude of notes. In vain. Before 1365, Guillaume de Machaut, canon of Reims, composed for his cathedral the Messe de Nostre Dame, in four voices: the oldest complete setting of the Ordinary of the Mass by a single composer.
textes.Ars nova vers 1322, rythmes libres ; bul: Ars nova around 1322, free rhythms; the bull of 1324; Machaut, before 1365, the first complete Mass by one author.
textes.Gamme majeure, gamme mineure, cycle des: Major scale, minor scale, circle of fifths, and the maqams of Arabic music.
textes.Dans la musique arabe, un maqâm est bien: In Arabic music, a maqam is much more than a scale: it sets the notes, but also the habitual phrases, the important notes, the development of the melody and the modulations. It is built from ajnas, singular jins, groups of consecutive notes, most often four, each with its own colour. A maqam scale stacks a lower jins and an upper jins, whose first note serves as the dominant.
textes.Les maqâms sont microtonaux : ils ne sui: Maqams are microtonal: they do not follow the twelve equal semitones of the piano. They are often written with an octave of 24 quarter tones, but that is a notational convention: musicians play finer nuances, passed down orally. In the 13th century, in Baghdad, Safi al-Din al-Urmawi divided the octave into 17 steps and, for the first time, notated melodies with letters and numbers.
textes.Maqâm : un mode, avec ses notes, ses phr: Maqam: a mode, with its notes, phrases and paths; intervals finer than the semitone.
textes.À Venise en 1501, Petrucci imprime de la: In Venice in 1501, Petrucci printed polyphony in three passes through the press; in Paris in 1528, Attaingnant did it in one.
textes.En 1498, Ottaviano Petrucci obtient de V: In 1498, Ottaviano Petrucci obtained from Venice the exclusive right to print music for 20 years.
textes.Le 15 mai 1501, il date la dédicace de l: On 15 May 1501, he dated the dedication of the Odhecaton: 96 songs in three or four parts, the first printed collection of polyphony.
textes.Sa méthode demande trois passages sous l: His method needed three passes through the press: the staves, then the text, then the notes.
textes.En 1528, à Paris, Pierre Attaingnant imp: In 1528, in Paris, Pierre Attaingnant printed notes, staves and text in a single pass: the method became the standard in Europe.
textes.Le titre Odhecaton promet cent chansons,: The title Odhecaton promises a hundred songs, but the book contains only 96: a title is not an inventory.
textes.Né à Fossombrone en 1466, Ottaviano Petr: Born in Fossombrone in 1466, Ottaviano Petrucci settled in Venice. In 1498, he asked the doge for the exclusive right to print music for twenty years. On 15 May 1501, he dated the dedication of the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, "one hundred songs of harmonic music".
textes.C'est le plus ancien recueil connu de po: It is the earliest known collection of printed polyphony: 96 secular songs in three or four parts, gathered by the Dominican Petrus Castellanus. It includes Ockeghem, Josquin des Prez, Obrecht, Busnois and Agricola. Petrucci followed with the Canti B in 1502 and the Canti C in 1504.
textes.1501, Venise : l'Odhecaton, 96 chansons,: 1501, Venice: the Odhecaton, 96 songs, the first book of printed polyphony.
textes.Imprimer de la polyphonie est un casse-t: Printing polyphony is a puzzle: it needs continuous staff lines, notes set on them at the right height, and words. Petrucci's solution: pass each sheet through the press three times, first for the staves, then for the text, finally for the notes.
textes.On lui connaît 61 publications musicales: He is known to have produced 61 music publications, including six books for the lute. In 1509, the war of the League of Cambrai drove him from Venice to Fossombrone, in the Papal States. There he obtained a papal privilege, which was withdrawn when he failed to produce keyboard music, in favour of a Roman competitor, Andrea Antico, who also took over his Venetian business in 1520.
textes.Petrucci : portées, texte, notes, trois: Petrucci: staves, text, notes, three passes. Beautiful, but slow and costly.
textes.À Paris, Pierre Attaingnant a une meille: In Paris, Pierre Attaingnant had a better idea: print each note directly on its own small piece of staff. Notes, staves and words are printed in a single pass. He used it from 1528 in his Chansons nouvelles en musique à quatre parties.
textes.Le travail diminue fortement, et la méth: The labour fell sharply, and the method became the standard for music printing in Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries. Attaingnant published over 1,500 chansons in 36 collections, and in 1537 Francis I named him the king's printer and bookseller for music. 111 of his publications survive.
textes.Attaingnant, 1528 : un caractère par not: Attaingnant, 1528: one type per note, with its bit of staff, and everything prints at once.
textes.Quintes pures, comma pythagoricien, et l: Pure fifths, the Pythagorean comma, and equal temperament, calculated by Zhu Zaiyu in 1584.
textes.À Florence, des lettrés veulent ressusci: In Florence, scholars wanted to revive the sung Greek theatre. They invented opera: a story entirely sung, with instruments.
textes.La naissance de l'opéra, dans le temps: The birth of opera, in time
textes.Vers 1573-1582, la Camerata florentine d: Around 1573-1582, Count Bardi's Florentine Camerata sought to recover the music of the Greeks and blamed polyphony for making words unintelligible.
textes.Dafne de Peri, en 1598, est le premier o: Peri's Dafne, in 1598, is the first opera; it is lost. Euridice, in 1600, is the oldest surviving opera.
textes.L'Orfeo de Monteverdi, créé à Mantoue en: Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, premiered in Mantua in 1607, is the oldest opera still regularly performed.
textes.En 1637, à Venise, le théâtre San Cassia: In 1637, in Venice, the San Cassiano theatre opened opera to a paying public: it was the first public opera house.
textes.L'opéra n'est pas né de la volonté d'inv: Opera was not born from a wish to invent a new genre: its inventors believed they were reviving Greek tragedy, which they thought was entirely sung.
textes.À Florence, des lettrés se réunissent ch: In Florence, scholars met at the house of Count Giovanni de' Bardi; the first recorded meeting dates from 14 January 1573. Among them were Giulio Caccini, Pietro Strozzi and Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father. They thought the music of their time corrupt and wanted to recover that of the Greeks.
textes.L'érudit Girolamo Mei les convainc que l: The scholar Girolamo Mei convinced them that Greek theatre was mostly sung, not spoken. The Camerata blamed polyphony for stacking voices until the words could no longer be understood. It championed a single accompanied voice, monody, and a singing close to speech, recitative.
textes.Camerata : retrouver les Grecs, une voix: Camerata: recover the Greeks, a single voice one can understand, recitative.
textes.En 1598, le compositeur Jacopo Peri et l: In 1598, the composer Jacopo Peri and the poet Ottavio Rinuccini created Dafne, a drama sung throughout: the first opera, now lost. On 6 October 1600, at the Pitti Palace, for the wedding of Henry IV and Maria de' Medici, they gave Euridice, with Peri himself singing Orpheus. It is the oldest surviving opera. Caccini, in a hurry, published his own Euridice on the same libretto even before Peri's was performed.
textes.Le 24 février 1607, à Mantoue, Claudio M: On 24 February 1607, in Mantua, Claudio Monteverdi staged L'Orfeo, on a libretto by Alessandro Striggio. Five acts, a trumpet toccata as an overture, and a score printed in 1609 that names some forty instruments. It is the oldest opera still regularly performed.
textes.Dafne 1598, le premier, perdu ; Euridice: Dafne 1598, the first, lost; Euridice 1600, the oldest surviving; L'Orfeo 1607, the oldest still performed.
textes.Les premiers opéras sont des fêtes de co: The first operas were court festivities. In 1637, in Venice, the Tron family opened the San Cassiano theatre to a paying public, with Francesco Manelli's L'Andromeda: it was the world's first public opera house. From then on, a ticket was enough to hear the gods sing. Closed by the French in 1805, the theatre was demolished in 1812.
textes.D'autres théâtres chantés existent aille: Other sung theatres exist elsewhere. In China, kunqu, one of the oldest surviving forms of Chinese opera, developed mainly under the Ming dynasty; its most famous work, The Peony Pavilion, is by Tang Xianzu. UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2001.
textes.1637, Venise : le premier opéra public,: 1637, Venice: the first public, paying opera house. In China, the Ming dynasty's kunqu.
textes.Accords parfaits, consonance et cadences: Triads, consonance and cadences, which Rameau turned into a system in 1722.
textes.Une onde de pression, que Chladni rend v: A pressure wave, which Chladni made visible with sand and Sabine learned to tame in halls.
textes.En 1895, à Harvard, on confie au jeune p: In 1895, at Harvard, the young physicist Wallace Sabine was handed a failed lecture hall: in the Fogg room, a spoken word resonated for about five and a half seconds. With his assistants, he borrowed hundreds of seat cushions, moved them around and timed how sounds died away. One listener absorbs as much as six cushions. He derived a law of reverberation, then advised on the building of Boston's Symphony Hall, the first concert hall designed by calculation.
textes.Chladni rend les vibrations visibles ave: Chladni made vibrations visible with sand; Sabine measured reverberation with cushions.
textes.Un pendule pour le tempo, une fourche d': A pendulum for tempo, a steel fork for pitch: in the 18th and 19th centuries, music acquired its standards.
textes.En 1711, John Shore invente le diapason,: In 1711, John Shore invented the tuning fork, a steel fork that gives an almost pure note, always the same.
textes.En 1814, Winkel invente à Amsterdam un p: In 1814, Winkel invented a spring pendulum in Amsterdam; Maelzel patented it in 1815 under the name metronome and mass-produced it from 1816.
textes.Un tempo s'écrit en battements par minut: A tempo is written in beats per minute: at 60, one beat per second; a mechanical metronome usually goes from 40 to 208.
textes.Le la a longtemps varié selon les villes: The A long varied from city to city; France fixed it at 435 Hz in 1859, a conference recommended 440 Hz in 1939, ISO adopted it in 1955.
textes.Le la à 440 Hz n'est pas une loi de la n: A at 440 Hz is not a law of nature: it is a convention, and many orchestras tune a little higher, between 440 and 444 Hz.
textes.Galilée étudie le pendule à la fin du XV: Galileo studied the pendulum at the end of the 16th century, inspired, it is said, by a chandelier swinging in Pisa Cathedral. In 1696, the French musician Étienne Loulié built a "chronometer": a lead weight on an adjustable string, in front of a six-foot ruler. It was silent, and nothing kept it moving.
textes.En 1814, à Amsterdam, Dietrich Nikolaus: In 1814, in Amsterdam, Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel invented a compact, spring-powered inverted pendulum. Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815 under the name metronome and mass-produced it from 1816: hence the abbreviation M.M., Maelzel's Metronome, on scores. In December 1815, Beethoven wrote his first metronome marking. Brahms, for his part, would judge that "the metronome is of no value".
textes.Loulié 1696, Winkel 1814, Maelzel 1815 :: Loulié 1696, Winkel 1814, Maelzel 1815: tempo becomes a number of beats per minute.
textes.Une note qui ne bouge pas: A note that does not move
textes.En 1711, John Shore, trompettiste et lut: In 1711, John Shore, trumpeter and lutenist at the English court, invented the tuning fork: a steel fork which, when struck, gives a fixed note. Its first overtone is about six times higher than the base note and dies away quickly: the sound is almost pure. The fork he gave Handel sounds a C at 512 Hz.
textes.Une corde change avec la température ; l: A string changes with temperature; the tuning fork keeps its note. But each city had its own: before the 19th century, the A could vary by several semitones from one city to another.
textes.Le diapason de Shore, 1711 : une note fi: Shore's tuning fork, 1711: a fixed, almost pure note. But each city long had its own A.
textes.En 1834, à Stuttgart, une conférence rec: In 1834, in Stuttgart, a conference already recommended A at 440 Hz, based on Scheibler's measurements. In 1859, a French law fixed A at 435 vibrations per second, the "diapason normal": the first attempt to standardise pitch on such a scale. In 1939, an international conference in London recommended 440 Hz, which ISO adopted in 1955 and reaffirmed in 1975.
textes.La norme n'empêche pas les écarts. En 19: The standard does not prevent deviations. In 1987, a survey found orchestras tuned between 440 and 444 Hz; the Berlin Philharmonic now plays at 443 Hz. Baroque music specialists have agreed on 415 Hz, about a semitone lower. As for the "natural" A at 432 Hz, its healing promises belong to legend.
textes.Stuttgart 1834 : 440 ; loi française 185: Stuttgart 1834: 440; French law 1859: 435; London 1939 and ISO 1955: 440. Baroque: 415.
textes.Fondamentale, harmoniques et timbre, que: Fundamental, harmonics and timbre, which Helmholtz dissected in 1863 with his resonators.
textes.Tracer le son sur du noir de fumée, le g: Tracing sound on lampblack, engraving it in tinfoil, magnetising it on tape: in a century, music learned to last.
textes.En 1857, Scott de Martinville brevète le: In 1857, Scott de Martinville patented the phonautograph, which draws sound but cannot play it back; in 1860, he sang Au clair de la lune into it.
textes.En 1877, Edison invente le phonographe :: In 1877, Edison invented the phonograph: a stylus engraves sound into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder, then plays it back.
textes.Berliner lance le disque plat et le mot: Berliner launched the flat disc and the word gramophone; his commercial discs came out in 1892.
textes.L'enregistrement magnétique, montré par: Magnetic recording, demonstrated by Poulsen in 1898, became practical with AEG's Magnetophon in 1935.
textes.Le premier enregistrement de voix n'a pa: The first voice recording was never heard by its maker: the 1860 phonautograph was only played in 2008, by computer.
textes.Le 25 mars 1857, le Français Édouard-Léo: On 25 March 1857, the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville received the patent for the phonautograph. A horn funnels sound to a thin membrane, like an eardrum; a boar's bristle about a centimetre long, fixed to the membrane, traces the vibrations on a glass plate blackened with lampblack. Scott wanted people to read sound, not listen to it: the device could play nothing back.
textes.Le 9 avril 1860, il y enregistre une vin: On 9 April 1860, he recorded some twenty seconds of Au clair de la lune with it. In 2008, researchers of the First Sounds project, with the Lawrence Berkeley laboratory, digitised the trace and made it heard. Played at first at double speed, it was thought to be a woman's or a child's voice; at the right speed, it is a man, almost certainly Scott himself, singing very slowly.
textes.Phonautographe : 1857, un tracé sans ret: Phonautograph: 1857, a trace with no playback; 1860, Au clair de la lune; 2008, finally heard.
textes.Le 30 avril 1877, le Français Charles Cr: On 30 April 1877, the Frenchman Charles Cros deposited with the Academy of Sciences a sealed envelope describing a device for reproducing sound, which he called the paleophone. That same year, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph: sound vibrates a membrane linked to a stylus, which engraves tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder; a horn gives the sound back. Edison tested it by reciting Mary Had a Little Lamb, but that recording was not preserved.
textes.Bell et Tainter brevètent en 1886 l'enre: Bell and Tainter patented recording in wax in 1886. Emile Berliner bet on the flat disc and coined the word gramophone; he began selling his discs in 1892, then replaced hard rubber with shellac in 1895.
textes.Cros et Edison, 1877 : rejouer le son. B: Cros and Edison, 1877: playing sound back. Berliner: the flat disc, 1892.
textes.En 1898, l'ingénieur danois Valdemar Pou: In 1898, the Danish engineer Valdemar Poulsen showed that sound could be recorded by magnetising a wire. The idea became practical in Germany: in 1935, AEG presented the Magnetophon K1 in Berlin, with a tape developed by Friedrich Matthias at IG Farben and BASF. Walter Weber then discovered AC biasing, which greatly improved the quality.
textes.Après la guerre, le chanteur Bing Crosby: After the war, the singer Bing Crosby invested 50,000 dollars in the American firm Ampex, whose Model 200 tape recorder came out in 1948. Tape can be cut and spliced: a recording can be edited. In 1963, Philips launched the Compact Cassette, and recorded music fitted in a pocket.
textes.Poulsen 1898, Magnetophon 1935, Ampex 19: Poulsen 1898, Magnetophon 1935, Ampex 1948, cassette 1963: sound is edited like film.
textes.Au début du XXe siècle, Schoenberg aband: In the early 20th century, Schoenberg abandoned the tonic and Stravinsky's Rite caused a scandal: art music changed its rules.
textes.Avec son Deuxième Quatuor, en 1907-1908,: With his Second Quartet, in 1907-1908, Schoenberg wrote his first piece without an explicitly stated key.
textes.Le 29 mai 1913, Le Sacre du printemps de: On 29 May 1913, Stravinsky's Rite of Spring caused a scandal in Paris; the "riot" is partly a legend.
textes.Vers 1921, Schoenberg met au point la mé: Around 1921, Schoenberg devised the twelve-tone method: a series contains each of the twelve notes once, and the whole work derives from it.
textes.Ses élèves Alban Berg et Anton Webern fo: His pupils Alban Berg and Anton Webern formed with him what is called the Second Viennese School.
textes.Atonal ne veut pas dire n'importe quoi :: Atonal does not mean anything goes: the twelve-tone method is a stricter rule than classical harmony, not an absence of rules.
textes.Le 29 mai 1913, au théâtre des Champs-Él: On 29 May 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the Ballets Russes premiered Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, choreographed by Nijinsky. The bassoon opens in such a high register that it is barely recognisable; laughter breaks out, then uproar.
